The registrar stared at her. "That gallery is coming down."

"Then unlock the doors."

"The controls are dead. Take what we need."

What we need. As if discovery had already made her part of his equipment.

The support cracked again.

Leora climbed onto the fallen scanner base. "Listen to me!" Her voice carried better from there. "I can hold an ability and give it back. I don't know how many or for how long. If you can help and you choose to lend me yours, say what it does. Don't touch me unless I say."

The crowd quieted by degrees, panic pulling tight around her words.

The pinned applicant raised a hand through the bent gallery rail. Dense brown resin formed a blocky lattice from his palm to his elbow. "I can set a load through anything rigid," he called. His breath hitched as he tried to shift his trapped leg. "I can't reach the support from here."

Leora climbed the sloping steps. The gallery shuddered beneath her. She crouched below him, separated by the twisted rail.

"If you lend it, you may not have it until I return it."

"I understand."

"Tell me to take it."

He looked at the people crawling toward the stairs. "Take it."

Leora reached through the rail and closed her hand around his.

The resin lattice softened into light. It entered more slowly than the silver had, heavy and hot, filling one dark branch after another. The man's palm went bare. Beneath Leora's skin, brown lines joined the hidden script from wrist to chest.

The weight of the gallery arrived all at once. Not its present weight, but every path it might take if the support failed. Her mind crowded with angles. She let go before the pressure could swallow the thought of her own body.

"I have it," she said.

She slid back to the floor and planted both hands against the cracked support. The resin ability sought rigid material. Leora pushed it into the stone and steel.

The gallery stopped sinking.

The force did not disappear. It traveled through her ability like strain through a wrench, down the support, across the floor, and somehow through the lattice burning under her skin. Her knees buckled. She locked them and felt the knot below her breastbone pull tighter.

"Clear the stairs," she said through her teeth. "One line. Help the injured first."

People moved. The registrar, perhaps because an order was something he understood, began directing them away from the cracked side. Two unmarked hands freed the pinned applicant's leg with a length of fallen rail as a lever. The soot-lettered boy damped the alarm around the stairs so instructions could be heard. Others supported shoulders, carried a child, counted those coming down.

Smoke thickened above the scanner. The damaged cable spat white fire onto a row of plastic chairs. Heat touched Leora's face.

"I can cool it," said the woman with blue across her cheek.

She stood on the safe side of the support, one hand out. The blue tattoo was not decorative ink but brine suspended in fine channels, trembling with each breath.

Leora could not leave the pillar. "Come to my shoulder. Tell me what happens when you use it."

"I draw heat into water. Too much, and the water flashes off."

"Can you lend it safely?"

The woman's eyes tracked the fire climbing toward the gallery. "Yes. Take it."

Her palm settled against Leora's shoulder.

Brine-cold light drove through Leora's body.

The hidden mark took it eagerly. Blue flooded across her chest and down the arm braced against the support. Resin heat and brine cold met around the dark knot. Pressure cinched her ribs. Her vision narrowed until she could see only the cracked pillar and the edge of the fire.

Two, she thought. Two was enough. Perhaps two was already too many.

She kept one hand on the support and pointed the other toward the burning cable. The cooling ability resisted the dry air. Leora dragged moisture from the puddle left by a ruptured cleaning pipe, feeling the blue pattern guide rather than obey her. Water sheeted across the floor, climbed the hot metal, and hissed into steam. The flames on the chairs shrank, but electricity snapped through the wet edge.

"Supply is still live!" the examiner shouted.

His silver bands shone again. He lifted a fallen beam clear of the service panel, but the breaker box was across the hall, beyond the sagging scanner arm.

"Guide him," Leora called.

Three applicants made a path through the smoke. One used a wind-bearing spiral to push the worst of it toward a ceiling vent. Another wrapped a coat around the examiner's hands. A third called out where the wet floor ended. The examiner climbed over the wrecked rig and wrenched open the service panel.

Leora's arms began to shake. The resin lattice inside her creaked in sympathy with the gallery. Cold climbed her throat. For one confused moment she could not remember which ability belonged to which body.

Then the main breaker slammed down.

The damaged cable went dark.

Leora pulled the remaining heat into the spilled water. Steam billowed, warm rather than scalding. Someone found the manual release chain behind the registrar's desk. The shutters rose a few inches, then a foot, and people knelt to lift them higher. Fresh air pushed into the hall.

"Gallery clear!" someone shouted.

Leora counted the footsteps above until there were none. "Brace it," she told the registrar.

"With what?"

"The emergency posts under the stairs. This is a licensing hall. You inspect them every month."

He blinked, then ran. Four people helped him drag the telescoping posts from their cabinet. Leora told them where to place the feet, judging the load paths crowding her mind. They raised the first post, then the second. Steel took the weight from her borrowed lattice.

When Leora lifted her hands from the support, she nearly fell.

The woman with the bare cheek caught her, then stiffened at the contact.

"I'm giving it back," Leora said.

She found the blue pattern amid the darkness and the brown. It no longer felt eager. It felt lodged, compressed into channels not made for it. Returning it required a slow, deliberate push. Cold passed from Leora's shoulder into the woman's palm. Blue brine reappeared across the woman's cheek, line by line, wetly bright.

The woman touched the mark, drew a breath, and cooled a cup of spilled water until a skin of ice formed over it.

"It's all there," she said.

The resin bearer sat near the stairs with his injured leg straight before him. Leora knelt and offered her hand.

"Ready?"

He nodded.

The brown lattice withdrew from her chest and arm. Its departure left an ache like a deep bruise. When the last block returned to his palm, he pressed it against the fallen length of railing. The metal steadied under his touch.

Only the hidden darkness remained inside Leora. Under the hall's ordinary lights, even that disappeared.

People had begun watching again. This time Leora understood the second look. Some saw danger. Some saw rescue. The registrar, standing amid broken equipment and damp paperwork, looked as though he saw a new red border for her file.

"This requires an immediate containment classification," he said. "Until the central examiners can establish transfer limits, you cannot leave unmonitored."

The woman with the restored brine tattoo stepped between him and Leora. "She asked."

"That is not the issue."

"It was the issue when you told her to take from us."

The examiner came back from the breaker panel. Soot marked his coat, and his silver bands were whole. "She returned mine too."

The registrar tightened his grip on the tablet. "We have no procedure for this."

Leora's work jacket lay beside the scanning square. She picked it up and put it on, though her wet sleeves clung to her arms.

"You do have a procedure for my credential," she said.

"Your classification has changed."

"My test results haven't. I completed the practical. I passed the written assessment. And I identified a failing support, placed emergency braces, and kept a live electrical fire from spreading in your hall."

"Using an unlicensed ability."

"Using two abilities their bearers lent me. If you want another examination, give me the request in writing. Include what you plan to do, who sees the results, and my right to stop. I will decide after I read it."

"You are in no position to set terms."

Leora looked at the raised shutters, the witnesses gathered beneath them, and the two people whose tattoos had returned unchanged.

"Then explain your position to everyone here while you deny the credential you promised before your machine broke."

The registrar followed her gaze. His shoulders lowered a fraction.

He went behind the desk.

The printer had survived the water. It clicked, warmed, and fed out a stiff card bearing Leora's photograph and structural maintenance authorization. The ability-classification field read PENDING REVIEW. She disliked the words, but they did not cancel the line beneath them.

QUALIFIED.

The registrar held on to the card when she first reached for it.

"You will be contacted," he said.

"In writing."

He released it.

Outside, late sunlight warmed the steps. Emergency crews pushed past Leora into the building, carrying braces, cutters, medical cases, and no interest yet in the girl walking the other way. People gathered on the pavement, checking injuries and recounting what they had seen.

Leora moved apart from them and held the credential in both hands until they stopped trembling.

Her skin looked as bare as it had that morning. No silver circled her wrists. No resin blocked her palms. No blue shone at her throat. Still, she could feel the colorless branches in the ache below her breastbone and along every finger, an unseen map whose edges belonged to her before anyone else could measure them.

She slid the credential into her jacket, pressed one apparently blank hand over the darkness written under her skin, and went to claim the work waiting for her.

stories.title: The Hollow Cask
stories.prompt: You purchase a crumbling, run down pub in rural country side, determined to bring it back to its once grandiose ways. But the pub hides an ancient secret..
stories.body:
# The Hollow Cask

The first roof tile fell before the cart carrying the conveyance clerk had reached the lane. It punched through a bladder of wet plaster and shattered on the counter where Agnes Wold meant to serve harvest ale in twelve weeks.

She stood beneath the dripping rafters with the deed rolled in one hand and watched brown water run among the shards. Three roof breaches showed white sky. The north wall plate had gone soft enough to take the point of her knife. A burst downpipe poured against the outer wall, the plaster below it bulged like soaked bread, and the gallery bowed over the room with a drop of nearly four inches from end to end.

There was still an honest hour in which she might call herself an investor. Board the place. Sell the old oak, the hearthstone, the acreage behind. Recover perhaps two-thirds of what she had spent and tell no one how close the remaining third came to all she owned.

Instead Agnes unloaded her props, wedges, adze, lime tubs, and the long box of planes she had carried from one rented workshop to another. She set a sole plate on sound flags, raised a temporary shore beneath the gallery's worst bay, and drove the top wedge until the timber answered with a dull, burdened note.

While pulling tarred cloth from a bracket, she found a carved vine beneath the flaking brown paint. Gold leaf still clung in the cuts. Across the hall, empty mortises showed where the gallery had once turned both corners and wrapped three walls. The floorboards were hollowed by feet before a broad hearth and a shallow speaking step. Not aristocratic grandeur, then. Better. A room made splendid by being full.

Agnes pinned the deed above the driest end of the counter. On the gallery fascia she chalked one word in carpenter's red.

SAVE.

Then she climbed onto the roof before the next tile could fall.

* * *

By the fifth day she had made the rain travel somewhere it was wanted. New lead lined the broken valley; the downpipe emptied into a cleared stone runnel rather than the wall; patched slates covered two breaches, while a tarpaulin and battens held the third. The building still smelled of wet ash and mice, but the upper courses had begun to dry.

Agnes was picking hard grey cement from the north wall when Silas Cray came through the door. He carried a sawyer's rule and looked first at the shore, then at the red word on the gallery.

“A shore isn't a cure,” he said.

“It isn't priced as one. I need two oak sisters cut to these measures.” She passed him a scrap of board. “Straight grain, no sapwood. I pay on delivery.”

Silas did not take it. “Pay won't make that gallery worth standing under.”

“No. Timber might.”

She turned back to the wall. The cement came away in sharp cakes, bringing some of the old face with it where damp had been trapped. Behind it lay soft lime plaster, still sound at the edges. Agnes misted a handspan and worked with a horn scraper. Brown became madder red. A procession emerged: sleeves, ribbons, the curve of a brass instrument, and a gold ground darkened to mustard beneath the dirt. Above it, square nail shadows marked the former places of blue-glass lamps.

At shoulder height, different hands had scratched feast days, grazing meetings, birth cups, and roof funds into the plaster. Some marks were formal; others wandered uphill as if their writers had been laughing.

Silas finally took the board. “Pretty wall.”

“Public wall.” Agnes nodded toward the gallery. “And those treads are worn to the left turn. It held dancers.”

“Then it held them badly.”

They measured together because numbers were harder to refuse than hope. The cantilever ran too far beyond the post line. The surviving joists were shallow, the outer rail absurdly heavy, and the wall mortises had spread under thrust. Even before rot, the span should have sagged under a quiet row of chairs, never mind generations of stamping feet.

Silas rapped the nearest post with his rule. “Take it down while it still agrees to come in pieces.”

Agnes pressed her thumb to one of the tiny bores polished through the mortise. There were hundreds, each no wider than a barley straw, running with rather than across the grain. “These aren't beetle holes.”

“A hole is a hole when the beam breaks.”

“Cut me the two sisters. I shore one bay and open no more than that. If the timber gives us no answer, we dismantle.”

“You dismantle.” He folded the board once, precise as a refusal. “My saw stays out of it.”

Agnes set a peg against one bore and tapped twice with her mallet.

From under the floor came two faint knocks. A pause followed, long enough for Silas to turn toward the door. Then came a third.

He unfolded the board.

* * *

The wet joist betrayed the route. Its upper face looked sound, but Agnes's awl sank to the haft beside a black iron nail. Rather than skin it over, she numbered the floorboards in chalk and lifted them from the gallery wall toward the middle of the room.

Beneath the ordinary boards lay an older sprung floor of elm laths. Bits of blue glazing glittered in the dust. A border of green-and-white tile survived under the later skirting, and in the dead spaces Agnes found three stamped dance tokens, a bone button, and enough bent pins to furnish a dozen lost sleeves. Whoever had built the grand room had spent money on light, color, and a floor gentle under moving feet.

They had also patched, generation after generation, around the same hollow oak dowels.

The dowels descended through the wall frame beside a copper gutter. Unlike the green metal around it, the gutter's inner lip shone where repeated pouring had worn it smooth. It sloped toward the swollen cellar door and vanished through older masonry.

“What did they pour?” Agnes asked.

“Cellars take ale.” Silas kept his eyes on the lifted boards.

“Ale goes down by cask and comes up by jug. It doesn't need a serving gutter inside a wall.”

He answered by fetching the pry bar.

They freed the cellar door a fraction at a time. Beyond it, stone steps fell into air warmer than the hall. Agnes's lamp showed a cracked drain, clay pipes, and a copper grille furred shut with verdigris. At the back, built into stonework older than any wall above, lay the curved shell of an enormous oak cask. Tool marks on it were broad and shallow, unlike the crisp later mortises that accommodated its shape. Three floors had been raised around it. None had disturbed it.

The smell was not rot. It was warm malt after rain.

Pale cords webbed the cask's broken staves and entered the hollow dowels overhead. They withdrew from Agnes's lamp, not all at once but in tightening ripples. Among them moved amber mites, grain-small and glossy. Some carried damp pulp toward a pale cluster of brood. Along one charred stave, old fungal tissue had ridged over a burn.

“The Underbreath,” Silas said behind her.

Agnes lowered the lamp. “You know it.”

“Knew the name. A cellar pest. Old folk blamed it for sour barrels.”

“Old folk built it a copper trough.”

“Old folk built many foolish things.”

One loose gallery peg stood proud above them. A fresh cord entered its dowel. As Agnes watched, the cord tightened and the oak grain drew fractionally closed. Upstairs, the peg settled by the thickness of a shaving.

The cord was fine as sewing thread. Its flesh could not by ordinary leverage have closed a handspan of old oak, much less shifted a peg upstairs. Yet its contraction had travelled through the dowel, and the old joinery had carried the impossible force. The life below supplied what the cask and pipe could only route.

Agnes shaded a dry margin with her hand, fed it a spoonful of water, and waited. Fresh translucent tips emerged along the damaged edge. A mite returned with pulp. Another followed.

“You wanted the cellar opened,” Silas said. “Now you've seen why it was shut.”

“I've seen why someone wanted me to think shutting it was sensible.”

She refused his jar of fumigating bitter. Instead she set shallow dishes of watered malt, opened three temporary vent runs, and marked every peg above with a hairline of chalk. Silas watched her work without helping.

“If that brings the gallery down?” he asked.

“Then I learn before there are customers under it.”

“And if it brings something else?”

Agnes looked at the brood gathered in the cask's damp seam. “Then you may try answering the question you keep stepping around.”

* * *

The drain had been laid with a mean little rise just before the outer wall. Agnes lifted two stones, reset the clay channel on packed lime and gravel, and gave the water a clean fall. She scraped the copper grille open and hinged it outward. Over the cask's split stave she fitted an oak sleeve with breathing gaps instead of packing the crack with mortar.

Only then did she test the structure.

She hung one measured sandbag from a colonized peg and gave two taps. Two taps returned through the dowel. That proved response, perhaps only habit. She needed a choice the old system had not taught.

From the cask she laid three covered channels. One held fresh air from the opened grille. One held watered malt. The third followed a smoke-stained clay branch toward the gallery wall; she placed malt there too, so food and safety would not point the same way.

The pale cords nosed first toward both dishes. At the bitter soot they recoiled. Mites left the nearer food untouched and began carrying brood toward the fresh-air channel. Agnes blocked that channel with a tile.

The sandbag peg released.

It dropped half an inch into its mortise, and the bag touched the floor. The cords did not take the offered food. They spread along the cask seam, found the edge of her tile, and sent one bright thread past it toward the copper grille.

Not speech. Not proof of a mind shaped like hers. But it was no echo either. Faced with three poor choices, the colony had refused two, protected its young, and surrendered a load.

Agnes removed the tile at once.

She traced the smoke branch upward. Behind the hearth, the flue divided through a shutter and a leather-bellows throat she had already rebuilt from fragments because its curve matched the earliest plaster. Bitter black lay only in the branches leading to structural bays. On one exposed beam, pale cords had grown around old burns and sealed them with scar tissue.

The wall tallies changed too. Early accounts paired malt measures with feast nights. Later hands bought more bitter fuel, recorded less feed, and demanded larger crowds from the same thin joists. That showed a change in practice, not what the first builders had intended. The oldest truth remained below the oldest readable wall.

Silas arrived near dusk and found Agnes scrubbing SAVE from the fascia. Beneath it she wrote, SUPPORT WITHOUT IT.

“That's a dear sentence,” he said.

“Less dear than a funeral.”

“You'll lose half the room.”

“I'll lose the part that doesn't know how to stand.” She held out a soot-black flue tile. “Who taught them to drive it with this?”

Silas looked past her to the chalked plan. “Put your roof on before the storm. Questions keep better than lime.”

He left the tile in her hand.

The deed still hung above the counter. It conveyed beams, stone, fixtures, and land by boundary. Nothing written there could turn the small lives below into stock. Agnes took up her rule and began drawing posts.

* * *

The storm arrived a day earlier than the carter's forecast. Wind rammed rain beneath the temporary roof and pressed smoke down the chimney. Agnes smelled the bitter residue before she heard the gallery move.

The rebuilt bellows shutter clapped open.

Smoke drove through the old clay branches into the hollow dowels. Beneath the floor, the Underbreath contracted in flight. Its force tightened the colonized oak, drew two pegs home, and lifted the bowed gallery almost level.

For one terrible moment the grand room returned. Gold brackets aligned. The rail rose straight. Agnes could see the lamps, the musicians on the speaking step, the crowd above moving as one body.

Then a rotten mortise split with the report of an axe.

Silas came through the main door carrying a wrapped book under his coat. “You've set the draw back.”

“I set it to the earliest profile.” Agnes braced a second prop beneath the inner beam. “The front bay is taking more than its share. Help me shore it.”

“Earliest you could see.” He put the book on the counter and opened it to a page of flue diagrams. “My forebear kept this. My family kept it after.”

The sketched branches matched the ones in the wall. Late entries grew meaner: *brood dead at east stave*; *feed shortened*; *drive the Underbreath hard for festival*. Beside one blot, a hand had drawn the same bellows shutter Agnes had restored.

“You had this while I was opening the floor?”

“I wanted the place shut.”

“You wanted the evidence shut.”

The gallery lurched. A peg sprang across the room and struck the hearth. Silas flinched, then caught the prop Agnes shoved at him.

“Blame me when the roof is holding,” he said.

Closing the shutter would stop new smoke. It would not cool the oak already hot, open a path for the colony, or support the frame when panicked cords let go. The outer bay had begun to peel away from the wall. If it fell uncontrolled, it would wrench the sound inner beam off its shores.

Agnes looked once at the gilded rail. Nearly all her savings, made visible.

“We're not shoring the front,” she said. “We're cutting it free.”

* * *

The safe door was behind them. The smoking hearth stood to their right. Across the room, beyond the bowed gallery, the cellar steps led to the drain and the copper grille. Agnes set out the order before fear could disorder it.

“Inner beam first. Both shores under sound heartwood. Then the grille full open. Then I break the shutter out.”

Silas looked up at the carved outer bay. “We can stand two more props under that rail.”

“On the sprung floor? It will punch through and trap us beneath it.” Agnes drove her rule into the scarf line where the decorated cantilever joined the inner beam. “This joint is already half opened. We support here, cut here, and wedge the dead bay outward.”

“That's the room you bought.”

“It's the room that was bought before.”

There was no time to make the sentence better. Another contraction jerked the rail upward and showered them with lime.

They raised the independent shores. Agnes held each plumb while Silas struck the wedges. The first seated under the inner beam with a clean knock. The second skidded on wet flagstone; she kicked grit beneath its sole and made him drive again.

“Three blows,” she said. “No more. One. Two. Three.”

The inner beam settled onto honest timber.

Silas ran for the cellar. Agnes crossed to the hearth, keeping outside the gallery's fall line. She hooked her pry bar behind the shutter she had so carefully fitted, levered until the new screws tore from old brick, and ripped the whole bellows throat into the ashes. Smoke burst into the hall, then thinned as the pressure found the open fireplace instead of the clay branches.

From below came the clang of copper and Silas shouting, “Grille's open!”

Cool wet air entered at floor level. It carried the smell of rain on nettles. Through a gap beside the dance floor, Agnes saw the pale cords still drawn taut, their edges gone translucent with heat. They did not release. Familiar smoke had taught flight into the beams too well.

She laid the long saw into the old scarf joint.

The teeth caught gilding first, then oak. Each pull cost her a month's rent, ten chairs, another strip of gallery she would never be able to claim as original. Sawdust fell red-brown through the gold. Above her, the outer bay shuddered as the Underbreath tightened; behind her, the independent posts held the inner beam without complaint.

Silas returned dripping. “Let me take the saw.”

“Take the wedge. When I reach the hollow, knock it outward.”

“The carving could be braced after.”

Agnes pointed with the saw handle. The scarf had split past its shoulder; rot ran through the decorated face; the colonized dowel bound the dying bay to the sound frame. “If we keep that, we keep the smoke route and the false load. The whole piece goes.”

He put the maul to the wedge.

Agnes cut. The saw passed solid grain, soft rot, then the hollow dowel. Warm, bitter air hissed from it. Beneath the floor, pale growth streamed toward the damp channel. Amber mites crowded the open route. A fresh cord touched the copper lip.

The load changed.

“Now,” Agnes said.

Silas struck.

For an instant the Underbreath pulled against the old command. The gallery rose a finger's width. Then the colonized peg slid free. Cords withdrew from the severed dowel in a pale rush, abandoning the outer bay.

The carved rail tipped away from them. It struck the cleared, roped floor in one vast cracking blow. Blue-glass fragments leapt from the dust. Agnes felt the impact through her boots, but the inner beam remained on its new posts. The roof did not follow.

Neither of them spoke until the last small piece of plaster had fallen.

In the cellar, the cask-shell was scorched but damp. Fresh cords filled its shaded seam and reached along the open grille; none returned to the separated gallery stump. The colony had stayed where it had a way to leave. That was a choice for tonight, not a promise Agnes could nail in place.

Upstairs, the deed had come loose from its pin. She picked it out of the dust, folded it, and put it in her pocket.

* * *

By the harvest gathering, the hall carried itself.

Two new oak posts stood where the gallery's front bay had been. Agnes had left them visible, their wedges and tool marks plain. She conserved the surviving madder procession and one jagged end of gilded rail, but she did not paint in the missing bodies or pretend the gallery still wrapped three walls. The smaller room held fewer tables. It also held no concealed load.

Beside the cellar door hung a notice describing the cask-shell, the living colony, the smoke damage, and the limits of what the records proved. The cellar was occupied habitat, not storage and not entertainment. The copper grille remained open. Water and malt went down whether or not any peg ever moved again.

Silas inspected both posts before he took off his coat. He had brought sound oak at his own cost and placed the maintenance book beneath the notice in a glass-fronted box. Agnes had thanked him for the timber. The notice still said how long the book had been kept back.

“Six tables lost,” he said.

“Five. I made the counter narrower.”

He read the notice again. “People will ask to see below.”

“They may ask.”

Silas tested the cellar latch, found it locked, and nodded toward the doors. “They're waiting in the rain.”

Together they opened the Hollow Cask.

Neighbors filled the speaking step and the floor. Musicians tuned where the dancers had once worn elm smooth. Agnes drew the first mug, listening despite herself for strain in the posts. There was none.

Music began. Warm barley air rose through the open copper grille, and one small, voluntary tremor dimpled the foam.

stories.title: The Strength of Ten
stories.prompt: Your kingdom is defenseless, and to secure an army, you, the prince, are promised in marriage to one of the daughters of the King of the North, a brutal warrior known for having the strength of 10 men.
stories.body:
# The Strength of Ten

The courier caught Prince Lysander beneath Harrowfast's gatehouse, before he could offer the gold wedding chain to the steward waiting on the steps.

Snow had packed white in the courier's eyebrows. His horse stood with its head down between six others, all seven animals trembling from the Frostroad. Lysander's own six escorts looked scarcely better.

"Greyglass is lost," the courier said. "The marshal sold the gate. Most of the four hundred border guards were taken in their beds. The rest came south without weapons."

Lysander felt the chain's square links through his glove. "How far is the Black Reed train?"

"A hundred and five miles from Ninepin. Six days, if the thaw doesn't speed them." The courier glanced at the northern steward and abandoned deference. "We have a hundred and eighty city watch and seventy riders. No seasonal companies. No border line. Come home."

Home had granaries worth an invasion, river locks worth a dynasty, and no army because Lysander had sent thirteen hundred hungry soldiers back to their farms before autumn. He had called that mercy. Later, when the Greyglass warnings came, he had called Redwater merely outnumbered.

"Ride back," he said. "Empty the three villages along Ninepin. Put every sluice worker under the watch. Assemble one hundred and twenty grain carts with fodder enough to reach the day-four post on the Frostroad."

"From what depot?"

"The river stores. Break my seals."

The courier's mouth tightened. It was not enough, but it was work that might be done. He mounted again.

Lysander gave the wedding chain to no one. He carried it into King Gorm's hall himself, resolved to marry whichever of Gorm's three grown daughters the king required.

* * *

An iron-banded oak table divided Gorm's hall. It was wide enough for maps, a winter feast, or a body laid out for judgment. The king of the North sat beyond it in shirtsleeves despite the cold, thick wrists bare, his old scar-lattice showing pale above his collar.

"Three thousand northerners," Gorm said. "At Ninepin before the reeds turn green."

A road clerk beside the wall cleared his throat. "Sixteen hundred can be spared without opening the northern passes."

Gorm held out one hand. The clerk went still, then removed the copper ration badge from his neck and laid it in the king's palm.

"Outer arch," Gorm told him. "Until the last bell. No brazier. Perhaps cold will improve your arithmetic."

The clerk bowed and left without his cloak. No one watched him go except Lysander.

Gorm smiled again. "Prince Lysander, my second daughter is thirty-two, unmarried, and more useful than many sons. You will have Princess Sigrun. Redwater will have my strength and my host."

The side door opened before Lysander could answer. Princess Sigrun came in carrying two ledgers and a roll of road maps under one arm. She wore a marshal's grey coat, damp at the shoulders, and had grain dust on one cuff.

"You will not have three thousand," she said. "And I will not marry him."

At thirty, Lysander had crossed one hundred and forty miles rehearsing surrender. "Princess Sigrun, I understand what is required. I accept the match."

Her eyes settled on him. "Did you come here to request my answer, or to carry it?"

The courtesy he had prepared offered no safe clause. "I came for an army."

"There is one honest quantity."

Gorm laughed. "At Rimegate they mistook counting for command too. They built a coal barricade across my road. Ten men could not shift it."

He stood and braced both hands beneath the table's edge.

The old stories said a living field-healer had laid those scar paths into him after a spear wound, decades ago, and that Gorm had learned to drive his own heat and strength through them in a single, ruinous effort. Lysander had assumed the strength of ten men was northern embroidery.

Gorm drew one measured breath. The scars along his throat darkened.

On the first heartbeat, the table groaned. On the second, its feet tore splinters from the floor. By the sixth, Gorm had dragged the massive thing sideways across the main doors. The iron bands struck stone. Anyone who left now would need his leave to pass through the private rooms behind him.

"Then I broke Rimegate," he said. "They yielded before dark."

His voice held, but one hand shook when he released the oak. A servant hurried forward with furs. Another brought heated stones and broth. Gorm lowered himself into his chair with the careful stiffness of a wounded man.

Sigrun did not look away from her father. "And you withheld their household coal until they did."

She placed an unsigned route ledger on the table he had moved. Six depot seals marked its first page. Twelve blank spaces waited beneath them.

"You may call troops," she said. "You may shut doors. But the keepers will not release grain, the remount masters will not open their barns, and the captains will not take the Frostroad until my ledger matches theirs. The seven reeves can replace me if you remove me. Their notices have ten days of road between them."

Gorm's face had gone grey beneath its weathered red. He had the strength of ten haulers for six heartbeats. Redwater had six days.

For the first time, Lysander saw that the bride and the army had never been one transaction.

* * *

While Gorm withdrew to be warmed, Sigrun took Lysander to the map room. On the way she stopped at the outer arch, dismissed the shivering clerk in the name of her office, and fastened the copper badge back around his neck.

Then she began counting what Lysander had tried not to name.

"Black Reed foot?"

"About forty-five hundred. Six hundred horse. Engineers and siege wagons."

"Your standing force?"

"Four hundred at Greyglass."

"No. Your standing force now."

The map between them showed Reedmarsh as a wash of green ink with one hard black line through it. "A hundred and eighty watch. Seventy couriers."

"Seasonal companies?"

"Released."

"Your letter said delayed."

"I released them early. There was not enough grain for soldiers and households both."

Sigrun waited.

"I chose the households," he said. "Then I discounted the warnings from Greyglass because calling the companies back would have admitted that the choice left us open."

She turned to a clean sheet. No comfort, no accusation. Only a sharper quill.

Three thousand soldiers, she showed him, would consume Redwater's promised carts before the fourth day and strip Harrowfast's passes. Sixteen hundred could cross in five days if six depots released grain, grease, socks, traces, and remounts in sequence. Eight hundred shield-spears. Four hundred bows. Two hundred and fifty pioneers. One hundred and fifty scouts. Two hundred and forty drivers, healers, smiths, and depot workers would sustain them.

"No foraging," she said. "If your carts fail, I turn the columns north."

"Agreed."

"I command until Black Reed retreats beyond Greyglass or twenty days pass. You command your watch and workers. Three captain-representatives may refuse pillage, pursuit beyond the border, or abandonment of Ninepin."

Lysander looked at the causeway. One firm road across thawing marsh, narrow enough to make five thousand less useful. "Evacuate the villages. Open both culverts when the train commits. Anchor wagons in the center."

"Harrowfast iron travels through your locks," Sigrun said. "If Black Reed takes the capital, our spring trade pays whatever tariff it names. This is not charity."

"If your sluice workers are there." Her quill moved. "Harrowfast supplies three days. Redwater supplies the carts and fodder. One third of the river-lock tolls for seven years goes to wages, injured households, roads, and the three displaced villages."

Seven years. His council would call it northern occupation written in columns.

"And a public tribunal," Sigrun said. "You testify about the demobilization, Greyglass, and the letter you sent us. If Redwater's lawful council finds you broke your office, you accept its decision on the succession."

There it was. The cost that could not be worn nobly around his neck.

"A wedding after the campaign might make these terms acceptable to your father," Lysander said. "When there is time to decide it freely."

Sigrun set down the quill.

He heard what he had done: taken her no, dressed it in a later season, and offered it back as compromise.

"Strike that," he said. "No wedding."

She drew a line through the blank marriage clause. "The compact can work without one. Can you?"

He stared at the tribunal provision. He had been ready to give his body to a stranger and remain prince. This asked him to give Redwater facts it might use to remove him.

"I don't know," he said.

"Find out before the road freezes without us."

* * *

A second Redwater courier arrived at dusk with his horse spent beneath him. Black Reed's siege wagons had turned onto the south road. The northern columns had to leave before dawn.

Sigrun read the compact aloud in Gorm's hall. The king sat under three furs, a hot stone against his ribs. His right hand still trembled. The table remained jammed across the doors.

"I remove you as road-marshal," he said.

Sigrun laid seven copied notices beside the route ledger, each bearing spaces for a reeve's mark. "Then no keeper opens a depot until the reeves appoint another marshal. The captains have been told. Ten days, if every road stays open."

"I have other daughters." Gorm looked at Lysander. "My eldest is grown and less enamored of account books. Take her."

Lysander thought of a woman not in the room being fitted to the empty clause. "No."

Gorm's gaze hardened. "My youngest, then. All three know their duty."

"I will not ask either of them to purchase soldiers for me. Princess Sigrun said no. The marriage promise ends there."

"Then take eight hundred of my household spears. Marry Sigrun tonight, and the Redwater tolls remain mine after seven years."

Sigrun tapped the force count. "Eight hundred cannot hold Ninepin and the depots will not feed an unauthorized levy."

The king rounded on her. "You would let his kingdom fall to spite me?"

"I have sixteen hundred people harnessing sleds while you ask which daughter will make you richest. Sign the call, or they unharness."

Gorm began a tale about Rimegate. His voice faltered when he reached for the table and his shaking fingers could not close on its edge.

Lysander unhooked the wedding chain. "My kingdom is not merely outnumbered," he said, loudly enough for the captains and clerks along the walls. "It is defenseless. I dismissed thirteen hundred soldiers, then concealed what I had done."

The words did not make him lighter. Good.

He signed the compact beneath Sigrun's name. He surrendered command of the northern host, one third of the river tolls for seven years, and any certainty that the tribunal would leave him heir. Then he laid the chain across the accounts.

"Weigh this into the casualty fund."

Sigrun examined the heavy clasp. "The gold, yes. The promise, no."

She cut the chain from its clasp with the clerk's shears. The twelve captains marked the route ledger. Three representatives countersigned the limits. At last Gorm pressed his seal into the levy call.

"You came north for the strength of ten men," he told Lysander, recovering enough breath for grandeur. "You have bargained hard for it."

Lysander looked past him to the ledger crowded with human marks. "So I have."

* * *

The host did not leave as a shining river of steel. It departed in staged columns, because the first depot yard held only so many sleds and the Frostroad only so many hooves.

At six depots, keepers compared Sigrun's page with their own before releasing grain. Drivers changed cracked traces. Remount masters inspected fetlocks. Soldiers collected dry socks and tins of runner grease with the solemnity courtiers reserved for relics. When a sled axle split on the second day, pioneers lashed it to a spare and lost three hours. No mighty hand descended to return them.

Lysander rode beside Sigrun with the route ledger under his coat. He urged shorter rests until she pointed to horses blowing foam into the snow.

"They can sleep at Ninepin," he said.

"Dead horses are famous for resting," she said, and kept the halt.

On the third day, scouts found the river shelf cracked where the road curved east. Lysander knew a charcoal track along the ridge. It added seven miles but stayed on stone.

Sigrun did not take a prince's memory as a bridge. She sent two riders with measuring cord, questioned a depot keeper, and changed the route when their figures matched his.

The Redwater carts reached the day-four post because the courier had carried Lysander's orders south. They brought grain and too little fodder. For one sick instant he saw the whole compact ending in an empty manger.

Then he opened his household horse train. His six escorts dismounted. Northern harness went onto Redwater animals, and the soldiers walked beside the sleds.

Late on the fifth night, the columns descended toward Ninepin tired, fed, and still together. Ahead, lamps moved away from the three marsh villages in orderly lines. Evacuation carts. Sluice crews. The orders he had given before asking what his authority could buy.

* * *

Ninepin Causeway rose scarcely a man's height above Reedmarsh, a stone-backed road with black water on either side. Two culverts ran beneath its shoulders. North lay Redwater's capital. South, torchlight multiplied along the road until the Black Reed League seemed to have brought down a strip of the night.

Sigrun anchored wagons wheel to wheel across the firm center. Shield-spears stood behind them, bows on two low mounds, pioneers at the culvert gates, scouts forward among the reeds. Redwater's watch waited behind the line with poles and shovels.

The thaw had begun. Water ticked under thinning ice.

"Open the culverts now," Lysander said. "Soften the shoulders before their train arrives."

"Our last village carts are still south of the western cut. So are twelve scouts."

"If the engineers lay fascines first—"

"Then we move them. I will not bury our own people to improve the ground. Bring me the clearance report."

He nearly told her he was prince here. Instead he took four riders down the drainage path until they found the last carts grinding north, one wheel sunk to its hub. Lysander put his shoulder beside the villagers and the watch. By the time the wheel rose, Black Reed horns sounded across the marsh.

The report reached Sigrun as the first cavalry tested the reeds and found water under the crust. Six hundred horse narrowed into a useless, stamping column. Black Reed engineers came on foot, laying bound reeds over the soft shoulders while siege wagons advanced along the center.

Northern bows slowed them. They did not erase them. Shafts struck shields and men fell on both sides of the wagons. Spears met at the first barricade with a sound like timber dropped on stone. Healers worked in the lee of the mound. Drivers carried water forward and the injured back.

When the last scouts crossed, Sigrun lowered her arm. "West culvert. Half gate. Hold the east."

Pioneers turned the windlass. Marsh water spread across one shoulder in a dark, deliberate sheet. Black Reed's outer fascines shifted.

"East gate!" she called.

The second windlass would not move.

A watch member hammered its pin with a maul. "Jammed below!"

Lysander knew the maintenance cut from childhood inspections, a narrow ditch behind the stone lip. "Poles," he said. "Six with me."

The water reached his thighs before he found the gate's lower brace. Cold punched the breath from him. Watch members wedged poles under the timber while northern pioneers held the crumbling bank above them. On the road, another siege wagon struck the barricade.

"Together," Lysander said.

The first heave slipped. The second cracked something in his shoulder. On the third, the brace tore free and the east gate dropped open.

Water flung him against the stone lip. Hands dragged him onto the bank, bruised and coughing. Five watch members came after him.

They called twice for the sixth. No answer came from the brown rush beneath the culvert.

There was no time to make that absence noble. The eastern shoulder began to dissolve.

Two Black Reed siege wagons tilted into the softened verge. One went over, slow and enormous, its wheels blocking half the causeway. The next driver tried to turn and wedged his wagon across the remaining road. Sigrun advanced shield-spears far enough to secure the blockage, then stopped them. Fresh companies replaced the exhausted ones. Grain came forward. Dry socks came forward. The wounded went back on sleds that had not been burned for cook fires or lost to hungry foraging.

Black Reed probed for two days. Its horse could not deploy. Its foot could not bring numbers through the blocked center, and its engineers could not clear the wagons under the northern bows before the marsh swallowed each new shoulder path. With its supply train stretched south and the siege road closed, the League withdrew toward Greyglass.

Lysander watched the banners recede. Somewhere beyond them rode the marshal who had sold the gate.

"We pursue," he said. "Your scouts with my riders. We can take him before Greyglass."

"No border pursuit," Sigrun said. She did not lift the compact. She did not need to. "The causeway is held. My people have marched and fought for seven days."

Rank rose in Lysander's mouth out of habit, ready to turn need into command.

He swallowed it. "Send riders to observe the retreat. The rest help the villages home."

Sigrun gave the order. The northern host remained at Ninepin, exactly as far as it had promised to go.

* * *

Before the twentieth day, the first northern columns started home. Redwater's watch held the repaired barricade. Families returned to damp houses. Greyglass remained in enemy hands, but the siege train was broken and the capital granaries stood unopened.

The victory accounts were less handsome. Wages. Horses. Three burned roofs. Road stone. Injuries. Eleven northern dead. Four from Redwater, including the watch member the culvert had not returned. The seven-year toll fund had begun spending before anyone could praise it.

Lysander's tribunal was set for the first week after the thaw. His council had sent no hint of its succession decision. Sigrun would face the seven reeves in Harrowfast, and Gorm had not answered any of her dispatches.

At Ninepin, they signed the final tallies on a field table repaired with plain wooden braces.

"One remaining article," Lysander said.

Sigrun read it before signing. The marriage promise between Redwater and Gorm's house was void. No debt survived it. No northern service depended upon it.

She placed the severed gold clasp beside his hand. The chain itself had already been weighed and paid into the casualty fund.

"Keep it," he said.

"It was yours. The part that bought anything is gone."

He closed his fingers around the cold metal, then opened them again. Formal release language waited on his tongue, clean and useless.

"After the tribunal," he said, "may I write to you? Myself, I mean. Not through a king."

Sigrun checked the last toll figure. "You may write one letter."

"And after that?"

"I may answer it."

It was not a betrothal, forgiveness, or even a promise of a second page. It was enough because it was exactly what she had offered.

The last supply sled creaked north. Its runners left two modest grooves among hundreds of boot tracks. Lysander and Sigrun walked beside it on separate footing, while the unused clasp lay cold in his open palm.

stories.title: All Accounts Due
stories.prompt: You have no magic, but as you've helped others you've amassed tons of favors, artifacts, etc. Today everyone woke up to find thier max mana is zero.
stories.body:
# All Accounts Due

The Ithrom Array hung where six world-curves crossed, and every kind of magic in the material world had come to kill Faris.

One hand bruised, Faris crouched behind ordinary stone. Six empty sockets ringed the Unwritten Axis beside cradled keystones; the Parity Astrolabe hung above. Three body-lengths away, the Mortal Latch waited cradled: bearing unseated, selector upward, plungers apart, lever folded, cotter strapped. Eight relics converged accidentally over thirty-one years—nine since he learned of the Yoke, four since he found the junction.

Beyond, a luminous city walked; black fire ate a fortress; dragons stitched horizons; palaces filled three skies; an aurora held a mountain; soldiers exchanged organs and wings.

Six-practice engineers built the Array three hundred and two years earlier as a last resort against coupled roots. Route custodians held the timing instrument; graft keepers guarded the final junction, whose selector protected material bodies. No practice held both.

The Absolute Yoke descended through six wonders, borrowing grace for command, fire for appetite, flight for pursuit, rooms for prisons, weight for chains, gifts for forced flesh. The Bound Ascendancy wore all six at their meeting.

Born as armistice councils after route wars and furnace invasions, frightened rulers, priests, users, and magic-dependent peoples decided peace required every root to obey. Using stolen Array studies and living contributions taken or volunteered across all six systems, the Ascendancy would preserve the magical world by ending refusal.

“Leave the Latch,” it said through conscripted mouths. “There can still be order.”

Then Seyathi stepped through a tessellated wall and reached for the Missing Tessera.

*Nine years earlier, at the Talarum Steps*

The pilgrims had been kneeling for four days.

Their knees bled through their clothes, but Tessellate Grace cared less about pain than arrangement. Every attempt to rise completed another line in the prepared pavement, and the completed line bent their bodies back into worship. Seyathi stood beyond them inside a shelter of rotating mineral color. She was holding the greater pattern apart by a finger's width. Sweat silvered her mouth. Each breath cost her another piece of her sense of place; when Faris shouted, she looked first in the wrong direction.

“Do not step on anything beautiful,” she called.

“That advice would have helped at the bottom.”

He lay flat in the drainage cut beside the stairs. He had no counter-pattern to wear and no inner gift for the pavement to recognize. That did not make him safe. A prepared surface could arrange an unmagical body as easily as a chair. He crawled where the mortar was still raw, testing it with the brass tongue from his sandal buckle. Plain grit crumbled. Worked grit hummed against the metal.

A blank white tile sat between him and the nearest pilgrim. No lines. No pigment. Faris put his palm on it.

The prepared underside turned him over and folded him to both knees.

His shoulder struck the step. His teeth met hard enough to fill his mouth with blood. The pilgrims' hands rose together, compelled into the next figure, and the shelter around Seyathi narrowed.

“Blank side inward,” she said, voice tight. “You were meant to notice.”

“I noticed when my ankle turned.”

He tried to lift one knee. The tile corrected him by twisting his ankle until his heel fitted the design. Nothing in the pain was mystical. Tendons were tendons even when a goddess's geometry chose how to pull them. Faris wedged the buckle tongue beneath his sole and used it as a lever, gaining less than a finger's width. Enough to keep the joint from breaking. Not enough to stand.

One of the kneeling pilgrims moved one finger. Not up, which the pattern would have caught. Sideways, scraping at a seam beneath the lip of the stair. Faris followed the scratch with his eyes. A maintenance pin held the prepared facing to an ordinary support bed. No holy geometry protected the pin. It was only iron, green with damp.

Seyathi understood his look. “One breath,” she said. “After that, I will not know which way you are.”

She turned two fingers.

The colored shelter opened. For one breath the compulsion loosened, and every pilgrim sagged without being forced into the next posture. Faris tore the buckle from his sandal and struck the maintenance pin. Once. Twice. On the third blow it slid free. The facing dropped a thumb's width, breaking the pattern's continuity. Forty-three people fell out of worship at once.

The hidden lines on the tile flashed before they died. They were not devotional. They were a trial lattice for the Absolute Yoke.

Afterward, Seyathi could not find the stairs without Faris taking her elbow. She gave him the Missing Tessera, a square of matte mineral two fingers wide. It had been made for her two hundred and thirty-three years before, she said, and contained one finite direction of her grace.

“One day,” she told him, “you may ask me to arm it against the Yoke. Say exactly what you mean. A promise protects only its exact shape.”

At the Array, the unarmed Sole Chamber rang inside nine Yoke-folded rooms.

*Twenty-four years earlier, at Mavorn Palace*

Faris entered the palace prison dressed as a laundry porter, carrying wet sheets and the confidence of a man nobody important intended to remember.

Nine prison wings occupied the same foundation. King Malrec's heartbeat chose which arrangement a corridor wore, and every arrangement beyond the base made that heart spend its years faster. With one beat, Faris passed cells full of debtors. With the next, the same doors held soldiers. Another beat revealed an empty banquet hall through the bars. Living people remained one body each, crossing between rooms only at permitted thresholds. The stone was less disciplined. It could be wall, stair, ceiling, and oubliette before a guard finished yawning. The king could maintain the palace's grandeur only by aging inside it.

The Sole Chamber governed Manyroom from a bronze model no bigger than a thumb. Faris had been told to follow a scratched line along the base wall until it ended under the royal archive.

He followed the wrong scratch.

The next heartbeat put him inside a locked cell. The following one put the cell behind the kitchens. Then under a chapel. Then nowhere he could name. He dropped the sheets and felt along the base, but each wall carried decades of scratches. He could not tell signal from damage.

The prisoner sharing the cell watched him sniff the air.

“What?” Faris whispered.

The prisoner pointed through the wall, then pinched their nose and mimed eating.

Faris held up one finger for each shift and let the prisoner tap his wrist when a smell returned. On the seventh heartbeat, soup and lamp oil repeated together. On the ninth, wet wool came back without the soup. The scratched walls were meant to defeat sight, but cooks still burned onions on schedule and laundries still made steam. The prisoner smiled when Faris finally began counting the palace as work instead of wonder.

Meal smells. Grease when the kitchens were near. Damp grain by storage. Wax by the archive. Faris stopped looking for the right mark and waited through the pulse of rooms, tracking the ordinary things each arrangement could not quite hide. When wax and mouse droppings arrived together, he found the true scratch under his heel. It led to a loose base stone.

Behind it sat the Sole Chamber, made by the first palace architects four hundred and eighty-six years earlier. Faris closed his hand around it. Nine wings shuddered toward one plain arrangement.

He could have left during the confusion. Then a heartbeat made the wall beside him share space with King Malrec's private room. Faris saw a blade emerging behind the king, its wielder hidden in another arrangement.

He threw the bronze model at Malrec's head.

The king ducked to rebuke him. The assassin's blade passed through the place his throat had been. Faris shouted where to strike, and the royal guard dragged the attacker across a threshold into one body and one room.

The prison settled. Every captive remained alive in the base structure. Faris was arrested before he reached the laundry door.

Malrec visited his cell three days later. “You stole the legal heart of my house.”

“I also threw it at you.”

“Yes. If treason must double as rescue, it might at least improve its manners.”

The king pardoned him, retained a witnessed claim, and granted one decision over the Chamber if that decision was made publicly and applied to the palace as well as its enemies.

At the Array, the Nearmost Vertebra knocked under the Yoke's stolen gravity.

*Fourteen years earlier, at the Aphalion Belt*

Qeluun was too large for Faris to see as a body.

He saw a dark plain curving through the upper air, ribbed with pale sensory tissue. He saw storms dragged into crescents by a contraction somewhere beyond the horizon. He saw poacher rigs fixed to that living surface, their drills chewing for fragments that could alter weight. He felt each wound as a change in which direction his boots wanted to fall.

The Nearmost Vertebra was in his coat: a porous length of shed bone stolen from Qeluun ninety-seven years before Faris was born. He had recovered it from the poachers' buyer. Returning it would have been simple if the rigs had not started drilling deeper when he arrived.

Faris crawled between them with an ordinary pry bar tied to his wrist. He cut power cables, opened fuel valves, and hammered wedges into drill gears. Magic shifted the sky around him. None of it made a rusted clamp less vulnerable to leverage.

At the fourth rig, he cut a tether he thought held the machine.

It held him.

The curved plain dropped away. Faris went outward, toward a seam of stars. The pry bar snapped to the end of its cord and spun behind him. His scream had no useful direction.

Qeluun contracted.

Weight returned sideways. Faris struck warm tissue, bounced, and caught the edge of a drilling frame. The catch tore both palms. Under him, the vast body pulsed. Three slow knocks traveled through the frame.

The poachers saw him hanging there and restarted the nearest drill. Its teeth did not need magic now; the flywheel already carried enough motion to cut. Qeluun shifted again, not to throw them off, but to bring Faris's dangling pry bar within reach. The movement opened a tear in the pale tissue wider than a road. Faris understood the scale of the choice only when dark blood rose past him in floating beads.

“I don't speak mountain,” Faris gasped.

One knock. Then two. Then a pressure beneath his left knee.

He understood enough. Qeluun could move masses, but every contraction tore more of the tender tissue the drills had exposed. Faris followed the pulses instead. Pry left. Brace right. Turn the bar. The clamps had been driven by spellwork, but they were physical iron once seated. One after another, they opened. The rigs drifted clear. The last drill stopped with its point resting against living flesh.

Faris placed the Nearmost Vertebra into the wound it had once bordered.

The slow voice reached him as pressure through bone.

SELL IT. COULD HAVE.

“It wasn't mine.”

OURS. NOT NEEDED. SHED.

“Still not mine.”

Qeluun entrusted the bone back to him. One day, it would align one terminal change. Faris promised never to speak of Qeluun as terrain while asking it.

At the Array, Yoke-fire opened the unarmed Cold Maw.

*Thirty-one years earlier, at the Ghorvane Underforge*

Faris was young enough to believe a good plan became better when performed quickly.

The demon young were trapped in a root-furnace during a coup. Black fire burned inward through their bodies, consuming flesh to draw heat and mineral toward the moving forge. The usurpers had sealed the air shutters. The young could feed the furnace or suffocate beside it.

Faris followed a draft through machinery that rearranged itself around appetite. He held a strip of cloth near each seam and watched which way the loose end bent. Hot metal hunted his boots. Chains slithered toward the iron in his blood. He kept moving because stopping would let the forge decide what use to make of him.

He found a wheel beside a sealed hatch and turned it with both hands.

The hatch opened onto slag.

A half-forged predator came through, all wet alloy and borrowed teeth. Faris threw himself behind the wheel. The creature bit the axle in half. Its second lunge ended in Hurzai's hand.

The demon lord crushed its head and burned the remains inward until nothing but a cold iron knot hit the floor. The effort took a strip of flesh from Hurzai's arm. Black fire filled the wound, bright at the edges and lightless in the center.

“You opened waste,” Hurzai said. “Air is above. Your nose has cheated you.”

“Then I read the draft wrong.”

“Review while moving.” Hurzai kicked the iron knot into a gear train and jammed it. The forge convulsed around them. “I can consume a wall or carry you. Not both.”

Faris looked at the half-closed passage, then at the ladder rising through heat toward the shutters. “The wall.”

Hurzai burned a path for him. The fire ate a visible hollow from the demon lord's side. Faris climbed through before the metal could flow back, knowing rescue had already placed him in debt and that the price was being paid in living flesh.

Hurzai could have left through the breach. Instead, the demon lord lifted Faris out of the predator's reach and showed him the real shutter chain. Faris climbed. He passed an artifact vault whose door had split in the fighting. Any one object inside could have bought him a quiet lifetime.

Below, the young struck the furnace wall with weakening hands.

Faris passed the vault.

He braced his feet on ordinary rivets and cranked the shutter until his shoulders failed. Hurzai took the wheel only after Faris had broken the seal. Fresh air crossed the furnace. The black flames steadied. The young survived, and what they shouted through the vents named the officers who had arranged the coup.

Later, Hurzai set the Cold Maw on a table between them. The paired heatless jaws had been forged by a predecessor six hundred and eleven years earlier. Turned inward, they preserved root authority over Inward Fire. Turned outward, they could reverse it once.

“Custody,” Hurzai said, “if you never call a terminal ending painless. One root act when you ask. You will name the meat cost first.”

At the Array, forced flesh made the unarmed Form flex.

*Four years earlier, at the Keruvan Fold*

Faris stole two relics from Jelveth Sorn because patrons were using Kindred Graft to turn consent into a ceremony performed after the cutting.

The Unhatched Form was a nonliving organoid shaped by six former keepers one hundred and forty-one years earlier. It stored possible exchanges without ever having been a person. The six-practice engineers had built the plainer Mortal Latch at the Array's commissioning; by Keruvan it was two hundred and ninety-eight years old. They assigned its bearing, lever, plungers, selector, and cotter to graft-keeper custody because the selector protected material bodies. It originated no charge.

Faris got both into a canvas sack before Jelveth found him.

She pursued him through a sanctuary where every resident carried a chosen faculty from someone else. One man heard through the soles of his feet. A woman breathed water through living folds at her ribs. Two people shared the effort of one damaged heart. Jelveth tracked Faris using their offered senses, never taking more than each had consented to lend.

He climbed a support membrane and cut what he thought was an alarm filament.

The membrane sagged.

Borrowed muscles failed along the gallery. The shared heartbeat stumbled. Water struck the floor around the woman who could no longer use her gills. Faris reached the outer door with the relics and saw the whole sanctuary folding behind him.

He went back.

“You severed a load-bearing exchange,” Jelveth said. Her fingers were inside the living wall to the knuckle. “Put down the theft.”

“Tell me where to brace it.”

“You cannot perceive the strain.”

“I can perceive people falling.”

The woman with gills convulsed beside them. Jelveth pressed her free hand to the woman's ribs and took the drowning reflex into her own lungs. Pain folded the keeper over, but her directions stayed clipped and exact. “Pole under the third seam. Not the red tissue. That is sensation. The gray band. Lift on my count.” Faris obeyed without pretending he understood the body he was helping hold together.

At her direction, he jammed ordinary poles between the gallery and its physical foundation. One split. He doubled the next with a bench leg. Jelveth rerouted sensation, muscle, and breath long enough for material supports to take the weight. Faris held a pole against his shoulder until the last resident crawled clear.

The patrons arrived claiming the keeper had endangered everyone by resisting their program. Faris still had their signed orders in his coat. He read them aloud.

Jelveth did not forgive him. She did establish a public bargain. He would repair the sanctuary, never call a fixed grafted body counterfeit, and hold lawful custody of the two relics. In return, she would perform one bounded root act after reading its selector herself.

At the Array, a Yoke-folded horizon stirred the unarmed Arc.

*Eighteen years earlier, at the Skairrift*

Ekkorath rescued Faris before Faris rescued Ekkorath.

The dragon was pinned inside a corridor knot around a falling ruin. Bent distance kept bringing the same broken towers back beneath them. Faris had no wings, magical or otherwise. He rode a slab of masonry with a ballast rope around his waist and tried not to look at the repeated sky.

His first knot slipped.

Ekkorath could have spent the remaining fold of one wing to free themself. Instead they snapped their neck across the gap and caught Faris against their scales. The motion tore cartilage along the trapped wing. Distance opened and closed inside the wound.

“You are falling toward the western edge of your own mistake,” Ekkorath said.

“Tell me which way is physical.”

“The beam beneath you still belongs to the ground. Follow its length before the western horizon folds over it.”

Faris crawled onto a grounded beam that passed through the knot. The magical horizons lied, showing cliffs above and valleys behind. Falling chips of stone did not lie. Each chip found ordinary down whenever it crossed the beam. Faris followed them to a physical pin holding two ruins in the same flight circuit.

Halfway there, the beam rolled. Faris flattened himself and looped the loose ballast rope around a crack rather than trusting another knot. Ekkorath's trapped wing swept overhead, opening a destination that looked one step away and was probably a mile beneath them. Faris shut one eye. With depth reduced to shape and falling grit, the unenchanted beam was easier to read.

The dragon shouted headings. Faris translated them into left, right, duck, and hit this. He hammered the pin with a loose block until it bent. The circuit tore open. Ekkorath pulled their wing free and carried them both out while towers resumed their separate falls.

The Unflown Arc came loose from Ekkorath's damaged flight horn during the escape. It held the Horizon Flight counter-circuit they had chosen not to spend on themself. They gave it to Faris as a rescue gift.

The Astrolabe was why Ekkorath had entered the ruin. Skairrift had been an Array calibration station; route custodians had sealed the instrument beneath a marked roof tile. The corridor knot buried the recess, but Ekkorath knew its marks. Built at the Array's commissioning, the frame was then two hundred and eighty-four years old, with one passive indicator metal per root. Ekkorath lifted the tile; Faris freed its bent nail. He asked before taking the instrument, and Ekkorath made him name its cost.

“One flight,” the dragon said. “If you state every destination you will close and everyone you expect to fall.”

Now, at the Ithrom Array, all six keystones remained unarmed.

Faris turned first to Seyathi. “Arm the Missing Tessera, and before this hour ends the Absolute Yoke will be powerless. I will not take its power, wear it, or pass it to anyone.”

Every clause was true. Thirty-one years had supplied relationships and relics; nine since Talarum had supplied the Yoke and Tessera; four since Keruvan had supplied the Latch. Faris had shaped this promise only after those pieces met, and deliberately left one word out.

Seyathi studied him and the six keystones. From her side, they appeared to be six strikes against the Yoke's six borrowed faces; the terminal connections stayed hidden until the Latch was seated. Trust, not carelessness, supplied what Faris withheld.

“Against the Yoke, within this hour,” she said, setting each boundary in place. “I agree.” She pressed her thumb to the matte square and set it blank-side inward. Geometric light filled the first socket.

The other five had heard the whole request before they came, knew Seyathi had not, and had agreed not to supply the missing scope. They still had to choose here. Their complicity did not absolve Faris.

The Sole Chamber rang louder. Malrec stood at the second socket in a crown that occupied five possible shapes.

“If my capital's crossings remain,” he said, “I will renounce every foreign claim and submit the record to any witness you choose.”

“No exemption.”

“Then your terms reduce every royal door to carpentry, including mine.”

“Yes.”

Malrec looked toward the many palaces sheltering his people. “Let the record show that necessity has defeated negotiation. Witness this: I release every claim in the Sole Chamber, including my own.”

He folded its nine possible walls shut until one bronze room remained. The socket held the renounced claims behind the unfired Latch. Until the cotter came free, the armed Chamber retained one use: collapsing an imposed overlap into its material base.

The Nearmost Vertebra knocked hard enough to fracture stone. The immense curve of Qeluun tightened around the Array. The third socket waited.

END US? came the pressure, making Faris's broken brace tremble.

“You may die,” Faris said. “All who depend on Worldcoil may die. I am asking you to align it anyway.”

Silence pressed on him. Then Qeluun moved the Nearmost Vertebra into place. The bone pulsed once and became dust. Gravity convulsed. The third socket shone.

The Cold Maw opened wider. Hurzai's woundless older body gleamed with contained fire beside the fourth socket, but he did not touch the jaws.

“One quenched furnace does not cool a foundry. Show me why all six roots must die with this mold.”

Faris pointed to the band of black fire descending through a folded horizon. “Turn one jaw far enough to close its present furnace line. Not far enough to arm it.”

Hurzai narrowed the Maw. Its Yoke-band pinched out—and reappeared inside a Grace command, carrying black appetite through colored stone.

“Every Yoke branch holds all six adapter patterns,” Faris said. “End five and the sixth preserves their instructions, then compels its users to rebuild the entrances. All six must lose capacity together.”

Hurzai reopened it. “Then we pour out the metal, break the molds, and accept the workers caught by the heat. Name them.”

“Some demons will survive,” Faris said. “Some will not. Fortresses will collapse. Stored heat will break loose. Your lordship and your fire end with theirs.”

Hurzai's face hardened without becoming calm. “You have named flesh, furnace, and crown. I accept the burn.” He seized both jaws and wrenched them outward. They fused around the socket. Black light filled it.

Forced wings erupted from attacking soldiers below. Jelveth stood over the Unwritten Axis and the fifth socket.

Without lifting the Latch from its carrying cradle, Faris rotated its selector plate toward her. Two instructions were cut into the metal: end function; preserve matter.

Jelveth read twice. “Fixed tissue remains. No body is declared false. The shared heart?”

“Its impossible sharing ends. Each body keeps whatever its own matter can sustain.”

“Which is not a promise that each body lives.”

“It is not.”

She closed the Unhatched Form in both hands and opened the Axis with a precise incision of borrowed sight. The Form went still. The fifth socket accepted it.

Across the ring, the Unflown Arc lifted from its cradle as if remembering a route it had never flown. Ekkorath faced the sixth socket while cities flickered at the ends of their wings.

“Dragons will be grounded,” Faris said. “Crossings will close. Suspended cities will fall toward whatever is physically below them. You may tear your last flight holding the corridor long enough for me to reach the Latch.”

Ekkorath's long gaze stayed on the cities. “You have named roofs and routes. Name the people under them.”

“People inside falling cities will die. People below some of them will die. Dragons that cannot survive grounded will die. I cannot count them, and I am choosing the fall anyway.”

“Now you have named the country beneath your answer.” Ekkorath spread their wounded wings. “I will fly it once.”

Ekkorath lowered the Unflown Arc into the socket and flew the terminal counter-circuit. The shed horn lit along an old fracture. Five Astrolabe needles held their timings while the sixth swept toward them.

The Bound Ascendancy struck before it reached parity.

Prepared color raced across the hub, commanding bodies to kneel. Hurzai burned a hole through it; Seyathi folded the broken pattern away from Faris.

“The Yoke,” she said. “Finish the Yoke.”

Black fire consumed the stone's heat and drove cold at Faris's bones. Hurzai drew it into his chest, losing flesh as he fed its appetite into Cold Maw.

Soldiers arrived through shortened distance. Malrec struck the armed Sole Chamber. Its one-way failsafe collapsed their imposed overlap into the base room without making a new arrangement; his heartbeat paid in years, and his hair grayed as the soldiers met ordinary space alive.

The Ascendancy pulled weight from Qeluun. The Array lurched. Faris hauled the Latch from its cradle—selector fixed, bearing unseated, lever folded, plungers apart—and slid toward open sky. Qeluun's painful contraction held one last stable down.

Forced grafts tangled wings with arms and dragged breath between strangers. Jelveth's exact cuts separated imposed functions while preserving material bodies.

The Yoke ran through all six attacks. Every magical defense gave its command a cleaner path into that root.

The hybrid body stepped from a folded horizon into three rooms. Its weighted shadow cracked the hub; its hands opened toward Faris's Latch.

“Withdraw the Latch,” the mouths said. “The cities remain aloft. The crossings remain open. Chosen bodies keep their gifts. Gods keep their care. We end the war by making disobedience impossible.”

It was not lying. Faris could see the offered order descend along the Yoke: no battle, no refusal, no one falling because no one permitted to move without command.

Seyathi screamed as her spatial sense failed. Hurzai was half his mass; paid years bent Malrec; Qeluun's pressure came ragged; Jelveth shook; blood striped Ekkorath's wings.

Faris thought of forty-three pilgrims unable to rise.

“No,” he said.

The Ascendancy drove all six systems at him.

The mounting recess lay three body-lengths ahead. Faris dropped onto unprepared mortar and dragged the Latch through the first as command passed over him. A scratch marked the Axis's base surface; he followed its vibration through the second length and kept to the ordinary draft opposite the inward-drawn heat.

A horizon folded over the third and final length.

Ekkorath hit it wing-first.

“This span still reaches the place beneath your hands,” the dragon said, holding two false destinations apart.

Faris crossed the last length before stolen weight drove one knee down. He crawled to the recess, inserted the ceramic bearing, and twisted until its shoulder seated flush. The housing pivoted beneath the Axis; the lever remained folded, the cotter strapped, and all six plungers extended.

Their heads showed the selector's instruction: Preserve matter. End function. Faris pressed them in order, each stopping short of contact, and braced the housing with his belt. Insulation kept the six armed outputs apart.

The Ascendancy reached for him through every magical being on the hub.

It found no address in lifelong nonmagical Faris. He remained vulnerable to fire, stone, surfaces, talons, and blades; the Yoke merely had nowhere inside him to issue an order.

Faris slid the ordinary cotter through all six plungers, then swung the lever ninety degrees. Its cam loaded them against the cotter, a hair short of contact.

Above, the sixth Astrolabe needle met the other five.

Faris pulled the cotter free and said, “No More Magic.”

The words caused nothing. The physical release did.

The plungers dropped into contact together. All six terminal conditions propagated in the same instant. The breaking world-curves made that instant visible in six different grammars.

The Missing Tessera discharged. Tessellate Grace whitened through every prepared surface. Commands became pigment; walking sanctuaries settled or toppled with fatal collapses where ordinary walls failed. Compelled knees unlocked. Healing patterns left bodies in their material states. Seyathi's radiance and godhood vanished; her person remained.

Cold Maw ended Inward Fire. Black flames pinched out; held heat returned as ordinary expansion. Furnaces burst, fortresses slumped into slag, and occupants died in failing structures. Demons lost their bodily conversion: some lived mortal, some did not. No ember retained a root or reserve. The jaws softened into dead alloy.

Unflown Arc spent its counter-circuit. Horizons straightened and material-side anchors closed without claims about former destinations. Cities fell. Faris saw one break against a mountain, killing its occupants; others carried people and wreckage toward valleys below. Dragons beat ordinary wings: some descended, others fell. Stored distance emptied from bodies and routes. The Arc cracked into ordinary horn.
