Sole Chamber released Manyroom's last arrangement. Palaces became one material structure in one place. Crossers remained whole on the side containing most of their bodies, neither copied nor trapped. Malrec's crown became one heavy object; the bronze tore flat.

Nearmost Vertebra ended Worldcoil. Auroras became weather. The opening mountain dropped toward its inhabited crown and the valley below. Qeluun's leverage over weight ended, leaving them conscious, falling, and vulnerable to every moving mass. Their bone dust answered nothing.

Unhatched Form ended Kindred Graft. Chosen material bodies remained their own; scars and surviving organs stayed. Impossible faculties stopped, shared senses separated, and keeper awareness went dark. Hybrids failed without revealing a seventh system. Materially sustainable bodies lived; those dependent on an impossible breath, pulse, or exchange died. The Form became protein ash.

The extinction ranked no personhood. Gods lost power, not identity; worship, memory, relationships, grief, and responsibility remained. So did death: among occupants of falling cities and structures, people beneath released masses, and magic-dependent bodies. Others survived by ordinary matter or another person's hands. Faris could not count the dead, but that did not reduce the largest entry in his choice.

The wave emptied living capacity, workings, charge, structures, crossings, faculties, hybrids, reserves, relics, seeds, and every material restoration path. No artifact, descendant, or machine could recover magic. It could never return to that material world. The past remained real; afterlives and realities beyond closed material crossings remained outside Faris's act.

The Parity Astrolabe registered six perfect zeros. Its needles melted and frame fell apart. Mortal Latch split its bearing, bent its lever, and shattered its plungers around the cotter in Faris's hand. Nothing retained a repeatable action.

The world-curves straightened. Nothing held the Ithrom Array.

The hub dropped. The slab under Faris's palms fell beside him, contact without stable down. Arches pulled apart on different trajectories; the Axis cracked and tore free. Faris, Seyathi, and the mechanism were all in open fall. The powerless Yoke lost its faces and dispersed above them.

Faris saw Seyathi through it.

She looked from the powder of the Missing Tessera to Hurzai's dead fire, from the straight horizon to Malrec's absent rooms, from Qeluun falling beyond a broken arch to Jelveth staring at unanswering hands. Her own skin held no light now. She was alive. She was herself. She was no longer a goddess.

“Before this hour ends,” she said, each clause placed with terrible care, “the Absolute Yoke will be powerless. You will not take its power, wear it, or pass it to anyone.”

Faris did not look away.

Seyathi said, “You never said the Yoke would be the *only* thing made powerless.”

She struck her heel against the slab falling beside her, forced her body into the first position of Tessellate Grace, and turned two fingers at him—the gesture that had once made every prepared surface seize every body upon it.

Nothing moved. Nothing answered.

stories.title: A Friendly Little Game
stories.prompt: "While we wait for the rest of your party to arrive, would you like to partake in a friendly little game?" the hooded stranger asked as they sat down next to you at bar.
stories.body:
# A Friendly Little Game

The fourth cup had begun to sweat a ring into the bar.

You shifted it back onto its coaster and restored the row: your cup at the end, Gwen's on the right where she could watch the door, Alba's beside it, Felix's nearest the open stretch of counter. Four places, four tasks, everyone where they worked best. If they came through the door in the next twelve minutes, you could still reach the spillway before the river uncovered the lower stones. The old iron gate would open. The recovery crew would get inside. The rest of the fee would be yours by dawn.

If they came in twelve minutes.

River damp had silvered the windows. Wet grit rasped under boots behind you, and every time the door lifted on its leather hinges you looked up. Each time it was a stevedore, a pair of net-menders, a kitchen hand hauling in onions. Never Gwen's narrow shoulders, Alba's canvas medical bag, or Felix ducking under the lintel.

You rubbed a scraped knuckle against your cup. At the bridge, an overloaded cart had slewed sideways and tipped, its shafts blocking the narrow crossing. The driver had been dazed. One wheel had kept turning in the air. Gwen had called for rope; Felix had put a shoulder under the axle; Alba had crouched beside the driver. They had said they would handle it and follow.

You had squeezed past with the gate key knocking against your hip. Someone had to protect the low-water window.

The key was still there, heavy in the inner pocket of your coat. You checked it without seeming to check it.

A stool scraped beside you.

The hooded stranger had come from a rear booth, not through the door. They sat close enough that the wet hem of their cloak brushed your boot. Beneath the hood there was only an ordinary chin, a thin mouth, and skin made sallow by the bar lamps.

They studied the four cups. Then the door. Then the hand resting over your inner pocket.

“While we wait for the rest of your party to arrive, would you like to partake in a friendly little game?”

“No.”

“A decisive answer.” Their hands emerged from the cloak, bare and clean. “You must be the one who makes the plans.”

The door opened. A gust stirred the lamps. A man with a basket of eels came in.

“I'm waiting for people,” you said.

“So I observed.”

The stranger set a small leather purse on the bar. It landed with the dense sound of enough coin to replace the rope and oil you had bought with the client's advance, perhaps enough to cover meals besides. They did not untie it.

“Three predictions,” they said. “Surely a planner knows what their own party will do.”

That was when you should have picked up the key and gone back to the bridge.

Instead you said, “What predictions?”

The stranger laid down a shallow wooden rack and three thumb-sized pieces of dark, salt-glazed ceramic. Each piece was blank. They placed one in front of you.

“Before each companion arrives, you will tell me that person's first meaningful choice upon entering. You may define it narrowly. For ten breaths, you will give no instruction. If the choice matches your forecast, the point is yours. If it does not, the point is mine.”

“Who decides what counts?”

“Everyone present. Any uncertainty counts against my claim.”

“And the stakes?”

The stranger nudged the purse with one pale nail. “Two matches, and this pays for your party's drinks as well as your trouble. Two misses, and you surrender one useful thing brought to this table for tonight's work, chosen by you. The third turn is played regardless. It completes the account.”

You thought of the spare wedges in Felix's pack, Gwen's rolls of survey charcoal, Alba's excess bandage. Things used in common and replaced from the common purse. None worth half the coins before you.

“I can stop?”

“Before the first piece, freely. After a forecast is set, stopping concedes the game and the same forfeit. Nothing here compels you to pay.” The stranger tapped the ceramic. “Nor do the pieces compel your friends. They hold only what I put into them.”

“How far?”

The thin mouth moved, almost a smile. “Twelve paces, if I keep one hand upon the rack. The other writes a piece or wakes its marks. A piece cannot keep itself warm. Farther, or without my hand on the wood, the marks cool. The witnesses may remember the score if the pottery does not.”

No prophecy, then. No trap hidden in a speaking board. A little heat-work, a purse, and a boast dressed as a wager. Gwen would laugh at you for hesitating.

You put your thumb on the first piece. It was cold and slightly rough.

“Do you accept?” the stranger asked.

“Yes.”

They braced the rack with one hand and placed a forefinger of the other on the opposite edge. Warmth entered the ceramic between you. Fine orange lines followed the stranger's fingertip, branching over the glaze in letters too small to read from a distance. Their nail bed blanched.

“Gwen,” you said. “She'll come in, report the cause of the delay before anything else, then take the right-hand stool. She always takes the position with the clearest exits.”

The lines fixed into a compressed record: GWEN—REPORT FIRST—RIGHT STOOL.

“Always?”

“When we're working.”

“Does Gwen ever choose another seat?”

“Not if she has looked at the room properly.”

The stranger stopped asking. They slid the warm piece into the first slot.

Three minutes later the door struck the wall.

Gwen came in sideways against the gust, rain darkening one shoulder and bridge mud striped to her knees. You began to stand.

She passed you.

“Hot water and whatever food travels,” she told the bartender. She put down two small coins. “Send it to the driver at the bridge. Has anyone from here gone back that way?”

“My kitchen hand can go when the bread comes out.” The bartender glanced toward the oven door. “Five minutes.”

“Make it four.” Gwen stayed on her feet, watching until the coins disappeared into the till.

Keeping one hand on the rack, the stranger touched the first piece with the other. The heat-writing brightened. You did not need the repeated words to know the score.

“She reported the delay,” you said. “The request tells us the bridge is still blocked.”

“I told the bartender what the driver needed,” Gwen said. She looked from the stranger's fingers to her name glowing on the ceramic. “Why is that there?”

“A prediction. First meaningful choice.”

“Mine?”

“A small game while we waited.”

Gwen picked up the cup you had set at the right-hand stool. She moved it to the middle of the bar and remained standing. “You left before we had the first rope fixed.”

“You said you could handle it.”

“We did handle it.”

The stranger turned the piece so the words faced Gwen. “The forecast was a report offered first to the player, followed by that seat. I claim a miss.”

“I was about to sit,” Gwen said, though she plainly had not been.

For one bright second you thought she meant to help you.

Then she said, “Now I'm not.” She looked at the other two blank pieces. “What else have you promised?”

“One tool, if I lose. I choose it.”

“Whose tool?”

“A useful thing brought for the work. The wording was clear.” You heard the mistake as soon as you repeated it, but the purse sat within reach and two rounds remained. Alba would come through that door and see your hand. That was as reliable as low water.

You pressed your thumb to the second piece.

Gwen caught your wrist without touching the ceramic. “Don't.”

“If I stop, I lose now.”

“You've already lost one point.”

“Which is why I need the next two.”

The stranger waited. They did not urge you. That courtesy was worse than urging.

“Alba will see my knuckles,” you said. “They'll take my hand and start cleaning it before they ask what happened.”

“Take it?” Gwen asked.

“Alba always treats what's in front of them.”

“That's not what I asked.”

You adjusted the forecast because precision, at least, was still yours. “Alba will reach for my hand, and begin treatment before asking how it happened.”

The stranger kept one hand on the rack. Their other fingertip whitened as the second piece warmed. ALBA—REACH—TREAT BEFORE QUESTION. When they fitted it into the rack, a tremor ran through their index finger and stopped.

Gwen saw it. So did you.

“They're doing that,” Gwen said quietly. “Not the stones.”

“Pieces,” the stranger corrected. “Salt-glazed.”

The door opened before Gwen could answer.

Alba stepped in with their medical bag hugged high against the rain. The knees of their trousers were soaked. They paused just inside, taking in Gwen standing, the stranger's hood, your hand pinned beneath Gwen's, and the two pieces glowing between you.

Alba came closer. Their gaze settled on the red scrape across your knuckles. They unfastened the top flap of the bag, then stopped with both hands on the buckle.

“May I see?”

The hand was already halfway toward them before you understood that they were waiting. They had seen. They had opened the bag. They had not touched you.

Alba's eyes lifted from the scrape to your face.

Say yes, and the stranger could call it close. Say nothing, and ten breaths would pass. The stupidest part was how badly you wanted Alba to stop asking and simply become right.

“Not now,” you said.

“All right.” Alba buckled the bag again. “The driver is awake. Shoulder bruised, no break I could find. Someone local took over.” Then they turned to the rack. “What powers those marks?”

With one hand flat on the rack, the stranger laid two fingers of the other on the second piece. Its writing flared bright enough to shine on the damp leather of Alba's bag.

“A forecast freely recorded,” they said. “A clear miss.”

“Freely?” Gwen said.

“The recording was.”

It was an exact answer, and not an honest one.

Alba did not touch the ceramic. “Lift your other hand from the rack.”

“That is not a move in the game.”

“Then it costs you nothing.”

The stranger regarded Alba for a moment. They lifted the hand from the rack, leaving the other two fingers on the second piece.

At once the first piece dimmed. On the second, the word ALBA blurred at the edges. When the stranger returned one trembling finger to the rack, heat gathered again, slow and uneven.

“The pieces hold the pattern,” Alba said. “You're keeping it warm.”

“The marks are mine.”

“Do they make anyone do what was said?”

“No.”

Alba nodded once. It was not approval. “Then don't put my hand near them.”

“The game is decided,” Gwen said. “Pack it up.”

“The score is decided,” the stranger replied. “The third turn completes the agreed proof and clarifies the available forfeit. The player may stop, of course.”

Stop, and the stranger would point to the two warm failures and choose the story of what they meant. Finish, and Felix would prove that there was a difference between a plan and a trick. More important, the exact third result might narrow useful thing to something cheap.

You put your thumb on the last blank piece.

Alba let out a tired breath. Gwen released your wrist as if it had become someone else's problem.

“Felix will see a hooded stranger beside me,” you said. “He'll put a hand on his knife and wait for my order.”

Keeping that hand on the rack, the stranger's other pale fingertip rested opposite yours.

“Don't use that,” Gwen said.

“Use what?”

“What happened in the last bar. He has spent two years making sure it doesn't happen again.”

“Which means he knows when to wait.”

“Does Felix know that's the part you gave him?” Alba asked.

“He carries the knife.”

No one answered. The stranger drew the heat-lines without looking down. FELIX—HAND TO KNIFE—WAIT FOR ORDER. Their hand shook badly now, three pieces drawing color from the fingers that fed them.

The door lifted and stayed open on Felix's shoulder.

He carried a compact lifting jack under one arm. Grease blackened both sleeves, and rain ran from his hair down the sides of his face. He lowered the jack beside the door rather than bring its iron feet across the clean floorboards.

Then he read the room.

Gwen stood with her folded survey tucked under one elbow. Alba kept a full arm's length from the rack. You were rigid on the stool. The stranger sat close enough to touch your coat. Felix's right hand moved toward his belt.

There. You knew him.

His fingers closed on the hook above the sheath. His gaze found yours and stayed there. Whatever he saw made his mouth flatten.

Slowly, he unhooked the sheathed knife from his belt. He walked past you and laid it at the far end of the bar, beyond the cups, beyond anyone's easy reach.

“What do you want me to do?” he asked.

You had an answer ready. Get the knife. Stand by the door. Make this person leave.

Felix waited for what you wanted, not for an order he had already accepted.

“Nothing,” you said.

With one hand still on the rack, the stranger touched the third piece with the other. Its letters burned steadily, preserving every word you had supplied.

“He put his hand to the knife,” you said.

“To remove it,” Alba said.

“He waited.”

“He asked,” Gwen said. “You answered.”

The stranger turned the piece beneath one drained-white finger. “Your forecast described readiness to use the weapon at your direction. His first choice was to put it beyond you. Any uncertainty counts against my claim, but there is none. A third miss.”

Felix looked at his name in the heat-writing. “Start at the beginning.”

You tried. The bridge, the tide, the offered purse, the three forecasts. The explanation became less sensible with each clipped fact. You left out nothing except how easy it had been to accept the phrase useful thing.

The stranger listened without correcting you. When you finished, they looked at Gwen.

“A survey is useful for tonight's work.”

Their hand moved toward the folded paper under Gwen's arm. Gwen pulled it back and tucked it inside her coat.

“My survey,” she said. “No.”

The stranger inclined their hood toward Alba's bag. “Care is useful.”

Alba put the bag behind their legs. “You may not have the bag. You may not have my hands.”

“A small service would satisfy me. A short walk, a carried parcel, a door opened. The player may choose.” The stranger looked to Felix. “Strength was brought to the table as surely as any tool.”

Felix's hands hung open at his sides. He did not glance toward the knife. “I did not enter your game.” His speech had gone careful and formal, the way it did when anger had to pass through each word before release. “You have no answer from me.”

The bartender set down a cup hard enough to spill foam. “Nor from me. I heard one person make a wager. I heard none of these three offer you a thing.”

The ceramic pieces did not move. They did not brighten toward Gwen's survey or Alba's bag. No hidden hook pulled Felix across the floor. They held only your three predictions, kept hot by the stranger's failing hand.

“You said I chose the forfeit,” you said.

“You do.”

“You let me think you meant my property.”

“I let you decide what your party brought for your work.” The stranger's voice stayed courteous. “You were very specific about their uses.”

Route. Care. Force.

Not the words you had used, exactly. Worse: they were the shapes underneath.

The key pressed against your ribs. You had carried it for six years, bought from the old gate keeper with money from your first independent route. It opened one iron gate, nothing more. Without it, the spillway stayed closed. The mud shelf flooded on the returning water. The client's lost equipment stayed where it was, and the remaining payment vanished with the chance to retrieve it.

You took the key from your coat.

Its shaft was as long as your palm, its teeth brown with old rust. Gwen shifted between the stranger and the door. Felix looked once toward his knife and did not move. Alba watched the scraped hand close around the iron.

You placed the key beside the three pieces.

“Mine.”

The stranger's sustaining hand left the rack and closed on the key. The heat-writing began to fade at once.

“It qualifies,” they said.

“You knew I had it.”

“At the bridge, it swung from your coat when you climbed past the axle. You hid it, then guarded that pocket while the others took hold of the cart.”

There had been no glimpse of the future. Only the four cups, the turning wheel, and your own hand giving away what mattered.

The stranger swept the cooling pieces into the rack and put it inside the cloak. The purse followed. When they rose, Gwen had already moved into the path to the door. Felix could have reached it in two strides. Alba's voice, quiet behind you, said, “That bargain was built crooked.”

It had been. The stranger had shown you the stake in pieces, each harmless enough to accept, and saved the ugliest reading for after refusal had acquired a price. Nothing in the cooling pottery made that fair.

Nothing in it made the key jump from your hand, either.

“Let them go,” you said. “The key was mine.”

Gwen did not move for you. She looked at Felix. Felix looked at Alba. Then Gwen stepped aside because she chose to, and the others left the doorway open.

The stranger went out into the river damp. The hood passed the silvered window and was gone among the quay lamps.

For a while, nobody sat.

Beyond the glass, the river drew down the embankment stones toward low water. There was no spare key. Even if you found the gate keeper tonight, no replacement could be cut and hauled to the spillway before the turn. The recovery was over. The unpaid portion of the fee was gone, and the advance already spent on oil and rope would have to come out of your account.

You reached for the cups, meaning to put them back in order. Your hand stopped above Gwen's.

“I should have stayed at the bridge,” you said. “And I shouldn't have made three people into a route, a bandage, and a knife.”

Gwen's mouth tightened. “We said we'd handle the cart. We didn't say it was nothing.”

“I know.”

“You know now.” She drew the right-hand stool away from the bar and sat on it backward, facing the room instead of the door. “Tomorrow's route gets discussed tomorrow.”

Not your route. Not your decision. You nodded.

Alba set the medical bag on a stool of their choosing. “May I see your hand now?”

This time you opened it and offered it across the gap. “Yes.”

Alba cleaned the scrape with warm water from the bar. It stung. They wrapped it without forgiving you, which was not the same as refusing care.

Felix retrieved his knife only after the bandage was tied. He fixed it to his belt, pulled a stool from the far end, and sat where no cup had been waiting for him.

“We should—” you began.

Three faces turned toward you.

The rest of the plan went unsaid. “What do you want to do?”

Felix considered the question. Gwen looked toward the rain. Alba tested the bandage with one finger.

Then, without agreeing on anything larger, they drew the four cups into an uneven ring. Your newly bandaged hand rested open among them, on the bar above the empty place where the key had been.

stories.title: Four Million Falling
stories.prompt: In a fantasy world much like our own, where magic has long since die out, the greatest wonder is a floating city that should not be possible. With over four million residents, it's ancient nuclear reactors are beginning to fail, and the results are catastrophic.
stories.body:
# Four Million Falling

### 0:00

The cup moved three millimetres before the alarms began.

Inez Arco watched it creep across Chief Damas's console, leaving a crescent of coffee on the old black surface. Above it, the calibration weight hung at half a degree from vertical. Half a degree was nothing in a city that crossed weather fronts. Half a degree during a routine load-transfer test meant the floor and the world had stopped agreeing.

Then Reactor Four's board went red.

PRIMARY COOLANT PRESSURE LOW. SCRAM COMPLETE. TURBINE TRIP.

Inez was already out of her chair when the generator trace snapped flat. The isolation lamps changed from amber to green: commanded open. Current continued to pour across the common bus.

"Breaker Four is still closed," she said.

Damas caught his cup before it reached the edge. "Confirm."

"Four commanded open. No contact change. Bus current rising."

The control room lights dimmed. Somewhere below the consoles, a relay began hammering fast enough to blur into a buzz. Reactor One vanished from the generation display, then Five. Three and Six followed so closely their alarms arrived on top of each other. Reactor Two held for two more seconds.

The floor dropped.

Not far. Perhaps the thickness of Inez's hand before the lift rings caught the city's weight again. Her knees knew, though. Four million sets of knees would know. Loose binders lifted and slapped down. Someone behind her shouted once.

"Authorize a bus retry," Inez said. "If the breaker rail resets, I can bring a converter bank back before the rings coast."

"No." Damas's voice stayed level because that was part of his job. "Arco, prove ring integrity. Reactor desk, confirm all scrams. Cooling desk, emergency trains by unit."

"The bus is the source. Give me one reset."

"Prove the rings."

Procedure had become a wall, so she stopped pushing at it. Inez pulled the six generator phase traces across the lift board. Four's trace had not simply died. It had broken into a violent comb, an arc reaching through damaged insulation onto the bus. Each remaining generator had fed the same fault until its protection tripped the turbine and shut its reactor down. The isolation commands had gone out. The old shared actuator rail, bridged last winter when replacement parts failed inspection, had opened none of the breakers.

The ring diagram steadied under her hands: six concentric bands, all intact, all losing stored field energy.

"Rings are continuous," she said. "No converter input. We're coasting."

Damas looked at the vertical-rate estimate. It revised twice, settling as the stored fields weakened and Orison's fall accelerated.

TIME TO LETHAL CONTACT: 00:51:08.

### 0:08

The bus-gallery camera showed a white scar where the copper spine had been. Smoke folded through the image until the lens disappeared.

"No restart to save," Damas said. "Confirm."

Inez hated confirmation loops when the answer was obvious. She hated more that they were useful. "Confirmed. Main bus physically destroyed."

All six fission cores were shut down. Five had scrammed cleanly after the load rejection; Four had suffered a primary-coolant rupture, and emergency cooling on Two was cycling badly. None was exploding. None needed to. Their generators were gone, the lift converters were dark, and decay heat still had to be carried out of six ancient reactor blocks by pumps now competing for emergency power.

Orison's phones woke together. Inez's vibrated across the console with the civic alert.

**LIFT INTERRUPTION. SHELTER IN PLACE ABOVE BLUE DECK. DO NOT USE TRANSIT. AWAIT DISTRICT ROUTES.**

The population line beneath it read 4,083,612. A planning number, ordinarily. Water demand, school places, grain allotments. Now every digit had weight.

Reports crowded the side screens. Trains had braked in tunnels and platforms were filling faster than stairs could clear them. Three hospitals were on reserve power. The western shelter map showed twice its rated occupancy; eastern districts reported a southward slope, while the Low Keels reported north, because the city was flexing between rings. Fire crews needed priority lanes that no longer existed. Almost half a million people worked or lived below Blue Deck during the day. They had forty-three minutes to climb.

Inez opened the emergency generator diagram. "Cross-connect Unit Three's black-start set to Converter Two. Six minutes at full output buys us nine minutes of field."

"It buys the rings six at best," Damas said. "And leaves Three without a cooling train."

"Three scrammed clean."

"Three is still hot. Four has one cooling loop. Two's pump is hunting. The generators stay with cooling."

She threw the calculation onto his board: megajoules, field decay, vertical velocity. "At least look at the gain."

"I have. No lift recharge at the price of a damaged core."

The refusal left no softer version of the same request. Inez closed her model. Five intact reactors had done what their protections demanded, and the city was still falling. She made herself look at what remained rather than what she wanted to restart.

"Then tell me what stored field we still own."

Damas nodded once. The ring desk sent the numbers.

Inez ran them against current mass and contact speed. Then she ran them again with a lower final deceleration, enough to break windows and bones but not whole districts. The result did not improve.

"We can reach the sea alive," she said, "if we lose twelve percent of mass."

The Low Keels lit beneath the city diagram: freight vaults, reservoirs, sewage works, workshops, and stacked housing bolted below the oldest ring deck.

Paz's clinic occupied Keel South Three.

### 0:17

There was no time to call her yet. That was the first lie Inez told herself.

She built the landing from forces she could still command. Clear the Keels upward. Fire their separation charges. Bleed the inner rings in sequence to keep the city level as mass fell away. Hold the outer two rings until the last minutes, then spend their fields in one deceleration pulse against the world's magnetic field. The rings did not abolish gravity; they exchanged momentum while powered and held a finite charge when they were not. Once that charge was gone, there was no hidden reserve, ancient spell, or clever restart waiting beneath the numbers.

Damas studied her model. "Keep South Three. Drop the freight keels and the northern tanks."

"Not enough."

"Recalculate at fourteen metres per second contact."

"I did. South Three drags the southern edge down first. Ring Four saturates correcting it, then we roll before contact."

"Council authorization for inhabited separation requires projected loss comparison."

"The Council has twenty-nine minutes to learn field balance."

"Then give me something I can order without guessing."

His calm finally cracked on the last word. Not much, but enough. Inez set the two descent curves beside each other. In the version he wanted, southern housing remained attached for eleven minutes longer. Then the outer rings exhausted above the sea, Orison struck nose-low, and the reactor quarter went under first. The other curve ended in a city-wide injury estimate and a permanent ruin, but it ended below the fatal line.

"All Keels," she said. "Evacuation cutoff at thirty-four minutes. Separation immediately after."

"Confidence?"

"Enough to act. Not enough to forgive us."

Damas's gaze moved to the green actuator commands that had never opened anything. "Not now, Arco."

"My signature is on the bridge waiver. Individual breakers tested green. The common rail didn't. I said thirty more days was an acceptable exposure. If you're waiting for me to sound certain before you destroy those homes, this is why I sound certain."

For one second, neither of them performed calm.

Then Damas keyed the command channel. "All desks, prepare full Low Keel evacuation and separation. This is not a drill. Route every available stair upward. Suspend equipment security and open maintenance passages. Confirm by sector."

A voice from the emergency office asked whether the public notice should call the order a temporary clearance.

"No," Damas said. Procedure had failed him; euphemism did not survive it. "Call it emergency jettison. Tell them the Keels will be lost."

Inez's model began counting down to the first ring bleed.

### 0:25

The passage to the manual sequencer sloped enough that Inez had to use the handrail. People were coming the other way: technicians carrying battery lanterns, two orderlies supporting a man with a bandaged scalp, a reactor worker stripped to an undershirt and shaking from exertion. Nobody asked her whether the city would remain in the sky. The public alert had answered that.

At the stair landing, an old mosaic showed robed magicians dissolving into gold dust while workers raised Orison above them. Every schoolchild knew the caption: *When magic died, human hands built the greatest wonder.* Inez had once corrected Paz for calling the lift rings enchanted. They were measurable, she had said. As if wonder and measurement were enemies.

She called.

Paz answered on the fourth attempt. Behind her came shoes on metal stairs, wheels knocking each riser, and someone counting to three over and over.

"You're moving?" Inez asked.

"Forty-one patients, twelve staff, six neighbours who came in when the lifts stopped. Two beds won't fit the south stair turn. What's our cutoff?"

"Use maintenance stair K. It opens beside your pharmacy wall. Code six-zero-one."

There was a pause, filled by the sound of a bedframe striking metal.

"Who else has that route?" Paz asked.

"You do now."

"That's not what I asked."

"Paz, you're losing time."

"So are the dialysis ward and the nursery upstairs. Did you give them the code?"

Inez reached the sequencer door. Its battery lock was dead, and she had to shoulder it while entering the mechanical override. "The maintenance stair isn't rated for a public load."

"But it's rated for your sister."

The door gave. Inez stumbled into a low room where six manual ring controls curved around a window. The sea had risen visibly toward the city, blue and impossible beyond the glass.

"The Keels are being detached," she said. Reassurance was another form of theft now. "South Three too. I can hold separation until minute thirty-four. I cannot hold it longer."

Paz did not answer at once. The counting behind her stopped, then resumed farther away.

"How many stairs stay open if the deck tilts five degrees?"

"K and the central paired shafts. Avoid west crossways."

"When do the lights fail?"

"They already might. Your phones should keep the route map."

"Then broadcast K to the whole clinic block. Not just us."

Inez opened the emergency route channel and stripped the maintenance restriction from stair K. Occupancy estimates jumped at once: hundreds diverting, then thousands. Too many for comfort, within the structural limit if they did not run.

"Done," she said.

"Good. Hold us until the stairwell clears. Don't promise anything else."

"I will hold South Three until the stairwell clears."

"Last bed is moving now."

The connection broke before Inez could tell whether Paz had hung up or the network had.

### 0:35

The first Keel released cleanly. Its indicator vanished, and Orison rolled half a degree as thirty thousand tonnes fell away. Inez bled Ring Two east to correct.

The second release tore a freight bridge in half. Through the sequencer window, she saw a dark platform turn under the city, its cargo containers spilling in a slow glitter. It struck the Inner Sea seconds later. The impact rose as a white disk, then as sound through the city's bones.

Keels North One and South Two followed. Warning boards reported fires where utility lines had failed to sever. A shelter stair collapsed in a district Inez could not see. The casualty field remained blank because nobody had time to count.

South Three stayed yellow.

LATCH BANK C: CLOSED.

The evacuation desk transmitted overlapping fragments: central shafts clear above Blue Deck; stair K traffic still moving; smoke in the west crossway; clinic group unconfirmed.

"Delay separation," Inez said.

Damas answered through the command speaker. "Negative. Continue sequence."

"South Three has a mechanical hold. I need evacuation confirmation."

"Outer-ring reserve is falling faster than model. Release it."

"Paz's stair is in that sector."

"I know."

"Then give them another minute."

"No minute available. You have nineteen seconds before Ring Four exceeds correction capacity. At zero, keeping that Keel risks the remaining city."

She waited for the order. Damas did not give it.

"Your sequence," he said. "Your call."

The latch had no remote mechanical backup. The original builders might have known why; their diagrams ended at the housings, and every later generation had copied the gap. Inez could force current through the nearest inner-ring segment, far beyond its converter limit. The field pulse would wrench the attached structure downward and tear the latch out. It would also burn the segment open forever.

Twelve seconds.

She could hold the Keel and watch the southern mass overwhelm Ring Four. She could drop it with Paz somewhere inside. Another calculation would only spend seconds while pretending not to choose.

Inez armed the overload. "South Three destructive release. Ring Three segment south-six."

"Confirmed," Damas said.

She pressed both switches.

The current meter struck its stop. Heat pushed through the console into her palms. Outside, the skyline bent: towers, antennae, and the low roofs of a district that had always hung beneath her feet. A line of blue light flashed along the ring housing, electrical and brief. The stuck latch tore free.

South Three fell.

For an instant it remained level below Orison, streets and clinic windows small enough to cover with her hand. Then it tipped into the smoke from its severed utilities. Inez kept her hand on the dead switch until the indicator went black.

"Mass target achieved," Damas said. No triumph entered the words. "Begin landing sequence."

Inez spent the inner rings one at a time. Each bleed reduced their stored field and slowed the growth of vertical speed; each correction bought level at the cost of the final pulse. Orison groaned as loads found paths no designer had intended. The sea filled the window. Rescue vessels below scattered from the city's shadow, leaving white wakes that looked motionless at this height.

Ring Two's western switch froze halfway.

The city rolled. Cabinets burst open. A drawer crossed the floor and struck Inez's ankle. Instrument tilt said four degrees, then six, but its sensor had lost power and continued reporting six while the horizon climbed.

She stopped trusting it. The visible sea was level. Orison was not.

"Burn east-five," she said.

"That is our second permanent loss," Damas replied.

"If we don't, the outer rings spend themselves fighting roll."

"Approved."

She overloaded Ring Two's opposite segment. A bang sounded somewhere deep in the structure. The horizon slowed, held, then settled almost straight across the window.

At minute forty-six, outer-ring telemetry corrected itself.

Not enough reserve.

The field estimate had been borrowing a failed temperature sensor, reading the outer conductors colder and more efficient than they were. Inez had three minutes of gentle braking on paper and less than one in metal.

"We can stretch the pulse," Damas said. "Keep ten percent for contact and buoyancy support."

He had shifted to bargaining because command could not change the charge meters.

"A stretched pulse leaves us at twenty-one metres per second," Inez said. "The lower decks won't survive."

"No reserve means the city settles with full weight."

"The sealed ring trunks may float long enough for boats. They won't matter if impact splits them."

"Contact speed?"

She shortened the pulse window until the line crossed survivable. "Eleven, if the field holds."

The civic channel filled with shelter confirmations. Millions crouched in schools, offices, stations, and reinforced corridors. There was no room to move them now, only time to tell them what was coming.

Damas keyed the public line. "Brace. Final deceleration in thirty seconds. Impact will follow. Stay away from exterior walls."

Inez set both outer rings to discharge together. No field remained in the inner pair she had burned, and none would remain in the outer pair after this. Orison would never hover on these rings again.

Ten seconds. The sea lost detail until it became a single hard surface.

Five. She locked her elbows around the console rail.

At zero, she spent the wonder.

The field took hold through the floor, a pressure in her teeth and spine. Vertical speed fell. Displays died one by one as the battery bus collapsed under the switching load. The horizon stayed nearly level.

Then Orison hit the Inner Sea.

Water erased the window. The first impact drove Inez to her knees; the second threw her sideways as the city settled unevenly. Metal screamed below. Glass burst somewhere behind her. Cold water punched through the door seam, climbed to her wrists, and stopped.

For the first time in its remembered history, Orison was no longer falling.

### After

The control room canted seven degrees to the south. Inez knew because the battery inclinometer had revived, but she checked the horizon anyway.

The window was cracked and half above water. Smoke trailed from two lost districts. Steam rose from the reactor quarter where emergency cooling continued on local generators. Four's damaged loop still demanded work; a contamination boundary would have to be drawn across part of the sea. Below Blue Deck, water moved through streets built for rain but never tides.

Damas sat against a console while a medic wrapped his forearm. "You're finished here, Arco."

"Ring trunks?"

"Three flooded. Two holding. One uncertain. Boats are approaching from windward."

The first rescue craft could take hundreds. The next wave, thousands. Orison had held 4,083,612 residents that morning, plus visitors nobody had counted. Moving the survivors would take days if the weather stayed kind. Feeding them on a dead city would begin before that. None of them had a home that could rise again.

Inez tried to stand. Her left ankle refused her weight.

"Sit," Damas said.

"I can bring up the shelter ledger."

"No console. That's an order."

She almost argued that work was rest if the alternative was waiting. The lie had worn thin.

"Did the clinic stairwell clear?" she asked.

Damas looked toward the emergency desk. He did not soften his face before answering. "Partial receiving list came through Central School. Paz Arco arrived with thirty-seven patients and nine staff. Four patients and three staff from the clinic group are still unlocated. Other names are coming in."

Relief hurt differently from impact. It did not restore South Three. It did not fill the blank casualty fields or lift the freight workers whose platform had struck the sea first. It only gave Paz back to a world that now required somewhere else for her to live.

Outside, responders had stretched a rope along the tilted avenue. People passed water, bandages, and children hand to hand toward the rescue boats. Above them, the old school mosaic had broken along its caption. The golden magicians ended at the waterline; the workers raising Orison were gone beneath it.

No magic arrived to dispute the lesson. No dormant power lifted the city. The rings were burned and empty, the reactors shut down, and the sea kept what had fallen into it.

Inez took a place in the line. Her ankle shook each time she accepted a water tin, so the woman beside her shortened the distance without comment. Farther down, someone called for room for a stretcher, and the line opened, then closed again.

The horizon lay level at last. Against it, Orison rested crooked, terribly still.

stories.title: What I Hate Most
stories.prompt: ”You know what I hate most? That I have to share you~.” “Wait are we fighting or flirting because I’m getting mixed signals here.”
stories.body:
# What I Hate Most

Stormglass reached Vantress before Queen Draxenne did.

It lay across the northern dark like a bruise: violet at the advancing edge, black behind, dense with mineral grit torn out of the Cinder March. The last evacuation wagons labored through the gate beneath her while she climbed the parapet. Wet ropes slapped stone. Wheels struck cracks that should have been repaired three seasons ago. On the road behind them, people ran with cloth bound over their mouths and one hand on whoever could not run as quickly.

Draxenne had brought twelve ceramic plates, four carts of powdered stone, and a channeling plan that could keep that road alive. At thirty-nine, she had learned not to arrive at a border dispute with only an argument.

Night-Sovereign Ombria stood at the central pylon with one bare hand spread upon its palm-worn surface.

Five brass pressure studs knocked beneath her fingers, each carrying the mechanical pulse of a different ward district. Ombria listened to all five, but gave active shadow to four: four thin planes rose beneath her boots, barely visible except where the lamps broke against their edges. The fifth stud carried pressure only until she chose to answer it. Her black coat streamed in the grit. Her face was composed, severe, and much too pale.

Forty-two years old, and still determined to spend herself as if the city had appointed her an inexhaustible resource.

“The Ninth Conduit is split,” Ombria said without looking around. “I am pulling the lattice inward.”

On the slate pressure map, a fresh white fracture crossed the border junction. The inward seal would keep the crowded inner streets behind layers of angled shadow. It would also strip the March road and the outer settlements bare.

“No,” Draxenne said.

Ombria's smallest finger twitched as a southern district called. The nearest shadow plane flexed. “An unusually concise objection.”

“I save my ornament for listeners.” Draxenne laid one prepared plate over the conduit housing. Its clay surface was grooved for venting, its edges already dusted with mineral fuel. “The old spillway is empty. Give me the Ninth. You baffle the gale; I fuse the glass and drop it before it reaches either side.”

“Your heat passes below the inner market.”

“Contained heat.”

“A phrase beloved by people standing outside the container.”

Another stud struck Ombria's palm. Her shoulders did not move, but the words came a fraction slower. Draxenne touched the back of Ombria's wrist. Cold bit through her glove.

Ombria withdrew before the touch could become anything but evidence. “Do not make my body your argument.”

There it was: a fault line cleaner than the one on the slate. Draxenne could press it, or she could save the people choking on her road.

“Thirty breaths,” she said. “Whoever holds the conduit at the end commands it for this breach.”

At last, Ombria turned. She released one district plane long enough to face Draxenne fully, and darkness fell flat behind her. “A spoken yield, a spoken withdrawal, or loss of contact with the housing ends a claim. No cast enters a body. No strike touches a ward sheltering civilians.”

“Agreed.”

“The winner gains the Ninth Conduit for this breach. Nothing else. No office, no territory, no future audience, no touch.”

Draxenne smiled despite the storm crawling toward them. “You make victory sound dreary.”

Ombria put her free hand on the housing. “The first breath has begun.”

* * *

Draxenne locked her left hand around the lower lip of the housing and opened her right fist.

Blue-white cinders ran from the plate beneath her palm, thin as wire and hot enough to paint both women's faces in hard light. She sent the stream for the conduit latch. Ombria folded her own shadow up between them. Flame struck the dark plane, compressed, and spat backward through the plate's vents.

Draxenne turned her head before the flare took her eyes. Four breaths.

She dragged the stream sideways through grit lodged in the parapet seam. The cinders obeyed her attention, eating a bright path through mineral dust toward the housing's western edge. Ombria changed the angle of her wrist. Her plane changed with it, shunting the heat toward open air.

She could have angled it into Draxenne's ribs. She did not.

Draxenne could have let the stream lick across Ombria's bare hand. She broke it around her fingers instead, a white fork close enough to raise steam from damp stone.

Ombria's mouth curved by the smallest treacherous amount.

Eight breaths.

Draxenne drove a second stream through a ceramic groove. Ombria let one quiet district plane flatten into ordinary darkness, stepped onto the maintenance bridge, and drew a second contesting plane from the shadow of her moving body. She crossed the two like shears across Draxenne's route, four planes active in all. The bridge shuddered beneath the approaching gale. Ombria's dark silhouette held at its center, coat snapping, one hand shaping the planes while the other kept contact with the iron-rimmed housing.

Dark-queen nonsense, Draxenne thought. Appointed by a council, worked to numbness, answerable to half a million complaints, and still somehow composed like night had dressed itself for her.

Draxenne advanced.

Her first stream curled low. Her second climbed. Ombria constricted them between two shadow planes, stealing the open air cindercraft needed. Heat flashed back along the mineral path. Draxenne snapped her hands open, ending both streams before the ceramic burst.

The planes passed an inch from her throat as Ombria repositioned them. No contact. No claim beyond the conduit.

“Twelve,” Ombria said.

“You count beautifully.”

“You breathe loudly.”

“You have noticed.”

The provocation went unanswered. A pressure stud hammered beneath Ombria's distant hand on the housing, and her gaze cut past Draxenne toward the eastern roofs. One plane turned grainy at its edge. Ombria stiffened it, pulling more heat from her own body.

Draxenne hated that precise, disciplined choice. Hated the five demands in one hand. Hated every ward that could reach into this woman and receive an answer, while Draxenne got a visit between council sessions, a duel between crises, one almost-kiss on a rain stair two years ago before a messenger had come pounding up it.

Sixteen breaths.

She drove her right palm against the parapet. Cinder flashed through three hairline cracks at once, not three streams but one divided path. Ombria caught two. The third fused the grit beneath her heel into slick glass. Draxenne kept her left hand fixed on the housing rim.

Ombria shifted exactly as Draxenne knew she would. Draxenne rose inside her guard, close enough that heat met cold between their faces. Ombria's back stopped one handspan from the conduit housing. Her shadow pressed around Draxenne's flame, neither able to close without violating the terms.

Twenty breaths.

Draxenne could smell rain on Ombria's coat and the clean scorched-clay scent of her own gloves. Ombria looked at her mouth, then at the flame threaded between them.

Another district pulse struck.

“You know what I hate most? That I have to share you~.” Draxenne let the cinder brighten, a dangerous promise pointed safely into stone.

Ombria's brows lifted. She was still crushing Draxenne's hottest route between two planes, still keeping two other districts intact, still cold enough that her next breath shook. “Wait are we fighting or flirting because I’m getting mixed signals here.”

There were a dozen answers Draxenne might have given on an easier night. Each was polished, possessive, and useless.

The eastern stud struck again.

Draxenne cut her flame to a dull line and leaned back as far as her grip allowed. Ombria watched her, waiting perhaps for the joke, perhaps for proof that Draxenne could hear an uncertainty without turning it into permission.

Draxenne gave her neither pressure nor reassurance. She drove the dull cinder line into the bridge seam, then flared it against the western rim as if she meant to circle the housing.

Ombria blocked west.

The attack was a feint. Without releasing the housing, Draxenne snapped her right hand across and slapped it against the eastern ceramic plate.

The district pulse struck a third time.

Ombria chose.

Her housing hand tore free. The agreed rule ended her claim the instant her palm left iron. With that freed hand Ombria released the western contesting plane and used the freed capacity to raise a district plane toward the eastern roofs, while Draxenne's safe feint ran over the empty edge of the housing. Draxenne closed both hands around the conduit rim.

“Twenty-nine,” Ombria said.

The eastern roofs settled on the pressure map.

“Thirty.”

Draxenne held the Ninth. Ombria stood exposed beside her, shadow stretched elsewhere, throat bare to any cruelty the rules forbade.

Draxenne opened her casting hand. The flame vanished. Residual heat hissed harmlessly through the plate vents.

“Mine for the breach,” she said.

Ombria's gaze moved from Draxenne's empty palm to her face. Whatever answer lived there, she kept it. “Then command it.”

* * *

For eleven breaths, Draxenne was right.

Ombria kept four costly planes active: two angled into baffles without contesting Draxenne's grip, and two covering the districts still under load. The storm front struck the outer lattice. Violet-black dust plunged into the Ninth, compressed between Ombria's baffles, and met Draxenne's cinder in measured bursts. Each burst fused a cloud of razored grit into heavy black beads. They fell rattling into the empty spillway.

On the pressure map, the March road remained a steady gray line. The last wagons cleared the gate.

“You may say it,” Draxenne told her.

“The eastern baffle needs four degrees more pitch.”

“Not that.”

“Your second vent is narrowing.”

The old stone gave a thick internal knock.

Draxenne felt the wrongness through the housing: pressure returning from below instead of leaving. A buried crack opened across the spillway wall. The gale struck it, climbed, and began forcing Draxenne's cooling beads toward the inner market.

Ombria had seen the shift half a breath earlier. “Drop your heat.”

“I can clear it.”

Draxenne opened a third stream. Her vision haloed white. The air thinned inside her chest as cindercraft consumed what her body could give it. She melted the first clot of stormglass, only to send it deeper into the outlet, where it hardened across the crack like mortar in the wrong wound.

Pressure doubled. The ceramic beneath her palms whined.

Brute force would seal the route completely. Then the trapped heat would flash back through the housing and burst into the street.

Her winning plan had become the weapon Ombria warned her about.

Draxenne closed all three streams. Darkness crashed back into her sight. She kept one hand on the housing because she had won it, because surrender tasted worse than blood, because queens did not release a wall while their people stood behind it.

Ombria could have invoked the failure. She could have taken the Ninth and sealed the city, leaving the outer road to the storm.

Instead she asked, “What do you need?”

No triumph. No rescue disguised as command. The choice remained Draxenne's long enough to become a better one.

Draxenne lifted her hand from the housing. With the other, she pried the vented plate free and tucked it beneath her arm; it was warm, but no longer molten.

“Vents inside the channel,” she said. Without heat to sharpen her, the words came plain. “Three angled baffles. I can carry the eastern load through the ceramic. You would hold three planes, not four. Which two anchors can you give up?”

Ombria stared at her. Then another crack sounded below them.

“Come down,” she said. “We decide on the bridge.”

* * *

The storm reached the wall as they descended.

Grit shrieked across the stone. Ombria held four planes, turning one above the stair so stormglass streaked along its angled surface in luminous purple threads while the other three strained toward their anchors. The maintenance bridge dropped into the conduit throat, narrow, wet, and crowded with ceramic braces that Draxenne's crews had fixed to the old masonry. Draxenne dropped the recovered housing plate atop the eleven waiting along the bridge wall. Below, the clogged spillway boiled with dust.

“I release road east,” Ombria said. Cold had shortened her words. “You take its pressure in the braces. I keep three.”

“And lower east?”

“It is open. To put its load into your brace cleanly, I must catch it first.”

“With a fifth plane.”

“For no more than three breaths.”

The plane above them rippled. Ombria's fingers had gone gray at the tips.

Draxenne fastened both hands around a ceramic brace. Heat cracks opened across her skin beneath the gloves. “The parapet is empty.”

“The transfer may burn through your hands.”

“They are my hands.”

“An argument you found objectionable when applied to mine.”

Draxenne nearly ordered her. The old impulse rose hot and regal: give it to me, let me decide, stop making me watch you die by fractions. Command would be quicker. It would also prove Ombria right to resist.

She swallowed smoke and pride together. “Which two anchors can you live without?”

Ombria studied her grip, her breathing, the open vents behind her. “Lower east and road east. I catch the first, then taper both. The remaining three become baffles. You hold two streams, no more. If either of us says stop, I turn the three inward and you vent into the spillway.”

“And if the spillway closes?”

“We stop anyway and get off the bridge.”

It would cost both sides of the wall. It was still a real exit.

“Accepted,” Draxenne said.

Ombria lifted her smallest finger. A fifth plane sprang across the unshielded lower-eastern gap and caught its loose pressure. Cold stripped the composure from her face.

On the first breath, Ombria bent that emergency plane toward the first ceramic brace.

On the second, Draxenne fed a narrow cinder stream through the prepared brace. Ceramic glowed red, softened, and locked against the masonry. Ombria released the fifth plane. It became ordinary shadow, and the physical load hit Draxenne's brace. Her shoulder slammed into stone.

On the third, Ombria released the road plane. It became shadow and nothing more. Draxenne ignited the second brace.

The bridge lurched. Her boot skidded to its outer edge.

The fifth plane had existed for two breaths. Even so, Ombria swayed before she reached for Draxenne, then stopped rather than take either of her casting hands. “Can you hold?”

Draxenne's first instinct was to make the flame broad enough to blind the night.

Instead she made it smaller.

The braces cooled from white to a sustainable red. Her muscles still shook, but the mineral paths held. “Yes. Three planes. Now.”

Ombria stepped to the bridge rail. With one hand braced on basalt and the other cutting exact positions through the darkness, she changed the angles of her three remaining planes and anchored them across the broken channel. Not a wall. A descending series of blades turned sideways, each with a deliberate gap.

“First vent,” Ombria said.

Draxenne pulsed heat through it. A dense ribbon of dust whitened, rounded, fell.

“Second.”

The next pulse staggered Draxenne. Ombria widened the gap before the flame could choke. She did not take the work away. She changed only what was hers to change.

Stormglass fell around them in hot black beads, bouncing off the bridge and clicking into the spillway. Ombria advanced one step. Draxenne followed, dragging the load along the braces through molten seams.

They moved into the breach together.

There was no elegance left for flirting. Ombria's instructions broke into nouns. “Upper gap. Wait. Now.”

Draxenne had no breath for wit. “Wider.”

“Too much draws gale.”

“I need air.”

Ombria widened it.

Draxenne drank one harsh breath and cast. Her cinder changed the storm one handful at a time: knife dust to liquid, liquid to bead, bead to weight. Ombria made the paths that let each change happen without killing them. When numbness made Ombria's third finger fail to lift, Draxenne called the timing. When the tremor in Draxenne's arms sent her flame high, Ombria vented the pressure into bare stone.

The cracked section came into reach.

A slab above the outlet shifted.

Draxenne saw the load path before it fell: fractured edge, failing brace, the last open spillway directly beneath. If the slab closed that mouth, the conduit would burst toward both the market and the March road.

Her twelve prepared plates were stacked along the bridge wall. Enough fired ceramic to replace the failed brace, if she melted every one into the gap. The Cinder March would have no fitted plates for its own defenses when the next front came.

Ombria saw her look. “I can take the east anchors back.”

Her voice dragged with cold. A fourth plane would make her slower; a fifth might stop her heart. She offered it anyway, not as a sovereign issuing terms, but as a woman willing to carry the cost Draxenne had not yet chosen.

“No,” Draxenne said. “Keep the vents open.”

She tore the first plate from the stack and drove cinder through it. The ceramic slumped into the fracture, bright as a piece of fallen noon. A second plate followed, then a third. Each one drank water and oxygen from her body. Each one hardened into an ugly, load-bearing mass beneath the slab.

Ombria held three planes. She did not reach for a fourth.

Draxenne melted the last plate.

The slab dropped.

The new brace caught it.

All the trapped pressure found Ombria's three gaps at once. Her planes turned grainy, edges shivering under the load.

“Final pulse,” Draxenne said.

Ombria's hands were nearly still. “On you.”

Draxenne set both feet against the bridge lip. She opened two streams and no more. Ombria angled. Draxenne fired.

Blue-white cinder crossed load-bearing shadow. The stormglass front folded through the vents, fused, and came down in a black glittering fall that filled the spillway without sealing it. The last of the gale went over the wall as ordinary wind.

For one breath, neither woman moved.

Then Ombria lowered her first plane through a three-count. Draxenne opened her casting hands and let the braces cool. Ombria lowered the second, then the third. Shadow became shadow. Ceramic ceased to glow. The pylons held only the harmless residue of their charge.

The ward was inert.

The road and the market remained standing.

Draxenne sat down hard on the bridge because remaining upright had become a vanity she could no longer finance.

Ombria sat beside her, shoulder against shoulder, and laughed once without grace.

* * *

Before dawn, they occupied a ward room that smelled of soot, wet wool, and boiled water.

Unnamed crews moved beyond the open door, shoveling cooling beads from the channels. Each scrape proved another route remained open. Draxenne's fingers were wrapped in clean linen. Ombria held a steaming cup between both palms, though she seemed to take warmth more readily from the shared cloak over their shoulders.

The pressure map lay across their knees.

“One moon cycle,” Draxenne said. “I take personal casting responsibility at the two eastern stations, holding their pressure through rebuilt ceramic braces, and I supply the maintenance crews. I replace the plates as soon as my kilns can fit them. You retain the other three anchors and your office.”

“Your veto remains yours,” Ombria said. “Mine remains mine. Either may end the compact after a safe transfer.”

“Either may withdraw immediately from unsafe casting.”

Ombria marked the terms in chalk at the map's margin. Her handwriting was usually architectural. Tonight it leaned drunkenly downhill.

“No magical bond,” Draxenne said. “No penalty beyond the ordinary consequences we arrange for.”

“And no pretending this is permanent because permanence saves us another conversation.” Ombria drew two small blocks on the weekly duty slate. “These hours are private. The ward office does not summon me except for immediate danger to life.”

Draxenne looked at the blocks. “Private for whom?”

Ombria gave her a cold, level glance over the cup. The effect was impaired by the cloak, which had slipped over one eyebrow. “Administration first.”

“Cruel woman.”

“You did fight me for my conduit.”

“And won.”

“Then clogged it.”

There was the late humor, quiet and exact. Draxenne could have hidden in the familiar exchange all the way to sunrise.

She touched the chalk marks instead.

“What I said on the bridge was true,” she said. “Badly shaped. Still true.”

Ombria waited.

“I don't hate the city for needing you. I don't hate that you answer. I hate being given whatever remains after you have answered everyone until your hands cannot feel mine.” Draxenne looked down at her bandages. “And I have behaved as if the remedy were to make your attention mine. It isn't.”

“No,” Ombria said.

The word landed without softening. Draxenne respected it enough not to flinch.

“I want time you choose before there is nothing left of you to choose with,” Draxenne said. “Emergencies will interrupt it. Your duty will remain yours. I will be angry sometimes, and I will try not to make the anger a claim.”

Ombria set down the cup. “Vantress cannot grant me to you. Your victory cannot. Your crown cannot.”

“I know.”

“Do you?”

Two years of almosts stood between them: rain stairs, council corridors, visits cut to pieces by pressure calls. Draxenne had always thought clarity meant losing ground. Tonight she had learned what happened when one kept exclusive control of a broken channel.

She turned beneath the cloak until she faced Ombria fully.

“May I court you?”

Ombria's expression changed by degrees. Weariness remained. So did authority, and the aggravating precision with which she inspected any proposal likely to affect her city. Underneath them, desire arrived without disguise.

“Yes,” she said. “I would like that.”

Draxenne let out the breath she had been rationing. “May I kiss you now?”

“Yes.”

Ombria closed the distance.

Her mouth was warmer than her hands and less careful than her speech. Draxenne tasted boiled water, smoke, and the sharp little sound Ombria made when Draxenne touched her jaw. She kept the kiss brief because they were injured, exhausted, and still sitting under a municipal duty slate. Brief did not mean uncertain.

A brass stud knocked beneath the pressure map.

The eastern ward.

Ombria began to reach from habit. Draxenne's bandaged palm was already waiting on the contact point. The signal traveled into her hand: weight, direction, an ordinary public need passed through ordinary metal. She took it. Ombria watched the signal settle beneath Draxenne's palm and did not reach again.

Outside, cooling stormglass clicked beneath the first gray light. Ombria used her free hand to pull Draxenne closer.

stories.title: Transitions in Common
stories.prompt: Your friend got so excited when you said you're trans like them. You just figured out too late they meant transgender, not actually a shapeshifter like you. - update the rate for this story to YA-14+ - male vs female identity play
stories.body:
# Transitions in Common

The black jacket was going to betray me by fitting perfectly.

I stood in the costume-room mirror late Friday, one arm through a sleeve, and watched the shoulder seam land exactly where it should on the masculine body I wore to school. On my practiced feminine body, the same seam would slide down my arm and the button would pull. The jacket didn't know that. Clothes were loyal to measurements, not people.

"Are you planning to return that," Hugo asked, "or form a permanent attachment?"

"I'm waiting for it to admit it has limitations."

He usually would have told me the jacket's greatest limitation was me. Instead, he checked the corridor, shut the costume-room door, and tested the latch twice.

"I need to ask you about the portrait," he said.

Monday's arts-night display required a self-portrait. Hugo had been avoiding his with the dedication of someone studying for an exam in avoidance. I pulled my arm free and rehung the jacket.

"I can take it. You can veto every shot."

"That's part of it." He flattened a crooked paper label on a box of gloves. "I want to control the clothes and who sees it. And I want you to understand why."

The room held its usual smells of dust, hot stage lights, and fabric that had survived too many imaginary centuries. Beyond the door, a rack squeaked along the auditorium floor and faded away.

Hugo said, "I'm trans."

I knew the common meaning of the word. Of course I did. But he had locked the door. He had mentioned photographs and clothes and being seen as the wrong version. For years, I had shortened my own impossible secret to the same four letters inside my head, because naming a thing privately was safer than explaining it aloud.

Hope reached the sentence before sense did.

"Me too," I said.

His whole face changed—not into another face, which should have warned me, but from braced to bright. "You're serious?"

"Completely. Nobody at school knows."

"I had no idea." He laughed once, mostly breath. "I thought maybe, because of the they/them, but I wasn't going to decide for you."

I heard *decide for you* and thought of body maps held behind my teeth, each one mine and none safe to show. "Thank you."

"How long have you known?"

"I started changing a few years ago. I got better at it slowly."

His excitement softened. "Yeah. Slowly sounds familiar."

That could have been the moment. So could half a dozen moments after it. Instead, we traded truths with the important noun cut out. He said photographs could pin other people's expectations to you. I said one version of me had ended up on every school record, so I kept using it even when another fit better. He said telling parents could be complicated. I said mine expected consistency.

Neither of us asked the question that might demand an answer we weren't ready to give.

"This stays here," Hugo said at last. "You don't tell anyone about me."

"Never. Same for me?"

"Obviously." He looked offended that I needed to ask, which made me trust him more. "Will you help me find something tomorrow? For the portrait. Then Sunday, we can change here and take it before anyone arrives."

I looked at the jacket, then at my friend, and imagined opening one locked door in my life.

"Yes," I said.

We meant different doors.

* * *

At the secondhand shop on Saturday, Hugo rejected three vests for being too shiny, too square, and "designed for a child magician with tax problems."

The fourth was charcoal gray and plain enough that he went quiet when he saw himself in it. He rolled the sleeves of an open-collar shirt beneath it and shifted under the fitting-room lights, checking the line from shoulder to waist.

"That one," I said.

"You didn't even make a joke."

"I respect the vest."

"Terrifying."

I had kept my school body for the trip. It matched the face people knew, and shopping already required enough arithmetic without changing height halfway through. Still, I took a soft blue blouse from the next rack and pulled it over my T-shirt. Its narrow cut sat oddly across my current shoulders, but I liked the drape of the sleeves.

Hugo glanced over. "Also that one."

"It doesn't fit."

"It doesn't fit *like that*."

I stared at him. The sentence was so exactly right under my meaning that it felt like a hand offered in the dark.

I added the blouse to our basket, then found a sharply cut jacket one size larger. The jacket worked over the blouse. Neither garment changed who was inside it, but together they made my reflection feel less like a form waiting to be filed under one heading.

Hugo watched me gather trousers in two sizes and another shirt in a third. "Planning several lives?"

"Same life. Unreliable measurements."

"Bodies are inconsiderate that way."

"Do your shoulders take long to settle?" I asked.

His attention snapped from the mirror to me. "I'm not discussing my body in detail. Or medical decisions. If I bring something up, fine. Otherwise, no."

Heat reached my ears. I had been trying to ask how quickly he transformed without making him prove anything. I had managed to be invasive under either interpretation.

"Right. Sorry. You don't owe me mechanics."

He studied me for another second, then tugged the vest straight. "Bodies don't move on command just because someone wants them to. That's all I'm saying."

I nodded, privately impressed by what I mistook for discipline. My own first changes had taken months of failed concentration before I learned the trick of holding a body-map and releasing my breath into it.

At the shop's little counter, Hugo paid for the vest and shirt. Outside, we divided the bags and reviewed Sunday as if precision about logistics could compensate for the noun neither of us had supplied.

"No portrait gets displayed unless I approve the exact picture," he said. "No posting it."

"Agreed. And when I'm changing: no camera, no coming in, no touching."

"I wasn't planning to tackle you into your trousers."

"Good. They're fragile."

The joke landed badly enough that I hurried on. "We could each show the other a version not many people see. If you want."

Hugo adjusted the paper handles cutting into his fingers. "You first or me first?"

"Same time? Screens between us."

"Then we come out when we're ready."

"Yes."

"Okay," he said. "I trust you."

That should have slowed me down. Instead, it felt like permission to run.

* * *

On Sunday, I put a PRIVATE FITTING sign on the costume-room door, checked the latch, and turned Hugo's instant camera facedown on a table. I set my water bottle and two oat bars beside it. A full change always left me thirsty, hungry, and weak in the muscles, and it made another full change unreliable for twenty minutes. Preparation was how I made danger look like tidiness.

Hugo arrived carrying the vest and shirt. "You brought emergency rations?"

"Wardrobe is strenuous."

He gave the food a puzzled glance but took his clothes behind the left screen. I went behind the right in loose trousers and a sweatshirt with enough room to forgive several versions of me.

Fabric rustled on his side. A button clicked against the floor, followed by a quiet, heartfelt complaint. Then Hugo said, "Ready."

I put my hand on the screen's wooden edge. "Ready for me to change?"

"Yes."

He had agreed to witness a change of clothes. I had asked permission to do something I had never named. My excitement called the difference unimportant.

I chose the familiar map of my feminine body. I held it whole: shorter reach, lighter frame, a different line to my face, longer hair, a voice that resonated higher without becoming anybody else's. Then I let out the breath I had been holding.

Warmth spread from my ribs through my shoulders and down my legs. The sweatshirt loosened, then caught at one hip as my balance shifted. My heels pressed differently into the floor. The top of the screen rose in my vision as I lost a few centimeters of height. I kept breathing. My jaw eased under my fingertips; hair brushed my neck, then the cloth between my shoulder blades. Every few seconds, the remembered map tugged against the body I was leaving, not painfully, but with the deep fatigue of holding a difficult pose.

At thirty seconds, my hands were trembling from effort. At forty, the warmth settled. I was still Cody. I had the same scuff on my left knee, the same promise to protect Hugo's secret, and the same terrible habit of believing preparation made me careful.

I stepped out.

Hugo emerged at the same time in the charcoal vest and open-collar shirt. It was exactly the look he had chosen: simple, sharp, entirely his.

Then he saw me.

My hair was still shortening by a final fraction around my face, and the last warmth was leaving my throat. His hand tightened on the screen.

"Hey," I said. My changed voice made the ordinary word unmistakably strange. "It's me."

His gaze went from my face to my unchanged sweatshirt to my face again. "Cody?"

"Yes." I waited for astonishment to become delight. "So. When do you change?"

He looked down at his vest. "I did."

"No, I mean—"

"I changed my clothes."

We stood there, each waiting for the other to catch up.

Hugo said, very carefully, "When I told you I was trans, I meant I'm a transgender boy."

Every double-edged sentence from the last two days turned at once. Not magic. Not body maps. Not a secret ability. Hugo had trusted me with himself, and I had answered from a private dictionary he had never seen.

"Oh," I said.

His face closed. "Did you understand what I told you?"

"I thought you meant—what I can do. I use it as a shortened word. For transmutable. Only in my head, mostly, but everything you said about changing and pictures and—"

"Did you know I might mean transgender?"

The technical defense crowded my mouth. I hadn't lied. I had told him something true. We both had secrets and complicated clothes and versions other people expected to see.

"I knew that was one meaning," I said.

"The usual meaning."

"Yes. But with the locked door, and you said—"

"You let me keep talking." His voice narrowed rather than rose. "You said 'me too.' I told you more because I thought you understood that part of my life. Did you?"

"I understand hiding. And people deciding what they see. There are similarities."

"That's not what I asked."

I reached for the body-map of my school form. If I changed back, maybe the room would contain one less impossible thing. I pulled in a breath.

"Stop," Hugo said. "Don't turn into someone else to win the argument."

"It's not someone else. It's all me. I can show you."

"I said stop."

I should have listened. Panic made the choice for speed, though the power still waited for me to initiate it. I released my breath too soon.

Heat lurched through me and stalled. My shoulders shifted wider; my height returned halfway; my face found a stable line between two practiced maps and refused to move farther. Dizziness tipped the room. I caught the screen, but my hand shook hard enough to knock a hanger from its hook.

The metal clattered across the floor.

Three knocks struck the door. "Hello? I need the rolling rack."

The handle pushed against the latch.

My school face was gone. The feminine one was gone too. The mixed body I had once imagined showing Hugo with a ridiculous flourish now felt like evidence under a bare bulb. Another full change wasn't available. The camera was facedown, but memory needed no lens.

Hugo stared at the door, then at me. He could have picked up his bag and left the problem with its owner.

Instead, he stepped into the corridor, pulling the door shut behind him.

"Private wardrobe fitting," he said through the thin panel. His voice had gone calm in the way it did when calm was work. "I'll bring the rack out. Give us ten minutes."

Wheels rattled. The other student said something too muffled to catch. A minute later, Hugo returned alone and locked the door.

"Thank you," I whispered.

He picked up the camera and capped its lens. "I protected your secret. That wasn't forgiveness."

"I know. I'm sorry, I just thought the word meant the other thing, and you have to understand I've never told anyone, and—"

"You're doing it again."

The sentence stopped me more cleanly than the cooldown had.

Hugo folded the charcoal vest with exact, angry care. He put it beside the reflector and spare film instead of in his bag. "I don't want your explanation right now. I don't want to take a portrait. I want to leave."

This time, I listened.

He took his camera and shirt. The vest and the rest of the gear stayed behind. The latch clicked after him.

I sat on the floor in the body I had wanted him to see, drank water with both hands around the bottle, and waited until I was strong enough to go back to the face on my school records.

* * *

Twenty minutes later, the familiar map held. I ate both oat bars before walking home with Hugo's vest, the reflector, and the spare film in a shop bag.

That evening, I wrote him four explanations and deleted them. One described body maps. One explained why *transmutable* was technically accurate. One listed all the things I thought we had in common. The fourth was six paragraphs long and contained the word *but* nine times.

I deleted that one twice.

What I sent was shorter.

*I assumed what you meant instead of asking. I said "me too" and let you believe I shared an experience I did not understand. I accepted more of your private disclosure because of that claim. Today I asked if I could change, but I did not say shapeshift, and you did not give permission to witness that. I'm sorry.*

*What you told me stays private. My ability is a separate secret, and you can decide whether you want to keep it; you do not owe me a reply, forgiveness, or an explanation of being transgender. Tell me where to return the vest and portrait gear.*

Nothing came back Sunday night.

On Monday, at lunch, my phone buzzed.
