*Costume room after school. Bring the gear. No shifting until we've talked. I still want my portrait.*

It was not forgiveness. It was an appointment, which was more than I had earned the right to expect.

* * *

I arrived in my masculine school body because Hugo had named the limit plainly. The vest lay folded over my arm. The reflector and film were in the bag. I set all of it on the table and left the camera where he had placed it.

Hugo locked the door, but this time the sound offered no secret meaning.

"I'm sorry," I said. "For all four things in the message."

He leaned against the table, arms folded. "What do you think we have in common?"

My mind produced a careful twelve-part answer with definitions. I let it pass.

"People make guesses about us," I said. "We both care who gets private information and what words people use. That's some common ground. My body changing is not the same thing as you being a transgender boy. I don't know your history or what you need, and I shouldn't have claimed I did."

"And what you can do doesn't tell me your gender."

It was not a question, so I didn't treat it like one. "Right."

He watched me long enough that I noticed every piece of lint on the vest.

"Can I ask what your gender is?" he said. "You can say no."

"You can ask." I looked at my hands, familiar in this form because school had made them routine. "I don't have a finished answer. Cody is right. They and them are right in every body. Masculine feels good sometimes. Feminine feels good sometimes. Mixed feels good sometimes. None of that hands me a label. Questioning, maybe. Genderfluid, maybe. I'm not choosing today."

Hugo nodded once. He did not tell me what I was.

"I don't want questions about anatomy or medical history," he said. "If I decide to talk about something, I start it. You don't tell anyone I'm trans."

"Agreed. I don't want anyone told I can shapeshift. No filming a change, no touching me during one, and no demonstrations unless I say yes to that exact thing."

"And 'changing' means clothes unless somebody supplies a better noun."

"Yes." A weak joke presented itself. I put it down before it could hurt anyone. "I'm retiring my private shorthand. Transmutable was never useful enough to cause this much damage."

"Can I ask one question about the shapeshifting?"

"You can ask. I might not answer."

"Can you look like anyone?"

"No. Only human versions of me. I can adjust them, but I can't copy another person. And fear can ruin a change; it can't start one unless I choose it."

"Okay." Hugo nodded and did not reach for a second question.

Hugo reached over and turned the vest so its buttons faced upward. "I'm willing to keep being friends. I'm not willing to pretend this didn't happen. I may ask extremely literal questions for a while."

Relief tried to make me promise everything forever. "Okay," I said.

"Good. I still need a portrait."

"Can I ask what you want the display to tell people?"

"That the vest was worth twelve." His mouth shifted, almost a smile. "Nothing about what I told you on Friday. If that changes, I decide."

That was how Hugo chose to continue: not with a speech, but by putting on the shirt and vest he had selected and standing on the strip of faded tape that marked the portrait corner.

I checked the latch. I asked whether he wanted the curtain in frame. He said no. I asked whether I could raise the camera. He said yes.

The first print caught him glancing toward the door. He studied it while the image developed, then handed it back.

"Again. Move left so the light isn't flattening the vest."

I moved. Hugo reset his shoulders, lifted his chin by a fraction, and looked into the lens because he had chosen to. The second picture emerged slowly: open collar, dark vest, steady expression.

"That one," he said. "That one can go in the display."

I wrote nothing on it. It was his image.

Hugo took the camera from me and set it down on the table. "Do you want a portrait?"

"Yes."

"Do you want to change first?"

"Yes. Specifically, shapeshift."

"May I stay in the room?"

"By the door. Don't touch me. Camera down and capped until I say I'm finished."

He placed it facedown, clicked on the cap, and moved to the door.

I changed with water and food ready, though Sunday was far enough behind me that the cooldown had long passed. I held the feminine map first. Warmth loosened my jaw and shortened my reach; the blouse settled closer as my shoulders changed. Then I chose deliberately between the practiced maps—not a truest body, not a compromise, simply the one I wanted for this picture. I stopped with my height and face in their mixed range. The same old scuff marked my knee. The same nerves made me check the jacket seam twice.

I put the sharply cut jacket over the soft blue blouse.

"Finished," I said.

Only then did Hugo lift the camera.

"Name?" he asked.

"Cody."

"Pronouns?"

"They and them."

"Can I take the picture?"

"Yes."

He waited until I chose how to stand. The shutter clicked.

As the print darkened between us, Hugo asked, "May I keep this?"

"One copy. Private. No display, no sharing."

"Okay."

We sat at the costume table with the two approved prints between us. Beneath the portrait in the charcoal vest, Hugo wrote **HUGO — DISPLAY**. Beneath the face no school record knew, I wrote **CODY — PRIVATE**.

We left them side by side while the images finished developing, each label in its owner's hand.

stories.title: The Unrepeatable Working
stories.prompt: You've "accidentally" created a new kind of magic. Its only an accident because youre not sure how it happened. The board of magical researchers is demanding you to show them how you've discovered this magic.
stories.body:
# The Unrepeatable Working

The tile on the hearing table had been sealed in three kinds of wax, as though it might split again out of spite.

It had already done the interesting thing. A hair-thin opening crossed the stone precisely along the line I had mapped, neat enough to admit light and too narrow for the board's smallest gauge. My working had shaped it. My power had held it. Melek had spoken the release phrase.

The chair rested one finger beside the unbroken seals. “Who cast the working?”

“I did.”

“Who said *Parting Line*?”

“Melek did, but the phrase only released my pattern.”

“Then Melek cast it?”

“No.” I heard the trap after I stepped into it. “The release was theirs. The working was mine.”

The chair looked to the two board members taking notes. Neither rescued me with a better noun.

I had brought six pages of better explanations. The brass listening tube might have resonated with a particular overtone in Melek's voice. The crowded bench might have altered the contact geometry. Their breath might have disturbed the chalk dust in a useful way. I presented all three theories, in descending order of elegance.

“Which did you test?” the chair asked.

“The room was sealed before I could test any of them.”

“So none.”

“Sealing the room does tend to impair research.”

Nobody wrote that down. The board was capable of humor but preferred it submitted in advance.

The chair turned the tile so the split caught the window light. “An unfinished working that can be released by a nearby voice would change how we safeguard every teaching room in this college. A false report could do nearly as much damage, particularly when it names a records technician as the unexplained cause.”

“I did not name Melek as the cause.”

“You named them under accidental influences.”

That phrase was mine. It looked worse when returned to me.

“By the next bell,” the chair said, “you will show the board the conditions under which this recurs. Untouched tiles. Board-kept apparatus. Predicted controls. No more than seven live holds between both shapers.”

“By the next bell I can offer a hypothesis.”

“We have six already.” The chair tapped my pages. “You may test the effect, or withdraw the incident report. If it recurs, we can investigate why. If you cannot explain why, the recurrence will remain real. If it does not recur, your explanation will not improve it.”

I disliked the distinction mostly because it was exact.

“Seven holds,” I said.

“Fewer if your hands lose precision. Melek will set their own limit.”

The chair broke none of the seals. I was dismissed with my discovery sitting on the table, grammatically ownerless.

* * *

Melek's notes were better than mine in the way records technicians' notes were always better: they contained what had happened rather than what ought to have mattered.

We stood on opposite sides of the sealed workbench while an attendant watched through the open door. Chalk marks from the accident remained under a sheet of glass. The flat brass contact lay where we had both crowded against it. The listening tube curved across the bench to a narrow horn, its shutter fixed open with sealing cord.

“You were here,” Melek said, pointing to a scuff at the bench edge. “I was beside the ledger. You turned the timing bead. Then I called.”

“Yes. The question is which acoustic property let your voice enter my working.” I slid my draft protocol toward them. “If you stand at the horn, I can separate direct sound from conducted sound.”

Melek read the first column. “You have me listed as witness.”

“You witnessed it.”

“And as vocal control.”

“That is the function I need you to perform.”

They took their hand off the listening tube. “Then your control can perform it.”

I tried reassurance first. “Nothing drew power from you. I would have felt any transfer into the pattern.”

“I didn't say it did.”

“The board has required your testimony. Participation is only the practical extension of—”

Melek closed their notebook and began wrapping its cord.

Rank, I discovered, was a tool that could be dropped on one's own foot.

“Wait.”

They did, though they did not put the notebook down.

“What have I left out?” I asked.

“You asked me to read the phrase back to you.”

“Because my hands were occupied.”

“You said, ‘When I turn the bead, say the release exactly.’ I asked whether you meant both words. You said yes. I said I would.”

I remembered the exchange. I had omitted it because it was ordinary laboratory coordination, like asking someone to move a lamp.

Melek pointed beneath the glass. “We were both touching the plate. I moved the ledger to make room. You turned the bead with your other hand.”

“Shared contact, instruction, answer, timing.” I began writing the variables in the margin. “And the tube. Present sound. Possibly breath.”

“Possibly several things. Not necessarily any one of them.”

There went my elegant overtone.

I redrew the protocol while Melek watched. The first column became **participants**. I put my name on the first line and theirs on the second. Beside each attempt I wrote who would hold the pattern, who would speak, what would be changed, and what failure should look like. A collapsed *Parting Line* left the tile whole and my fingers numb for several minutes. I wrote that down. Melek added that repeated phrases through a dry brass horn had roughened their throat after the accident. I wrote that down too.

“Three fresh calls,” they said. “I stop after any one of them if I choose. Not during an open pattern unless there is danger.”

“Three will not complete the full transfer test.”

“Then choose what you most need to know.”

I disliked that limit for the same reason I had disliked the chair's distinction. It moved uncertainty onto my side of the table.

“Three,” I said. “Between attempts, you decide again.”

Melek unwound the notebook cord.

We predicted the failures before the board could call them excuses. An echo-vial replay should not release the working if a present living speaker mattered. A live but unappointed phrase should fail if our first exchange had done more than organize us. A call after eight bead-drops should test the brief readiness I remembered holding. A shut listening path should fail if the brass carried sound rather than power. Only then would we combine the witnessed conditions.

At the bottom I wrote: **Recurrence does not identify cause.**

Melek read the sentence twice. “Keep that one.”

* * *

By the next bell, the board had turned my workroom into a place where even the dust had witnesses.

Untouched palm-sized tiles sat in a numbered rack. The board inspected the listening tube, the flat contact, the white timing bead, and the echo vial, then resealed every joint. The brass was inert: useful for marking geometry and carrying nearby sound, incapable of choosing a line or supplying a spark. I said so for the record before anyone could promote it to accomplice.

The chair pointed to the first tile. “Ordinary control.”

I set my palm over the stone and traced one short opening through its grain. Living power came up my arm, cold and familiar, whitening the mapped line beneath the surface. I held the last gap open and spoke the designated phrase myself.

“Parting Line.”

The tile opened with a small, dry click.

The chair gauged the split and recorded it. My established working functioned. I could shape it and call it alone. Nobody applauded; a control that behaved properly was expected to have the decency not to seek attention.

For the echo-vial test, I prepared a fresh tile while the vial repeated my recorded phrase into the open tube. The sound was exact, including the slight impatience with which I had made the recording. The white line under the stone trembled, then went dark. The tile remained whole.

Cold numbness filled my thumb and first two fingers.

“Stored sound failed in this arrangement,” the chair said. “Nothing more.”

I flexed my hand. “Agreed.”

For the next test I did not appoint Melek. They stood at the horn, hands clear of the plate, and waited until I turned the bead.

“Parting Line.”

Their living voice traveled cleanly through the tube. My open pattern folded shut without releasing. Whole tile. Numb fingers.

Melek made one mark beside their limit.

The late-call control belonged to the chair. We touched opposite edges of the plate. I asked the chair to speak for that pattern; the chair agreed. When I turned the bead, the eight white drops fell through their glass channel one by one. The chair waited for the ninth.

“Parting Line.”

The pattern had already begun to collapse. The fresh voice reached brass, stone, and nothing open enough to answer it.

“Late failed,” I said through my teeth.

“Under this count,” the chair corrected.

“Under this count.”

For the blocked-path control, Melek and I both touched the contact. I asked them to call for this one pattern. They said they would. At readiness I turned the bead; the chair closed the listening-tube shutter between us.

Melek spoke their second fresh phrase into the horn.

I heard only a dull blur through the shutter. The shaped line vanished from the tile. This collapse reached my wrist, leaving my hand as precise as a mitten.

The chair called a pause.

“I can continue,” I said.

Instead of answering, the chair put the smallest gauge between my fingers. I dropped it on the first attempt and held it on the second.

“One hold after the full-condition test,” the chair said. “If that succeeds, another shaper uses the last.”

Melek swallowed and took water. “One fresh call left.”

“The echo proves the brass needs living breath,” I said. “The plate may tune that breath through sympathetic—”

“No,” Melek said.

The room became very still.

They touched the two whole control tiles, not the apparatus. “A stored phrase failed. An unappointed living phrase failed. A late phrase failed. A blocked phrase failed. We haven't separated breath from attention, sound, touch, timing, or the appointment. We may not be able to.”

Every eye in the room turned to me. I could have objected to a records technician correcting my magical analysis. The evidence did not offer the same objection.

“Melek is right,” I said. The admission cost less than the numbness and felt less pleasant. “The predicted substitutions failed. The cause remains undivided.”

I placed my unreliable hand flat on the next tile. “I request the full-condition attempt.”

* * *

Melek met me at the brass contact for their third call.

“This pattern only,” I said. “One line through this tile. You speak after I turn the bead, before the eighth drop completes. You may step away now.”

“I accept this pattern,” they said.

Their fingers warmed one edge of the brass while mine marked the geometry from the other. The plate contributed no power. It merely gave our hands one exact place to be while we did what we had agreed to do.

Melek moved to the open horn. I mapped the line, fed it power, and held it unfinished. The white bead turned.

“Parting Line.”

Their words reached me through the unobstructed tube before the third drop.

The pattern closed.

The tile split along my mapped line with a sound like a fingernail drawn once across slate. Light appeared where there had been stone. My power had chosen the target and made the opening possible; no releasing sound had left my mouth. Melek's hands were empty; no shaping light had touched them. Yet without their present act, every matched control said the tile would have remained whole.

For one excellent second, nobody spoke.

Then the chair measured the split.

“You two may share an unrecorded peculiarity,” the chair said.

“The procedure succeeded exactly as predicted.”

“Once. With the original pair.”

“Changing the shaper changes the pattern, power, handling, and target discipline at the same time.”

“Yes.” The chair slid the final untouched tile forward. “That is why we change the shaper.”

I kept my annotated sequence under my palm. Methodologically, my objection was respectable. Privately, I could feel my name detaching from the only new magic in the room.

Melek set down the horn. “Without transfer, it remains a report about Dorram.”

“It is my working.”

“Then call it yourself and report nothing new.”

The chair held out a hand for my notes.

I gave them over.

The chair read my sequence without improving it, which was the first kindness the board had shown me. At the contact, the chair asked Melek to serve for one pattern under the same conditions.

Melek did not touch the brass. “My three calls are spent.”

The chair withdrew their hand at once.

The room waited. My demonstration had reached the edge of another person's throat, and no amount of standing could turn that into my property.

“If the form names both functions as participants,” Melek said, “and if this is the final call today, I will make one more.”

The chair looked toward the record sheet. “Agreed, subject to the ruling's terminology.”

“Before the attempt,” Melek said.

The chair struck out **vocal control** and wrote **participating caller**. Melek read the change, drank again, and touched the plate.

The chair's shaping entered the stone in short blue segments, unlike my continuous white trace. The line itself curved slightly around a dark inclusion I would have cut through. Different judgment, different living power, same bounded working. The chair held the incomplete pattern and turned the bead.

Melek spoke their final phrase. It came rougher now but complete.

“Parting Line.”

Blue joined blue. The second tile opened around the inclusion, exactly within the chair's mapped boundary.

I had done nothing. I had not powered, shaped, targeted, appointed, spoken, or released. My notes lay open on the table between two other living people and had worked better without me than my theory ever had.

The discovery became mine in a form I could not own alone.

* * *

The board's ruling began badly enough to be plausible.

“Dorram,” the chair dictated, “discoverer and responsible practitioner. Melek, living acoustic control.”

Melek capped the ink and pushed the unsigned witness line away.

The chair stopped dictating. “The phrase distinguishes you from the echo vial.”

“The successful working distinguishes me from it.”

“You supplied no shaping or power.”

“I have not claimed either.” Melek stood. “Write the report you prefer. Do not put my name beneath it.”

The offered wording would have repaired my standing almost perfectly. I would be the discoverer of a new method in the college records. Melek would be thanked in the apparatus section. Future readers would see one mind and one useful noise.

I looked at the chair's split tile.

“Acoustic control is false,” I said.

Melek paused but did not sit.

The chair folded their hands. “Offer a more exact classification.”

I wished, briefly and intensely, that accuracy came with its own vocabulary.

“The person holding power, pattern, target, and direction is the shaper,” I said. “The appointed person supplying the live release is the caller. They are not equal contributions in kind. They are both necessary contributions in the paired result.”

“Under the tested conjunction,” the chair said.

“Under the tested conjunction.”

“And either role may be occupied by the same practitioner, as your control showed.”

That provision restored something familiar. “Yes.”

The chair revised the ruling in wet black lines. Paired research would continue only under board supervision until its limits were better understood. Every paired test would name shaper and caller. Training and independent accreditation would still require a practitioner to shape and self-call, because the college knew how to examine one person's competence and had one afternoon of evidence for examining two.

“A caller may be essential to a paired working,” Melek said, reading over the chair's hand, “and still be absent from the definition of complete competence.”

“Complete independent competence,” the chair said.

I considered the failed tiles, Melek's rough voice, and how little we knew. “For now, that is defensible.”

Melek looked at me, not the chair. They did not agree. They also did not leave.

The final finding occupied less space than my smallest theory: a single *Parting Line* could be divided between a living shaper and a living caller under the witnessed appointment, contact, timing, and sound-path conditions. Stored sound and the tested broken conditions had failed. A second shaper had repeated the result. Why the conjunction worked, whether every element was necessary, and how far it extended remained unresolved.

The board accepted the new effect without pretending to understand it. Institutions managed courage best when it could be written as caution.

* * *

In the archive, an attendant boxed the two split tiles beside the four whole failures. The echo vial went into a padded compartment. The timing bead went into another. Last came the flat brass contact, cooled now that no living hand touched it.

Melek and I reviewed the final form at a narrow desk. Where the old form had offered one line for **practitioner**, the new one had two ruled columns.

I signed under **shaper**.

Melek inspected every page before uncapping the ink.

“I should have recorded the appointment in my first report,” I said.

“Yes.”

“I treated your answer as laboratory furniture.”

“You treated it as something that could matter only after you explained it.”

That was worse, being more precise.

“I was wrong.”

Melek signed under **caller**. “The record is right now.”

It was not forgiveness. It was something the archive could use.

The cause line still contained my overtone hypothesis, cramped into the available space with two qualifications and an arrow into the margin. I crossed it out. Underneath, I wrote **unresolved** and left the rest blank.

At the bottom of the form, the college had already pressed its separate seal for independent competence: shape and self-call. I noticed it. I let it stand.

The attendant closed the box. Through its glass lid, the brass contact lay dull between two living names, while the line that should have explained us remained open.

stories.title: The Sky Remembers Us
stories.prompt: Long ago, the Earth was part of the greater magical universe, but were cut off due to a cosmic war, leaving them magicless. Recently, the magical universe has started to take action in restoring the Earth back to its former glory, much to the dismay of the government.
stories.body:
# The Sky Remembers Us

The last shutter stopped six centimeters short of closed.

Naomi Basto stood calf-deep in the test channel and watched brown water needle through the gap. The shutter was ordinary steel, its lower edge furred with salt, its motor loud enough to shake birds out of the restored marsh. Ordinary steel had been the government's preferred answer to the extraordinary for three months. It was reassuring right up until it failed.

She signaled the operator to reverse it. The steel rose with a wet complaint.

"Six centimeters," Minister Ochoa said from the boardwalk. "Your certification said zero."

"My draft certification said the motor could close an unobstructed channel." Naomi hooked a strand of eelgrass off the track. "The marsh has declined to remain unobstructed."

Ochoa did not reward the joke. Beyond her, floodlights silvered the research island's low sheds, the ring of inert pylons, and the mainland gates across a kilometer of dark water. Behind those gates lay the low district. At spring tide, a failed barrier there was not a metaphor about sovereignty. It was water in ground-floor bedrooms.

Veyru waited barefoot in the pilot pool. Thin membranes along their wrists opened and closed with each breath. They had eaten twice during the shutter test and still looked diminished, their skin losing the faint copper warmth it had held at sunset.

Ochoa turned to them. "If you lose consciousness, does contact end?"

"My part does." Veyru's voice was careful, each phrase given time to arrive. "The chorus cannot reach your apparatus without a living bridge here. The pylons focus what we provide. Alone, they provide nothing."

"And if your chorus refuses to stop?"

"Then I stop being its bridge."

"That makes your body our emergency control."

Veyru's wrist membranes tightened. "It makes my body mine."

Naomi climbed out of the channel before Ochoa could turn the exchange into a jurisdictional finding. "The shutters can narrow the pilot and change where the pressure goes. They cannot switch off a living source. Veyru can reduce that source. Either side needs to be able to call staged contraction."

Ochoa looked across the marsh. "My office is responsible for the island, the gates, and every resident below the surge line. The compact has no enforceable liability here. It cannot even promise that every other actor beyond Earth will respect a refusal."

"We cannot promise for those who did not join us," Veyru said. Ceremony had left their voice. "We can give you eighteen minutes from a finite chorus, through one bridge, across two kilometers. My blood oxygen, temperature, and response time are yours to measure."

"And if the ecology changes?" Ochoa asked. "If exposure does not stop at your surveyed population? If the gates become something our crews cannot operate?"

There it was: not hatred of magic, but a failure path. Naomi knew the minister expected the pilot to supply grounds for a moratorium. Veyru expected it to prove that an old injury created a present duty. Both had arrived with their conclusions packed and labeled.

"Conventional response stays with the government," Naomi said. "Supply stays with Veyru. Either may order contraction, and it happens in the rehearsed stages. No abrupt halt unless there is immediate loss of life."

Ochoa studied the six-centimeter gap. "Repair that. Then you have conditional approval."

It was less trust than Naomi had wanted. It was enough to reach low tide.

* * *

The basalt core had been cut from beneath the island before anyone knew where to look.

Naomi set it in its cradle beside the archive wafer. Under magnification, a pale fracture forked through the black stone, doubled back, and ended in a plane too smooth for cooling stress. Three laboratories had dated the glassed edge to the same impossible interval. The result had survived blind samples and a cabinet team determined to make it go away.

The wafer offered no light of its own. It was a gray sliver until Veyru cupped it between both hands. Their pulse quickened on Naomi's monitor. Mineral flecks inside the wafer turned one by one, spending the current Veyru and the distant living chorus supplied.

An image gathered above the table: not a globe, but a curved field crowded with branching lines. Some moved like roots toward water. Others struck, recoiled, and struck again. At the center, living figures pressed their hands into a bright mesh. The record broke there. When it resumed, one region had gone dark behind a doubled scar.

"Defenders cut Earth away as a firebreak," Veyru said. "The war could not follow what it could no longer touch."

"Defenders according to whom?" Ochoa asked.

The image trembled as Veyru shifted their grip. "According to the surviving side of a damaged record. I do not have the names of the decision-makers. I do not know whether the people here agreed."

"Then the record establishes no inherited permission."

"It establishes an inherited injury."

Naomi leaned over the core. "It establishes a shape. Interpretation can wait. Show us the inverse."

Veyru breathed in, held it, and sent one brief diagnostic pulse through the wafer. The inert flecks aligned. A second geometry appeared above the basalt: the missing half of the fracture, fitting its fork and smooth return with the intimacy of a healed bone broken apart again.

The air over the core cooled. Naomi smelled rain where there was none.

For ordinary life, the severance had worked almost perfectly. Almost mattered. Earth had kept its disputed incidents, its isolated survivals and impossible people, all the things institutions filed as fraud, folklore, or somebody else's sealed problem. But a sparse remainder was not connection. This wound was real, and it was older than any present government or compact.

Ochoa stopped disputing the event. "A true history does not decide who may alter my coast tomorrow."

Veyru lowered the wafer. Its light died at once. "No. It decides only that silence was made."

Naomi looked from the dead wafer to the fracture in Earth stone. Truth had arrived. Authority had not come with it.

* * *

At low tide the island smelled of mud, diesel, and cut saltgrass. Naomi walked the perimeter with both of them: pylons bolted to concrete pads, three drainage basins below the old tide mark, manual shutters in the channels between them, sirens and painted evacuation arrows facing the mainland. A sealed tank of broad-spectrum biocide waited beside the pump house. If released through the spray bars, it would kill the root mat and the microbial film beneath it within minutes.

It would also erase eight years of marsh restoration.

"The raw telemetry remains inside the operations room," Ochoa said. "A verified summary can be released afterward."

"Afterward is when summaries become arguments," Naomi said. "Public feed."

"No."

Veyru touched one pylon with the back of two fingers. Nothing happened. "Witness would protect all parties."

"Your compact is not a party recognized by our courts."

"Then recognition is another thing we cannot wait for."

Ochoa's mouth narrowed. "That is precisely the problem."

Naomi stopped beside the pump house. "Automatic safety feed if a perimeter breach holds for five seconds or a flood gate misses a commanded position. Raw safety instruments and exterior cameras go public, and the resident warnings start. Operations audio, command logs, and crew channels stay restricted. If neither trigger occurs, you keep the data sealed pending review."

Ochoa considered the mainland gates. "Those two triggers, that data. Agreed."

They ran the one-second calibration from the pilot pool. Veyru knelt with both palms in the water. The chorus entered through them—not as voices, exactly, but as layered changes in their breathing. The pylons caught and narrowed what those living bodies supplied.

A cool blue impulse passed through the nearest saltgrass.

Naomi had one glove off to check a salinity probe. The impulse reached her bare fingertips through a bent blade. For one second she felt the marsh as pressure and appetite: not words, not intention, but water seeking more than one route through roots, biofilm, and brackish channels.

Then Ochoa cut the calibration timer. Veyru lifted their hands. The blue vanished.

"Conductivity noise in living tissue," Naomi said, because that was the box on the form and the reading had lasted less than a heartbeat.

Veyru sat back on their heels. "A hard edge may teach it to seek around the edge. Contraction should remain gradual."

"On whose authority?" Ochoa asked.

Veyru looked at the dark grass. "Responsibility is not sovereignty. I have no authority here unless you give it. I am telling you what the pressure felt like in my hands."

Naomi logged the response as noise. She staged the steel shutters around three basins and told herself that several physical paths were the same thing as redundancy.

* * *

At the start of the pilot, the sky changed color without becoming brighter.

Veyru stood ankle-deep in the central pool. Every pylon remained dark until they pressed their hands to the living root mat below the water and the remote chorus found them. Then light traveled from their fingers through the pool in thin blue veins. The pylons took that supplied current and bent it inward, describing a two-kilometer contour over the marsh.

Naomi watched numbers. Water temperature fell six-tenths of a degree. Dissolved oxygen rose, then settled. The saltgrass conducted blue at the speed of a slow breath. Above them, the severance's counter-pattern appeared as faint branching lines, a scar remembered from the other side.

At minute nine, Veyru drank sugared broth without removing one hand from the water. At minute twelve, their wrist membranes fluttered fast enough to blur.

"No boundary excursion," Naomi reported. "No gate deformation. Metabolic load high but inside the agreed limit."

Ochoa stood at the threshold board with one hand beside the stop control. "Your model covers eighteen minutes. What does the root uptake do in eighteen days?"

"We don't have an eighteen-day exposure," Naomi said.

"Then you do not have the projection residents will ask me for."

Veyru's next breath caught. "Flow stable. Chorus reduced by one voice. I can hold the interval."

They had abandoned history. Each report was bodily and short.

At minute eighteen, Naomi called the first contraction. The outer shutters lowered. Veyru reduced the chorus's supply by a quarter. Blue withdrew from the high grass.

The western channel brightened.

"Hold stage one," Naomi said.

Beyond the pylons, a thread of light moved under the perimeter float. It did not leap the boundary. It followed the submerged root mat into a brackish creek, passed beneath the service causeway through a film-lined culvert, and surfaced on the mainland side.

Ochoa's hand closed on the stop control. "Boundary breach."

"Staged contraction," Naomi said. "Do not make the gradient sharper."

The breach timer counted through five seconds. The automatic safety feed opened: raw thresholds and exterior cameras went public, and the low district's warning network began its evacuation tone. Ochoa did not reach for an override. She took the operations radio instead. "Begin the low-district evacuation. Keep the emergency channels clear."

Veyru tried to ease the supply down. The blue in the pilot pool dimmed, but the creek brightened further. Earth life had learned the borrowed practice while the bridge remained open. Roots and microbial film were not generating the current; Veyru's shaking body and the distant chorus still paid for every blue centimeter. But the marsh had become its own set of conductors, branching beyond the apparatus meant to shape them.

Warning lights flashed on the gate monitor.

The mainland gates were six hundred meters beyond the causeway, half open for low-tide drainage. Along their submerged tracks, pale mineral crust flowered wherever the living film touched steel. It packed the drive slots, thickened around the hinges, and locked both gates before they could close against the returning tide.

Naomi killed power to the pylons. They went inert. The blue continued through grass and creek, bypassing them.

"Gate cycle failed," Ochoa said. She did not sound vindicated. She sounded frightened. "Tide turns in eleven minutes."

On the mainland camera, crews struck the new crust with pry bars. It cracked and grew back along the wet film.

Naomi stared at the branching channels on her map. Ochoa had predicted transformation in the one place they could not tolerate it. The government's risk was no longer a pretext.

* * *

"Release the biocide," Ochoa ordered.

The pump house alarm changed pitch. Valves armed the spray bars above the marsh.

"It will kill the active conductors," Ochoa said. "The gate crews get a clear cycle. The district gets a barrier."

She was right about the sequence. The remedy would work by turning a living wetland into dead mud, and after the surge there would be oxygen collapse, fish loss, and years of exposed shoreline. Those costs were not as immediate as water in the low district. That did not make them imaginary.

Veyru sagged against the pool rail. Blue traced the veins in their forearms. "Widen the contact along the unoccupied coast. Lower the pressure everywhere."

The sky contour bowed outward.

Naomi saw it move on three cameras. "No."

"The compact can carry the greater load."

"The compact was authorized for this island."

"The injury is ours to repair."

"You inherited responsibility, not the coast." Naomi stepped between Veyru and the outer channel, absurdly, as though her body could block a horizon. "You don't own the wound because your predecessors made it."

The contour held. After one terrible second, it stopped widening.

Ochoa spoke into the operations radio. "Remove Naomi Basto from the active zone. Biocide release in thirty seconds."

Naomi opened the red cover beside the command console. The agreed safety feed was already public; this switch added the excluded operations-room audio and the command log showing who had armed which system and when. Crew channels and evacuation routes would remain protected.

"Release the command record," Ochoa said, "and your clearance ends now."

Private appeal had failed. Naomi pressed the switch.

The public could already see the jammed gates, Veyru's metabolic readings, the armed spray system, and the unauthorized bend that had appeared in the sky and stopped. Now they could hear Ochoa order the rehearsed biocide, Veyru propose widening the contact, and Naomi refuse them both. The log also carried Naomi's own dismissal of the calibration response as noise.

"Evacuation is running," Naomi said. "Give me the three basins and two minutes."

"You logged the calibration as noise."

"I was wrong. The response found several living paths. We can give it lower-resistance paths away from the gate."

"We have no Earth-side operator."

Naomi pulled off her remaining glove. "We do for two minutes."

Veyru shook their head. "You cannot supply this."

"I know. You supply. I shape only what is already in the marsh, and you stop when I call it."

The calibration had touched her for one second. It had not chosen her, blessed her, or taught her anything beyond a pressure map she understood because wetlands had been her work for half her life.

Ochoa's gaze moved from the armed biocide display to the rising tide gauge. "If this does not reduce gate accretion in sixty seconds, I release it."

Naomi stepped off the boardwalk into the marsh.

* * *

Cold water filled Naomi's boots and dragged at her knees. She reached the root mat near the first manual shutter, pushed both hands into the saltgrass, and shouted, "Now."

Veyru opened one measured thread to the chorus.

The marsh arrived all at once. Naomi felt pressure in the roots, salt on living membranes, the hard bright resistance of mineral building against steel. She could not make the current. She could barely bear its passage. What she could do was press a preference into the connected local life: not there, where the culvert narrowed toward the gates; here, where mud and water opened into the first empty basin.

"Take control back," Veyru called. Their voice seemed to come through water as well as air. "I can pull it from you."

"Don't pull. Follow. First shutter."

She hauled the wheel. Ordinary gears lifted ordinary steel. Brackish water poured downhill into the nearest basin, giving the living current a broad wet route. Blue unstitched itself from the culvert and spread across the basin floor.

On the gate camera, mineral growth slowed.

"Thirty-eight seconds," Ochoa said over the loudspeaker. Her formality had burned away. "Crews, clear the left drive slot. Pumps two and four, start."

Naomi waded to the second shutter. The borrowed sense did not extend beyond the connected roots. She could feel none of the district, none of the wider coast, none of the world. Only this marsh, only while Veyru and the chorus held the source open.

The second wheel stuck at the same cursed six-centimeter gap. Eelgrass knotted the track.

Naomi plunged her arm into the channel, tore the strand loose, and shoved the wheel again. The shutter rose. Water struck the second basin. Blue followed, cooler now, divided between two root systems instead of forced through one narrow creek.

"Accretion has stopped," Ochoa said. "Hold biocide. Gate crews, cycle on my count."

Veyru gasped. The current surged toward Naomi as their control slipped.

"Less," she said.

"The chorus fears losing the bridge."

"Then tell them fear is not a flow rate. Less."

The dry impatience in her own voice sounded ridiculous, but Veyru understood it. Their breathing changed. The blue pressure eased.

Crews broke the softened crust from the drive slots. The gates moved a handspan, stopped, then moved again. Ochoa counted through the radio with the gate operator. Conventional pumps drew water from behind the barrier while the tide pressed from the other side.

Naomi reached the third basin with her vision stippled blue. This shutter had been set for the final staged return. She opened it one notch, waited for the root pressure to branch, then another.

"Fixed stopping point," Ochoa demanded. "How long?"

Naomi could no longer manage an explanation. "Gate closed. Third basin full. Then Veyru steps down on my hand."

"Two minutes total. You have twenty-one seconds."

The mainland gates ground shut. Water behind them stopped rising. Pumps pulled it below the first red mark.

Naomi flattened her palm against the root mat. "Half."

Veyru reduced the living supply. The distant chorus thinned in their breath.

"Half again."

Blue faded from the culvert, then from the two nearer basins. The third held it as a cool sheen across black water, a wide place instead of a hard edge.

"Close."

Veyru lifted both hands from the pilot pool.

The chorus was gone. With no living source beyond Earth sustaining the contact, the practice ended. Blue left the roots. The mineral crust at the gates became ordinary brittle scale beneath the crews' tools.

Naomi's borrowed sense vanished so completely that for a moment she mistook absence for falling. Then Ochoa's emergency team caught her under the arms and lifted her onto the boardwalk.

Across the water, the pumps kept running. The level in the low district fell.

* * *

At the public inquiry, Naomi's clearance was suspended for releasing the restricted command record and entering the active zone. Her hands still carried thin cuts from saltgrass.

The automatic safety feed had been copied too widely to seal. So had the command record Naomi added. Everyone had seen the government's forecast come true and Veyru begin an unauthorized widening before stopping. Everyone had also heard Ochoa order the rehearsed biocide, then seen her hold it when another method began to work.

Ochoa sat at the end of the hearing table with the proposed moratorium before her. "The pilot exceeded its legal boundary, altered protected ecology, disabled flood infrastructure, and required an evacuation. Those facts justify suspension."

"Of this method," Naomi said. "Until the next method has local approval and an Earth-side living operator who can refuse it. Not permanent silence."

Veyru's membranes had regained their color, though they still kept sugared water close. "The compact treated Earth's ecology as passive ground. That was our error. We will provide the damaged records, restoration labor, and compensation whether another pilot is authorized or not."

"Compensation assessed here," Ochoa said. "Not valued by the compact and presented as settlement."

Veyru paused. Under resistance, history had finally given way to bargain. "Assessed here."

The charter that emerged bound only one coastal government and one repair compact. Baseline studies and live data would be public. Communities inside any proposed exposure contour would authorize each attempt; an independent ecology review could stop it before activation. Every pilot would have a willing living operator on Earth, gradual rather than hard boundaries, mutual stop authority, and a new decision afterward. No successful test licensed the next one.

Ochoa added the last condition herself: conventional crews and evacuation systems would remain funded and under local command. Naomi accepted review of her conduct but refused the line that would have made her permanent operator. No method got to depend on one heroic body.

The moratorium became a pause with terms.

At dusk they tested the smallest of them beside the repaired mainland gate. Residents watched from the seawall. The pylons were disconnected. Veyru stood in the marsh and supplied one narrow thread from the finite chorus; Naomi, one hand on a living clump of saltgrass, guided the local response over open water.

"Five seconds," Ochoa said, watching the public clock. "Beginning now."

A single blue contour rose above the gate. It held without spreading, thin as a tide mark drawn on the evening sky.

At five seconds, Veyru withdrew and Naomi opened her hand.

The contour went dark on time.

stories.title: The Last Monster
stories.prompt: you don’t know how long you been lost in this dungeon but you are losing your mind and just want to get out. You can’t tell what a monster or an adventurer anymore so you just been killing anything in sight. It gotten to a point where the dungeon monsters are now scared of you
stories.body:
# The Last Monster

The shape comes around the corner carrying a lantern, and you kill it before the light reaches its face.

Your sword catches first on something hard, then goes through. The lantern swings. In its orange pass you see a hand wrapped in clean cloth, worked leather at the shoulder, a metal buckle stamped with a curling line. You also see a jaw too narrow, perhaps, and teeth too many, perhaps. Then the shape folds against the wall and the lantern settles upright between its knees.

It had been turning away.

Movement means attack. You know this. Waiting is how the others died.

Still, it had been turning away.

You take the lantern and fasten its strap at your shoulder with the stamped buckle. The dead shape's bag contains four strips of dried meat beside a wad of pale cave growth, food gathered by an adventurer or carried by a monster. Its flask gives you three swallows. You take all three too quickly. The corridor tilts, the flame divides into twins, and the next thing you know you are crouched with your shoulder against the wall and your sword lifted at the sound of pursuit.

Water drips into water. Nothing else moves.

Your gear keeps the count that your mind cannot. There is rust on the lower half of the blade. Your belt closes through a hole punched with the knife point, two holes beyond the last proper one. Cord holds both soles to your boots. A white seam crosses your forearm beneath three newer cuts. You remember receiving that shallow wound yesterday.

You remember several yesterdays. They cannot all have been yesterday.

The lantern gutters. When you cup a hand around it, the flame leans toward the left-hand passage and stays there. You hold still. A loose thread at your cuff lifts the same way. Against your wet fingertip, the air is cold.

Air goes somewhere.

From the left passage comes a measured sound.

Knock. Knock. Knock.

A pause. Farther ahead, three knocks answer. The signal travels away through the stone.

A hunting call, you think.

But the flame bends left. The thread lifts left. Cold touches the wet side of your finger. For the first time since counting stopped, three things agree.

You step over the body and follow the light it carried.

* * *

At every branching you make the same tests.

You shield the flame. You watch the thread. You wet one fingertip with water you should be saving. When your eyes insist that one corridor rises and your knees insist that it falls, you trust the air instead. The draft strengthens by degrees. Enclosed rot thins. Beneath it comes the smell of leaf mold, so faint you almost mistake wanting for evidence.

Then the flame bows, the thread trembles, and the damp of your finger turns cold. Evidence enough.

Something scrambles ahead.

You raise the lantern. A long-limbed figure crouches at a wall crack, hauling a smaller shape through by two of its four—or perhaps merely bent—arms. Its eyes catch the light. It bares its teeth.

No. The teeth are already bare. The lips may not close over them.

The figure shoves the smaller one into darkness, tears down a woven sleeping mat, and stuffs it into the crack between you. It never advances. It never reaches for you. When you take one step, it disappears after the smaller body.

Knock. Knock. Knock.

The warning races ahead. Claws answer it from a ceiling niche. Feet answer from below a broken stair. A cluster of low, gray scavengers abandons a fresh carcass without feeding and squeezes beneath a slab, the largest going last. Points of reflected light vanish whenever your lantern turns toward them.

They are taking positions. They are drawing you on.

The corridor ahead goes silent.

You slash at a dark shape hanging in a niche. Hide parts beneath the sword. The thing gives no cry because it is an empty sling, still warm where a body lay in it. The stroke pulls pain down your ribs and bursts sparks across your vision. For several breaths you cannot make the two lanterns become one.

At the next narrow place, stones and cracked boards fill a side opening. Their rough ends point toward you. Beyond them, tracks lead away: narrow feet, broad pads, dragging knuckles, a sweep like bundled reeds. They all overlap in one direction. A sack has split in flight, spilling cave bulbs and scraps of bedding. There are no spear points waiting through the barricade. It has been built from the far side to keep you out.

The word ambush remains ready in your mouth. The facts will not fit inside it.

Behind you, a stone grinds across stone. One of the passages you passed has been sealed. The creatures are closing the route after themselves, and if they close the airy route ahead, you will be left with the drip, the dark, and however many yesterdays your body has survived.

You begin to run.

The warning runs faster.

* * *

The passage spills you into a cistern chamber broad enough to swallow the lantern light. Bedrolls huddle near old fire pits. Gear lies scattered where a waiting party has dropped it for quick hands. Cuts score the wall in groups you cannot count at this distance.

You stop at the threshold, sword forward.

Nothing charges.

The flame shows a soot patch on the floor. Beside it sits a cup fashioned from the cheek plate of a helmet. Its rim bears one square dent.

Your thumb knows the dent before you do.

You made the cup. You slept beside that soot. At arm's height on the wall, one of the counting marks has a crooked tail because the notch in your knife catches when you pull it downward. You fit the knife to the groove. Stone dust flakes out.

The last time you stood here, the cut along your forearm was open. Now that cut is the white seam beneath the newer ones.

You have not found a new chamber. You have found a place that already survived you.

More things return as the lantern moves: a shield split through its painted face; a small wooden splint tied with careful knots; a blackened cooking spoon. Behind the cistern, a blanket-wrapped bundle has been dragged partly out of sight. One end is weighted by the unmistakable shape of a foot. The boot might fit you. The toes beyond it might not.

You do not uncover the face.

At the far side, tracks of every shape converge on a rising arch. Mud has been slapped across the walls at the height of your shoulder. Three blunt finger streaks here. Three charcoal bars there. Three scratches cut by a claw or a tool. Old signs have dried. New ones gleam wet.

When you move toward the arch, the knocking begins again.

Knock. Knock. Knock.

Nothing has followed you into this room.

The thought arrives whole, and you cannot starve it back into pieces. Nothing has been following you. Everything that could move has moved before you. You remember a horned silhouette dropping a bowl and flattening itself against a wall. A mail-clad figure backing away with both palms out. A face hidden behind thin hands while you approached.

Fear can be bait. Surrender can hide a knife. The old rule answers at once: if a shape can reach you, kill it before it decides.

But all the barricades face backward.

You cross the room. The strongest current of cold air passes over the bundle and pulls you toward the rising arch. The way out and the record of what you have done are the same trail.

* * *

The arch climbs into a steep spillway. Roots probe through mortar high above. The lantern flame streams almost flat, and beyond it, at the top of a broken stair, a seam in the stone is gray instead of black.

Not lamplight. Something paler.

A corroded grate covers the human-width throat. A fallen block pins its lower corner. Beside it, a smaller opening disappears behind a curtain of moss, its edges scored by fresh passage.

You strike the grate.

The clang fills the spillway, hits the curved walls, and comes back larger. You strike again. Rust showers down. On the third blow the sound becomes screaming: not here, not now, but close enough to lock your elbows. Someone is shouting behind you. Someone is not getting up. There was a bridge, or a stair, or a floor that gave way. You waited once. Waiting is how—

Light blooms below.

Two figures stand in the lower arch. Their lantern is bright and clean. One carries a coil of rope. The other says words that should have meaning.

“—hear me? Put—”

The grate's ringing sits inside your skull. The voice breaks around it. One figure lifts empty hands. The other reaches across its body, toward the rope, toward a hilt, toward either.

Your feet choose before the words can reform.

You descend with the sword high. The first figure stumbles backward, palms still open. The second throws the rope between you. Your boot catches it. When you wrench free, the coil whips upward, snags the lantern hanging from your shoulder, and tears its strap at the iron loop. Your lantern tumbles loose and skitters toward the moss-hung opening, still burning. Steel rings once; the bright lantern falls and bursts dark against the stones. One figure goes down and does not rise. The other makes a sound too raw to be a battle cry, snatches up the dying stub of your lantern, and crawls through the moss-hung opening.

Then you are alone with your breathing.

The fallen figure's hand is open. There is no weapon in it.

You turn over the pack. Clean bandages. A stoppered bottle of water. Two iron wedges. A charcoal map drawn on oiled cloth: the curve of the spillway, the grate, the side opening. Above them, a circle with short lines around it.

An open sky, drawn by an adventurer. Or a mark copied by a scavenger. The doubt comes as faithfully as hunger.

It changes nothing about the empty hand.

You drink, slower this time, though every part of you demands the bottle. You bind the fallen figure's wound, though the bandage stays unstained by any living pulse. You do it because the cloth was carried for saving someone and because you have ruined enough of its purposes.

The dropped rope reaches a ledge below the grate, but from there the stone still will not move. Your repeated blows have bent the bars inward and spoiled the best place for a wedge. The better lantern is gone. Yours, abandoned by the small opening, burns with a wick no brighter than a red pin.

The escaping figure has torn the moss aside. Cold air pours through the gap hard enough to stir the hair at your temple.

You cannot force the broad way. The only open route is the route taken by something fleeing you.

You take the rope, the map, and your failing light. You leave the bandaged dead where it fell and crawl into the crack.

* * *

Stone closes around your shoulders. The sword must go ahead of you, shoved along on one forearm. Your breath returns hot from the wall inches before your face. Behind you there is no room to turn. Ahead, the last flame shrinks until darkness seems to lean over it from every side.

The thread at your cuff lifts. Cool air touches the sweat between your fingers.

The flame goes out.

For a moment there is no route, no stone, no hand. The dark is complete enough that your body invents motion inside it. Teeth graze the back of your neck. Nails hover above your eyes. You know they are inventions because the cold current continues across your knuckles, steady and indifferent, and because the thread brushes your wrist in the same direction.

You crawl toward the air.

Gray light appears as a flaw ahead. In it, a small figure stands at a crack in the rising floor. Its knees bend backward, unless the joints are merely long. One hand grips a sharp strip of metal. Behind its legs, a smaller body curls beneath a bundle of woven fiber.

The metal points at the floor.

You reach forward. The guardian strikes the stone with its free hand.

Knock. Knock. Knock.

No answer comes from above.

It shifts over the smaller body. Its limbs shake. Its face turns away from what remains of your light, though the light is only a gray stain now. When it crouches, you see teeth. When it tightens its hand, you see claws. When its weight moves forward, you see the beginning of a spring.

You see these things second.

First: the shaking. The averted face. The sharp scrap held down. The guardian folding its own body over the smaller one and leaving its narrow back bare to your sword.

You pull yourself close enough to reach the crack. Its weapon could enter the soft underside of your wrist. You feel the point touch your skin.

It does not push.

Your sword rises as far as the low ceiling allows.

Movement means attack. Waiting is how the others died. The lantern-bearer had been turning away. The barricades faced backward. The hands below were empty. Every warning traveled ahead of you, never toward you.

Your ragged breath fills the chamber. The guardian flinches at each exhale.

The warning is not telling hunters where you are.

It is telling everyone else.

You lower the sword.

Not a slip. Not weakness. You make yourself finish the choice. You slide the weapon flat across the floor until it lies beyond your immediate reach. You open both hands. Then, though the air lies beyond the guardian and death may lie behind you, you push yourself backward through the tight stone.

One body length. Two.

You wait with your palms visible.

The guardian could close the crack. It could come after you with the metal. It does neither. For one breath, then ten, it watches. At last it gathers the smaller body against its chest and retreats through the opening. It does not bow. It does not soften. It bares its teeth once, whether from effort or terror, and vanishes.

The gray flaw remains open.

You retrieve the sword only because the shaft may still be barred. You hold it by the middle of the blade so the hilt trails behind.

From somewhere above comes a faint sound.

Knock. Knock. Knock.

Then roots rustle, and small feet move away.

You follow at a distance.

* * *

The bypass joins a slanted shaft where your shoulders no longer touch both walls. Cool air flows downward around cords of root. At the upper end, loose leaves tremble against a grate outlined in dawn.

Dawn. The word hurts more than the climb.

Fresh scrapes score the shaft. Bedding fibers snag on stone. Prints stipple the dust, some still crumbling at the edges. This is not a private path offered to you. It is the road along which the dungeon has been emptying itself.

The guardian moves ahead as a bent shadow, the smaller one clinging to its back. When it stops, you stop. When it turns its head, you lower your eyes. Twice the old need surges through you: close the distance, control the hands, strike before the turn. Twice you put your palm against the cold wall and wait until the air confirms itself by flowing over your fingers.

At the top, a shifted stone pins the grate. Roots as thick as rope have pried its frame from the mortar but not freed it. The guardian thrusts its metal scrap into a narrow retaining gap. The tool bends. The grate lifts no more than a finger's width.

The smaller body whimpers. The guardian answers with three soft taps against its own chest.

Your sword will fit beneath the frame.

You set it down where the guardian can see. It drags the dependent to the far side of the shaft, teeth bare, scrap raised at last. You do not approach until it lowers the point.

Then you wedge the blade beneath the grate and lean on the hilt.

Your arms shake. The grate rises. Soil showers your face. One root snaps with a noise that nearly makes you release the sword, but above the opening the leaves jump in open wind. The guardian understands the gap before you can gesture. It pushes the smaller one through, wriggles after it, and disappears into brightness.

The stone shifts.

You throw both hands against it. The sword bows beneath the grate. For one instant you could pull it free and let the opening close. Instead you shove until your shoulder enters the gap. The stone drops onto the flat of the blade and holds there, trapping it between iron and earth.

You leave it.

Your head clears the drain. Wet grass touches your cheek. Your shoulders scrape through, then your hips, then your knees. You crawl until no part of you remains beneath the stone.

You are outside.

The sky is colorless with early morning and vast enough to make you clutch the ground. Wind moves over the hillside without striking a wall. Damp earth yields beneath your fingers. Birds call from more directions than you can endure. You press your face into the grass, not to hide from a vision, but because daylight is real and your eyes have forgotten how to bear it.

In the brush, the guardian pauses with the smaller one clutched close. You see only a narrow back, long joints, the glint of its metal scrap. Then leaves close behind them.

They do not thank you. They owe you nothing.

* * *

Boots beat through wet grass.

Voices overlap. Metal leaves sheaths. Your hand closes on emptiness where the sword should be, and terror makes the whole bright hillside into another narrow passage.

“Down,” someone orders. “Hands where I can see them.”

You can see almost nothing. Human shapes, perhaps, ring you in the glare. One carries a bow. One has a hooked pole. One comes close enough that you hear their breath catch.

“Salken?”

The sound passes through the ringing in your head. It does not tell you what the shapes are. It tells you what you are: not innocent, not safe, not nameless.

You open your hands and kneel.

They bind your wrists. The cord burns the cuts beneath it. Someone holds a cup to your mouth and lets you take one measured swallow, then pulls it away while you beg for the rest. Care and restraint arrive together, and your body knows how to understand neither.

A searcher touches the stamped buckle at your shoulder.

“That belonged to one of ours.”

You look down at the curling line in the metal. It might have come from the lantern-bearer. It might have come from someone dead many passages ago. You cannot build certainty from the fact that it is easier to survive.

“I killed people below,” you say. Your voice sounds scraped hollow. “I killed others. I don't know what they were. I don't know how many.”

The hands on your bindings tighten, but no one strikes.

You turn your face toward the drain. “There may be survivors. I can show you the chambers.”

“And the monsters?” someone asks. “The tracks in the grass?”

The brush has stopped moving. You cannot tell where the guardian went.

“They led me out,” you say. “Let them go.”

No one promises. Judgment does not arrive in a clean shape. Neither does forgiveness.

Sunlight clears the hill and falls across your bound, open hands. Behind you, the sword remains wedged in the dark mouth of the drain, holding the way open.

The air is free.

You breathe it while they take you away.

stories.title: The Healer's Measure
stories.prompt: witchknights are not only master mages, but are also the most capable warriors. When one chose you to become their apprentice you were confused; You trained to be a healer. Apparently that's why they did.
stories.body:
# The Healer's Measure

Ruva saw the wrist before she saw the opening.

Vekran's practice blade was high, his right shoulder bare to a clean strike. That was the opening. The wrist beneath it was the truth: two tendons drawn tight under the skin, the thumb turned inward, one narrow line where a shallow cut would empty the hand without ruining it.

She went for the shoulder.

Three paces of sand vanished under her boots. Vekran did not retreat. He set the iron length of his blunted blade against hers, breathed out, and turned.

Pressure traveled through the blades like a kick from a mule. He had declared one turn before they began, and he spent it neatly. Ruva's own charge carried her past him. Her back foot crossed her front; the yard tipped; she landed hip-first in the sand.

Vekran stopped his blade a finger's width from her ribs.

"Halt."

Ruva lay still until the iron went away. The packed practice yard had been raked, its boundary checked, both blades inspected in her hands. Six weeks of bruises had taught her that Vekran meant every safety rule he gave her. They had not taught her how to fall without feeling personally insulted by the ground.

"Again," she said.

"What did you decline to strike?"

She sat up. "If you're looking for a graceful description of my failure, you'll have to recruit a poet."

"I recruited a healer."

There it was again: an answer shaped like a shut door. In every village along the road, children played at witchknights with broom handles. Soldiers lowered their voices over stories of warriors who could read a blow through iron and send it elsewhere. Vekran could have chosen any fighter who knew which end of a sword to hold. Instead he had walked into Ruva's treatment tent, watched her work for half a day, and offered her an apprenticeship she had spent six weeks proving she did not deserve.

He waited.

Ruva brushed sand from her sleeve. "Your wrist. Inside line. I could have stopped the hand without cutting the tendons if the blade were sharp."

"Yes. Next pass, that is your target."

"You want me to hesitate better?"

"I want you to reach the choice while someone is attacking you."

Hooves struck the road outside the yard. A rider pulled up hard enough to spray grit through the open gate. "The roadside infirmary. Medicine cart caught in an attack. The roof's going in."

Vekran was already exchanging the blunted blade for his edged one. "Ruva. Edged blade, warm cloak, healer's satchel."

She buckled on the edged apprentice blade and caught up the cloak and satchel from beside the fence. "All three?"

"All three."

The sword pulled at one hip. The satchel dragged at the other. She followed him through the gate with neither weight settled.

* * *

The medicine cart stood crooked across the infirmary courtyard, one wheel wedged against a stone trough. Bolts had punched through its canvas cover. A driver lay beside it with blood in their hair, and two attackers had the cart pinned from opposite sides while pressure groaned through the low building beyond.

Vekran touched the flat of his blade to the gatepost.

For one breath, nothing visible happened. Then his attention moved across the yard: roof, doorway, cart, hands. Ruva had learned enough of the measure to feel only a muddle through her own iron. He seemed to find every load at once.

A crossbow snapped.

Vekran stepped into the bolt. His blade met it at an angle too slight to stop anything. Breath and warmth moved from his living grip through the iron focus; the bolt changed course and buried itself in the empty water trough with a crack.

He was at the cart before the shooter had lowered the bow. An attacker cut for his neck. Vekran caught the sword close to its guard, bound it, and drove one shoulder into the wielder's chest. The same turn of his body put his free bracer under a lintel that tore loose above the driver. He sent the timber sideways into bare paving, twisted the sword from the attacker's hand, and kicked it under the cart.

One step, two threats, no wasted reach. This was why soldiers lowered their voices.

"Ruva. Take the driver. Rear route."

It sounded too much like stay out of the way.

She slid beside the driver anyway. "Can you hear me?"

The driver's eyes opened. Their pupils matched. Breathing quick, no wet rattle. The scalp wound bled freely but the skull beneath felt sound.

"I'm going to move you behind the wall. Press here. Hard." She put their hand over a folded cloth. "Ready?"

At their nod she pulled, keeping the neck straight, until the stone well curb lay between them and the crossbow.

The infirmary door bowed inward. Two walking patients stumbled into the yard, one supporting the other.

"Rear gate," Ruva called. "Stay low. Take the driver when you pass."

The crossbow attacker reached for another bolt. Vekran slapped his blade against the cart's iron rim, read the incoming pressure, and turned the next shot high over the wall. The magic took heat with it. His knuckles had gone pale. His next breath ended short.

The disarmed attacker rose behind him with a knife.

"Left rear," Ruva shouted.

Vekran pivoted before the knife reached him. He caught the wrist, folded it without breaking it, and sent the attacker face-down across the cart tongue. The crossbow shooter met him on the other side; Vekran slipped inside the stock, struck once with his sword guard, and caught the weapon before its owner hit the dust.

Ruva bound the driver's head, checked the two walking patients, and found a third person beneath the cart with a bruised leg but a strong foot pulse. She showed the mobile pair where to lift the axle, freed the trapped leg, and sent the driver and injured passenger through the rear gate. While Vekran stood between them and the fallen attackers, Ruva and the mobile pair rocked the wedged wheel clear of the trough. The axle cracked as they shoved the cart through the rear gate and left it behind the stone wall. The strip from the infirmary door past the trough stood empty. Three hurt. None bleeding to death. No red priority.

She drew her edged apprentice blade. "My route is clear. I'm coming to the door."

"Keep evacuating."

"You took me as an apprentice, not a porter with bandages."

The building groaned again. Dust streamed from the eaves.

Vekran looked at her then, not away from the doorway but somehow through the same attention. "You own the rear route until there are no red-priority patients. Report."

"None red. One head wound controlled. One leg injury, stable. Two mobile."

"Then advance under a shield-sized hold. No farther than you can retreat in three steps."

It was not reassurance. It was usable.

They crossed the threshold together. Inside, two patients crouched behind an overturned table. At the far roof post, a figure in a dark coat had one shoulder pressed against the wood and one hand clenched around an iron clasp fixed through torn clothing. Four lines of pressure ran from that point into the ceiling braces. The person held a knife in the other hand.

Vekran moved between the table and a falling beam. He planted his sword point in a crack between two floorstones, set his palm to the doorframe, and made a fixed brace from one surface to the other. The intact posts still carried most of the roof while the caster's working divided its pressure among four braces; Vekran took only the beam's sliding weight. It spent his warmth and fixed him at the doorway, but it was not yet the full crisis load. The beam stopped dropping. Timbers creaked around him.

The knife flashed from beside the post. Vekran shifted enough to keep it from his ribs, but the edge opened his sleeve under the upper arm.

He did not lose the ward. His jaw tightened once.

"Lane," he said.

Pressure gathered along Ruva's bracer, no wider than a shield. It gave her a path past the hanging beam.

She went in.

* * *

The knot-caster's knife had fallen after the strike. Ruva kicked it away before she knelt. Their skin had the gray cast of worsening shock, and the hand below the injured shoulder was darkening at the fingertips. Blood soaked the coat around the iron clasp, though not fast enough to explain the pulse Ruva could see jumping there.

It beat twice for every beat in the caster's throat.

"Don't touch it," they said. Their breath came shallow. "I let go, the roof comes down. Your witchknight cuts me, it comes down faster. So perhaps we discuss a door."

Behind Ruva, Vekran's partial brace hummed through stone and iron. "I can part the hard line through clasp and shoulder. I cannot map past it while I carry even this crossing load."

The fastest cut would end the living source. It would also cross muscle, vessels, perhaps the joint. Ruva looked at the four braces, each drawn toward the wounded shoulder as if the caster had tied the room to their own body and pulled.

"If I open a door," she said, "you can't walk to it. Your hand is losing blood. Your breath is failing."

"Then promise I leave alive."

"I can't promise freedom. I can examine the shoulder and press the wound, or I can stay back while he prepares the cut he can make. Those are the choices we have now."

The caster's mouth tightened. "A healer traveling with a witchknight. How comforting."

"Pressure, or no touch?"

The post creaked. One of the patients behind the table made a small sound.

"Pressure," the caster said. "The clasp stays."

Ruva set clean folded cloth around the iron, not over it. "I'm touching you now."

She pressed. The caster hissed and tried to turn away.

"Still. Or tell me to stop."

They held still.

Only then did Ruva give the healing working a little of her warmth. It passed through her palms, living attention following the gross boundaries beneath them: skin, torn muscle, the hard foreign edge of the clasp. She could encourage the small vessels to close and hold damaged edges where they belonged. She could not replace what had already been lost. She could not clean the wound while the iron remained, or give the caster back the heat shock had taken.

Cold climbed into her fingers.

The false pulse changed. Not a pulse at all. A second rhythm had been laid alongside the wound, tightening whenever the caster's breath stumbled. As Ruva held the tissue steadier, the pressure in the ceiling eased by a fraction.

Vekran felt it. "Again."

"I can't do more without spending what I'll need to move."

"Then don't. Name what changed."

Ruva followed the imposed rhythm as far as her touch allowed. It did not end at the clasp. It ran beside living tissue, borrowed the easiest path around the joint, then divided toward all four roof braces.

She took her hands away. "The working is braided along the wound. If you cut through the shoulder, all four loads release together."

The partial brace shuddered under Vekran's hand.

"My map was incomplete," he said at once. "I can keep the roof or attempt a second working. Not both."

No excuse. No performance of certainty. The partial brace was already cooling him. Taking all four roof lines would leave still less room for error.

Ruva pulled her cloak around the caster's uninjured side and looked for another line.

* * *

Blood had reached Vekran's cuff.

"Your arm first," Ruva said. "Thirty heartbeats and I can bind it."

"Assess it from there."

"You need stitches."

"First death?"

She hated the answer. "No. Painful. Steady loss, but the arm still bears weight. Your hand?"

"Cooling. Full feeling for now."

He had not dismissed her judgment. He had asked her to use it.

Ruva returned two fingers to the caster's shoulder. With the wound steadier, she could feel a narrow interval where the iron clasp touched the shaped pressure without crossing flesh. A finger's width at most. It shifted with each breath.

"There," she said. "Nonliving line. But it moves. I can't mark it once and trust it."

"Then you cut from the live map," Vekran said.

"I've parted chalk cord twice. Once cleanly."

"Name what you require."

"Someone qualified."

"Unavailable."

The caster gave a breath-short laugh that broke into a cough. "Your standards inspire confidence."

Ruva ignored them. Listing reasons had not changed the room. She changed tactics.

"A shield lane. A count I don't have to keep myself. Permission to abort if I lose the line."

"Yes. I drop the lane if my fingers go numb. If you lose the line, you stop. No blind cut."

"And the roof?"

"The posts carry most of it now, and the knot keeps its pressure divided. When you begin the final map, I take all four lines. About sixty heartbeats at full load."

The caster's hand closed over the clasp. "It stays. It's the only reason your people haven't killed me."

"It's also killing you," Ruva said. "Hold still and warn me when the false branch moves. I will try to separate it without cutting your shoulder. If you live, you go to treatment under ordinary guard. Not free. Alive."

"Try?"

"That's the true word."

The caster looked past her to Vekran. "And him?"

"Those are the terms," Vekran said. His voice had gone plain and thin. "Your companions have fled or fallen. Choose."

Dust spilled from a new crack overhead.

The caster released the clasp, though their fingers hovered beside it. "After each tightening, the false branch starts across on one. It lies over the living line on two and three. It clears on four. The gap after four lasts until the next tightening. I call every beat."

Ruva took chalk from her satchel and settled the edged apprentice blade in her grip. Stabilize for three breaths. Trace. Shift to guard. Turn the defensive pressure into bare floor. Part the braid. If the map blurred, stop.

Narrow enough to attempt. Too narrow for courage to improve.

* * *

Ruva tucked both hands into the warm fold of her cloak until her fingertips stung.

"Do I still have your yes to touch the shoulder?"

"Yes. The clasp stays until you cut it."

"If you pull away, I stop."

"This pass only settles the wound," Ruva told Vekran. "Keep the partial brace until I call the final map."
