She cleaned the accessible skin, replaced the blood-wet cloth, and set her palms around the wound. Her warmth moved again. One breath: tissue edges, unsteady but distinct. Two: the caster's true pulse, quick beneath her little finger. Three: the imposed rhythm sliding beside it.

"Tightening," the caster whispered. "One."

Movement sounded at the broken side door.

An attacker from the courtyard lurched through, one hand braced on the frame, a short sword in the other. Their eyes found the caster.

"Traitor," they said, and drove forward.

Ruva released the healing working and stood. Six weeks had not taught her how to win a sword fight. Six weeks had taught her one short parry and how badly her guard recovered afterward.

The sword struck her bracer hard enough to bruise through leather. She caught it late, gave ground, and saw the attacker's wrist turn beneath the guard.

Inside line. The hand, not the shoulder.

Ruva cut once. The edge opened sleeve and skin shallowly across the exact disabling line. The attacker's grip sprang open. Their sword hit the floor.

She kicked it through the broken doorway. The attacker clutched the useless hand, stared at her, then stumbled after their fleeing companions rather than try Vekran's ward unarmed. Ruva did not pursue.

"Position," Vekran said.

Not praise. The thing she needed.

Ruva dropped beside the caster and raised a shield-sized hold as pressure snapped outward from the working they were still struggling to sustain. Her back foot slid in blood-damp dust. The hold buckled, flinging strain into her shoulder.

She let it go.

The pressure struck the wall above them and showered grit. Forcing the hold would have thrown it through the patients—or through Ruva.

"New count," she said. Her breath shook. "I lost the footing."

She shifted half a pace to dry stone. Her arm throbbed where the bracer had taken the sword. Vekran's hands shook now, too, but his partial brace remained fixed.

"Still yes?"

"Yes. Hurry."

"Call the branch. Nothing else."

The caster swallowed and nodded.

"The full load starts with my first breath," Ruva said.

"Ready," Vekran said.

Ruva put her palms back to the wound. Vekran drove his sword point deeper and, with one long exhale, interposed his fixed ward across all four roof lines. The ceiling settled the width of a finger as the intact posts shed their strain into him. His next breath stopped short.

"Full load," he said. "Sixty."

"First breath," Vekran counted.

Ruva found the living pulse.

"Second."

She found the false rhythm alongside it.

"Third breath. Forty-six heartbeats."

She drew chalk across the clasp where the narrow gap lay at that instant. Then she released the healing hold. The wound stayed bound by cloth and its own encouraged clotting, not cured, not safe for long.

Ruva shifted to guard.

The caster's trained reflex tightened the working as pain caught their breath. Pressure lashed from the clasp toward Ruva's chest. She met one bounded line with her bracer, set her weight through the dry back foot, and turned.

Force hammered into the floor. Tile split with a flat crack. Numbness rushed from her wrist to her elbow.

Moved, not erased.

"Thirty-four," Vekran said.

"One—moving," the caster gasped.

Ruva began the stroke toward the chalk mark, intending to land before the second beat.

"Two. Across. Stop."

The false branch slid across the living pulse.

Vekran's breath hitched. The beam above him dropped the width of a nail before his ward caught it again.

Every urgent part of Ruva wanted to finish the stroke. Faster. Stronger. Before the room chose for them.

But there was no safe line beneath her blade.

She aborted, drew back, and waited.

"Twenty-eight," Vekran said.

"Three. Hold," the caster said. Their whole body strained against the need to move. "Four. Clear. Now."

The false branch passed beyond the living pulse. In the promised gap before the next tightening, healer-sense gave Ruva the boundary her eyes could not: warm living tissue here, cold clasp there, shaped pressure crossing only the iron.

She cut on that line.

The blade passed through the edge of the clasp and the braided working with a sound like cloth tearing under water. The caster cried out but the edge cleared their shoulder.

The four roof loads released unevenly.

"Eighteen," Vekran said. He pulled his sword from the floor and turned with his whole body. He opened the ward toward the cleared strip between the doorway and the trough. Timber, tile, and force went outward through the path he chose, bursting across the empty paving in a roar of dust.

Then he dropped the hold before it could take the last warmth from his hands.

Part of the roof fell across the cleared strip, stopping short of the cart behind the rear wall. The inner beam settled onto the overturned table instead of the people behind it.

Vekran sank to one knee, conscious, his sword point resting on stone.

Ruva did not check whether anyone had seen her cut. She put the blade down, caught the caster before they slumped against the post, and pressed fresh cloth to the shoulder.

"Stay with me," she said. "The spell is over. The wound isn't."

* * *

By the time guards arrived from the road, Ruva had found six injuries, none immediately fatal. The driver needed watching for confusion. The patient with the bruised leg needed a splint for the journey. The caster needed warmth, fluids if they could keep them down, and proper cleaning before anyone considered removing what remained of the clasp.

Vekran needed stitches.

"Cloak first," Ruva told him.

"The caster—"

"Has mine and two warmed bricks. Give me your arm."

He did. His cut was shallow but longer than she had hoped, and his skin had the waxy chill of spent measurework. She cleaned and bound it; stitching could wait until there was better light and a roof that did not shed dust into open wounds.

The caster watched from a litter while a guard secured their uninjured wrist. Ruva checked the restraint for circulation, then checked the shoulder binding again.

"This isn't pardon," the caster said.

"No. It's transport. Keep that hand still."

They looked as if they had another taunt available. Exhaustion won. The litter went toward the road under guard.

The infirmary had lost half its roof. The medicine cart had a split axle and three bolts through its canvas. Those who could walk gathered blankets and unbroken jars from the dust. There would be repairs, statements, custody, more treatment. Nothing Ruva had done made those costs vanish.

Vekran sat against the wall with his bandaged arm inside the cloak. "Assessment."

Ruva was too tired to pretend not to know what he meant. "Of me?"

"By you."

She wanted one word: worthy or mistaken. He had never offered comfort where evidence would do, so she gave him the evidence.

"My recovery is weak. I failed the first hold because I didn't clear my footing. The turn worked and numbed my arm. The parting worked because the caster corrected my timing. I stabilized two patients." She looked at his bandage. "And one mentor who still needs stitches."

"Accurate."

"Is that why you chose me? To keep a witchknight alive after the work?"

"Partly. Not chiefly." He flexed his fingers, stopped when they trembled, and put the hand back under the cloak. "Anyone can be taught where to cut. I needed an apprentice already trained to ask what has to live through it."

Ruva glanced at the ruined room. "Then you should have said you wanted a healer. Not someone you meant to turn into a former healer."

"I thought bringing the satchel made that plain."

"It did not."

He considered this with the same seriousness he gave a bad map. "My error."

"The satchel stays in every field kit. Healing shifts count as witchknight training, not time away from it. Those are my terms."

"Agreed."

No ceremony. Ruva found that she preferred it.

Vekran nodded toward the broken tile where her turn had landed. "Your back foot was late."

"I noticed."

"Tomorrow—"

"Tomorrow you sleep. The day after, perhaps you may criticize my feet."

His mouth moved at one corner, too tired to become a smile.

When the damaged medicine cart finally rolled toward town, Ruva walked beside the patients. Her healer's satchel crossed one shoulder. Her edged apprentice sword crossed the other, cleaned and returned to its sheath.

The two weights pulled differently. After a dozen steps, Ruva stopped and shortened the sword strap until they balanced. Then she walked on.

stories.title: Hello, Lover
stories.prompt: A demon appears before your party, exclaiming “Hello lover!” Everyone looks at the bard, but then the cleric speaks up. “Actually, my ex is referring to me.”
stories.body:
# Hello, Lover

Emet Sarn had one hand on the stolen brass when he recognized the file mark.

Three shallow strokes crossed the lower hinge leaf, the middle one wandering crooked because Lacrixa had laughed into his shoulder while he worked. He had once known that scratch by touch in the dark. Now the leaf was bolted into an iron scaffold in a ruined roadside sanctuary, between three black loops and jars of salt-glass cloudy with someone else's stored charge.

“Familiar workmanship?” Udren asked from beneath the cracked arch. Her shield was already angled toward the doorway, the road settlement downhill, and every person who had ignored their warning to stay indoors.

Emet removed his thumb from the scratches. “Familiar principles.”

Not a lie, if one filed truth as badly as brass.

Bosk, the party's bard, crouched beside him, keeping his embroidered sleeves clear of the iron. “Can you quiet it?”

Emet pressed the stamped medallion at his throat, not for help from the inert silver but for the shelter-count cut into it. Breath in. Heat gathered behind his sternum. On the exhale, he fed a thread of his own ward-light through the stolen leaf to feel for the trap's edge.

The scaffold took everything he offered.

Heat drew an upright line in the air. The line opened hand-wide, showing red tile, white glare, and one amber eye.

Emet stopped breathing.

The opening widened. Lacrixa stepped through in a scorched traveling coat, a living demon from the far Cauterized Reach, one horn wrapped in a strip of copper cloth and her boot soles smoking against the sanctuary floor. She looked straight past Bosk and smiled at Emet with all her teeth.

“Hello lover!”

Everyone looked at Bosk.

It was, Emet had to admit, a reasoned response. On three previous jobs, Bosk's stage acquaintances had arrived through a window, a funeral procession, and a magistrate's evidence cupboard. All three had greeted him as if entering to applause.

Bosk put a hand to his chest. For once, he looked genuinely unprepared.

“Actually, my ex is referring to me.” Emet said it because collapse procedure began with correcting dangerous assumptions.

“I had a line,” Bosk said faintly. “It has left the stage.”

No one laughed. Iron slammed against iron behind Lacrixa. The first black loop cinched around the scaffold, brass reddened, and the sanctuary inhaled hard enough to lift ash from the floor.

Udren raised her shield. “Threat.”

Lacrixa's smile vanished. She caught the frame with both hands, the skin along her knuckles glowing the color of banked coals. “Three borrower loops. Freight pattern.” She looked at Emet. “What did you open?”

The pressure pulled at their clothes, toward the red seam.

Emet reached for the severing verse engraved inside his medallion. “I can close it.”

“If you want to cut a street in half.”

Lacrixa did not grab him. She stopped her hand a finger's width from his wrist and pointed instead. A shape wavered in the opening behind her: an apron, an upraised arm, a person backing away through kiln glare.

“Worker on the far side,” Udren said.

Emet lowered his hand.

“Good,” Lacrixa said. “The cleric can still be taught by evidence.”

“The frame is holding your passage open.”

“Our passage.” She tapped the brass with one claw. “This leaf has your keying. Mine signaled a forced expansion, so I supplied heat and breath to inspect it. You supplied ward-work here. The loops stored both contributions and bent them into this.”

The iron and glass had not invited her, chosen her, or made power of their own. They had redirected what two living people deliberately put in. That distinction would have comforted Emet if the redirect were not trying to tear two buildings together.

Ordinarily, their courtesy hinge admitted one traveler or stayed open eighty heartbeats, with fresh assent and living power at both ends. Mounting the stolen leaf in a new frame had not opened a road; the fence's work remained inert until its keyed bearer supplied a fresh living opening. By recognizing the leaf and powering the rig, Emet had knowingly met that condition, and Lacrixa had answered from her side.

Bosk edged toward the wall, out of the suction's straight path. “For the record, I prefer entrances with a rehearsed exit.”

Lacrixa did not glance at him.

His mouth shut. “What beat do you need?”

“Not yet.” She leaned close to the scaffold. Ember-light moved from her palm into the metal; her own, spent by choice. The black loops answered by brightening at three separate joints. “North jamb. Under the floor. Behind the throat. Remove them in that order, bleed each charge into stone, and then we withdraw together after I'm home.”

Emet watched the salt-glass turn milk-white. “Or sever before the next pulse and accept damage to an empty endpoint.”

“It isn't empty.”

“We evacuate it.”

“In the time you took to say that, the scaffold pulled another six feet of my kiln court into alignment.” She pointed to the stolen leaf. “Why is your private half in a freight rig?”

Udren's gaze moved to him. “Compromised?”

“The leaf was stolen with other brasswork. We caught the fence. We followed the components here.”

All true. None sufficient.

“And you recognized it,” Lacrixa said.

Air reversed.

The first pulse struck with a sound below hearing. Emet's teeth rang. The opening flared wider, revealing a crowded court of red tile and copper awnings. Two workers dragged a third away from a rack of cooling vessels. A tool cart rolled toward them without anyone touching it. Here, a crack raced through the sanctuary arch, and hot wind poured downslope through the broken wall.

“Answer,” Udren said.

Emet looked at the arch, the road, the widening seam—every exposure except Lacrixa. “After the first loop.”

Lacrixa's tail struck the floor once, a hard refusal.

“We lose both sites if we debate provenance now,” he said. Formality settled over his voice like ceremonial cloth. “Give me the discharge order, and I will answer after the first loop is safe.”

“One loop,” Lacrixa said. “Then no more careful fractions.”

Udren wedged her shield under the sagging arch. “Deadline accepted. Move.”

* * *

The north-jamb loop hung twelve feet up, its iron collar sunk behind rotten stone. Udren planted her boots and took the arch's weight on her shield while Emet climbed the scaffold. Below, Bosk unhooked the small frame drum from his pack.

“Eight beats,” Lacrixa said. “We feed on one and five. Pull the pin on seven. Stone takes it on eight.”

“A sparse arrangement,” Bosk said. He struck the drum once, listened to the sanctuary answer, and adjusted his grip. “Again.”

The second beat came clean and low.

Emet set his palm against one side of the brass. Lacrixa took the other. They had done this hundreds of times in two years: her heat rising as his breath left, his ward steadying when hers flared. His body found the old timing before his pride could object.

One. He fed the smallest possible thread.

Five. Lacrixa answered. The brass warmed between them.

Seven. Udren drove out the inert pin with the boss of her shield.

Eight. Emet turned their joined charge down through the scaffold's foot. Foundation stone flashed white. The loop dropped, empty and ordinary, and shattered a floor tile.

The sudden relief made his knees loosen. Lacrixa's glow had faded around her knuckles.

“Question,” she said.

“Second loop first.”

She stared until he added, “Please.”

Udren did not look up from the arch. “He bought one loop. Debt's due.”

The floor bucked beneath them. The second collar tightened under a fractured paving slab, dragging its iron staples deeper. Bosk moved his drumbeat faster at Lacrixa's signal while Udren lowered the arch onto a surviving pillar and crossed the room. Emet knelt, hooked numb fingers beneath the slab, and lifted with her.

“Cut?” Udren asked.

“No,” Emet said.

“Not the leaf. The staple.”

“Left one only.” Lacrixa was already bracing the opposite edge. “Right carries the throat.”

Udren struck left. The staple split. Emet and Lacrixa breathed on one and five, and the old coordination returned in humiliating details: the slight turn of her wrist that meant hold; the way his thumb shifted before he sent power; the shared half-breath they had used when a hearthframe caught in wet weather.

He remembered her bare feet on the table in their rented room, polishing hinge pins while he wrote shelter reports. They had been twenty-eight and thirty-one when they began, adults with separate work and keys and the belief that asking clearly would keep them from hurting each other. For a while, it had.

The second loop came free.

The second pulse caught its stored charge before it could discharge. The salt-glass flashed.

The kiln court disappeared. In its place stood their old room: narrow bed, blue washbasin, rain stippling the window. On the table lay two unfinished cups and the little file Lacrixa had jostled when she laughed. The image was no memory Emet had meant to offer. But the charged metal had been shaped to widen whatever route-impressions its living bearers supplied, and his trained intent had reached for safety as it had once looked.

Lacrixa went very still.

Then she saw the repaired corner on his leaf, the bright solder line made after the last winter they shared.

“You kept it keyed.”

A roof slab broke loose.

Udren shoved Bosk clear and caught the worst of it on her shield. Stone struck stone. Dust erased the room, the court, and half the sanctuary. Emet fell into the side alcove with Lacrixa. A tilted pillar blocked them from the others, though Bosk's drum continued through the dust—slower now, a pulse they could follow.

Lacrixa's eyes found him in the red gloom. “You kept it keyed.”

Emet put his shoulder against the pillar. It did not move. “Yes.”

“The letter said your oath required a clean severance.”

His silence had once passed for dignity at council tables. Here it was simply an answer.

“I won't trust final withdrawal to another silence,” she said. No endearment now, no ceremony. “Tell me what I am trusting.”

* * *

Ash blew through the alcove. Each breath scraped. Emet's right hand shook against the frame, and Lacrixa's skin had cooled from ember-red to dull brown at the fingertips. Beyond the pillar, Udren cursed once, concisely, while stone ground over metal.

“I was offered the permanent circuit,” Emet said. “Six shelters. Twenty years.”

“I remember your chronology.”

Of course she did. He had used dates in the letter the way a mason used rubble: to fill the space where a proper stone should go.

“The House of Common Shelter did not forbid us,” he said.

Lacrixa stopped examining the frame.

The third pulse gathered in the salt-glass, a cloudy brightness that grew with every breath they lost.

“They did not ask me to choose the circuit over you,” Emet continued. “You asked whether I wanted a shared home. I was afraid to leave my work. I was afraid to ask you to leave yours. And I was more afraid to say that I didn't know which fear mattered more.”

“So you invented a prohibition.”

“Yes.” The word hurt less than the long explanations had. That was no credit to him. “I made myself obedient instead of cowardly. I let you believe the institution I served had judged you unfit. Then I kept the leaf because calling uncertainty a safety precaution sounded better than admitting I wanted a door I had refused to walk through.”

“And today?”

“I recognized the file marks before I powered the rig. I did not tell them.”

Her face changed by almost nothing. It had always been dangerous to mistake her stillness for absence.

“I spent three years preparing arguments,” she said. “Rules of residence. Kiln-court protections. Precedents from mixed households in the Reach. I had an answer for every objection your House never made.”

The charge brightened behind her. Bosk's beat came through the pillar: steady, asking nothing.

“I am sorry,” Emet said. “For the lie then. For the concealment now. Both were choices. Neither protected anyone.”

He did not add that he had loved her. That fact was visible in the danger around them and useless as a claim.

Lacrixa crouched beside the second loop and worked a claw under its split edge. “I kept my leaf locked away because breaking one half without neutral de-keying can leave a dangerous echo. That was the technical reason.” She pried. Iron screamed. “The other reason was that I wanted you to have to answer me someday. Pride can wear procedure too.”

The admission did not divide fault equally. It was not offered to do so.

“Do you forgive me?” Emet did not ask.

Instead he said, “Will you trust me for one synchronized withdrawal?”

“I will trust the count. I will trust what you do on it.” Her eyes held his. “We are finishing the road, Emet. We are not beginning again.”

“Understood.”

The third pulse broke.

He and Lacrixa threw their remaining power down together. The second loop released its charge into the foundation, and the tilted pillar jumped aside. Udren hauled Emet through the gap by his collar. Bosk caught Lacrixa's forearm, failed to hide his surprise at how cold her skin had become, and adjusted his grip without comment.

No one had time for relief. Behind them, the third loop glowed white.

* * *

“Full account,” Udren said.

Emet forced air into his lungs. “The leaf is mine. I kept it keyed. The last loop sits behind the throat. Once it's removed, Lacrixa crosses, and we both revoke future access on Bosk's count.”

Udren compressed everything she wanted to say into three questions. “Other traps?”

“None I know.”

“Can she close her side?”

“Yes.”

“Will you release on count?”

The honest answer arrived before the respectable one. “I am afraid I won't.”

“Then I stand with you.” She turned to Lacrixa. “Shield before or behind?”

Lacrixa pointed into the widening seam. “Behind me until I clear. The court roof is shedding tile.”

Udren moved without hesitation, placing her shield between Lacrixa and the falling stone of her own home.

Bosk tightened the drum strap around his burned fingers. “Eighty heartbeats until this tries freight width?”

“At most,” Lacrixa said.

“One tempo. On sixty, Udren takes the pin. On seventy, Lacrixa crosses. On seventy-eight, the leaves break. On eighty, nobody is between.” He looked from face to face. “That is the arrangement. No solos.”

Emet nodded.

“Good,” Bosk said, and began.

* * *

At twelve, the opening widened to the height of the arch.

At twenty, kiln wind struck sanctuary air. Heat blasted one way while tools, roof tiles, and loose stones skidded the other. Emet held the near edge with both palms, feeding ward-light through muscles that no longer wanted to close. Lacrixa held the far edge. Her coat snapped in the crossing wind; her horns were dark against the furnace glare.

At thirty-four, Udren advanced behind her shield. The third loop lay behind the throat, visible whenever the opening shuddered: black iron, a hot clasp, one pin driven through the scaffold's rear brace.

At forty, the sanctuary roof began to peel.

Bosk's beat did not change.

Emet's ward-light had once illuminated whole refuge halls. Now it barely silvered his fingers. The scaffold held no strength of its own, but its salt-glass reservoirs returned his earlier contribution in distorted surges, each one demanding that he spend more to keep the person-wide center clear.

At fifty-two, Lacrixa missed her handhold.

Emet shifted as she recovered, matching the old half-breath. Intimacy lived in the body longer than permission. It told him what she would do. It did not entitle him to decide for her.

“Clasp won't lift,” Udren called.

Lacrixa pressed both cooling hands around the hot iron. A last ember-glow moved out of her skin by choice. The clasp softened, then sagged around the pin.

“Foundation,” she ordered.

Emet took one hand from the edge. The throat narrowed, throwing a strip of kiln light across Udren's shield. He drove what remained of his ward down the rear brace. The foundation stone whitened, ready to receive the stored charge.

Sixty.

Udren hit the pin.

It moved the width of a thumbnail and jammed.

She hit it again. The shield slipped in the suction. A tile from the kiln court struck its rim. Lacrixa caught Udren's shoulder before she pitched into the throat, and the three of them lost the count beneath a roar of moving air.

The drum tore free of Bosk's hands. It sailed through the breach and vanished among the copper awnings.

“Sixty-four!” Bosk shouted. His voice cracked, but his tempo did not. “Sixty-five! Sixty-six!”

Udren planted one boot against the scaffold and drove her shield boss into the pin.

At sixty-nine, it came free.

The final loop dropped. White fire ran harmlessly down the prepared line into dead stone, but the throat convulsed around the sudden absence of its brace.

“Cross!” Emet shouted.

Lacrixa backed through first, facing them. Udren followed just far enough to keep the shield over her while remaining on the sanctuary side. At seventy-three, falling tile struck the top edge. At seventy-five, Lacrixa stumbled.

Emet poured more of himself into the leaf.

“Seventy-six!” Bosk called.

Lacrixa rolled, rose on the red tile, and turned. One boot was visible. The other vanished behind the warping edge.

Emet held.

“Seventy-seven!”

The opening drank his breath. Red spread through the brass again. The empty loop sockets began to shine as his continued supply recharged the route.

“Emet.” Lacrixa's voice crossed the narrowing distance. “Both feet clear.”

He could not see them.

He held.

Udren abandoned the pin. She caught his forearm in both hands and planted his palm flat against the stone beside the leaf. She did not tear him away. She made him feel something that was not the open road: grit, weight, the shaking of his own muscles.

“Off,” she said.

Across the breach, Lacrixa reached her hearthframe. “You do not keep me safe by keeping access.”

No ornament. No technical argument. A command he had spent three years earning.

“Seventy-eight!” Bosk shouted.

Emet withdrew.

The loss of power struck like a missed stair. He sagged against Udren, but his right hand found the stolen leaf. He wrenched it from the loosened bolts, set its keyed edge against the foundation, and bent with what little strength remained.

Across the narrowing sight-window, Lacrixa pulled her leaf from its hearthframe. Embercraft lit one fingertip. She melted the keyed edge into a bright, useless curve and let the ruined brass fall onto the red tile beside the frame.

Emet's brass folded under his weight.

“No future invitation,” Lacrixa said.

“None,” he answered.

The opening shrank to hand-width. Behind her, people lifted the fallen kiln worker. Here, the sanctuary settled by inches instead of collapsing. Both places remained themselves.

For one beat, Lacrixa's face filled the small square of light.

Emet did not ask if they would meet again.

“Goodbye, Lacrixa.”

She studied him as if accuracy still mattered, because it did. “Goodbye, Emet.”

The window closed.

* * *

At first light, the road settlement still stood. Smoke marked one scorched field below the sanctuary, but no freight breach had opened above it, and no one had been pulled from the kiln court.

Before dawn, they spent an hour shoring the wounded arch with salvaged beams. Emet could lift only with his left hand. Bosk worked without turning the labor into a performance, and Udren accepted no assurance about a brace that she could not test with her own weight. Each time the wind stirred ash through the scaffold, Emet looked at the warped loops. The iron stayed cold.

Bosk wrapped his burned fingertips in strips torn from the lining of his least embroidered sleeve. Udren bound Emet's strained wrist with considerably less tenderness and considerably better tension.

Emet gave them the fuller account: the two adult years he and Lacrixa had chosen together, the false letter, the retained leaf, the moment he recognized it and said nothing. He kept his sentences plain. Neither oath nor magic received the blame.

Udren tied off the bandage. “We discuss field trust after we deliver the evidence.”

“Yes.”

Bosk glanced at the dead scaffold. There was room for a joke in his expression. He let it pass. “Can you walk?”

Emet tested his legs. “Slowly.”

“A tempo I can manage.”

They left Emet's folded leaf, the three warped loops, the spent salt-glass, and the dead iron scaffold for the local authorities. Udren propped the sanctuary's ordinary door open with a fallen stone. Cool morning moved through it, and Emet followed his companions outside.

stories.title: The Voice of Silence
stories.prompt: In a world where people must call out the names of their spells to use them, a mute person has managed to become an archmage.
stories.body:
# The Voice of Silence

Kethra laid two fingers on the brass node and felt the examination tower through it.

Not heard it—felt it: the drag of the loaded gallery, the thrust of six stone ribs, the little wrongness where an old joint met new mortar. Those forces gathered in her mind as bright lines waiting to be bent. Around her, three floors of examiners and students watched from behind the railings. Above them, the tower crown glittered with the speaking rails she had spent four years designing.

Ulan placed his fingers beside hers. The brass was only brass. It could carry a living voice and mark the geometry of a spell, but it could not choose, consent, or supply so much as a spark.

Kethra marked the registered shape for *Weightward* against the node. Ulan signed **yes**.

One caller. One spell. One cell. The link would last thirty breaths unless either of them broke it first.

Kethra drew power up through her legs. It burned cold along her bones as she mapped the weight of a suspended block into the grounded rails. The pattern remained deliberately unfinished. In the callwright practice taught here, no spell could cross that last gap until its full name was spoken by its authorized living caller.

She gave Ulan the two-finger ready sign.

“Weightward!”

His voice traveled through the brass on one clear exhalation. Gold light raced along the load path Kethra held. The suspended block sank half a handspan, stopped, then glided sideways as she redirected its weight from one grounded rail to the next. Ulan’s hands stayed open. The shaping was hers; she felt every crushing measure of it.

Applause rose from the galleries. Kethra did not look up. She lowered the block precisely onto its painted square before letting the power go.

Dorram, the chief examiner, tapped four marks on his slate: original architecture, control, safe instruction, judgment. The four requirements of the local archmage office. Then he signed, *A beautiful lattice. But is it mastery, or dependence hidden in brass?*

There it was—the question she had built the glittering lattice to answer. Her pulse kicked, but her hands were steady.

*Remove me,* she signed, *and there is no power, target, or spell. Remove Ulan, and the prepared pattern cannot release. Two necessary arts are not one art.*

She turned the slate so the gallery could read what she added beneath: **A caller completes. A shaper powers and directs. Neither is equipment.**

Dorram studied the block, the rails, and Ulan’s empty hands. At last he drew a fifth mark.

“Proceed to the resilience trial,” he said.

Kethra let herself breathe. The title was not hers yet.

* * *

At the tower’s central table, Kethra briefed Ulan and the two apprentice callers again, although each knew the procedure.

She pointed to the three isolated cells of her voiced lattice. For each, shaper and caller would touch one node; she would mark one registered spell; the caller would choose **yes** or refuse. After her ready sign came a window of twelve heartbeats. The complete name had to arrive in order, on living breath, through an intact rail or directly into the shaped acoustic field. A late call, a broken syllable, or silence meant no spell—only a collapsed pattern and fatigue for her.

Kethra tapped the field signs painted on the table: **yes**, **wait**, and the crossed hands of **stop**.

“Stop cancels the cell,” one apprentice recited.

Kethra nodded and signed, *Immediately. No penalty. No argument.*

The apprentice signed **yes**. So did the other.

Ulan rubbed his throat. “Two safe calls left,” he said. His opening call had been clean, but Kethra heard the rough edge beneath it. “No more than two.”

Dorram glanced toward the panel. “A substitute caller is available.”

Kethra kept her hands still. The choice was not his, and it was not hers. She looked at Ulan.

He considered the rails, then signed, *I stay. Two.*

She wrote the limit beside his name on her caller roster and showed it to him before he initialed the mark. Two meant two, even if the examination turned on a third.

On the emergency edge of her slate she reviewed *Crown Release* and *Safe Descent*. Neither belonged in the ceremonial sequence. Both had been tested on stone frames in the court below, because preparation that assumed nothing would break was decoration, not safety.

As Kethra turned toward the first cell, a pale line near the western joint caught her eye. A crack no longer than her smallest finger crossed the old mortar.

She signed for a manual check. Dorram climbed the short stair, pressed both palms to the joint, and sighted along it while wind worried the high shutters.

“No movement,” he reported. “The masonry is within tolerance.”

It was. Kethra still erased the upper third of her planned load.

Dorram’s stylus hovered, then marked down her impressiveness score.

The loss stung. She had wanted the panel to see the lattice at its fullest: three spells held separately by one living mind, not a choir dragging her power behind their voices. Yet the hairline remained in her thoughts, a tiny white refusal.

She showed the revised loads to every caller. One by one, each touched a node and signed **yes**.

* * *

Kethra opened the first cell, then the second, then the third.

Three patterns pressed against the limits of her attention. The lattice kept them isolated, each aligned to its own caller and sound path. It did not make the work light. A tremor began deep in her left wrist as she placed the ceremonial loads.

Dorram raised one hand. The resilience trial would begin with the planned loss of a caller.

Wind struck the shutters.

The pale crack flashed across Kethra’s memory an instant before a grinding blow shook the floor.

This was not the trial.

The western joint split under the occupied gallery’s ordinary weight. Stone lurched. Kethra slashed the abort sign before the next spell name could be called, collapsing its pattern unspent. Pain bit up her arm anyway. Dust burst from the wall and erased half the room.

Somebody screamed. The long speaking rail tore from its brackets with a metallic shriek.

Through the dust, one apprentice found Kethra’s eyes and crossed both hands: **stop**.

Kethra dropped that cell at once.

The failed pattern struck her like a missed step in darkness. Her knees dipped. With the rail broken and a caller withdrawn, the rehearsed three-cell solution was gone. The lattice held no stored commands to play back. Even if it had, old sound could not complete a living link.

A slab broke free above the gallery.

Dorram moved before Kethra could finish mapping its fall. He planted his staff against the floor—not for power, only to mark the roof’s geometry—then caught the nearest brass node between his hands. With one hand he marked the registered shape for *Roofstay*; with the other he signed **yes** against the node, authorizing himself as both living shaper and living caller for that one cell. Amber lines climbed his arms as he gathered the familiar pattern into his body and selected the sagging ribs. When the shape was ready, he gave the two-finger ready sign to open the same twelve-heartbeat window Kethra used. One heartbeat later, he drew a single breath and called his own spell.

“Roofstay!”

The live name closed his pattern. The falling slab stopped with a crack that shivered dust from every seam. Around it, the roof ribs burned amber, sustained by Dorram’s power.

The gallery occupants stumbled toward the central exit. Then the exit arch buckled inward and jammed.

Dorram had caught the roof. He had caught it fast, alone, and wrong.

Kethra saw the load pouring down his target lines. *Roofstay* had concentrated the western weight on the central exit column. A black fracture was already climbing its face.

She seized his sleeve and pointed.

His expression changed as he followed the crack upward.

The examination was over. The rescue had begun.

* * *

Kethra swept dust from the floor and sketched in chalk: roof ribs, tower crown, trapped gallery, central column, broken rail. The map made the choice plain and terrible. If Dorram released *Roofstay* now, the roof would drop. If he sustained it, the exit column would split. They could preserve the tower or clear the people below it, but not both.

Coughing filled the chamber. Before anyone could follow her plan, they needed air.

Ulan stood beside the mouth of the one short rail still fixed to the central node. Kethra met his eyes, touched the brass, and marked *Airclear*. The previous link was gone; consent could not be assumed from it.

Ulan touched beside her and signed **yes**.

Kethra shaped one narrow corridor from the gallery to the open court. She could not clear the whole tower. She could not spare the power to try. When the pattern was ready, she raised two fingers.

“Airclear!” Ulan called.

His living breath traveled the short rail. Kethra’s power released in a cool spiral, and dust peeled away from the mapped corridor as if drawn through a glass tunnel. Trapped students bent into the cleaner air.

Ulan coughed hard afterward. When Kethra looked to him, he signed **wait**.

Every part of her wanted the final cell ready now. She closed her hand and waited.

Dorram stared at her chalk map. “*Crown Release* would destroy the upper ring.”

Kethra nodded.

“And your lattice with it.”

She nodded again. Four years of measured brass, revised diagrams, and evenings spent proving that a caller’s sound did not own the shaper’s art. Her masterwork shone above them through the dust. She wanted the title badly enough that the thought of tearing it apart felt like tearing out a bone.

The exit column cracked loud enough to silence the room.

Kethra drew three load arrows. She showed how *Roofstay* pinned the crown joints and drove force into the column. She crossed out every sustaining route. Then she marked the only sequence that left time for descent: ground the gallery; end *Roofstay*; separate the crown; lower the occupied platform and loose stone into the cleared court.

Dorram began to object. Kethra struck the chalk against the point where his spell met the column and signed in the standard field language, *Your sustain lasts until your strength fails or the exit does. Either failure kills the route.*

Another chip sprang from the column.

Dorram looked from the map to the people pressed inside the air corridor. Then he laid his staff down.

“Kethra has incident command,” he told the room.

She did not waste a heartbeat on relief. She climbed onto the examination table and tore the first ornamental rail free.

Her beautiful lattice became raw brass in her hands.

* * *

Kethra rebuilt for survival.

She bent one speaking rail down to the gallery footing and anchored it against sound stone. She ran another across the crown joints, following every fracture she wanted *Crown Release* to open and none she wanted spared. From the central node she mapped a descent field around the stranded platform and the loosened upper stones.

The rails chose nothing. Her diagrams powered nothing. Kethra held the three spell cells in her body and attention until her teeth ached.

An adult volunteer from the lower gallery stepped into the court and raised a hand. “I know *Weightward*. I can call.”

Kethra showed the volunteer the grounded path and its danger: the spell moved existing weight; it did not create support. A bad map could drive the load through the floor. The volunteer studied the chalk, touched the first node with her, and signed **yes**.

At the second node, Kethra marked *Crown Release*. Dorram checked the traced joints himself, then placed his fingers beside hers. He signed **yes**.

Ulan had rested against the wall with a wet cloth over his mouth. One safe call remained. Kethra showed him the descent target, the short duration, and the place the platform must reach before her power failed. She pointed to **wait** and **stop** as deliberately as she pointed to **yes**.

Ulan lowered the cloth. He touched the third node and signed **yes**.

Three living choices. Three isolated cells. Kethra’s maximum.

Her hands had begun to shake visibly. Holding the gallery’s map while tracing the crown and enclosing the descent field made each movement slow, as if the air had thickened around her. If one call failed, its collapsing pattern could tear the sequence out of her grasp. She looked at the volunteer.

The first ready sign.

“Weightward!”

The full name rang out at conversational strength, each syllable clear. The live call closed Kethra’s first pattern. Power surged from her into the grounded rails. The gallery settled with a deep stone knock as she moved its load away from the cracked exit and into the tower footing. She held the map until every gold line reached sound foundation.

One major release. Her left arm shook from shoulder to fingertips.

Kethra faced Dorram and made the cutting sign.

He ended *Roofstay*.

The amber ribs vanished. For one plunging instant the unloaded crown shifted above them. Kethra maintained the grounded gallery and thrust her second cell toward the joints. Two fingers rose.

“Crown Release!” Dorram called.

His voice was living and chosen; the spell was Kethra’s shaping, Kethra’s power, Kethra’s exact target. White light snapped along the repurposed rails. The upper ring split at its joints in a thunder of shearing mortar. Blocks peeled outward instead of crushing the exit column.

The tower crown—and the ornate lattice fixed across it—came apart.

Two major releases. Kethra’s vision narrowed. The second pattern tried to pull her down with the falling stone, but she held its separation long enough for the crown to clear the gallery.

Then the platform dropped.

Kethra turned to Ulan and gave the final ready sign.

The remote speaking rail snapped.

Its broken end lashed through empty air. Ulan’s call position was cut away from the shaped field. No matter how loudly he spoke, no living sound could reach the active node through a severed tube.

Twelve heartbeats.

Kethra could not call the name herself. Her throat could make no ordinary words, and neither terror nor magic changed that. The incomplete pattern burned inside her, draining strength with every beat.

She wrenched the third cell’s small brass node from its rail and carried it.

Eleven.

The target geometry pulled against her grip. She kept one hand shaped around the falling platform and ran with the other clenched on the node.

Ten. Nine.

Stone struck stone behind her. A fragment clipped her shoulder and spun her sideways. She stayed upright.

Eight. Seven.

Ulan saw what she was doing and pushed away from the wall. His face was gray beneath the dust.

Six.

Kethra reached direct speaking range. She could have ordered with her eyes. She could have treated his earlier assent as permanent because people were falling.

Instead she showed him the node, pointed once to his throat, and opened her hand in a question.

Five.

Ulan looked at the descending platform. Then he looked at her and chose **yes**.

Four.

“Safe Descent!”

The words came hoarse but complete on one living exhalation. The nearby node caught and modestly carried them into Kethra’s active field. Her third pattern closed.

Power tore through her. She spread it beneath the platform and falling crown stones, slowing rather than stopping them. The spell could not hold them aloft. It bought only a few breaths, and Kethra spent those breaths steering.

The platform sank into the cleared court. People jumped away as its edge touched down. Crown blocks followed in a grinding curtain, slow enough for rescuers to pull the last apprentice clear. Kethra guided the largest slab aside by half a pace—only half, but enough.

Three major releases.

Her legs stopped obeying. She remained standing until the platform rested on stone and the final white line faded. Then her knees struck the dusty floor.

For a moment she could hear nothing but her own pulse.

Then came crying, coughing, and the astonished noise of people discovering one another alive.

* * *

By dusk, the open court had become a place of cups, bandages, and blankets. The injuries were bruises and shallow cuts. The tower crown lay in ordered wreckage around the platform, its broken brass rails dull in the fading light.

The apprentice who had signed **stop** sat with a cup between both hands. No one blamed the apprentice for withdrawing. Kethra made certain of that before she allowed anyone to look at her shoulder.

The volunteer received water and thanks. Dorram’s voice had roughened on *Crown Release*, and a healer wrapped a warm cloth around his throat. Ulan declined every spoken question. He rested his voice and answered in sign, with his usual sharp precision.

Kethra sat before the panel with a blanket around her and her ruined masterwork behind them. She knew what they had seen: three voices where she possessed none; an examiner forced to intervene in her trial; a tower sacrificed on the day she was supposed to prove she could be trusted with one.

Dorram set the office seal on the table.

“The examination has four requirements,” he said, his voice quiet. “Original architecture. Precise control of power and consequence. A method others can learn safely. Discretionary command that values lives above prestige, property, and the candidate’s own work.”

He touched the first mark. “You designed the voiced lattice, then proved you understood it well enough to dismantle it.”

The second. “You diagnosed my error, mapped every load, and ordered three effects so none destroyed what the next required.”

The third. “Your callers understood their tasks, named their limits, stopped, waited, and chose again. That cost time. It also kept them people.”

The fourth. “You destroyed the work meant to win this seal, because keeping it would have killed those we teach.”

Kethra looked at the broken crown. She had spent years trying to make interdependence look like independence, afraid that any visible need would be counted as someone else’s mastery. Today the need had been visible, dangerous, and real. So had the limits of Dorram’s solitary spell.

“The calls were not yours,” Dorram said. “Their courage and labor belong to the callers. The architecture, power, diagnosis, sequence, and command were yours. I mistook resilience for self-sufficiency. The evidence corrected me.”

He pushed the seal across the table.

“The panel finds Kethra qualified for the office of archmage.”

Ulan grinned and applauded silently, striking one palm against the back of his other hand. Kethra laughed without a voice, shoulders shaking until it hurt. Nothing opened in her throat. No hidden word arrived. The rules of the practice had not bent for her, and neither had she been diminished by them.

The next morning, the office seal rested beside a fresh caller roster. Kethra had drawn spaces for voluntary assignments, individual voice limits, and the signs for **yes** and **wait**. The crossed hands of **stop** stood at the top, where no one could miss them.

Students gathered around the scarred court. Ulan sat among them, still resting his voice.

Kethra raised her hands and began her first safety briefing as an archmage.

stories.title: The Five-Minute Warranty
stories.prompt: Goblin's aren't terrible engineers, they can make anything work. And I mean anything. Just... not for very long.
stories.body:
# The Five-Minute Warranty

The North Rise died in three sounds.

First came the kiln-shed blast, a flat blow that struck soot from the upper landing's rafters. Then the lift cables sang as the lower terrace jumped beneath them. Last came a crunch so deep and expensive that Kezli, standing two streets away in her workshop yard, knew a crown gear had lost more than one tooth.

In the echoes, she reconstructed the likely sequence: broken teeth punching through the inspection cover, the cable drum lurching half a turn, the ratchet brake catching with a crack. If one cage had been at the upper landing, its twin would be stranded somewhere in the smoke below.

By the time Director Nalda Vick's runner reached the workshop, Kezli and Olbit had already packed gauges, oakcloth, and every wrench that could be carried at a trot.

When they arrived, Kezli found the failure she had heard. Two iron wedges lay on the Rise's landing stones beside the holes they had punched through the inspection cover. The cable drum stood half a turn out of position, held fast by its ratchet brake.

Four signal flags hung from the lower station: ten people ready, ten behind them, ten more behind those, and a fourth group still coming out of the quarry sheds. Forty in all. A bruised lift attendant below worked the speaking wire with one arm. Beyond the flags, black smoke moved across the kiln yard toward the station. The stair road had vanished under a spill of rock and brick.

Two human lift mechanics knelt beside the opened gear housing. One held up half a tooth as if the rest might apologize and come back.

"The crown is finished," he said. "Casting and cutting another takes six days. Resetting that pedestal may take ten."

"You have minutes," Nalda told Kezli. Her gray coat was powdered white from the blast. "I need a proper repair. Permanent."

Kezli looked at the drive pedestal. A hairline crack ran through its masonry footing exactly where her rejected maintenance bid had warned it would. *Excessive short-term work,* Nalda had written across that bid. *The lift office requires lasting solutions.*

All around the upper landing, people were watching Kezli as though goblin pride might be hammered flat enough to fit where the gear had been. She wanted the civic contract. She wanted Nalda to regret every word of that rejection. For one hot, foolish moment, she wanted to say yes before she knew what yes would cost.

Olbit crouched beside the cable drum and put two fingers against the brake pawl. "Still holding," he said. "That is one useful fact. Shall we collect more before making promises?"

Kezli let out the breath she had been saving for a boast.

"A permanent repair? No," she said. Nalda's face tightened. Kezli pointed past the wrecked teeth to the smooth iron collar left on the engine shaft, then to the clean outer rim of the cable drum. "But the boiler still turns, and the drum can still turn. They can't mesh anymore. They might be persuaded to touch."

***

Kezli checked the engine while Olbit checked the load path. They worked separately because agreement was useful only when it survived two sets of hands.

Boiler pressure held steady. The piston rods ran true. The engine-side shaft had gained a bright score but no bend. Kezli chalked a line on the flywheel and watched three slow revolutions under steam. Across the housing, Olbit measured cable lay, tested both landing brakes, and sent an empty cage two handspans down and back on the emergency windlass.

"Cables pass," he said. "Cages pass. Brakes engage. Drum collar is sound. Pedestal offset is eleven fingers at the crown and worsening under weight."

One of the lift mechanics proposed welding the broken teeth into place.

"The crown is brittle," Kezli said. "The first passenger load would pull the welds out with larger pieces attached."

The other suggested a leather belt around both rims.

Olbit stretched a cord between the misaligned shafts. It wandered to the edge before he had pulled it taut. "The belt would walk off before the first cage cleared the lower roof."

"Then couple the drum directly," Nalda said.

"The engine turns six times too fast," Kezli said. "Direct drive would bring the cage up promptly. It would not stop at the landing, which is where passengers generally prefer to leave it."

Nalda pressed her mouth shut. Below, the speaking wire clicked twice: smoke had crossed the kiln yard.

Kezli sighted along the two bare rims. Rigid teeth demanded alignment. Friction did not, if the contact could follow the offset and if something gentler than iron carried the heat. She drew two circles in the soot on the housing, then a smaller circle pinched between them.

"A contact roller," she said. "Spring-mounted. Sleeve it in oakcloth so it grips both rims."

"One roller will climb," Olbit said. He drew a second small circle under hers. "Two will share the side thrust. Put them in a flexure brace so they can follow the shifted axis instead of arguing with it."

"The piston pulse will eat the cloth."

"Sorter flywheel. The cracked ore sorter behind the coal shed still has one."

"Too heavy."

"Which is why it will smooth the pulse."

Kezli grinned despite the smoke. That was the pleasure of working with Olbit: he disagreed in completed calculations.

They measured the shaft speeds and chose roller diameters that reduced the engine's turns to the drum's safe rate. Olbit took two brass weights from a platform scale and sketched a ball governor to hold that rate under load. Kezli cut a strip from a standard resin-bound oakcloth leaf, clamped it to a test roller, and pressed it against the powered engine collar for ten counted seconds.

The sample emerged hot, glazed, and thinner by a measurable shaving.

They ran it again at the pressure required to lift the heaviest declared cage. Kezli marked wear against time. Olbit measured the available collar clearance.

"Five standard leaves," he said.

Kezli stacked them around the test roller: white, blue, yellow, orange, red. Five fitted snugly. A sixth made the roller too fat to engage. She tried six thinner strips; the test heat burned through the outer pair so quickly that iron would meet iron before the fourth load arrived.

Nalda watched the red layer disappear beneath the others. "How long?"

"Under a declared load, at governed speed, five minutes from clutch engagement to bare iron," Kezli said. "Not six. Not five and a favorable opinion. Five."

"People say your workshop can make anything work."

It was a local joke, usually told when someone wanted a miracle at the price of a hinge. Kezli rolled the ruined test strip between her fingers.

"We can make these parts agree," she said. "For five minutes. If you want anything else, call someone who lies."

***

The apparatus looked improbable only to anyone who could not see what each piece did.

Cart springs became the flexure that kept the rollers pressed against both offset rims. A straight length of ore rail braced the frame. The salvaged sorter flywheel went on the engine side to swallow the pistons' hammering pulses. The scale weights spun on hinged arms above it, opening the steam throttle linkage when speed fell and closing it when speed rose. Five resin-bound oakcloth leaves wrapped the main contact roller, each dyed a different color and chalked with a wear line.

Olbit riveted a copper tab into every layer. As each leaf stripped away, its tab would strike a hanging clapper. Kezli notched a bronze shear link to part at the force expected when compliant cloth gave way to bare iron. The parting link would release the spring brace, pull the rollers clear, and trip the steam-dump latch. After that, the Rise's own tested ratchet brake would hold the drum.

Nothing in the chain was decorative. Even the shield of dented boiler plate had one purpose: keeping curious people away from the harmless but alarming pieces.

Nalda returned with a passenger sheet while Kezli fitted the final pin.

Olbit read it and frowned. "It says 'forty, roughly adult.'"

"There are also three children," Nalda said.

"Then they are remarkably roughly adult. Any tools? Ore samples? Family trunks?"

"One hand bag each."

"A hand is not a unit of mass."

Smoke rolled above the lower terrace roof. Still, Olbit would not sign for a mystery. They weighed upper-landing volunteers with ballast, established ten marks on the cage floor, and sent instructions down the speaking wire: four balanced groups of ten, bags on laps, quarry tools left behind. The bruised attendant confirmed each group against the marks.

Kezli wrote the operating ticket on a board and read every line aloud.

"Four passenger loads. Governed speed at the painted line. Five minutes beginning at clutch engagement. White, blue, yellow, orange, red, then bare iron. Smoke expected. Clatter expected. Copper strike at every cleared leaf. Everyone behind the shield line when red appears. Terminal sequence: shear, roller withdrawal, steam dump, brake engagement. No restart after terminal shear."

At the bottom waited signature lines for engineer, loadwright, director, and use priority.

Five minutes looked miserable in ink. Six looked almost generous. Six might look like confidence to Nalda, and permanence's smaller, respectable cousin to the council.

Kezli's pen hovered.

Olbit glanced at it. "Will the extra minute be made of ink?"

She scratched out the beginning of a curve before it became a six, wrote a hard-edged five, and stamped the ticket in red.

"Five," she said.

Director Vick signed beneath her. "Five."

The speaking wire bell rang before Nalda could fill in the use-priority line.

The council courier bent to the mouthpiece, listened, and went pale. "Order from the council. Two guards take the first empty cage down. The returning cage carries the civic strongbox. Passenger evacuation follows."

Nalda stared toward the smoke. "The strongbox holds the quarry receipts and the reserve for wages. Without it, half the lower district may not be paid. We may not be able to rebuild this lift."

The order was not foolish. That made it worse.

Olbit laid four square washers on the ticket, one for each passenger group. Then he set a brass nut beside them for the strongbox cycle. There was no room for the nut.

"Find another minute," Nalda said to Kezli. Quietly, as if quiet words weighed less. "Or slow the lift and stretch the five."

"Slower means the cloth sits under pressure longer and cooks," Kezli said. "Faster means the landing brake takes more speed than we tested. The four passenger loads use the travel and loading time we have. Send guards and retrieve the strongbox, and ten people remain below when red clears."

"Then tell me what to do."

Kezli felt the invitation inside the demand. If she chose, the director could later say the goblins had forced her hand. If Kezli invented a sixth minute, everyone could pretend the machine had erased the choice.

She moved the washers and nut apart.

"I can price your choices in loads and minutes," she said. "I cannot decide whose future counts. That line is yours."

For one breath Nalda looked furious. Then she took the pen.

On the use-priority line, she wrote: **PERSONS BEFORE PROPERTY. FOUR PASSENGER LOADS. STRONGBOX REMAINS BELOW.** She signed the addition and made the council courier witness it. Then she took the speaking-wire mouthpiece herself and transmitted the order to the bruised attendant.

The four lower flags dipped in acknowledgment.

"Engage," Nalda said.

***

White showed on the roller. Five minutes remained.

Kezli opened the boiler feed, watched the governor weights lift to their painted line, and pulled the clutch lever.

The roller train gripped.

For a terrible half second, every piece merely strained: engine collar against white oakcloth, cloth against rollers, rollers against the hoist rim, drum against forty lives' worth of cable. Then the empty upper cage descended. Out of the smoke, its loaded twin began to rise.

The impossible connection worked because every part was doing exactly one possible thing.

"Speed on line," Kezli called.

"Contact pressure true," Olbit answered.

Nalda read the first ten names from the passenger sheet, then caught herself and called, "First load rising."

The drum turned steadily. Resin warmed into a bitter smell. At the first chalk line the white leaf frayed, tore into smoking ribbons, and flung itself against the shield. Its copper tab struck the clapper once.

Several onlookers cried out.

"Expected transition," Kezli said. "Blue exposed. Four minutes. Keep the landing clear."

The first cage settled onto the upper stops. Ten soot-streaked people spilled out while the other cage reached the lower station. Nalda counted them herself. Below, the second group loaded according to the marks.

The council courier appeared at her shoulder. "The council repeats its order. The strongbox—"

"Remains below by my signed direction," Nalda said, loudly enough for the arriving passengers to hear. "Send the cage back."

The blue leaf darkened along Kezli's chalk line. The governor weights held steady. Kezli reversed the drum for the empty cage's exchange, then took up the second load. The connection changed direction without wandering off the rims. That had been Olbit's second roller. She glanced at him; he was already watching the brace, not seeking thanks.

The clapper rang. Blue strips snapped away, and yellow appeared with three minutes remaining.

The second load climbed. Halfway up, heat widened the engine collar. The contact roller edged toward the limit mark. The flexure brace kicked hard enough to dent its wooden stop.

The crowd recoiled.

"Expected brace correction," Olbit said.

He did not improvise. He pulled the premeasured second fulcrum pin from his belt, drove it into the waiting hole, and shifted the spring weight one notch. Contact pressure dropped. The roller recentered between its chalk lines.

"Pressure true," he called.

Kezli kept her hand off his work. Trusting a partner was another form of accuracy.

Ten more people reached the upper landing. Twenty safe. Yellow glazed, blistered, and peeled away. Its tab hit the clapper. Orange emerged with two minutes left.

The third cage rose through resin smoke and a shower of black scale. The bruised attendant stood inside, one arm strapped to their chest, while another worker below organized the final group. The apparatus looked as though it were burning itself apart because it was, in the measured and useful way stated on the ticket.

"Governor still on line," Kezli said.

"Drum steady," Olbit said.

Nalda no longer watched their hands. She helped the third group off the cage, supported the attendant by the good arm, and cleared all ten behind the shield line.

Orange reached its final chalk mark. The orange tab dropped against the clapper, and red turned on the roller like a warning lamp.

"One minute," Kezli called. "Operating trio only. Everyone else behind the shield."

The final cage began to rise.

The lower signal flag fell. No people remained at the station. Through a gap in the smoke, Kezli saw the squat civic strongbox still chained beside the speaking-wire desk.

"Final wear mark approaching," Olbit said.

The red leaf looked thicker than it had on the bench. For one treacherous instant, Kezli imagined it lasting another passage. Perhaps the measurements had been conservative. Perhaps she could wrap on another leaf, fetch the strongbox, save Nalda from the inquiry, and turn five good minutes into six glorious ones.

Then she saw the heat score spreading across the shaft and the flexure spring sitting at the end of its useful travel. Hope was not a measurement.

"Cut fuel," she told the boiler tender. "Dump ready."

The council courier gripped the edge of the shield. "The sleeve can be packed again. When they arrive, send it down once more."

"No," Kezli said. "After shear, the shaft is scored, the brace is spent, and the lower station will be inside the fire. The warranty includes stopping."

The fourth cage broke through the smoke. Nalda and the lift mechanics hauled it onto the upper landing. Ten people crossed the stop line with seconds left.

Forty.

Red vanished.

Bare iron caught against iron instead of slipping compliantly. The jolt loaded the notched bronze link past its threshold. It parted with a clean metallic crack. Released springs snapped the contact rollers away. The same motion tripped the steam-dump latch, and white vapor burst above the housing. The ratchet brake dropped into the drum and caught it against the landing stops.

Sparks scattered across the boiler-plate shield. Scale pattered onto the stones. The clapper rang one last time, nearly lost beneath the hiss of vented steam.

People screamed.

Then nothing moved.

Kezli looked down the sequence on the ticket. Bare iron. Shear. Withdrawal. Dump. Brake.

"Terminal behavior as warranted," she said, and discovered that her voice was shaking only after the words were out.

Olbit checked the brake pawl and held up his thumb. "Forty passengers. Five minutes. Zero unpriced adults."

The upper landing laughed, a thin and astonished sound that became cheering.

A second rumble rolled up from the terrace. The roof of the lower station folded into the fire, and rock swept across it from the broken stair road. When the dust cleared, the speaking-wire desk and the strongbox were gone.

Nalda watched the place where they had been. She did not look away from the price she had signed for.

***

By noon, the North Rise was quiet enough to hear cooling iron tick.

Kezli and Olbit inventoried what remained: five stripped oakcloth leaves, one cleanly parted shear link, one heat-scored shaft, a flexure spring with no safe travel left, and a brake still locked around the drum. Olbit punched each completed color on the ticket as they checked it. Beneath all of it, the pedestal crack remained. The crown gear was still ruined. Their success had not repaired a single permanent fault.

It had only kept every one of those faults from mattering for five minutes.

At a makeshift desk, Nalda dictated two records. The first admitted that she had deferred the pedestal work after Kezli's maintenance bid and recorded her decision to leave civic funds below. The second listed the emergency rig's declared duration, four-load capacity, five warning colors, and terminal sequence. Every item had occurred within its stated bound.

"The council will hold an inquiry," she said.

"Probably several," Olbit said. "Committees multiply when stored near missing money."

Nalda gave him a tired, unwilling smile. Then she paid the emergency invoice in full from the lift office's upper reserve. On a fresh work order, she commissioned a new pedestal and crown gear, named Kezli's workshop as paid lead, and assigned the ordinary lift mechanics as independent inspectors.

"A permanent repair," Nalda said, offering Kezli the pen.

This time the phrase did not sound like a verdict on everything temporary.

Kezli signed.

They pinned the red-stamped warranty to the silent lift housing beside the rebuild order. All five colored boxes had been punched through, exactly as promised. Below them, in the space for witnesses, forty soot-marked fingerprints crowded one another nearly off the board.

Kezli looked past the spent leaves to the cracked pedestal they would set right next. The five-minute machine had not lasted.

Its consequence would.

stories.title: The Tenth World Needs No Hero
stories.prompt: The purpose of Isekai is to reform the previously shut-in heroes into people that believe in their own importance and self. It’s clear that you haven’t learned your lesson yet, because you’ve been sent to your 10th world and that goddess is getting exhausted.
stories.body:
# The Tenth World Needs No Hero

Ryo Sato came through the door sideways, because heroism had done nothing for his balance.

He struck the floor on one shoulder. His sword followed, then a white ceremonial spear, then a jeweled staff he had never learned to use. Beyond the narrowing doorway, thousands of voices were chanting his name.

“Ryo! Ryo! Ryo!”

“Zero casualties,” he reported.

Steward Eiren used both hands to pinch the shining filament that formed the door’s edge. It grew from the centers of her palms, fine as spider silk and bright as a cut in the air. Usually she closed it with a neat twist. This time her fingers shook. The chanting squeezed to a silver line, then vanished.

Eiren stepped backward, missed the only chair in the threshold room, and sat on the floor.

“Delightful,” she said. Her shawl had slipped halfway down one arm. Ink-dark stains filled the beds of her nails. “And how are you?”

Ryo pushed himself upright. “What?”

“A cunning ambush. I thought I might catch you between statistics.”

He unbuckled his ruined breastplate. Nine marks shone across his body: pale bands at his shoulder, palm, ribs, throat, temple, spine, ankle, heart, and brow. The first burned whenever he remembered the floodgate chain snapping. He had braced his shoulder beneath the falling beam while brown water climbed his legs, held until his knees ground craters into the stone, and walked away as children on the wall began a song about him.

The mark in his palm recalled a fevered well turning clear beneath his hand. The one along his ribs remembered a plain of burning grass and the seed grain he had carried through it. In both places, doors garlanded for his feast had stood open behind him. He had left before anyone served the food.

Eiren watched the marks fade. “Nine worlds. Nine victories. You collect ceremonial weapons like a hallway collects shoes, and you still cannot answer a question about yourself.”

“You said there was another pull.”

“This will be your tenth world, Ryo.” She pressed her stained fingertips to her eyes. “If nine triumphs have not taught you that you matter, I am running out of strength, ideas, and tact. The tact went first.”

He looked at the blank wall where a door might appear. Tenth mission, he thought. A pleasing round number. A completion marker.

“What needs saving?” he asked.

Eiren laughed once, without amusement. Then, because she was as trapped by the question as he was, she held out her hands.

* * *

The next doorway opened slowly.

Living filaments slid from Eiren’s palms and stitched a rectangle of darkness into the air. She had to stop twice, breathing through clenched teeth. Within the dark, Ryo saw not the destination but the reflection of another door: cheap wood, a peeling apartment number, a chain he had once kept fastened even while awake.

“Before you say yes,” Eiren said, “listen. You are alive. You have been alive through every crossing. Same body, same memory, same extremely poor habit of landing on your face.”

“Shoulder.”

“A magnificent distinction. You may refuse. This filament is nearly spent. If you cross, I can open one return during the storm’s peak, and only briefly. I cannot follow you. I cannot see the whole problem from here.”

Ryo kept looking at the reflected apartment.

Before the first door, he had stopped going outside because outside had become a sequence of demands his body treated as emergencies. At work, his chest had tightened until he could not feel his hands. He had lost the job after too many mornings spent dressed on the edge of his bed, unable to make himself touch the front-door knob. Messages accumulated. Concern became advice; advice became silence. Delivered groceries waited outside until the hall was empty.

Games had helped. Their rules held still. A failed task could be tried again without disappointing anyone who loved him. The apartment had been shelter when he needed shelter. Later, it had tightened by degrees, until safety and shame occupied the same rooms.

Then Eiren had opened a door and offered him a problem with a health bar.

The mark at his throat warmed. He remembered forcing his mouth around the warning cries of a furred hunting clan while arrows rattled on their gate. At his temple, a corridor of mirrors broke into shining fault lines and showed him the one safe path. Along his spine, impossible strength returned him to the fortress arch he had lifted while soldiers crawled from beneath it. There had been an alliance table, a ruler’s bow, a room full of the newly bereaved. He had stayed for none of them.

At his ankle: a step through shadow into a besieged gatehouse, followed by victory horns. Over his heart: a ward held all night above a refuge while snow buried the road, and a child offering him soup at dawn. At his brow: two armies halted because Ryo saw the single act that would end their war—the stolen water maps laid together on one table, the sustaining lie made visible. That crowd had still been chanting when he fell through Eiren’s door.

“The assignments made me better,” he said.

Eiren’s exhausted gaze did not leave him. “Better at what?”

“Endurance. Languages. Strategy. Saving people.”

“I asked what you wanted for breakfast yesterday. You told me which grain had the highest survival value.”

“It did.”

“The grain was blue.”

He had no defense against that except accuracy. “It was nutritious.”

Eiren flexed her trembling hands. “This pull is centered on the ending of a hero’s job. I chose it because I thought—” She stopped. “I do not know the full circumstances. That is the truth.”

An ending implied something large enough to end. Ryo imagined a concealed tyrant, a buried monster, a final form waiting beneath an innocent surface.

“I consent,” he said.

Eiren’s face tightened. Still, she opened the door.

* * *

Ryo arrived under a clear sky in a town taking its miracle apart.

The storm engine occupied the center of a stone tower open to the wind. It was a black metal column three stories high, ribbed with copper conduits. Nine conductor vanes reached from it like the spokes of a wheel. Crews in leather aprons were unbolting them one by one and lowering them toward nine squat stations built around the tower floor.

Beyond the open arches, roofs crowded down a hillside. Far past them, a purple cloudbank pressed against the horizon.

“Put that down,” someone said.

Ryo realized he had drawn his sword.

The speaker was a young engineer with cropped hair, soot on both cheeks, and a wrench braced over one shoulder. “Unless the storm has developed a throat, that will be decorative.”

He sheathed it. “Ryo Sato. I was sent to help.”

“Jori Vale. Carry that vane to station four.” Jori pointed to a curved slab of copper taller than either of them. “No powers through it. It’s inert, and we worked hard to keep it that way.”

Ryo lifted it. Four crew members let go with visible relief. He carried it across the tower floor and eased it into a cradle while Jori called measurements.

“Good,” Jori said. “Stop there.”

The words landed strangely. “I can carry the others.”

“So can the hoists. I need you clear of the conductor paths.”

Jori showed him the plan because he kept asking where the real emergency was. Long ago, every resident’s small ability to turn wind or bleed lightning from a roof had been gathered by the engine into one operator. The old plaques called that operator the Necessary One. One body could protect the whole town with wonderful efficiency, right up until the storms burned it out.

“People prefer a miracle with a face,” Jori said, tightening a clamp. “Easier to praise one person than maintain nine stations. We chose maintenance.”

For years the town had built manual channels that could divide the storm among hundreds of hands. Today they meant to cut the last central conduits before the seasonal front arrived.

There was no tyrant. No monster. No one even seemed interested in Ryo’s sword.

A siren wailed.

Crew members dropped into practiced positions. Gauges jumped along the column.

“Pressure test,” Jori shouted. “Hold your stations. Ryo, stay where you are.”

The mark at Ryo’s brow blazed. His gift had never been wrong. Every line in the room—the stress fractures in the copper, the shadow beneath the central rail, the angle of the rising gauges—pointed toward a white control circle at the engine’s base.

Necessary action.

He stepped into shadow and emerged inside the circle.

Jori shouted something sharp. Ryo did not hear it. He seized the central rails, drove cleansing warmth into one and raised a ward through the other. The tower lurched. A seam in the column opened with furnace light; he forced it shut with both hands.

The pressure dropped. The siren died.

For one perfect second, everyone stared at him.

Then the nine detached conductors snapped upright.

Mechanical letters clattered across an old brass panel.

NECESSARY ONE ACCEPTED.

The white circle closed around Ryo’s boots like cooling glass. Outside, the purple storm turned toward the town.

* * *

The engine became very interested in everything Ryo could do.

When a copper rib buckled, he held it straight. The shoulder mark burned brighter, and a second conductor lit.

When heat rolled up his arms, his fireproof skin hardened. A third conductor lit.

He saw fractures before they spread, warded sparks away from the crews, stepped through the engine’s own shadows to catch a falling brace. With each success, white light climbed higher around his legs. Each time he took a task, one of the manual stations went dark.

“Stop helping!” Jori shouted.

“I’m preventing a rupture.”

“You are teaching the engine where the power is!”

Residents had gathered in the archways below. Some recognized the old pattern faster than the crews did.

“A Necessary One,” someone breathed.

“He can hold it.”

“The hero came back.”

The words reached a hollow place in Ryo and filled it with light. His arms were burning. His feet had gone numb. He smiled anyway.

Jori saw. Their expression changed from anger to something worse: understanding without admiration.

“Every job you take disables a station,” they said. “It is not choosing you because you are destined. It is choosing you because you keep volunteering for the whole load.”

A slim doorway flickered at the edge of the circle. Eiren knelt on the other side, one palm braced on the threshold-room floor. Her other hand reached toward him, but the filaments around her fingers blinked in and out.

“Ryo,” she said. “Stop proving the problem correct.”

“If I leave and anyone dies, it’s my fault.”

“That sentence has eaten nine years of my life, and considerably more of yours.”

“Argue later,” Jori said. They shoved a diagram against the glassy boundary. Nine radial lines. Nine stations. “Your powers are distinct charges. We can bleed one into each station, and each crew can use it to break one central bond. The stations consume the charge. You lose the gifts.”

Ryo looked at his shining marks.

“Then what?”

“Then you step out before station nine cuts the core.”

“Will it work?”

“We have tested each station separately. Never all nine in a live storm.”

“So you don’t know.”

“Correct. Welcome to engineering.”
