Lightning moved inside the approaching clouds. Eiren’s return door dimmed.

Ryo searched the room with his fracture-sight. There had to be a cleaner line: one cut, one ward, one decisive act that placed uncertainty on his shoulders and nowhere else.

He found a bright seam at the top of the engine.

“Ryo, no,” Eiren whispered.

He shadow-stepped upward, caught the seam, and poured his strength through it. He tried to turn the whole storm aside.

The engine took the offer.

All nine conductors flared white. The seam sealed around his hands. Station nine went black with a sound like a slammed coffin lid.

At the doorway, Eiren fell to one knee.

Ryo dropped back into the circle. He had fixed nothing. His certainty had merely become another conduit.

* * *

For three breaths, the engine held perfectly still.

Rain struck the tower in hard, scattered coins.

Eiren looked older than she had an hour ago. The door-filaments cut red grooves across her palms.

“People called me a goddess once,” she said. “Not everywhere. Not forever. Just frightened people who prayed for an exit and saw me open one.”

Ryo gripped the central rails. “This is not the moment for your biography.”

“It is the moment for my confession.” Her voice shook, but did not soften. “I learned to feel real when I was needed. Every door cost me, and I mistook the cost for evidence that I loved people properly.”

The filament pulsed between them, ragged and bright.

“Then I found you,” Eiren said. “You looked at the first crisis and stood up. I thought if I gave you enough proof—enough victories—you would carry that feeling home. When you asked again, it reassured me. Your success made my mistake look like care.”

Ryo’s hands tightened until the rails bent. “So I was a lesson.”

“In part. You were also someone I cared about. I asked each time, and you said yes. I used those facts to avoid asking what our yes was serving.”

“Tell me the correct choice now.”

Eiren closed her eyes. “No. I have made too many assignments out of your life already.”

At station nine, Jori and six crew members hauled open the dead housing. Wind threw rain through the arches. They reached bare hands into the mechanism and fed their own small currents into it: a tremor of diverted air, a blue crawling spark, a pressure change Ryo felt in his teeth.

“We do not need you to be sure,” Jori called. “We need you to stop taking away everyone else’s chance to act.”

The ninth station’s indicator stuttered amber.

Ryo looked down at the circle holding him. It promised fixed inputs and measurable outcomes. Stay here. Take every danger. Receive praise. Never answer what you wanted.

His apartment had made no such promise. It had been a refuge from pain no one else could see, until fear and shame narrowed his choices to the size of one room. The control circle was brighter. The control circle had an audience. But disappearing into it would still be disappearance.

The return doorway shrank to the width of Eiren’s shoulders.

“Ryo,” she said, barely audible. “I cannot hold it much longer.”

He did not know whether the town would survive without him.

For the first time, not knowing could not postpone the choice.

* * *

“All right,” Ryo told Jori. “Your plan.”

Jori pointed at the first station. “On my count.”

“Wait.” He swallowed. The engine thrummed approval through his bones, certain he had reconsidered. “I want to live.”

The statement sounded embarrassingly small beside the storm.

It was not small to him.

“I want a chance to find out what I like when nobody is scoring it,” he said. “Those are my reasons. Count.”

Jori did.

At one, Ryo opened the pale band on his shoulder. Years of impossible endurance rushed out of him in a white stream and struck station one. For an instant he was back beneath the broken floodgate, water climbing his chest, children singing above. Then the station’s crew caught the charge in copper arms and forced a lever down.

The first central bond broke.

Ryo’s knees began to shake.

At two, he released the cleansing warmth from his palm. He smelled fever-sour stone and remembered clear water welling between his fingers. Station two flashed gold. Its crew missed the first catch, swore, reset their clamps, and caught the second.

The engine offered the power back through the rails. Ryo let the offer pass.

At three, heat resistance peeled from his skin. The burning plain vanished from his ribs. The control rails became instantly, honestly hot, and he cried out. Station three’s crew broke their bond with a hammer because the release catch jammed.

At four, the voices of every creature he had ever understood crowded his throat—warning cries, jokes, mourning songs—then dissolved into rain. The crew at station four needed no miraculous language. They shouted ordinary instructions until everyone understood.

At five, fracture-sight left his eyes. The tower became terrifyingly opaque. No bright lines marked the safe places to stand.

“Your left hand,” Jori called. “Move it down.”

Ryo obeyed someone else’s sight. Station five engaged.

At six, strength poured from his spine. The rails sagged in his grip. Two crew members thrust a brace through the boundary and took the weight he could no longer hold alone.

At seven, shadow-step unstitched itself from his ankle. Every distance in the tower became real distance. There would be no skipping the space between danger and help, no private shortcut through darkness. Station seven groaned, hesitated, then locked.

At eight, the ward over his heart broke into sparks. Wind hit him full in the face. Rain found every burn. The engine opened a path for the storm and invited him to take the sheltering power back.

He did not.

Eight station crews held eight imperfect lines. One conductor remained white. The glass around Ryo’s boots loosened until he could lift one heel.

The final mark blazed at his brow.

His decisive instinct showed him the necessary action with the clarity of revelation: stay in the circle. Reclaim the load. Guarantee the town’s survival. Be consumed, and never again face a day in which his worth was uncertain.

Station nine flickered. Jori’s crew fought to keep their handmade current alive.

The old gift had never been wrong about how to win.

It had never been asked whether Ryo should survive the winning.

He tore the light from his brow and threw it into station nine.

Certainty went dark.

The crew caught the charge. Ryo no longer knew whether they had caught it correctly. He no longer knew the best angle for his foot, the perfect second to move, the outcome waiting beyond the next breath.

He stepped out anyway.

The tower lights failed.

The storm struck.

For one deafening moment, Ryo thought he had abandoned everyone. Then eight channels opened across the floor, messy and uneven. The ninth sputtered, died, and flared again as Jori and the others forced it by hand. Lightning divided through the stations instead of converging on one body.

The black column split along its central seam. Beneath the casing, the sacrificial core hung exposed: a fist-sized knot where all nine lines had once become one.

The return door was now barely wider than Eiren’s hand.

“Use the filament,” Ryo said.

Her fingers were inches from his. “To pull you out?”

“To cut that.”

Eiren stared at the core. “If I do, your assignment thread burns out. No powers. No eleventh door. I may not be able to reach you again.”

Fear opened under him. It had no bottom and no victory condition.

“That’s the point,” he said, and then, because it was more honest, “I am terrified. Please do it.”

Eiren moved.

The living filament lashed through the inert doorway, bright with the last strength in her bleeding palms. It looped the exposed core. Eiren pulled once.

The knot came apart.

Thunder punched cracks through the tower walls. Roof tiles spun into the streets. Every lamp on the hillside went dark. But the storm ran outward through nine ordinary channels, into hundreds of waiting hands, and no single person burned at its center.

Jori staggered against a station, laughing or coughing. “You followed the plan,” they told Ryo.

“Eventually.”

“I remain angry about the first part.”

“That seems fair.”

No one crowned him. No crowd began a chant. Crews were already checking the cracked tower and calling damage reports into the rain.

Eiren’s doorway folded inward.

Ryo wanted to stay long enough to prove the lights would return. He wanted a final count, a clean result, permission to call his choice correct.

Instead he took Eiren’s hand.

He left before certainty.

* * *

They collapsed together on the threshold-room floor.

For a while Ryo could hear only their breathing. His arms burned. His muscles trembled with the indignity of supporting exactly one exhausted human body. The nine marks had faded to ordinary skin.

Eiren turned her palms upward. The filaments were gone. Thin burns crossed her hands where they had grown.

“I cannot open another assignment door for you,” she said.

Ryo waited for grief and found it. He also found relief, fear, resentment, affection, and a powerful desire to sleep for a week. None canceled the others.

“Thank you for bringing me back,” he said. “That does not make everything you did right.”

“I know.” Eiren’s apology arrived without defense. “I am sorry.”

“And I’m not fixed.”

“No.” She considered. “You are extremely singed.”

He laughed, which hurt. “You should rest.”

“An outrageous proposal.”

“You are not allowed to make me your project again.”

“Agreed. You are not allowed to make yourself mine.”

They slept on opposite sides of the blank room. Later—Ryo did not know how much later—Eiren found enough strength for one last one-way fold, back to the physical doorway where she had first found him. It was not an assignment and held no promise of return.

“If an ordinary road ever lets us meet again,” Eiren said, “we could try being two people.”

“What would we do?”

“I hear some people consume blue grain voluntarily.”

“Anything but that.”

It was, Ryo realized, a preference.

He stepped through.

His apartment had preserved all its unfinished problems. Dust silvered the desk. Unread messages waited on his phone. The grocery app still remembered his order. No music swelled to certify his return.

His first impulse was to answer everyone at once and promise he was better now. His second was to find some emergency large enough to delay answering at all.

Ryo ate crackers over the sink, drank two glasses of water, and slept.

When he woke, daylight lay across the floor. He opened one message from a relative who had kept writing long after questions became weather reports and small photographs from ordinary days.

Ryo typed: *I’m back. I’m not okay yet. Could you help me make one appointment?*

He nearly replaced it with a joke. He nearly added a list of miraculous qualifications. He sent the message as it was.

Then he wrote one item on a sheet of paper.

*Visit the neighborhood garden.*

It would save no one. He remembered liking the smell of wet soil after rain. That seemed sufficient.

Ryo opened the curtains. The room felt exposed, and he left them open anyway.

At his apartment door there was no silver filament, no chanting crowd, no mark to reveal the necessary action. There was only the hall, one appointment he could not make alone, and a garden he might not manage to visit today.

He put his hand on the knob without knowing what waited behind it.

Then Ryo opened the door himself.

stories.body:
# The Two-Tug Rule

At twenty-nine, Miles Arden had learned that adulthood mostly meant putting warning labels on things no reasonable person would mistake for safe. Living with Luz Navarro in their third-floor apartment had merely improved his materials.

On Saturday morning, a yellow strip crossed the unplugged countertop mixer: **DO NOT PLUG IN—LUZ WORKING.** Another blocked its speed dial. A third marked the bright nonslip mat where Luz, twenty-eight and already wearing the fitted work clothes that changed with her, planted both feet.

“Fifteen centimetres,” she said. “Ten minutes.”

Miles checked the exhaust fan, burner knobs, taps, drain plug, door, and mixer cord. “Air still. Water off. Machines dead. Route clear.” He lifted both ordinary battery radios. They resisted splashes, not soaking; hers sat snug beneath her sleeve, dry and well under the two-hundred-and-fifty-gram limit for things she could take with her. “Radio check.”

“You are standing half a metre away.”

“Radio check.”

Her voice crackled from his speaker. “Your devotion to procedure remains extremely attractive.”

Luz took one controlled breath to a five-count. The change belonged wholly to her; Miles could neither start nor stop it. Over the next five seconds, she diminished smoothly toward the height she had chosen until she stood fifteen centimetres tall on the mat, still unmistakably the adult woman who had shared his apartment, bills, and terrible weekend breakfasts for four years.

Because she was below half her ordinary height, her own living process would begin an automatic return at twenty-four minutes. Miles started independent timers for twenty and twenty-three, warnings that neither controlled nor extended the change. She planned to be done long before either sounded. He opened the shallow emergency tray: flashlight, glucose gel, utility cord, and a dry towel folded into a ramp.

Luz glanced at the card beside the spool. “One tug, stop. Two, pull steadily. Three, give slack. Did you think we forgot overnight?”

“Redundancy saves lives.”

“Are you labeling gravity next?”

“Only the dangerous direction.”

She laughed and climbed the towel into the dry mixer housing. At that size, short falls worried him less than moving parts or drafts. She weighed very little and could scale the internal ribs easily, but useful relative strength did not grant full-sized torque. Their rule was plain: Miles did not touch, lift, enclose, or carry her without a direct request. He steadied the unplugged housing, never her, while she reset its jammed latch with a screwdriver she had kept against bare skin during the change. Anything loose would have remained behind at ordinary size; anything picked up now remained whatever size it already was.

Eight minutes later she descended without help and stepped onto the mat.

“Returning,” she said. Three slow breaths, then eight seconds of growth restored her ordinary hundred and sixty-eight centimetres. Only when she had finished did Miles offer a hand.

Her fingers trembled faintly against his.

“Cold?” he asked.

“Hungry.” Luz withdrew her hand and reached for toast. “Which is your fault. You turned breakfast into a safety audit.”

They logged eight minutes and the tremor together, then added toast, water, and a warm mug to the recovery. The record was supposed to be shared evidence, not permission Miles issued. For six hours Luz would not start another safe cycle; attempting one sooner risked an immediate uncontrolled return and a much longer recovery.

Miles looked at the untouched glucose gel, then at the protocol sheet. Checking its boxes was easier than asking why he had seen that tremor before.

* * *

The drip beneath the kitchen sink had learned patience.

It waited through breakfast, then tapped once against the basin while they cleaned. Miles crouched and aimed a flashlight behind the fixed toe-kick. A cold-water branch line vanished into the narrow void. Green-white corrosion furred a bend deeper than either of them could reach, and the wood beneath it was dark with damp.

The apartment stop valve turned grudgingly under his hand. The dripping slowed, but did not stop.

Luz knelt beside him. “There’s a quarter-turn handle behind the bend.”

“I see it.” Miles tried reaching through the toe-kick gap and scraped his knuckles. “Maintenance can’t come until Monday.”

“On a fresh cycle, I could inspect it.”

“No plumbing.”

The words came too fast. Her gaze moved from his face to the protocol sheet on the counter.

“You actually wrote that in?” she asked.

After a fan had kicked on during a routine two months earlier, Miles had added three new strips to every fan switch. Luz had been safely on the mat across the room, but the sudden current had knocked her flat. He still sometimes woke hearing her radio clatter.

“Water moves harder at your size,” he said. “Cold hits you faster. Pipes have edges, gaps—”

“All useful facts. None of them lets you turn our checklist into your list of permissions.”

“It’s one line.”

“About what I may do with my body.”

He wanted to say he was only trying to keep her safe. The sentence felt noble right up until he imagined hearing it from someone who had edited his choices while he slept.

“The fan was a near miss,” he said instead.

“And we changed the fan protocol together.” Luz rubbed her fingers, then tucked both hands beneath her arms. “This isn’t that.”

He noticed the motion. “Has the shaking happened again?”

“I told you. I missed breakfast.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“Neither is ‘no plumbing.’”

The drip struck the basin between them.

In the end, they agreed to stop using the sink, leave the basin under the line, and wait. No shrinking for the repair, not because Miles had forbidden it, and not because Luz had conceded the principle. They had postponed both the plumbing and the argument.

* * *

Rain pressed a grey evening against the windows. Six hours after her morning cycle, warmed, fed, and recovered, Luz prepared for a different job: a dropped hinge pin in the dry cabinet beside the sink.

“Twelve centimetres,” she said. “Fifteen minutes.”

They cleared it together. Sink taps off. Drain plugged. Dishwasher disabled. Exhaust fan dead. Cabinet empty and dry. Both radios tested. The bright mat and open emergency tray stood beside the cabinet. Miles set an electric hotplate across the room, safely beyond the marked work zone, and put soup on low.

Luz changed on the bright mat, five counted seconds from ordinary height to her practiced minimum, and Miles started both warning timers. At twelve centimetres, her voice kept its familiar adult pitch but could barely cross a quiet metre. The radio made conversation easy.

“Pin’s aligned,” she reported from the cabinet. “I’m setting the clip.”

Miles stirred the soup. “Three minutes. I should label this spoon.”

“Warning: may contain spoon.”

The corroded bend, weakened past endurance by the damp, gave way under ordinary building pressure with a crack like a plate breaking.

Cold water punched through the base cabinet, struck the opposite wall, and sheeted across the kitchen floor. Miles killed the hotplate, yanked its plug, and lunged toward the cabinet.

Luz stood on the dry mat outside it. She had made it clear of the hinge before the flood reached her.

“Reverse now,” Miles said.

Her expression sharpened. “Facts, Miles.”

He heard the command in his own voice and hated that it had arrived before thought. He forced himself to look.

“Branch line split behind the toe-kick. Apartment stop still isn’t holding. I can see the hidden handle, but I can’t reach it. Water’s moving toward the outlet.” His timer showed eighteen minutes left before her hard return. “Eighteen minutes.”

“Cut the kitchen breaker.”

He ran to the panel. The kitchen went dark; the refrigerator hum and hotplate light died. When he returned with the flashlight, water had spread halfway across the floor, but Luz remained on the mat.

“I can reach that handle,” she said.

“Luz, I’m afraid.” The admission felt less useful than a wrench and twice as heavy. “I don’t think that makes the choice mine. But I am afraid.”

She held his gaze for one beat. “Good fact.” Then she pointed at the emergency tray. “I’m going in. Ramp.”

Miles laid the towel from the mat to the cabinet threshold. He set his open palm beside it as the other option, still and uncurled.

Luz chose the ramp.

* * *

In the cabinet, the broken line turned the flashlight beam into a field of flying silver. Luz stayed behind the pipe braces, climbing where they shielded her from the direct jet. Water that would have been spray against Miles’s wrist could sweep her into the dark gap behind the cabinets.

“Clip on the handle,” she said over the radio. “I can move it.”

Miles rolled towels into a dam between the flood and the dead outlet. With his other hand he called the unit below, warned that water was coming, and then called emergency maintenance. Each glance away from the cabinet felt like a betrayal, but containing the flood was work only his reach and speed allowed.

“Clip’s clear,” Luz said. “Handle’s seized. I can’t get the torque.”

Relative to her weight, she could climb like a champion. Against a corroded full-sized valve, twelve centimetres of leverage remained twelve centimetres.

Miles pulled the utility cord from the tray. “I can feed this through the gap.”

“Do it.”

He pushed the dry end beneath the toe-kick. A ricochet struck the cabinet wall and became a sudden sideways sheet. Luz disappeared from the brace.

“Luz!”

Her radio hit something, crackled, and gave him a burst of static. He saw her land on the shallow shelf below, roll, and push upright. A short fall at her weight was usually forgiving. The cold water was not. It washed around her boots and dragged at her legs.

Miles thrust his hand toward the gap.

“Don’t,” her radio managed.

The word vanished beneath static.

He stopped with his fingers at the opening. Every frantic part of him demanded that he reach in, close his hand, tear wood away until he had her out. But a blind grab could drive her into the pipe, and wrenching the cabinet could split the line farther—or block the only clear route for her forced return.

Lost communication had a protocol. Freeze or de-energize hazards first. Offer a route. Do not seize.

The breaker was off. He withdrew his hand, fixed the flashlight on the shelf, and laid the cord end within her reach.

For several seconds he saw only water. Then the cord twitched and began sliding into the dark.

* * *

Miles knelt in the flood with the cord wet between his fingers. Luz vanished behind the pipe, visible only in fragments: a sleeve, one boot, the brief shine of the radio that no longer worked.

The cord moved around the hidden valve. He waited.

Two distinct tugs reached his hand.

Pull steadily.

He leaned back, building force instead of jerking. The line quivered. The valve handle shifted a fraction—and the wet loop slipped free.

One tug.

Miles stopped instantly.

His twenty-minute alarm sounded. The bright little chime was absurd under the roar of the leak.

Three tugs.

He fed slack into the gap. When Luz crossed the flashlight beam, he saw her hands shaking hard enough to make the cord jump.

“I can tear the toe-kick out,” he called.

One tug: stop.

He closed his eyes for half a second. There it was again, fear dressed as a solution. He could make the opening larger, but he could also collapse wet wood into her route and worsen the rupture.

“Options,” he said toward the gap, forcing his voice level. “The valve failed on the first pull. The exit is still clear. I can keep the cord slack, build the dry ramp, or pull when you signal. We are past twenty minutes. The hard return starts at twenty-four.”

Luz edged close enough that her unamplified voice reached him between surges of water. “I’m colder than I told you. It’s happened on the last three cycles.” She braced a hand against the pipe. “My early return may hesitate. Less than three minutes to the hard limit.”

Miles’s throat tightened. Cold or low blood sugar could hold off a chosen early reversal by as much as twenty seconds. Nothing extended the twenty-four-minute maximum. If automatic return began inside that narrow void, the cabinet would trap her before she reached half height.

“Exit now is safest,” he said. He made himself add, “That’s my assessment. What are you choosing?”

“One more attempt. The loop slipped because it sat in front of the clip. I can get behind it.”

He wanted to say no. He could say that he would not participate in a plan he believed certain to kill her, but this was not that. It was dangerous, legible, and required both of them.

“At the twenty-three-minute alarm, I stop pulling and open the exit, whatever the valve is doing,” he said. “That is what I can do.”

Luz nodded once. “Agreed.”

She took the cord back into the dark.

* * *

The water chilled Miles through his trousers while he waited. He imagined Luz crawling behind the stiff handle, using strength enough to lift her own body many times over but not enough to turn the metal. He imagined the safety clip she had shifted, the narrow angle she alone could see, the countdown neither of them controlled.

The cord moved. Slack vanished one centimetre at a time.

Two deliberate tugs.

Miles leaned back on Luz’s rhythm. The cord tightened. For a breath, nothing yielded. Then the valve handle groaned around its stem.

The changing angle drove the spray harder. White water erased the interior of the cabinet.

One tug snapped through the cord.

Miles froze. The handle stopped moving.

He could not see Luz. His timer counted upward. Twenty-two minutes, thirty-eight seconds.

The cord loosened, shifted, tightened. Luz was changing position before the handle could pin her. Miles supplied no help she had not requested. He barely breathed.

Two tugs.

He pulled.

The cord bit across his palms. Somewhere beyond the spray, Luz kept the loop seated behind the cleared clip. Miles leaned with his full weight, steady, steady, until the handle struck its stop.

The jet died.

Water pattered from the cabinet roof. In the sudden quiet, the twenty-three-minute alarm began to chime.

Miles released the cord. He wanted to reach into the dark so badly his hands hurt. Instead he swept the shallow dam into dry towels, fixed the flashlight on the toe-kick gap, and spread a clean cloth from the shelf to the mat.

“Exit is lit,” he said. “Ramp is dry.”

Luz emerged on hands and knees. She stood once she cleared the cabinet and walked down the cloth, slower than before. At the last wet gap she looked up.

“Hand,” she said.

Miles placed his palm flat and still. She crossed it as a bridge, stepped onto the bright mat, and lifted both arms away from her sides.

“Returning.”

She chose three slow breaths.

One.

Two.

On the third, nothing happened.

Miles saw the tremor in her legs. He kept his hands off her. “You’re on the mat. The route is clear. Breathe again.”

Luz inhaled. Five seconds passed, then ten. Her change finally began. Over eight long seconds she rose to ordinary height, wet clothes changing with her while the full-sized cord fell loose from her hand. She was back before the twenty-four-minute limit.

“Blanket?” Miles asked.

“Yes.”

Only then did he wrap it around her shoulders. She accepted glucose gel, water, and the chair he nudged into place. Emergency maintenance was already on the way. The outlet remained dead. The valve remained closed. Below them, the water stopped spreading.

Miles crouched beside Luz, close enough for their knees to touch. He did not mistake the ending of danger for the end of the argument.

* * *

After warmth, soup, dry clothes, and the branch line’s professional isolation, they sat at the kitchen table beneath the old protocol sheet.

Miles took down the page he had amended alone.

“I’m sorry I wrote a veto about your body into something we’re supposed to share,” he said. “I made fear sound like authority. And I kept labeling things because labels let me pretend I could guarantee your safety.”

Luz held a warm glass between both hands. “I’m sorry I hid the tremor. It happened three times, and I kept thinking that if I told you, the information would become permission for you to decide.”

“It almost did.”

“Yes.” She met his eyes. “But you needed the truth to spot for me. I can owe you accurate information without owing you the final choice.”

“And I can say I’m afraid without turning it into an order.”

They wrote the next page together. Symptoms had to be disclosed before a cycle because coordination required facts. Bodily decisions remained Luz’s. Either partner could decline their own part in a plan. Until they installed an accessible shutoff extension, waterproof communication, and a verified dry route, Luz chose no shrinking around live plumbing. Not forever. Not as punishment. A boundary for conditions they could change.

Days later, with the branch repaired, the water isolated, and the kitchen power off, they installed an external valve pull. Luz chose a twelve-centimetre cycle and inspected the cord routing from the bright mat.

Miles offered his open palm beside the towel ramp.

She grinned and pointed to the towel. “That route.”

He moved his hand away.

At the valve, she checked the seated loop, then gave two tugs. Miles pulled steadily. The handle closed with a smooth, satisfying turn.

When Luz had returned beside him, they taped up the new protocol sheet. Half the lines were in his square handwriting and half in her quick slant. At the centre, beneath the rules for honest facts and chosen help, they had written the one instruction neither of them could use alone:

**TWO TUGS: PULL STEADILY.**

stories.body:
# The Courtesy of Blades

Fiora Halwick set her travel case beneath the spectator rail, where it looked
like an accusation.

The buckles were fastened. Her teaching coats were rolled around two pairs of
boots. At dawn, a hired cart would carry her upriver to East Weir and the yard
that had trusted her with its head instructor's keys. Everything about the case
said *settled*. Everything about Fiora standing in the Lacebridge civic blade
yard in a padded practice coat said otherwise.

Across the strip, Jasper Renlow tightened his throat guard. He caught her
watching and lifted his chin in question.

Fiora lifted hers back. If he wanted reassurance, he could earn it point by
point.

Between them, Quade inspected the flex of one chalk-edged blade, then the other.
Evening light slanted through the open side of the yard and turned the chalk
dust pale gold. Beyond the wall came the river's slap against pilings and the
more persuasive hiss of onions hitting hot iron at the supper stalls.

Quade sighted along Fiora's blunt blade. “No cracks. Edge freshly chalked. Eye
guards down when I call ready. Marks count only on the dark torso and upper-arm
panels. Head, throat, hands, and joints are out. Either of you may halt or
surrender. I may halt you whether you like it or not.”

“You've been waiting years to say that to us,” Jasper said.

“I've been saying it to you for years. Tonight I have witnesses.” Quade handed
the blade to Fiora. “First to three. Clear touches are mine to judge. If you
both land and I cannot see the order, you call your own truth. Understood?”

“Understood,” Fiora and Jasper said together.

That earned a ripple of amusement from behind the rail. Fiora did not look
toward it. The bronze trial badge pinned inside her case had been won in this
same strip, three points to two. For six months, people had admired it by asking
whether Jasper had let her have the last touch.

Quade opened the yard ledger. “Now the personal stake. So if you win the duel,
you get to take her on a date.”

They both nodded.

“And if she wins the duel, she gets to take you on a date.”

They both nodded.

Quade looked from one of them to the other. “So why don't you both just... skip
that and go on a date?”

They both glared.

Quade waited a beat. “Yes, very frightening. For the record, *take* means the
winner gets the first invitation and chooses the place. The loser may decline.
The winner may decide not to ask. Nobody owes anyone a hand, a kiss, a change
of town, a second evening, or even dessert. This is a courtesy-bout stake, not
custody. Do you each enter freely?”

“Yes,” Jasper said.

“Yes,” Fiora said.

“Do you understand that this entire business could have been accomplished with
two sentences and clean shirts?”

“Ready, Quade,” Fiora said.

Jasper lowered his eye guard. “Very ready.”

Their mutual glare had been agreement of a kind. The absurdity was admitted.
The necessity was not. Fiora raised her blade and stepped onto the strip.

***

Jasper saluted with the crisp economy that made him infuriating on patrol and
worse in a fencing yard. He had the sort of balance that never looked hurried,
even when Fiora knew perfectly well she had him worried.

She intended to worry him quickly.

“Ready,” Quade called. “Fence.”

Fiora advanced behind two small testing cuts. Jasper yielded half a step, blade
quiet, his gaze fixed through the guard on the center of her coat. She pressed.
His retreat put him exactly where she wanted him: weight shifting back, right
side open, attention dragged low.

She snapped her blade high.

Jasper was already there.

His parry turned her familiar feint aside. Before she could recover, his blade
flexed against the padded panel of her upper arm and sprang away, leaving one
clean white bar.

“Halt.” Quade stepped between their lines before either could continue. He
examined the mark. “Touch, Jasper. One to nothing.”

The yard murmured.

Fiora stared at the chalk on her sleeve. Jasper had known the attack. Not
guessed—known. He had remembered the hitch of her shoulder, or the fraction by
which she shortened her second step, and he had trained an answer precise
enough to make the point look simple.

It was deeply annoying.

It was also the first thing she had wanted from him all evening.

Jasper returned to his mark without smiling. “You still announce the high line
with your left eyebrow.”

“My eyebrow is a master of deception.”

“It told me everything.”

“Then do keep listening.”

Quade checked the chalk edge, backed away, and called them on.

Fiora gave Jasper the same two testing cuts. This time his mouth twitched. He
settled to meet the high feint again.

She sank instead.

The new pivot had been born from three weeks of preparing lessons for East
Weir, where the shortest practice strip was hemmed in by two inconvenient
pillars. Fiora folded low without surrendering her balance, turned beneath
Jasper's parry, and came up past his outside shoulder. Her chalk edge kissed
the dark panel over his ribs.

Quade's “Halt” arrived on the same breath as Jasper's startled laugh.

The mark was a bright crescent.

“Touch, Fiora. One to one.”

Jasper looked down at it, then across at her. There was no embarrassment in his
face, only sharp interest. “That's new.”

“East Weir.”

“You developed it for the new yard?”

“I developed it because the new yard has pillars, and pillars refuse to adjust
their style for my convenience.”

“I always said you should train with more reasonable opponents.”

“You have never been evidence for that argument.”

This time he did smile, quick and unwilling and much too handsome. Fiora's
heart made a tactical error. She covered it by returning to her mark.

One to one. He knew her, but not all of her. She could work with that.

***

On the next call, Jasper came forward.

The lazy-looking patience vanished from his feet. He drove Fiora down the strip
with compact attacks that made her give ground honestly. Chalk whispered once
past her shoulder without touching. She caught his next blade and turned it,
but he was already angling for her ribs.

He was not easing against her. The realization warmed something under her
breastbone at the least convenient possible time.

Fiora broke his rhythm with a stop, then another. Jasper adjusted. She let him.
On his third advance she offered the opening he had been trying to create, a
sliver of dark panel under her arm.

He took it.

Her blade was waiting on the line he abandoned.

She rotated out, struck his upper-arm panel with a flat white line, and was
already clear when Quade called halt.

“Touch, Fiora. Two to one.”

The cheer behind the rail came fast enough to lift the rafters. Fiora stepped
back, breathless and grinning despite herself.

Jasper rubbed a thumb near the mark, careful not to smear it. “A trap.”

“A lesson plan.”

“Your pupils are doomed.”

“My pupils will learn.”

“I am learning.” His gaze held hers. “That's the trouble.”

It would have been easier if he had sounded flirtatious. He sounded sincere.

Then a voice behind the rail said, not quite softly enough, “Still easing off,
then.”

The grin left Fiora's face.

Quade turned toward the onlookers. “The next person who offers an unofficial
judgment may enjoy the rest of the bout from the street.”

Silence followed, but the words had found the old bruise.

Still easing off. Still giving her room. Still letting the ambitious assistant
instructor leave town with a badge she had not properly earned. She could
already hear the story traveling upriver ahead of her: Jasper had indulged her
again, out of affection this time, and East Weir had appointed the beneficiary
of his gallantry.

Jasper returned to his mark. His shoulders were loose, his attention on her,
as if the rail did not exist.

“You're not going to answer that?” Fiora asked.

“I can argue with the rail,” he said, “or I can fence you. Which do you want?”

“I want your best.”

“You have it.”

Quade studied them. “Do either of you need a halt?”

“No,” Fiora said.

“No,” Jasper echoed.

“Then leave the rail outside the rail. Ready. Fence.”

Fiora attacked before the last word had settled.

Anger lent speed and stole judgment. Her first advance forced Jasper back; her
second beat his blade wide. She saw the opening at his ribs and chased it with
the fierce satisfaction of a door flying open.

It was too wide.

Jasper dropped his point under hers, turned, and let her own forward drive
carry her onto the flex of his blade. Chalk struck squarely across her rib
panel. The padded coat absorbed the touch with a firm thump.

“Halt!” Quade was already moving between them, one arm extended until both
blades were safely down. His eyes went from Fiora's panel to Jasper's edge.
“Clean touch. Jasper. Two to two.”

Fiora's lungs objected to every part of the situation.

Jasper did not apologize. He did not soften the point by calling it luck or
looking ashamed of the mark. He only waited while she found her breath.

She had asked for his best. He had respected her enough to make the request
cost something.

“That,” she said, “was obnoxiously clean.”

“Your eyebrow told me nothing.”

“It was distracted by your personality.”

Quade pinched the bridge of his nose. “Mandatory pause. Re-chalk. Water. Try
not to court each other into heatstroke.”

***

Fiora pushed up her eye guard. The evening air cooled the sweat at her temples.
Across the strip, Jasper did the same.

Quade ran a practiced hand along each blade for damage, then worked fresh chalk
over their edges. “Two to two. Final point decides. Before it does: hands?”

“Sound,” Fiora said.

“Sound,” Jasper said.

“Vision?”

“Clear.”

“Clear.”

Quade gave them water and moved several paces away. Close enough to intervene,
far enough to offer privacy that fooled no one in a yard full of listeners.

Fiora drank, then stared at the old chalk on Jasper's arm. “At the trial,” she
said, “did I land first?”

Jasper lowered his cup. “Yes.”

The answer came without decoration. That almost made her angrier.

“Then why did you never say so afterward?”

“I called your touch in front of Quade and half this yard.”

“And when they said you gave it to me?”

“I thought the call was the answer.” Jasper looked toward the strip rather than
the rail. “I was wrong. I should have said it again when the story changed. I
should have said it every time someone made my honesty into your humiliation.”

Fiora had prepared for denial, chivalry, or some noble nonsense about wanting
her to leave with the badge. An admission fitted nowhere in her defenses.

“If I simply went to supper with you,” she said, “they would call that proof.
They would say you wanted me, so you spared me. And I wouldn't know which
version you believed. I would sit across a table wondering whether you saw me
or someone you had to be gentle with.”

Jasper met her eyes. “I do want you.”

Her fingers tightened around the cup.

“I also wanted to win that trial,” he continued. “You touched first. Both are
true.”

“And tonight?”

“Tonight I want to win. If I do, I get to ask one question and choose where we
eat. You can say no. You leave for East Weir at dawn. I have no claim on that,
or on a second supper, or on any day after tonight.” His expression shifted,
not quite a smile. “Though I reserve the right to be intolerably hopeful.”

It was, Fiora thought, remarkably unfair to become more attractive while
renouncing all rights to her.

Quade returned and offered Fiora her blade hilt-first. “You may agree to a draw.
You may surrender. You may continue. Separately, please, so neither of you can
hide inside the other's answer. Fiora?”

The easy refuge waited. A draw would leave her badge technically untouched and
her doubt perfectly preserved.

She took the blade. “Continue.”

Quade turned. “Jasper?”

Jasper took his. “Continue.”

Fiora lowered her eye guard. The truth of the old match could no longer be
proved by winning this one. It could only be tested by what they did when the
truth hurt.

***

They returned to their marks with two white scores on each coat.

Fiora heard the crowd settle behind the rail. She heard the river and the
supper fires and the faint clink of the buckle on her waiting travel case. The
world had become offensively full of things that would continue after the next
touch.

Quade raised one hand. “Ready.”

Fiora set her feet.

Jasper's blade hovered on the line that had defeated her high feint at the
opening. But his weight had shifted a degree lower. He was preparing for the
East Weir pivot now.

Good.

“Fence.”

Neither moved.

Jasper's eyebrows rose behind his guard.

“Mine say nothing,” Fiora told him.

“They say you intend something unkind.”

“That's not prediction. That's experience.”

He advanced.

The last exchange began almost quietly: blade to blade, a light scrape, two
measured steps. Jasper tested her outside line. Fiora gave him no answer. He
pressed again, quicker, and she turned the attack without taking the opening
that followed.

He knew her patience was borrowed. She knew his was a weapon.

Jasper changed pace. Fiora retreated once, twice, until the end mark brushed
beneath her heel. He expected her to spring high rather than be crowded off the
strip. She saw it in the angle of his guard, the answer waiting where it had
waited for her first attack.

So she began the new pivot.

She dropped her center. Jasper adjusted at once, blade falling to catch the low
turn that had scored against his ribs. Fiora let the motion carry halfway—then
drove upward, unwinding the pivot into the old high attack.

Surprise flashed across his face.

Not enough surprise.

Jasper recovered with brutal neatness. His low parry swept up as Fiora's point
cut toward his upper arm. Their shoulders crossed. For one compressed instant,
his body blocked Quade's view of both target panels.

Two chalked blades flexed.

Quade called halt.

Fiora froze with Jasper so close she could hear the catch in his breath. Her
blade rested against his upper-arm panel. His rested against the dark padding
over her ribs.

To the rail, the touches had been one sound.

To Quade, hidden by their crossing bodies, they had been one motion.

To Fiora, they had not.

She had felt Jasper's blade bow against her coat. She had seen white chalk
bloom at the lower edge of her vision. Half a beat later, her own edge had
drawn its line across his arm.

Jasper eased his blade away but said nothing. He looked at her, waiting.

Six months earlier, in this strip, he had stood where she stood. He had owned a
fraction of knowledge that could cost him the match, and he had spoken it.
Courtesy, Fiora understood at last, was not making the world painless for
someone. It was trusting them with the truth and trusting that they could bear
what came next.

She could say she did not know. Quade would order the point refenced. She might
win. The badge in her case might feel defended for an hour, perhaps even a
week.

And every time she looked at it, she would know what she had withheld.

“Jasper's touch landed first,” Fiora said.

The words passed through the yard with more force than a shout.

Jasper glanced once at the white mark on her ribs. He could have disputed her.
He could have performed generosity and handed the point back until neither of
them knew what anything meant.

Instead he nodded. “My touch first.”

Quade inspected both marks. He looked at Fiora, giving her room to correct or
withdraw the call.

She held his gaze. “The point is Jasper's.”

Quade straightened. “Touch, Jasper. Match to Jasper, three to two.”

For a moment no one behind the rail spoke. Then the applause came, less like a
victory roar than a release of breath.

Fiora lifted her guard. Jasper did the same. He was smiling, but not as a man
who had been awarded her company. He looked as she must have looked at the old
trial: astonished, relieved, and fiercely proud of the person who had beaten
him to the truth.

They saluted.

Quade carried the ledger to the rail and wrote the result in a firm hand:
Jasper, three; Fiora, two. Beneath the notation, he added the final touch as
self-called by Fiora. The old trial remained in its own place in the book:
Fiora, three; Jasper, two, with Jasper's call beside it.

Quade studied the two entries. “I withdraw my objection to the rematch.”

“Thank you,” Fiora said.

“I maintain every objection to your methods of conversation.”

“Also fair,” Jasper said.

***

The onlookers drifted toward the supper stalls, already arguing cheerfully
about the final exchange. Quade made Fiora and Jasper return their blades,
remove their guards, and submit to one last inspection before he would let
either of them near food.

“No damage except to judgment,” he pronounced.

“Whose?” Fiora asked.

“Mine, for officiating.” Quade shut the ledger. “The match is recorded. What
happens now is not.”

He walked away with enough determination to prove he was not about to arrange
the rest for them.

Fiora knelt by her travel case and checked the nearest buckle. Still fastened.
The cart would still come at dawn. East Weir's yard would still be hers to
lead. Losing had altered none of that.

Jasper stopped beside her. The chalk marks on his coat made him look like a
particularly elegant piece of disputed arithmetic.

“The bout is over,” he said. “Your answer belongs to you.”

Fiora stood.

He took a breath. This, apparently, frightened him more than facing her blade.
The discovery was so charming she almost rescued him, then decided equality
required letting him suffer properly.

“Fiora Halwick,” Jasper said, “would you have supper with me at the riverside
stalls tonight? One supper. I choose the place; you choose whether to come. You
leave for East Weir at dawn either way.”

There it was: no ritual left to speak for him, no point pretending the question
was anything but a hope placed carefully in her hands.

“Yes,” Fiora said. “Because I want to.”

His whole face changed.

“You may choose the stall,” she added, “but if you choose the one that burns
the onions, I reserve the right to regret my consent.”

“Continued consent was explicitly covered.”

“Good. You were listening.”

They left the yard in their chalk-marked practice coats, Fiora carrying the
travel case and Jasper carrying both guards. At the riverside, canvas awnings
snapped above iron cooking plates. Warm bread steamed in baskets. The lamps
along the pilings laid wavering paths across the dark water.

Jasper selected a stall where the onions were merely browned. He bought two
folded breads full of vegetables and sharp cheese, then waited until Fiora had
chosen a bench before sitting beside her.

The date began with her stealing one of his crispest onions.

“When may I visit East Weir?” he asked.

Fiora chewed thoughtfully. She could picture the new yard's narrow strip, the
awkward pillars, the rack waiting to be filled. She could picture herself at
its center in the head instructor's coat she had earned. Jasper belonged
nowhere in that picture unless invited, which made room for wanting him there.

“When you've devised a respectable counter to my pivot,” she said.

“I countered it.”

“Eventually. After it scored.”

“Then I may need a rematch.”

“You may need several.” Fiora raised her supper in salute. “Come prepared to
lose three to two.”

Jasper touched his folded bread to hers with grave courtesy. “I'll come
prepared to call what lands first.”

Fiora smiled and took another bite. Dawn would carry her east. Tonight, beside
the river, neither of them asked it to wait.

stories.title: The Last Thing I Could Fix
stories.prompt: You are a legendary blacksmith, sought out for your ability to fix anything. Talking swords, obsidian breastplates, staves made of crystal, daggers forged from dragon scales, you've done it all. The real challenge today is a young hero asking you to fix what they call their 'plot armor'.
stories.body:
# The Last Thing I Could Fix

I had corrected the manners of talking swords, which is harder than sharpening them and only slightly easier than convincing their owners to pay. I had mended obsidian breastplates without turning their wearers into pincushions of black glass. I had spliced crystal staves whose two halves disagreed about the direction of lightning. I had even reset the scales on dragon-scale daggers, a task best undertaken after establishing whether the dragon was finished with them.

In short, I was Hadrik, and I fixed anything.

The sign over my forge said so. The words were cut deep enough to outlive me and gilded thick enough to suggest they might. Travelers came up the valley to point at it, then at some impossible wreck in a velvet box. Nothing left my bench until it did what its maker had intended.

That last part was not on the sign. At the time, I thought it too obvious to carve.

Aven arrived in a thunderstorm with a bundle under one arm and bloodless determination holding their young face together. Water ran from their hair, their sleeves, and the toe of one split boot. They put the bundle on my bench. Scorched metal showed through the wrapping.

“I need you to fix my plot armor.”

I waited for the grin. Aven did not provide one.

“That is what the court chroniclers call it,” they said. “Because it keeps the hero alive for the next great deed.”

“Chroniclers,” I said. “Of course. Smiths call things by what they are. Chroniclers call them by what rhymes with the wine.”

I unwrapped a close-fitted under-harness: small overlapping plates, a mesh of silver-gray response wire, and enough scorch marks to trouble me. Then the reservoir bell sounded uphill, one iron note rolling beneath the thunder.

Aven told me the relief gate had jammed. The reservoir was climbing toward the rim. On their first attempt, a gate bolt had torn loose above them. Their guide had reached out—and the harness had dragged the guide beneath the falling iron. The bolt broke the guide’s leg instead of Aven’s back.

“They told me to try again alone,” Aven said. “Nothing near me for the armor to hurt.”

“A practical solution, if one is a wheelbarrow.”

“I am not wearing it again until I understand what it does.”

That was the first sensible thing anyone had said about the harness, myself included. I still gave the answer expected of a legend.

“You will have it by midday.”

The reservoir bell sounded again before the echo of my promise had died.

Off Aven’s body, the harness was as magical as a soup pot. I laid it in salt, passed a lodestone over every plate, warmed it by the forge and cooled it in rainwater. Nothing answered. The response wire held a faint stored tension, but no heat, pulse, or motion of its own.

“It needs someone living,” I said. “Likely you. Put it on.”

Aven’s hands stopped at the buckles.

“We test with cloth, not gate bolts,” I said. “And I stop when you say.”

They searched my face long enough to make me glad I had said it plainly. Then they stripped off their wet coat and fitted the harness over their shirt.

I blackened every wire junction with soot and hung a sack of rags from a ceiling chain. It made a gentle pendulum, by heroic standards. By mine, it was still a weight moving toward a client.

“Do nothing,” I told Aven. “I will catch it.”

I drew the sack back. Aven nodded. I let go.

The sack swung. Nothing warmed in advance, no invisible hand tipped it aside. The canvas touched the center plate with a padded thud.

Only then did the wire tighten.

A rivet at Aven’s sternum flashed hot. A line of lampblack leapt outward along one narrow hook. I had planted my boots and sworn to hold still, but some older part of me saw a young person in danger and reached before pride could stop it.

That reach completed the open circuit.

My arm jerked across Aven’s chest and into the sack’s path. I caught the chain with my other hand before the returning weight could crack my elbow. The pendulum had not swerved by a finger’s width. I had.

Aven went pale. “That was how the guide moved.”

I examined the hot center rivet under a lens. A hairline split ran through the metal and left its tiny assent gate jammed open. The outward hooks were made to take the intention of a nearby protector, but the choice rivet was supposed to admit only someone who actively joined the circuit. Cracked, it could turn a flinch, a reach, the bare wish that Aven not be hurt, into a bodily pull.

The wire had not foreseen the sack. It stayed cold until contact. Then Aven’s alarm and my protective reflex supplied the current, and the open circuit routed the pull through me as the nearer shield.

I drove ceramic wedges beneath the witness hooks and swung the sack again. It struck. The plates cinched hard around Aven; the split rivet heated; but the soot stopped at the blocked hooks, and I did not move.

There are diagnoses one enjoys being right about. This was not one of them.

“The central rivet is split,” I said. “I can drill it out, forge another, and reconnect the hooks. With the assent catch sound, it will take only a willing protector. Two hours.”

I reached for my smallest punch.

“No.”

“It is the proper repair.”

“It is the same purpose with a better latch.” Aven touched the reddened cloth over their sternum. “The latch broke once.”

“Everything breaks once. Most things make a career of it.”

“Then I won’t wear a thing whose failure turns people into shields.”

Outside, rain hissed on my chimney cap. I looked at the sign through the open forge door, its gold letters blurred by water. Anything fixed. A promise is an excellent servant until it hears a deadline; then it becomes a magistrate.

“The adults below expect that harness to bring their hero back,” I said.

“They expect me to go where they won’t because they think it has always brought me back.” Aven swallowed. “I don’t know how many times somebody else moved because of it. I don’t know which victories were mine.”

That landed harder than the sack had.

“The armor did not climb the road for you,” I said. “It did not learn the gate or decide to return here. But it changed who paid when things went wrong.” I put down the punch. “Tell me what fixed means.”

Aven looked surprised. So was I.

“It means I choose what I do,” they said. “It means nobody else pays unless they know the price and say yes. It means if it can’t save me honestly, it doesn’t pretend it can.”

The reservoir bell began ringing in strokes of three.

“That,” I said, “is a much slower repair.”

“Can you do it?”

“I did carve the sign very deeply.”

I cut away the witness hooks. One curved piece—the old bypass hook—could bridge an assent gate without a rivet and leave the outward path permanently open. I coiled it and dropped it into my tool roll, because smiths save dangerous scraps with the faith that labeling them dangerous makes us wise. Then I unfolded the response braid, turned every other outward path inward, and stitched it back through the plates.

The split choice rivet came out under my drill in bright curls. In its place I forged a will-catch: one contact beneath Aven’s sternum, one beneath the palm of their working hand. Aven stood beside the quench trough with their fingers on both while I tempered the fitted circuit. Their intent ran warm through the wire; my tongs and fire shaped it but supplied none of their own.

Last, I forged three rivets from soft iron, heated them to straw, then violet, then the blue of deep water. I set them where overload would break them before the braid could seek another body or hide the strain.

“Three hard uses,” I said. “Visible ones. After the third, this becomes rather uncomfortable ordinary armor.”

“What counts as a use?”

“First, danger must actually touch you. No warning. You must be conscious, understand the motion, press the will-catch, and say what you choose to do. One verb. One direction. The braid will brace that line for about one breath.”

“And the force?”

“Still exists. It spreads through the plates and through you. A blow from the side remains a blow from the side. Too much force will injure or kill you, whether the rivets have admired your courage or not.”

Aven gave the three blue heads a sober glance. “Better.”

I retained one outward loop of copper, isolated from the rest. “A second person may share the load by taking this consent ring with bare skin and saying yes, then and there. Let go, and the join ends. No stored permission. No borrowed reflex.”

We tested the redesign before trusting a town to it.

First I swung the padded sack slowly. Aven watched it come and stepped aside. It passed them. Nothing warmed; nothing pulled. They laughed once, mostly from surprise.

Then they returned to the mark. The sack touched the breastplate.

Aven pressed sternum and palm. “Stand.”

The inward braid lit beneath its soot. The plates drew tight along the line from their boots to their shoulders. The sack drove them back half a step and left a bruise they would feel by supper. It did not throw them. One blue rivet snapped with a crack like a seed in flame.

My arms remained entirely my own.

For the consent check, I gripped the copper ring while Aven leaned into a lightly padded press. They said, “Stand.” The mesh warmed around them. The ring stayed cold in my hand.

“Yes,” I said.

Heat crossed my palm, mild but unmistakable, and the resistance divided between us until I let go. The remaining two rivets stayed blue.

The bell above us rang three strokes again, with less silence between each set.

I packed my hammer, wedges, and tool roll.

“You said I would have it by midday,” Aven said.

“You have it.” I tied on my rain cloak. “I did not say you would have the poor judgment to field an unproven redesign without its smith.”

I had serviced the spillgate years before, an ordinary job of rust, hinges, and a locking wedge that swelled every wet season. Less glamorous than dragon scales. Considerably more useful that morning.

The path climbed beside the relief channel. Rain had turned its stones black and slick, and water boomed behind the reservoir wall like something enormous objecting to architecture. Aven led. They knew where the first attempt had torn loose railings and which stair had split.

Halfway across the upper catwalk, a support gave way under me.

There was no omen. One moment I had iron under both boots. The next, the bracket peeled from wet stone and the walkway dropped. I caught the rail with one hand. My hammer dragged at my belt while the relief channel hammered below.

Aven turned. For one naked instant, they stood perfectly still.

They were waiting for rescue to happen.

Nothing did. The wire could not choose. The old hooks were gone. The harness offered no warning and took no one’s body.

Then Aven saw me, saw the intact support behind them, and made a decision.

They dropped flat, hooked one knee around the support, and caught my wrist. The load struck their shoulder. They pressed the will-catch against the rail with their free hand.

“Catch.”

The braid braced backward along their chosen pull. Aven hauled; I kicked against the wall; together we got my chest over the broken edge. The second rivet sheared.

When the breath ended, Aven rolled onto their back with their injured arm clutched close.

“Shoulder?” I asked.

“Strained.” Their face said more than the word did.

I checked the joint as gently as my hands allowed. Painful, still placed. I looked at the single blue rivet remaining.

“We can go back,” I said.

Below the clouds, the valley town was a huddle of slate roofs beside a river already too broad for its banks. Aven stared down at it.

“The armor didn’t make me catch you,” they said.

“No.”

“And it didn’t make me freeze.”

“No. That habit came from people teaching you rescue was automatic.”

They flexed their good hand. “Then I can learn a different one.”

We went on.

The relief gate shuddered in its stone throat. Water sprayed through every seam. The release bar had jammed halfway, exactly where rust had always loved it, and the locking wedge beneath it had swollen fast. Worse, the final retaining bracket was peeling from the wall. Each surge bent it farther. When it tore free, the bar would kick loose and the gate would stay shut until the reservoir overtopped.

I laid out the work. Aven would brace beneath the release bar while I drove the wedge through its lock. When the wedge seated, the gate would fall open toward the empty relief channel. We would both drop left, behind the stone pier, before the first water struck.

“One rivet,” Aven said.

“One breath,” I agreed.

“Will it work?”

The old answer rose easily. Of course. Hadrik fixed anything. The words even sounded like courage if one did not inspect them closely.

“It can work,” I said. “The upward load is within the design. The bar may twist. Your shoulder is already strained. I cannot promise either of us leaves unhurt.”

“Can we retreat?”

“Yes.” The bracket shrieked. “We would probably live. The lower town would flood.”

Aven shut their eyes. When they opened them, there was fear in them and room beside it for thought.

“I’m not doing this because the court called me a hero,” they said. “I’m doing it because I know what happens if we leave, and because you told me the truth.”

“You may still say no.”

“So may you.”

That was the soundest safety rule either of us had made.

We took our places.

The release bar slammed down until it met Aven’s raised hands. Contact first. Metal groaned against metal. Aven perceived the direction and set their boots. They flattened their working palm beneath the bar, compressing that contact against the iron, and leaned into the breastplate until the second contact seated beneath their sternum. Their other hand never left the bar.

“Hold.”

The last blue rivet began to whiten at its edge. The inward braid tightened from Aven’s palms through their back and legs. They cried out as the real weight spread through them, but the bar stopped descending.

I swung my hammer.

The first blow cracked rust. The second moved the locking wedge the breadth of a thumbnail. The gate shifted under water pressure—not down, but sideways.

Aven’s protection held the upward line they had chosen. It did nothing about the lateral wrench. Their strained shoulder buckled toward the wall.

One breath was not enough.

My tool roll lay open at my knee. The old bypass hook gleamed among the wedges. I could jam it across the empty assent seat in a heartbeat. The open path would seize the nearest protective impulse—mine—and turn my body into whatever brace the harness required. It was the old guarantee, close enough to touch. I could preserve the legend and call the coercion sacrifice afterward.

I dropped the hook.

Instead I tore off my glove and seized the copper consent ring.

“Yes,” I said. Not forever. Not for the court. “Yes, now.”

The ring burned into my palm.

My living intent joined Aven’s for that single hold, and the fitted wire divided the upward strain between us. It did not erase the sideways force. Aven’s shoulder still took that; my hand took heat enough to make the hammer swim in my vision. But their knees stopped folding. The whitening rivet endured one moment longer.

I struck the wedge a third time.

It seated.

The release bar leapt. The gate dropped open. Water roared into the empty channel, exactly where stone and old iron had directed it, not where luck preferred. The third rivet sheared. The response braid flashed once and fused black against the plates.

“Left!” I shouted.

We fell behind the pier as planned. The first wall of water tore through the place where we had stood, carrying rust, branches, and the discarded bypass hook down the safe channel.

For some time there was only stone under my cheek, rain on my back, and Aven’s breathing beside me.

Then the reservoir bell changed to the long, steady toll for water falling.

We had opened the gate. The lower town remained a town rather than becoming a shallow and badly planned lake. Aven could walk, though their shoulder needed a sling. I kept my burned hand wrapped against my chest. The harness hung from them as dead weight: all three blue rivets broken, the response wire fused, no warmth left anywhere in it.

Back at the forge, I laid the harness on my bench.

“Failed repair,” I said.

Aven, pale with exhaustion and dry at last, looked at me as if I had announced that anvils were migratory birds.

“It did exactly what I chose,” they said. “It stopped when you said it would. It charged nobody who hadn’t agreed.”

“The wire is ruined.”

“Then it spent itself honestly.”

I had spent my life returning objects to what their makers intended. It had never occurred to me that an intention might deserve refusal, or that a thing could be fixed by giving it an honorable way to end.

“I could make another,” I said. The offer came from habit, but not entirely. “More rivets. A stronger braid.”

Aven shook their head. “Ordinary mail. A crew. A plan. And the right to refuse the next great deed before anyone starts writing about it.”

“Ordinary mail I can guarantee against reasonable stabbing.”

“Reasonable stabbing?”

“The sign is under revision.”

The next morning, with my good hand and a narrow chisel, I climbed a ladder outside the forge. The gilding came away first. Then the wood. I cut the word *anything* out of the promise I had made so deeply.

In the space beneath, in smaller letters because truth is seldom brief, I carved: *Before I take the job, I will tell you what the repair can do and what it will cost.*

The new sign brought fewer velvet boxes. It brought better questions.

I remained Hadrik. I remained a blacksmith. I fixed many things after that, though never everything, and never by myself merely because my name was over the door.

The plot armor was the last thing I ever claimed I could fix alone.

stories.title: The Last Bus to Briar Hill
stories.prompt: A fairytale about going on an adventure but set in modern day.
stories.body:
# The Last Bus to Briar Hill

At 12:47 a.m., with rain ticking against her helmet and somebody’s noodles
cooling in the insulated box on her back, Miriam Velez promised her brother an
adventure for the thirty-second time.

“After this month,” she said into her headset, braking at a red light. “Rent
first. Briar Hill when things settle down.”

Mateo was quiet long enough for the courier app to offer her a surge block:
three deliveries, guaranteed bonus, accept within twenty seconds.

“Things don’t settle down,” he said.

“They do if people stop adding emergencies.”

She regretted it before the words had finished leaving her mouth. Fifteen was
old enough to hear the accusation inside a joke. Miriam watched rain polish the
empty intersection. Her battery showed thirty-one percent; the offer counted
down from twelve.

“I didn’t mean you,” she said.

“You never do.”

The call ended. Miriam accepted the block.

She delivered the noodles to a lobby bright as an aquarium, photographed the
paper bag beneath the apartment number, and turned her bicycle toward the next
pickup. The bonus would cover the short edge of rent. That was not imaginary.
Neither were the electric bill, Mateo’s growing feet, or the fact that two years
ago their mother had died on a dry road in ordinary traffic while going
somewhere she had gone a hundred times before.

Briar Hill had been their mother’s idea. The old voicemail was still saved
offline on Miriam’s phone: traffic hissing behind her voice, a bus number
remembered wrong, then laughter interrupting the promise that they would all go
up to the hill together—

Miriam never played the final second. There was no final second, only breath
and laughter cut off by the recording limit.

Her phone chimed.

The message had been scheduled rather than sent live. Mateo had used the safety
check-in settings Miriam had taught him.

*I found our adventure. I researched the route. Location is on. If I’m not back
by sunrise, follow it. I’m sorry.*

Below the message, his live-location pin moved along the last ordinary bus line
toward their apartment.

Miriam called. No answer. She called again while riding hard enough that rain
needled through her gloves. The pin crossed the municipal bus terminal, paused
at its western shelter, then acquired a transit label she had never seen:
`Route 0`.

She opened the city app one-handed at the next light. There was no Route 0.
Mateo’s pin moved north along two streets that ran parallel, crossed a canal
without using either bridge, and vanished into a gray patch where the map stored
no road at all.

Miriam pulled over beneath a leaking awning and inspected everything the fear
in her wanted to skip. Mateo had packed his transit card and rain shell. His
location sharing had been switched from one hour to indefinite. The safety
message had been written that afternoon and scheduled for the last ordinary
service of the night. He had not stumbled onto the route or been snatched from
his bed. He had planned an adventure using every emergency precaution she had
taught him, except the one where he asked permission.

The courier app vibrated: *Proceed to pickup. Late arrival may affect your
standing.*

Miriam swung west.

The terminal shelter was empty when she arrived. The last scheduled bus had
gone. Sodium lamps burned through the downpour, making every drop look briefly
solid. She locked her bicycle to a rack and discovered Mateo’s green charging
cord was missing from the side pocket of her delivery box. He had taken that
too. Planning, not panic.

A pair of headlights appeared where the terminal lane ended at a concrete
wall.

An unmarked white bus rolled out of the rain. It was old enough to have square
windows and new enough to carry a contactless fare reader. Its front display
held a plain service label: `Route 0`.

The doors folded open under the driver’s hand.

The woman behind the wheel wore a charcoal coat over an ordinary transit
uniform. Silver hair brushed her jaw. A brass name badge read **Maude Dallow**.

“You are late,” she said.

“Where is Mateo Velez?”

“Ahead of you.”

Miriam put one wet shoe on the step.

Maude raised two fingers. The fare reader remained dark. “Not yet. You should
understand what you’re choosing.”

“I’m choosing my brother.”

“You are trying to choose two destinations.” Maude glanced at the courier
countdown glowing on Miriam’s phone. “This crossing opens for a person willing
to leave the destination the city already expects. Cancel it. Name whom you
seek. Pay the usual fare. There are three request stops before Briar Hill and
one return at sunrise. Miss that return, and I promise nothing.”

“This is a bus.”

“Yes. Metal, glass, wiring. None of it is alive, and none of it makes bargains.”
Maude laid her palm against the fare reader. Fine green light traveled from the
creases of her hand into its black screen. “I tend this end of the crossing.
The Briar Host tends the Hill. The bus carries what I give it. It decides
nothing.”

The courier timer showed forty-three seconds. Miriam could board, find Mateo,
and preserve the block if she hurried. The thought lasted until Maude looked at
her.

“Unchosen destinations do not count as abandoned,” Maude said.

Miriam opened the courier app. *Canceling after acceptance forfeits the
guarantee and may reduce future offers.* Her thumb hovered. Rent first, she had
said, as though fear had never hidden behind arithmetic.

She canceled the block.

“Mateo Velez,” she said, and tapped her ordinary fare card.

The reader chimed because Maude’s green light had awakened it. The doors closed
at her touch. Maude drove into the terminal wall.

For one instant the windshield held only wet concrete. Then Maude pressed her
hand to the wheel, green light ran beneath its vinyl, and the bus passed into a
street Miriam had never seen.

Thorn hedges crowded the sidewalks. Rain shone on them like strings of beads.
Behind the glass, the city still appeared in fragments—laundromat, tower block,
all-night pharmacy—but never in an order any map would accept.

At the first request stop, an exhausted woman in scrubs stood beneath a broken
shelter with a dead phone in both hands. Maude braked and opened the doors.

“Finally,” the woman said, climbing aboard. “I need to call my client again.
The first call dropped. Then the regular service disappeared from the board,
so I have to tell her what changed.”

She was real: rain-reddened eyes, plastic grocery bag, an identity card turned
backward on its clip. No crown beneath her hood, no bird feet, nothing from a
storybook. Just someone stranded between night shifts.

“We continue when she has made her call,” Maude said.

Miriam’s phone showed Mateo’s location frozen somewhere ahead. Twenty-four
percent remained in the power bank clipped inside her delivery box. Enough to
keep tracking him—or enough to lend.

“How long does that call have to be?” Miriam asked.

“Long enough for someone waiting to know she has not been forgotten.”

Miriam almost laughed. Instead she pulled out the power bank.

The woman’s phone drank charge slowly. One percent, then two. Miriam watched
Mateo’s pin fail to refresh and imagined sunrise bleaching an empty hill.

At three percent, the woman made the call. “I’m safe,” she said, hunching over
the borrowed power. “We got cut off. The service changed. I’m still coming.
Lock the door until I buzz.”

She stayed connected until the person at the other end understood the new
arrival time. By then, the power bank had fallen to nine percent.

When she finished, she unwound a green cord from her phone and held it out.

“A boy lent me this at the last bus,” she said. “He said his sister would be
angry if he gave away the power bank too.”

Miriam took Mateo’s cord. Warmth from the woman’s phone still clung to the
connector.

“Which way did he go?”

“Up the steps beside the stop. He waited until my first call connected.” The
woman looked from Miriam to Maude. “Said he was going to finish something.”

Maude drove on after the woman transferred at an ordinary lit corner. Within a
block, rain erased the corner from view.

Miriam connected her own phone to the power bank. Its remaining charge kept
Mateo’s location trace and the municipal text service running until the thorn
ring road came into view. Then the bank’s indicator lights went dark.

“The Briar Host makes copies,” Maude said. “Stored maps. Old signs. Anything a
screen or a memory has already shown within its hedge.”

“Why are you telling me?”

“Because a test with no rule is only cruelty.” Maude watched the road. “The
Briar Host can repeat what it has received. It cannot forge a new reply freely
made outside the crossing after you entered.”

The thorn hedges opened onto a ring road divided into three identical exits.
Each sign said **BRIAR HILL**. Each navigation preview on Miriam’s phone showed
the same blue line. Rain struck all three roads at the same angle, and beneath
each sign stood a municipal stop placard.

The numbers differed.

Miriam enlarged the map, but the roads crawled and exchanged places under her
fingertip. She held to Maude’s rule: the Briar Host could repeat stored images,
and some such copy was reaching the screens and signs. The phone itself was
only displaying what reached it.

“You have six minutes,” Maude said.

“Until what?”

“Until this stop becomes your destination.”

Miriam knew the municipal text service because couriers used it when the app’s
arrival times lied. She sent the three stop codes in one message. Two automated
replies returned at once, both naming ordinary neighborhoods miles apart. The
third request passed to a late-night responder.

The battery fell to eleven percent.

*Stop 4312: Briar Hill park entrance. Temporary service access only. No
scheduled pickup at this hour.*

A current reply, written beyond the hedge. By Maude’s rule, the Briar Host
could not have stored it before she asked.

“Middle exit,” Miriam said.

Maude turned the wheel. The other two roads folded behind curtains of thorn,
as though the Briar Host had drawn its hedge closed behind them. The bus
continued along the only strip of wet municipal asphalt underneath.

The third request stop was a closed shopping concourse. Steel grilles covered
the storefronts. A children’s ride sat unplugged beside a vending machine.
Maude opened the doors.

“I don’t see anyone,” Miriam said.

“Truth is waiting,” Maude replied. “It usually does. The Briar Host will shape
what reaches your eyes and ears from material already stored here. An offer is
not a person. An imitation is not an answer from the dead.”

As Miriam stepped down, her phone screen filled with notifications.

*Bonus reinstated. Return to pickup.*

Then a message marked as Mateo’s: *All clear. Went home. Don’t follow.*

Then an incoming voicemail bearing their mother’s old number.

Miriam stopped under the dead strip lights.

She knew. Knowing did not stop her hand from shaking.

She pressed play.

Her mother’s voice came smooth and near, without traffic or breath. “Miriam,
sweetheart, you were right. Loving someone means keeping them away from danger.
Go home. Mateo is safe if you stop.”

Warm kitchen light spilled from a storefront. Beyond the grille stood the old
table, the chipped yellow bowl, their mother in the raincoat from her last
photograph. The glamour smiled with her mouth.

Miriam held to Maude’s warning. It was not a ghost. It was not their mother
restored, nor a living copy of her. What confronted her was a sensory lure
assembled from cached photographs, recordings, and whatever grief supplied
when a shape was almost right.

Almost was terrible.

Miriam opened the authentic voicemail saved on her phone. Four percent.

Traffic hissed. Their mother said the wrong bus number, corrected herself,
laughed, and began, “We’ll take sandwiches up to Briar Hill when—”

The recording ended inside the laugh.

The kitchen imitation had no room for error. It offered certainty in her
mother’s voice because certainty was what Miriam had wanted from the dead.

“Money matters,” Miriam said into the empty concourse. “Rent matters. But it
isn’t why I keep saying later.”

The false kitchen waited.

“She died going somewhere ordinary. I thought if I chose anything unnecessary,
anything happy, it would be like asking the road to take somebody else.”

The confession did not make the fear foolish. It made the fear hers. Mateo had
been paying for it without ever agreeing to the debt.

Her phone went black.

For one breath Miriam stood without maps, messages, work, or the saved voice.
Then the kitchen light vanished. Steel grilles became steel grilles again, and
the mother-shaped lure broke into reflections on wet tile. Miriam could only
take the timing as the Briar Host’s reply.

Maude opened the bus doors. “Now you know what you came to finish.”
