At Maude’s last green-lit turn, she said, “The Briar Host is opening the Hill.”
A hedge drew aside. Briar Hill rose behind the last row of apartment towers,
though Miriam had never seen a hill there before. The rain thinned near its
crown. Roots surfaced through the pavement and braided themselves into steps,
lifting one after another as though something beneath the soil flexed.

Mateo stood at the top with his hood down and wet curls plastered to his
forehead.

Miriam ran. She stopped one arm’s length from him, because the urge to seize
him was so strong it felt like falling.

“You came,” he said.

“You left.”

“I sent the safety message. I shared my location.”

“You took an impossible bus after midnight.”

“Because if I asked, you would have said after this month.”

Both facts struck cleanly. Neither canceled the other.

Behind Mateo, a trunk wider than the bus shelter divided into the suggestion
of shoulders. Thousands of thorn twigs lifted and settled with a sound like
quiet applause. Two green hollows opened in the bark.

The Briar Host was alive. Miriam felt its attention move through root and leaf,
patient and immense.

“I didn’t get an exception,” Mateo said. “I was on the last ordinary bus home.
At the terminal, I canceled the saved trip in the city app even though I’d
promised to be home when your block ended. I named Miriam Velez. I tapped my
transit card and paid the normal fare.”

His eyes dropped. “I got the aide’s first call connected. At the false exits, I
requested the stop codes after we crossed the terminal wall. The fresh reply
came from outside, the way Maude said it had to. And I said no when it showed
me our mother.”

Pride arrived tangled with anger. Miriam let both remain.

“You still scared me.”

“You scare me too,” he said. “Every time you act like keeping me alive is the
same as us having a life.”

He rubbed rain from his eyes. “The posts about Briar Hill said it finished
promises. I thought maybe it could finish her voicemail. Not bring her back. I
knew that wasn’t—” His voice caught. “I thought there might be one real thing
she meant to say.”

The Briar Host bent its living branches low. “I know only what was brought
within my hedge. I can arrange stored sound. I cannot make your mother choose
new words, and I cannot turn an arrangement into her.”

Mateo nodded. Grief moved over his face without taking his decision away. “So I
said no to the thing it made.”

Miriam looked at the brightening edge of the sky. “I am taking him home.”

The Briar Host’s branches leaned toward her.

“That is not yours to complete,” it said. Its voice came from living wood, not
from the bus, the dead phone, or the wind. “This road grows toward promises
left unfinished at my Hill. I can complete a beginning. I cannot restore your
dead, and I cannot choose a living rider’s return.”

Mateo folded his arms.

“I’m sorry,” Miriam said.

He looked startled.

“I’m sorry I made later do the work of no. I’m sorry I made you test whether
I’d follow. And I’m angry that you made me.”

“I’m sorry for that part,” Mateo said. “Not for coming.”

“I know.”

“If I come home, you don’t get to call tonight proof I can never choose
anything.”

“And you don’t get to call precautions permission.”

“Okay.”

It was not forgiveness tied in a ribbon. It was a boundary they could carry in
both directions.

The Briar Host opened the hedge. A bridge of slick roots crossed a dark cut in
the hillside to the road where Maude had parked the bus. The sky above the
apartments had gone from black to iron gray.

“Will you finish the last path with me?” Miriam asked. “Then will you come
home?”

Mateo studied her face, giving the question the time a real choice required.
“Yes. If we schedule the next adventure before you accept another block.”

“Yes.”

They stepped onto the bridge.

Mateo led. His research had taught him that the roots with pale undersides were
new growth and would bend; he tested the dark, rain-hardened ones before
shifting his weight. Halfway across, a broken span opened above the cut.

“I crossed it when there were more roots,” he said.

The Briar Host drew those roots deeper into the hill. It would supply the test,
not the answer.

Miriam opened her delivery box. The power bank was empty, the food compartment
smelled of rain, and a length of repair cord remained beneath her tools. She
looped it around a stone post on their side, pulled twice, and tied the other
end around her waist.

“You know the anchors,” Mateo said.

“You know the path. Tell me where to put my feet.”

He pointed to a black root below the lip. Miriam lowered herself onto it,
crossed the gap, and braced the cord around the far trunk. Mateo followed. When
his wet shoe slipped, he caught the line; when the anchor shifted, Miriam
leaned back with all her weight. Neither hauled the other across. Each made the
other’s next choice possible.

At the far end, the Briar Host cast one last glamour across the road.

The warm kitchen appeared with two empty chairs drawn out. Their mother stood
between them, whole and dry, holding the yellow bowl. No demand this time. Only
the invitation to stop before leaving.

Mateo’s hand found Miriam’s.

“It showed me this before,” he whispered.

“I know what it is.”

“Me too.”

They walked through. The false kitchen scattered into rain, its borrowed light
withdrawing into the Briar Host’s hedge.

Maude opened the bus doors. Mateo boarded first by his own choice. Miriam
followed by hers.

Sunrise touched the thorns.

The Briar Host closed the Hill end of the crossing, and Maude drove the bus
through the narrowing gap. Her green light moved from her hands through the
wheel and along the window frames. Outside, impossible streets aligned one by
one with ordinary city blocks.

At 6:08 a.m., Maude stopped at the western terminal shelter. Rainwater lay in
the gutters. Commuters had not yet arrived.

Miriam’s fare card showed one ordinary charge. Mateo’s location history ended
at the terminal, resumed briefly beside an unlisted park access, and stopped
when his battery had died. The evidence looked like bad service and bad
judgment because most of it was.

Before they stepped down, Maude held out a flat brown token punched in the
shape of a leaf.

“The Briar Host grew it after you chose the return,” she said. “It completes
beginnings, not wishes. Plant it if you like.”

Miriam put it in Mateo’s palm.

“Ms. Dallow,” he said, “will Route 0 come again?”

“I promised one return,” Maude said. “Do not embroider that into two.”

They got off. Maude closed the doors and drove the bus into the thinning rain,
her hands steady on the wheel.

At home, charging cables revived their phones but repaired nothing else.
Miriam’s app recorded an abandoned block, removed the guaranteed bonus, and
warned that fewer offers might follow. The rent remained short. Her jacket
dripped onto the floor, her bicycle needed a new brake pad, and their mother
remained dead.

Miriam and Mateo sat at the kitchen table until the windows paled. They agreed
that safety messages were not permission to vanish. They agreed that fear was
not permission to make every decision alone. Mateo accepted a week without
unsupervised night trips. Miriam opened their shared calendar.

Together, they chose a Saturday morning two weeks away: municipal bus, free
greenhouse, packed lunch, home before dark. The leaf-punched token lay in a
flowerpot beside the window. It did nothing.

Two weeks later, the lost bonus still mattered. Miriam had taken extra midday
deliveries, and the numbers in her banking app remained unfriendly. Rain
threatened again. Every practiced part of her wanted to say they should wait.

Instead she zipped sandwiches into her cleaned delivery bag.

Mateo checked the ordinary bus time. Miriam locked the apartment. They left
together.

When they returned that afternoon with damp sleeves and an empty sandwich bag,
Miriam found the token split open in the flowerpot. A green shoot, small enough
to shelter beneath one raindrop, had pushed into the light.

stories.title: The Attendance Ledger
stories.prompt: A school teacher moonlights as a handler for magical girls, looking after their wellbeing in battle and the classroom, even protecting the girls' secret identities without alerting them.
stories.body:
# The Attendance Ledger

By the third name on the paper attendance ledger, Gideon Tolland knew exactly
how much sleep three of his students had not had.

Northbridge Secondary’s network had chosen community-showcase day to display a
spinning circle instead of the online register, so Gideon was using the paper
backup. The ledger was a grey administrative object with coffee feathered
along one corner. It possessed no insight. Gideon supplied the dangerous part
himself.

“Drita Ademi?”

“Present.”

Drita held her left wrist close to her body. The cuff of her uniform jumper
covered most of the bruise, but not the careful way she turned each page with
her right hand. Her fingertips were pale with cold.

“Bryn Ahn?”

“Here.”

Bryn had already drawn two routes out of the problem on the lab sheet, although
the problem concerned mineral samples and neither route was required. Her
pencil trembled once, stopped under the pressure of her thumb, then continued.

“Cassia Dominguez?”

“Physically.”

The class laughed. Cassia offered them a thin grin and lowered her face over
her folded arms.

Gideon marked all three present. At one seventeen that morning, in the
voice-scrambled privacy of an encrypted radio relay, Kiteglass had reported a
bad wrist and loss of body heat. Pulsewire had said that lights still had halos
after two difficult severances. Mothlight had joked twice as fast as usual,
which had been the clearest report of all.

Night Clerk had recommended a recovery day. The three girls had chosen school.

Mr. Tolland, who had no legitimate way to connect those reports to these
students, had prepared accordingly.

“Before anyone asks,” he told the class, “the revision token on the board is
for everyone. One deadline, moved once, no justification required. Lab roles
rotate every twelve minutes. The snack box is not charity; it is protection
against the paperwork generated by fainting.”

That earned a better laugh. He passed the box along the benches. Cassia took
two oat bars without looking up. Drita accepted one after seeing three other
students do it. Bryn chose the role nearest the door.

Kindness was easiest to disguise as policy.

Gideon had not meant to learn their secret. Six months earlier, three
voice-scrambled strangers had asked for practical help over an emergency-radio
frequency: routes, weather, first-aid supplies, someone to notice when brave
became reckless. They had named him Night Clerk as a joke, and the name had
stuck.

Then he had seen three transformed figures disappear into an alley and Drita,
Bryn, and Cassia emerge moments later. After that came matching absences,
matching injuries, Drita’s angle-cutting hand signal, Bryn’s insistence on two
exits, Cassia’s habit of making a joke before admitting fear. No single clue
had proved anything. Together, they left almost no room for him to be wrong.

He had kept that knowledge to himself. Their anonymity was not a puzzle he had
earned the right to solve.

“Feet on the floor,” he said. “Before we begin, five things you can see, four
you can feel, three you can hear. Yes, this is educational. I have declared it
so.”

The room settled by degrees. Cassia’s shoulders lowered. Gideon reached the
next line of his ledger.

From the ventilation grate above Drita came a papery whisper.

“Kiteglass?”

Drita’s head began to turn.

Gideon let the ledger fall.

It struck the floor flat, loud as a slammed door. Pages slewed beneath his
desk. Twenty-eight students looked at him instead of at Drita.

“A compelling demonstration,” he said, crouching, “of gravity’s refusal to
respect staff authority.”

In the shadow behind the grate, something black and thin withdrew. Not wire.
Not a shadow. A living filament, wetly quick, vanishing after it had enjoyed a
clear view of the page.

The Rollcaller had survived the night.

Gideon gathered the papers without hurrying. “Change of method. Mark yourselves
present on the silent check-in slips. Apparently I am no longer qualified to
hold a book.”

The class bent to the slips. Drita did not look at the grate again.

At the time, switching the register felt like protection. Gideon would later
understand that the Rollcaller had watched him protect exactly one reaction.

* * *

At lunch, Gideon locked himself in the equipment room behind the lab and
plugged an ordinary headset into an ordinary phone. The voice scrambler made
him sound like a courteous cupboard.

“Rollcaller survived,” Night Clerk said. “It entered the school ventilation,
heard me call one civilian name, and tested the alias Kiteglass. It had sight
of the paper register. I saw living filament.”

Silence held on the relay. Their health and location channels showed only what
each girl had chosen to share: three rough status lights, no names, no map
points.

“How many people reacted?” Kiteglass asked.

“One nearly did. I interrupted. The room did not appear to notice.”

“Nearly,” Kiteglass repeated, annoyed with herself.

“The creature engineered surprise. That is information about its method, not a
failure on your part.”

Pulsewire’s scrambled voice cut in. “It needs correlation. The ledger gives it
possible civilians, reactions narrow them, cameras prove them.”

“Agreed. My recommendation is evacuation and cancellation. Available
alternatives: separate departures, remaining in public view, or a contained
trap using the building map. You decide whether you engage at all.”

“Three of us leaving together would be a confession with backpacks,”
Kiteglass said. “And we built that presentation.”

“For six weeks,” Pulsewire added.

Mothlight had said nothing.

Gideon resisted the urge to fill the quiet with instructions. “Mothlight, do
you want options, quiet, or a grounding count?”

“Count. Then options.”

He counted five slow breaths. He could hear her match him by the faint hiss of
the microphone. No one hurried her.

“I’m scared,” Mothlight said at last. “That is not the same as voting no.”

“Understood.”

“I vote we stay,” she said. “I also vote we don’t improvise in front of a
guardian livestream, because I do have standards.”

Kiteglass proposed drawing the Rollcaller toward the empty rehearsal corridor
during showcase setup, away from the auditorium audience. Pulsewire requested
the building’s camera positions and traced two exits on the map Gideon sent:
the public auditorium doors and a service corridor with no camera sightline.
Three taps on the relay would be the hard abort signal. No debate afterward.

“If the network is compromised?” Pulsewire asked.

“Disconnect.”

“And if you order a transformation?”

“Night Clerk never orders a transformation,” Gideon said. It was the first
rule they had made together. “If you hear one, the channel is compromised.”

“Good,” Pulsewire said. “Because you are useful, but you are not in charge of
our bodies.”

The sentence pricked because it was true and because he had lately behaved as
though noticing everything entitled him to arrange everything. He looked at
the school map, at the three status lights, at every variable he wanted to
close his hand around.

“Send me your final route,” he said. “I’ll give you camera coverage and
evacuation timing. The plan remains yours.”

* * *

By midafternoon, the auditorium smelled of dust, hot projector plastic, and
the citrus cleaner used whenever guardians were expected.

Gideon rotated presentation jobs across the whole class. Anyone could hand
their speaking section to a partner. Anyone could use the revision token.
Drita kept her speaking part but let someone else carry the display board.
Bryn checked both exits before connecting the class laptop. Cassia stood in
the wing, named five things she could see under her breath, and walked onstage
when she was ready.

Their rehearsal was good. Not good considering the night they had endured.
Simply good.

On the second run, Drita lost her place when the display board shifted. Gideon
did not rescue her sentence. He reminded the entire class that a pause counted
as speaking, then waited. Drita reset the board with her right hand and
finished the explanation herself. Bryn quietly moved the laptop charger so it
would not cross either exit. Cassia shortened one joke, drank half a bottle of
water, and asked to repeat her closing section.

Those choices cost the schedule eight minutes. Gideon spent them without
hesitation. A showcase timetable was an invented emergency; cold hands,
sensory strain, and a student asking for another try were real. Because the
roles rotated, no one could call the accommodations special treatment. Because
the girls kept their own speaking choices, their project remained theirs.

Gideon checked the boring safety features while they reset: the heavy acoustic
fire partition recessed beside the stage, the breaker panel near the service
door, the blind corridor beyond it. Above the auditorium laptop, the stream
camera’s green indicator glowed beside a guardian-view counter reading zero.

At that moment, Bryn came from the laptop, Cassia came from the wing, and all
three girls leaned over the same cue sheet. A hair-thin filament beneath the
camera housing pivoted to follow them. The Rollcaller had pursued a trio the
night before and had one strong civilian candidate in Drita. Her two showcase
partners were only a guess, but a narrow, observable one. The ledger supplied
spellings, not truth. By using the public-address system, the Rollcaller could
test the guess.

The public-address speakers clicked.

An administrator’s voice said, “Drita Ademi, Bryn Ahn, and Cassia Dominguez,
report to the main office immediately.”

All three girls went still.

The guess had earned the Rollcaller a shared reaction.

“Continue setup,” Gideon said, pleasantly. “The office knows the traditional
method of contacting staff.”

He called from the wall phone. The actual office had issued no summons.

“An audio test entered the wrong channel,” he told the class. “A thrilling
preview of the competence adults will display this evening.”

The room loosened. Students returned to cables and cue cards. The three girls
did not leave together.

Yet when Gideon returned to his desk, the relevant ledger page was gone.
Along the baseboard, an ink-dark filament slipped beneath the auditorium’s A/V
rack. His protection had told the predator what it needed to know: those three
names mattered to him.

The camera counter changed from zero to one.

Then to six.

The livestream had begun forty minutes early.

* * *

The projection screen flashed white. Three civilian names appeared across it
in block letters: DRITA ADEMI. BRYN AHN. CASSIA DOMINGUEZ.

Beneath them jittered blurred images from the previous night—three bright,
human shapes caught at bad angles by an ordinary street camera the Rollcaller
had threaded with its own living filaments. The refraction veil had smeared
faces and voices in the recording, as it was meant to do. It could not hide a
visible transformation, and it could not stop someone patient from placing two
sets of evidence side by side.

Question marks blinked between Drita Ademi and Kiteglass, Bryn Ahn and
Pulsewire, Cassia Dominguez and Mothlight.

The class stared. The view counter climbed.

Black filaments spilled from the A/V rack, thin as drawn ink and moving with
the intent of fingers. They threaded the camera mount, the speaker cable, the
door hardware. The Rollcaller had not enchanted the equipment. It had put
living pieces of itself inside the machinery and was operating it.

From every speaker came Night Clerk’s copied voice.

“Kiteglass. Pulsewire. Mothlight. Transform now.”

Gideon’s heart lurched.

The three girls did not move.

Six months of insisting that consent be procedural, not sentimental, had just
done what surveillance could not. Night Clerk never gave that order.

“Everyone away from the screen,” Mr. Tolland said. “Leave bags. Service
corridor, two lines.”

The class knew his evacuation voice. Chairs scraped. A filament snapped across
the main doors and cinched them shut. Another reached for the camera, carrying
the Rollcaller’s living attention toward the growing audience beyond it.

Three taps struck Gideon’s earpiece.

“The wiring is one route,” Pulsewire said through the relay. Pain roughened
the scrambled words. “Our channel is the second. It bridged both. I need full
blackout.”

His screen still held three weak telemetry lights: cold, tremor, strain. Cut
the breaker, and the school network, cameras, and relay would all die
together. He would lose their reports. Their positions. His illusion that
enough data could make their choices safe.

The copied voice crooned from the speakers, “Transform now.”

Gideon could have used their civilian names on the relay. Three precise
warnings. Three betrayals.

Instead he pressed the transmit switch. “Facts once. The network is the
exposure path. Cutting it ends the stream and cameras, and it also cuts this
relay. The local power can be killed, giving you darkness but no telemetry or
handler contact. Engagement remains your choice.”

A breath.

Kiteglass said, “Dark.”

Pulsewire said, “Dark.”

Mothlight said, “Very, very dark.”

Gideon pulled the local breaker. A hijacked A/V rack was still electrical
equipment. School procedure gave the adult nearest the panel one sensible
action.

The view counter vanished at twenty-three.

The speakers died. The relay died. Every telemetry light went out.

For one terrible instant, caring felt exactly like abandonment.

The main doors were visibly bound. Mr. Tolland opened the designated service
exit, as the evacuation plan required. Gideon chose to trust the difference.

* * *

Emergency strips painted the corridor floor a weak amber. Gideon moved the
class through the blind turn by touch and voice.

“Hand on the wall. Keep moving. If you can complain, save it for the incident
form.”

They obeyed. One student held the service door. Another guided a classmate
whose glasses had fallen. Ordinary competence moved down the line without
waiting for Gideon to distribute it. His duty was here, with the whole class,
even while every frightened instinct tried to turn him toward the three status
lights that no longer existed.

Behind him came the sound of tearing cloth, though no cloth in the auditorium
was large enough to make it. A cold, angled gleam crossed the narrow window in
the acoustic partition.

He did not see who stayed behind. He did not see hands close on focus tokens,
or living power pass through those nonliving shapes and become transformed
light. By the time he dragged the partition from its recess, three refracted
figures moved beyond the glass, their features blurred even to his knowing
eyes.

The Rollcaller hurled filaments at the evacuation opening.

A translucent plane struck them aside. It appeared at a steep angle, flashed,
and settled across the service route like braced glass. Behind it, Kiteglass
held one arm tight against her ribs. The barrier shivered each time the
creature hit. She could have chased the sheet-thin body retreating toward the
A/V rack. Instead she planted her feet at the door.

“Route first,” Gideon heard her say.

With students still passing through, fire procedure required the acoustic
partition between them and the auditorium.

He pulled the heavy partition. Something caught its lower track. A filament
whipped through the gap and wrapped the handle. Gideon hauled back. Pain
streaked from his shoulder to his elbow, bright enough to turn the corridor
white at the edges.

On the auditorium side, a sharp blue flicker ran along the speaker cable. It
ended with a crack. Someone gasped. The lights stayed off, but Gideon heard a
body strike the stage steps and then get up again.

“One bridge cut,” Pulsewire said. Her voice sounded far too loud in the dead
room. “Two active.”

The Rollcaller answered in Cassia’s civilian voice.

“I can’t. I can’t. I can’t.”

It spoke from the stage, the ceiling, the dead speakers, each imitation
slightly out of time. One refracted figure stopped moving.

Gideon could see only fragments through the narrow glass: a pale hand lifted,
a shimmer gone ragged, filaments turning toward the stillness. He had no relay
and no right to break the darkness they had requested. He held the partition
and listened.

The real voice said, “One breath.”

The angled barrier widened. The blue flicker paused.

No one told her to hurry.

Gideon took one breath too, though his shoulder shook. Beyond the glass, the
still figure inhaled. Exhaled.

Then Mothlight filled the rehearsal corridor with liars.

That was all Gideon could make of it at first. Shadows ran where no bodies
could fit. Light folded against the walls and came away as half a dozen figures
shaped like Kiteglass, a scatter shaped like Pulsewire, Mothlight after
Mothlight lifting bright hands. Displaced voices called the three aliases from
opposite ends of the room.

The Rollcaller lunged at recognition. Filaments ripped out of the camera,
speakers, and cable channels to seize every apparent identity at once.

For a moment the A/V rack stood exposed.

Something behind it peeled upward: a narrow living body, ink-dark and
sheet-thin, its many extended pieces pulled taut toward false targets. A
translucent plane appeared above it. Another below. Two more folded inward,
not striking but enclosing.

The pressure against Gideon’s partition doubled. The filament around the
handle tightened. His injured arm began to fail.

“External lines and relay,” Pulsewire said somewhere beyond his sight. “All
remaining connections. Consent to cut?”

“Yes,” came one voice.

“Yes,” came another, after one deliberate breath.

Blue-white light snapped through every black strand.

The filament on Gideon’s handle went slack.

He dragged the partition closed with his good arm. The latch caught. On the
other side came a sound like a ream of wet paper dropped from a height, then
silence.

Gideon stayed against the partition, shoulder burning, while the last student
cleared the corridor. Through the window he saw only a clear angular cage, a
dark shape folded small inside it, and three blurred figures supporting one
another.

He did not know how they had changed their plan in the dark. He did not know
whether Pulsewire could still hear properly, whether Kiteglass’s wrist had
worsened, whether Mothlight’s remaining glow meant strength or the last of it.

He knew the exit was clear because Kiteglass had guarded it.

He knew the connections were dead because Pulsewire had asked before cutting
them.

He knew the decoys had worked because Mothlight had taken the breath she
needed, then chosen to act.

For the rest, he waited for whatever they decided to tell him.

* * *

At the outdoor muster point, the story available to ordinary witnesses was
strange but small.

The power had failed. A corrupted showcase file had displayed three students’
names beside fuzzy costume footage. The guardian stream had ended before
anything clearer appeared. Cameras had gone dark with the breaker. No one had
seen a transformation. Most of the class had been looking at Gideon or the
service corridor when the lights died.

By the time explanations passed from student to student, the likeliest theory
was an ugly promotional stunt interrupted by bad wiring. In a city where magic
belonged to old stories and cheap effects, that answer was easier to believe
than three exhausted classmates turning into the impossible.

Drita, Bryn, and Cassia emerged from separate gaps in the milling students in
civilian clothes. Gideon did not see where they came from. Drita’s hands were
still cold. Bryn flinched at a whistle from across the yard. Cassia ate the
second oat bar in four bites.

He accepted all three back without asking questions Mr. Tolland could not
know to ask.

The stolen page meant he had to rebuild attendance. He passed silent check-in
slips down the rows at muster, and each student marked their own presence.
Drita, Bryn, and Cassia made three honest marks. Gideon entered them without
alteration.

That evening, after food, warmth, an ordinary check of his strained shoulder,
and several hours in which the world remained blessedly unremarkable, Night
Clerk reopened the reset relay.

Three status lights appeared by choice.

“Containment?” he asked.

“Stable,” Kiteglass said. “I held it while Pulsewire checked the cuts. Then we
closed the body in an unplugged metal equipment case. We’ll decide what to do
with it when we are not exhausted.”

“That is a strong argument for rest. Available support: food delivery, medical
checks, deadline help, route coverage, or no contact.”

“Not a schedule?” Mothlight asked.

Gideon looked at the recovery plan he had already drafted and turned it face
down.

“Not unless requested.”

They chose food, injury checks, and two mission-free nights. Kiteglass
volunteered that she had abandoned pursuit because her wrist could hold a
stationary shield or a chase, not both. Pulsewire reported that the final
severance had been possible only after the decoys drew the living core out of
the rack. Mothlight said she had needed one honest breath before she could make
twenty dishonest versions of them.

They offered those facts. Gideon received them. He did not ask for more.

“New protocol,” Pulsewire said. “When we request darkness, you give facts once
and disconnect.”

“Even if I dislike it?”

“Especially then.”

“Agreed.”

The next morning, Mr. Tolland did not call the register aloud. Silent
self-check-in slips waited on every lab bench.

“Permanent?” Drita asked.

“Trial policy,” Gideon said. “It reduces the number of opportunities for me to
drop important documents.”

Cassia smiled. Bryn checked the door, then bent over her slip. None of them
looked at Mr. Tolland as though they heard Night Clerk’s scrambled voice. None
looked at Night Clerk, through the relay, as though they knew he had recognized
their civilian ones.

Their boundary held.

Gideon opened the replacement ledger. It was still only paper, incapable of
knowing what its marks meant. Beside Drita Ademi, Bryn Ahn, and Cassia
Dominguez, he recorded three simple presences.

Not pieces he had successfully controlled.

Students who had chosen, fought, returned, and answered for themselves.

stories.title: A Little Winter for Sale
stories.prompt: As a traveler, you've been exploring the desert for days, before coming upon a city so far from water, nestled against a mountainside. You find that in the mountains cave, is an ice dragon far from home, enjoying being paid to simply sell small bouts of it's power
stories.body:
# A Little Winter for Sale

On the fourth day beyond the last mapped cistern, I found a city where no city
had any right to be.

It clung to the lower face of a black mountain, pale walls crowded one above
another in the narrow mercy of its shadow. Terraces flashed with copper. A line
of green trees ran through the middle of it, offensively alive.

I checked my map, though I had checked it twice since dawn. No river. No
spring. No lake blue enough to justify a goat, let alone five hundred roofs.
Only the mountain, marked by an earlier surveyor as the Black Shoulder, and a
warning that the western salt road ended in broken country.

My water skin gave me one mouthful. It tasted of leather, hot brass, and poor
decisions.

Behind me, the southern sky had thickened to the color of a bruise. Glasswind.
Even at that distance I could see the high glitter where grit turned in the
sun. I had watched it growing all morning and continued west because I was
Tair Ked, route surveyor, and because turning back had always felt like asking
permission.

I took out my sunwheel. Its brass rim lay warm and familiar in my palm, its
silver heart balancing the needle so delicately that my pulse made it tremble.
Five years of bearings were cut into the outer rings in my own cramped hand:
salt pans, wells, safe noon shadows, three roads that merchants insisted did
not exist until they needed them. With the sunwheel and a clear horizon, I
could earn water in any settlement worth reaching.

Without water, I had until noon to become a cautionary engraving on somebody
else's instrument.

I walked toward the impossible trees.

The gate stood open. White cloth had been tied over its ironwork against the
coming wind. A woman in a dust veil took one look at me, held up a finger to
silence whatever proud idiocy I was about to say, and put a clay cup in my
hands.

The cup sweated.

I stared at the droplets running over my knuckles.

"Drink," she said.

The water was so cold it hurt my teeth. I drank too quickly, stopped because
she pinched the rim down, then drank again when she released it. The desert
inside me contracted around that cup.

"Price?" I managed.

"After you keep it down."

She poured a second measure, smaller than the first, and opened a narrow
ledger. "Name?"

"You give water before asking that?"

"I asked after. We are very strict."

"Tair Ked."

She wrote it. Beside my name she marked the two measures with a square of blue
chalk.

"Yara Mesk," she said, tapping her own chest. "Waterkeeper. Those are on
recoverable civic hospitality credit, at ration price. You can pay in coin or
work when your hands stop shaking."

My gratitude cooled. A debt entered in ink was still a hand around the ankle,
however politely offered.

"I can pay now."

"Your purse may be steady. You are not." Yara corked the jar. "There will be
work soon enough. The glasswind is early."

Across the city, shutters were closing in a rising clatter. Above the rooftops,
thin copper channels descended from the mountain, some beaded with
condensation. I put two small coins on her ledger anyway.

She pushed one back. "That is double."

"For speed."

"Water does not become more watered because you are impatient."

She recorded the first coin, then recorded the returned one. This seemed
designed to annoy me with accuracy.

I followed her uphill.

***

Qarsis was not sustained by a miracle. It was sustained by several
insufficient things lashed together with copper, lime, and aggressive
bookkeeping.

Yara showed me the flat fields east of the wall, where hundreds of sloped glass
panes drank damp from hot brine spread beneath them. The sun warmed the pans;
vapor gathered under the glass and ran through clay gutters into covered
cisterns. White crust furred every seam. Farther upslope, stone throats waited
to catch the rare rain that struck the Black Shoulder and tried to escape.

"Stills and runoff give us about half an ordinary day," Yara said. "More in a
kind season. Less in a year with a sense of humor."

"And the other half?"

She laid her palm on a copper pipe running down the lane.

It was cold.

Under its greenish skin, water ticked and whispered toward the lower cisterns.
The return pipe beside it was warm and smelled faintly of salt.

"The mountain seeps brine," she said. "Too bitter to drink. We lift it to the
exchanger. Six batches a day give roughly four hundred litres each. Add the
stills, stored runoff, and cistern carryover, and five hundred people receive
twelve litres apiece."

"Six batches of what?"

"You will ask less suspiciously if you drink another cup."

"I ask everything suspiciously."

"Yes. I had begun to notice."

We climbed through terraces where covered jars stood at every doorway. No
fountains splashed for beauty. Laundry water ran into garden troughs. A child
somewhere behind a shutter complained about being called indoors, but no one
wasted breath arguing with the darkening sky.

The cold pipe led toward a cave cut into the mountainside above the last
houses. A stone arch at its mouth had one word carved into it: COLDMOUTH.
Inside, channels crossed the floor toward a copper apparatus taller than I
was. Brine filled a shallow enclosed basin. Ribs of hammered metal clasped it,
all connected to a flared horn that pointed into the dark.

My suspicion, deprived of any sensible target, found a dragon.

Urumet lay beyond the exchanger on a shelf of black stone. Slate-blue scales
overlapped from its long muzzle to the folded hooks of its wings. Hoarfrost
edged every ridge. It could have crushed the copper horn under one foreclaw.
Instead it was holding a square of paper delicately between two claws and
reading it with an expression of profound injury.

"This receipt," Urumet said, "does not include the grit surcharge."

A thin clerk on the safe side of the exchanger consulted a slate. "The grit
has not yet reached the intake."

"I can taste tomorrow's grit from here."

"It is not tomorrow's batch."

"Then you may come back tomorrow and discover that foresight costs extra."

Yara leaned toward me. "Urumet likes invoices."

"Invoices," the dragon said without looking up, "are civilization made
portable."

The clerk added a line. Urumet read it, made a pleased sound deep enough to
ripple the brine, and pressed one clawtip into a pad of blue wax. It stamped
the receipt with a neat crescent.

"Fourth stroke," Yara said. "Four-count standard. Exchanger loaded and gates
checked."

The clerk pulled two levers. Brine flooded the copper ribs. A small bimetal
tongue in the regulator lifted across a numbered slot.

Urumet rose.

Cold did not come from the machine. It came when Urumet opened its jaws and
breathed one narrow, silent ribbon into the horn.

Yara counted aloud.

At one, frost raced over the copper ribs.

At two, the cave air turned white and my damp sleeves stiffened.

At three, clear ice thickened inside the basin while cloudy, concentrated brine
squeezed through lower slots.

At four, the regulator tongue curled across the aperture. Urumet shut its jaws.
The cold ceased.

For a moment the cave held its breath. Then drains opened and the bitter
remnant hissed down the warm return channel. Workers behind the casing loosened
the clean ice in slabs. Desert heat would melt those into drinking water before
they reached the cisterns.

Along Urumet's jaw, a line of hoarfrost had vanished. Heat shimmered faintly
above its scales.

"Four today," the dragon said. "Two remaining."

The clerk hesitated. "The dye works asked whether a seventh might be reserved.
They will pay the grit rate."

"No."

"Double."

"Still no, but more offensively."

Urumet settled back on the shelf. "Six strokes, then I spend the night shedding
the heat. A seventh is bad for me, bad for the exchanger, and worst of all,
unpriced by any responsible schedule."

That last reason seemed to cheer it.

The clerk passed payment through a hatch: small coins, a paper twist of red
pepper sweets, and a freight ledger. Urumet counted the coins twice, popped a
sweet between its teeth, and opened the ledger to a page marked with northward
routes. Its pleasure was so plain I felt foolish for having come uphill
prepared to discover chains.

"You are not from here," I said.

Urumet turned one pale eye on me. "Neither are you."

"The frost suggested it."

"The manners confirmed it."

Yara made a noise that might have been a cough.

Urumet licked pepper sugar from one claw. "There is an ice shelf far north of
every road on that ledger. I left it because I wished to leave. I work here
because I like precise jobs, small luxuries, and customers who can be taught to
fear amendments."

Its claw rested on the northern page.

"I can enjoy Qarsis and miss home," it said. "Even water manages to be more
than one thing."

The first grit struck the cave arch with a sound like dry rain.

***

The glasswind arrived all at once.

Daylight went copper. The mountain vanished behind its own dust. Wind drove
shards of pale grit against the stone hard enough to spark, and the city below
became a confusion of ropes, slamming shutters, and cloth snapping loose from
the gate.

Yara ran for the exchanger controls. The clerk dropped the freight ledger and
threw a cover over it. I had just bent to catch the northern page when
something cracked above us.

A stone came through the outer screen.

It struck the regulator casing with a bright metallic snap. The bimetal tongue
spun past my boot in two pieces.

Yara closed the brine gate. The basin shuddered as its flow stopped.

"Nobody touch the horn," Urumet said.

The humor had gone out of its voice.

Yara opened the casing. The regulator's brass frame had buckled inward. One
half of the silver-backed tongue remained trapped beneath it, curled like a
dead leaf.

"Can you aim without that?" I asked.

"Yes," Urumet said. "I can also put my foot through your chest with admirable
accuracy. Neither is relevant to whether it is safe."

Yara traced the split with one finger. "Without a regulator, the stroke can
freeze the feed throat before the brine clears. Pressure bursts the ribs. We
lose the batch and perhaps the exchanger."

"The two strokes are contracted," Urumet said. "They are not contracted
through broken equipment."

Another impact rang from outside.

The glass still field had disappeared under moving dunes. Yara sent the clerk
down with orders to seal the cistern vents and count every covered jar. When
the clerk was gone, she stood very still beside the ruined regulator, doing
figures against her thumb.

"Four thousand two hundred litres in emergency reserve," she said. "A little
more in household jars. The final two batches would add about eight hundred.
Enough for one reduced day while the storm passes and we uncover the stills."

"Without them?"

"Not enough without cutting everyone below safety, and not enough for the
clearing crews."

"A replacement?"

"Twelve caravan-days away, once caravans move." She looked at my hands.

No. She looked at what I held.

I had drawn the sunwheel when the sky darkened. Its needle lay folded into its
case, but the brass-and-silver center shone against my dusty palm.

Yara did not reach for it.

"May I examine your wheel?" she asked.

I closed my fingers.

The instrument had carried me across five years of country. Every calibration
was mine. Every nick in its rim recalled a place where I had been thirsty,
lost, paid, or right when a caravan master had been expensively wrong. It was
not merely metal. It was proof that I could leave any obligation behind if I
walked far enough.

"Why?"

"The heart is paired brass and silver, pressure-balanced. I could cut a
regulator tongue from it."

"And the wheel?"

"Would never take a true bearing again."

The wind screamed across the cave mouth.

I thought of twelve litres multiplied by five hundred closed doors. I thought
of the cold cup whose debt had irritated me more than dying alone would have.
The answer came out before fear could make it smaller.

"Take it."

Yara kept her hands at her sides. "At what price?"

"None."

"That was not my question."

"It is mine. I give it. You use it. No debt."

Urumet's tail struck the stone once.

"Absolutely not."

I turned. "It is not yours."

"Correct. That is why I object to your attempt to make its price everyone
else's problem."

"People need water."

"And therefore Yara may ask to buy your tool. She may not seize it. I may
choose to complete two jobs. I may not be squeezed into a seventh. Emergency
does not turn consent into a decorative flourish."

"I consented."

"To loss," Urumet said. "Very grandly. You have not consented to being paid."

I laughed once, because anger and fear had crowded everything else out of me.
"Why should that concern you?"

Urumet drew the freight ledger from under its cover and tapped the northern
page. "Because I am a professional."

***

Yara set the broken regulator pieces on a workbench. Beside them she placed a
small saw, a file, and her open ledger.

"If I cut the heart," she said, "the city owes you its replacement value. You
also lose time and earnings. Name those."

I wanted to say nothing. Nothing was clean. Nothing could be refused later,
called in, or held over me. If I walked out stripped of my livelihood, I could
at least tell myself the loss belonged entirely to me.

Then I looked at Urumet's blue-stamped receipts lined in a tidy stack. The
dragon did not look owned. It looked recognized.

I opened my route book to the page where I had priced a new survey-grade
sunwheel the year before and decided mine had another decade in it.

"A wheel of equal balance," I said. My throat tightened around the number.
"Delivered at city cost to the freight shelter beside the split-stone well,
eight days up the existing north caravan road. Twenty days' route wage for
delay. Another twenty to recut my recorded bearings. Provisions to the shelter
and while I wait there. I do not begin new survey work until the replacement
is in my hands."

Yara did not flinch. She worked the sum, showed me each line, then turned the
ledger around.

"Fair," she said. "The city agrees. Do you?"

The word weighed more than sacrifice.

"I agree."

I signed Tair Ked beneath the blue square that had begun with two cups of
water.

Only then did I lay the sunwheel on the bench.

Yara dismantled it with the care of someone preparing a body for burial and
the speed of someone who had no time for grief. She freed the paired heart,
marked a narrow curve against the surviving regulator half, and cut. The saw
made a thin, intimate sound.

My five years of bearings fell still.

I did not look away.

Yara filed the new tongue, riveted it into the buckled frame, and tuned its
resting angle by fractions against the numbered slot. I held the lamp. Urumet
watched from beside the horn, correcting the alignment twice and refusing it a
third time until Yara adjusted the stop.

Yara bolted a calibration strip alongside the tongue. One end went into warm
return brine; against the other she packed shavings from the fourth batch of
ice. As she moved the strip through four marked temperature steps, the paired
metals bent the tongue across the slot. She warmed the casing, watched it
return, then repeated the bench test.

"That matches the old travel," Urumet said. "I accept Yara's calibration."

"I accept the repair for the two remaining contracted strokes," it continued.
"At the previously agreed grit surcharge. No extension."

"The city agrees," Yara said.

The three of us signed separate lines.

Then Urumet looked at me. "I also require a route surveyed north. Not a rescue.
Not an escort. A commercial road for letters and light freight. The first leg
requires no surveying: you follow the marked caravan road to the split-stone
well and carry one letter. Your new wheel travels there on the first northbound
freight after the road opens. Beyond the well, you survey only after it
arrives."

"The western salt road is my commission."

"The western salt road is under several tons of ambitious glass."

That was true.

Urumet pushed a small stack of its own coins across the bench. "First
installment. You may refuse. You may counter."

I named my weekly rate.

Urumet countered by adding meals but subtracting pepper sweets, which it called
a specialist expense. I asked for half the delivery bonus in advance. Urumet
asked what guarantee I offered.

"Five years of bearings," I said, touching the empty rim of my sunwheel.

"Temporarily converted into municipal plumbing."

"The best routes become infrastructure eventually."

Urumet's teeth showed. It stamped our receipt.

I read the handoff and start conditions back from it: known road first, letter
delivered at the freight shelter, replacement wheel received there, new
bearings afterward. Only then did I add my signature.

Yara loaded the exchanger.

For the fifth stroke, she counted and I watched the new tongue curl exactly
across the fourth mark. Clean ice filled the basin. Concentrated brine drained
away. Heat shimmered more strongly above Urumet's back.

For the sixth, Urumet paused with its jaws at the horn.

"Brine gate?"

"Open and checked," Yara said.

"Outlet?"

"Clear."

"My fee?"

"Entered, including grit."

Urumet breathed.

At four, the new tongue closed the aperture. Urumet stopped. No seventh stroke
came. No desperate exception. Just the crackle of nearly four hundred litres
of clean ice releasing from copper while the storm battered itself against the
mountain.

The last hoarfrost along Urumet's wings melted into dark beads.

"Sold out," it said, and lay down with a sigh that stirred snow-dry dust across
the floor. "Come back tomorrow."

***

The glasswind spent itself by the following afternoon.

Urumet's recovery had not taken that long. By dawn the heat shimmer above its
scales was gone and hoarfrost had returned along its jaw. It pronounced the
night's shedding complete, then declined to discuss fresh work until the
exchanger intake had been cleared and inspected.

Qarsis drank ten litres per person while the storm lasted. The sealed cisterns
held. The final eight hundred litres gave the clearing crews enough to work
without stealing from the old, the sick, or the small. When the sky cleared,
people swept glittering dunes from the still panes, flushed grit from the
gutters, and spread brine beneath the glass again.

By sunset, the first distilled drops were ticking into clay channels.

Yara gave me another cold cup. She opened the ledger before I could object and
drew a line through my blue square.

"Hospitality credit recovered," she said. "Included in your northbound
provisions."

"So the city paid itself for my water with money it owes me."

"You are learning civic finance."

"It resembles theft performed by very patient ink."

"That is the nicest thing anyone has said about my work today."

My ruined sunwheel fit strangely in its case. The outer rings and five years of
marks remained, but its center was an empty circle. Through it I could see a
slice of the northern sky.

Urumet gave me a letter wrapped in waxed cloth. It bore no grand seal, only a
blue claw crescent like the mark on a receipt. With it came a freight list,
three pepper sweets for the road, and a warning that all three were separate
items and only two were billable.

"Will you go back if I find the route?" I asked.

Urumet considered this while fitting coins into a little stack.

"Perhaps I will visit. Perhaps freight will travel better than I do. Perhaps
someone from the ice will come south and complain about my prices." Its pale
eye narrowed happily. "A road creates choices. That is what I am buying."

So I left Qarsis along a caravan road already marked by stone stakes, with the
city's signed promise to put a new sunwheel on the next freight caravan,
Urumet's first installment in my purse, and its letter tucked against my ribs.
Eight days north, I would meet the wheel at the freight shelter. Only beyond
that known road would I start cutting new bearings.

The Black Shoulder dwindled behind me. Below it, the still fields shone clean
again. The copper return pipe carried bitterness downhill, the cold pipe
carried drinking water, and high in the Coldmouth a fully recovered dragon had
gone to bed after an ordinary day's accounts.

For the first time in years, I could not cut a new bearing.

I had never been more certain what I was walking toward.

stories.title: The Gentlest Terror
stories.prompt: Every single noble family in your kingdom has an alliance with a dragon that watches over them. The royal family's dragon, despite being the biggest and scariest by appearance, is a total sweetheart.
stories.body:
# The Gentlest Terror

The swallow had chosen the worst possible crown in Ersene.

Princess Olyra stood on a scaffold beside Nyrzath's head, one hand hooked
around a black horn, while the other worked at the gold thread wound around the
bird's leg. Beneath her boots, the royal dragon kept so still that dust had
settled along the hooked ridges of his brow.

Stillness did not make him reassuring.

Nyrzath filled the convocation court from dais to doors. Black plates overlapped
down his neck like shields laid for a siege. Tusks curved past his lower jaw.
One eye was gold; the other, scarred milky-white. The ragged edges of his folded
wings rose above the galleries, and heat leaked between his teeth in a red glow
that made the ceremonial banners stir. The masons had rebuilt the west arch
after his last Dread Passage. Lord Osric Fane called that an unfortunate
expense. Privately, he had also requested a wider arch.

"If you twitch," Olyra murmured, "it will think the end of the world has
arrived."

"I have that effect on small creatures," Nyrzath said. His whisper sounded
like a cart overturning in a cellar.

The swallow trembled against the horn. Olyra teased free the last bright
strand. It fluttered once, failed to gain height, and tucked itself into the
hollow behind Nyrzath's forward horn.

"Stunned," she said. "Keep your head level."

"I had intended to nod gravely throughout your accession."

"You may nod gravely tomorrow."

"Excellent. I have been practicing for centuries."

Lord Osric's shoes clicked into the court. Olyra did not need to look down to
recognize the pace: brisk enough to rebuke everyone else for wasting time,
measured enough to suggest he never did.

"The noble pairs are assembling," he said. "Princess Olyra, we require one
complete rehearsal."

Olyra descended. On the lowest rung, the scale beneath her collarbone shifted,
cold and smooth against her skin. Nyrzath had shed it freely for King Ambric's
alliance and warmed it with his breath while her father held it. With her
father's death, it had become inert: a keepsake that could point nowhere and
draw heat from no living hand. A working focus required two living partners,
their spoken assent, and a new scale freely offered and warmed by dragon
breath. Today Nyrzath would have to choose her before any connection opened.

Lord Osric noticed her hand at her collar. "The old focus?"

"Only a memory now," Olyra said.

"Then we shall require the new one to function immediately."

"After both of us agree," Nyrzath said.

Lord Osric inclined his head, accepting the correction without enjoying it.
"And the Dread Passage?"

Nyrzath unfolded his wings.

The court vanished under shadow. His horn crown scraped stone. He drew one
breath; furnace-light brightened behind his tusks, and the damp on the flagstones
turned to mist. This was the face Ersene painted over gates and stamped into
wax: Nyrzath the Grief-Clad, largest of the kingdom's dragons, ruin wearing
scales.

Olyra heard King Ambric as clearly as if her father stood beside her: *A crown
sometimes needs a gentle friend to wear a monster's face.*

Three weeks dead, and he could still give terrible advice at exactly the useful
moment.

"Enter as rehearsed," Olyra told Nyrzath.

The red light dimmed.

"I will enter," he said. "I will witness. I will not force another dragon's
vow."

Lord Osric's mouth tightened. "No one anticipates that necessity."

They all looked toward the waiting doors.

No one believed him.

* * *

Every noble family in Ersene entered the convocation court beside its dragon
ally. There were long-legged dragons from the reed estates, copper-scaled
dragons whose human partners tended cliff roosts, and one elderly white dragon
who accepted a heated stone from her family before settling onto the tiles.
Each alliance represented a paired public service: watch and rescue from the
dragon; protected nesting ground, injury care, and a human voice in court in
return.

None of the dragons came on a chain. None bore a saddle.

House Cress renewed first.

Larkspur was considered large anywhere Nyrzath was not present. Beside him,
the green-and-violet dragon looked almost delicate, though one foreclaw could
have covered Lord Ruvik Cress from polished boot to thinning hair.

She plucked a loose scale from her shoulder and dropped it into Lord Ruvik's
waiting hands.

"Do you offer watch over the Cress orchards and storm channels?" Nyrzath
asked.

"I do," Larkspur said. Her voice had the crackle of dry leaves.

"Do you offer the care you agreed?"

Lord Ruvik bowed to her before he answered Nyrzath. "We cleared her molting
ground, rebuilt the upper cisterns, and greased every gate."

"You missed three."

"Two."

"Three. The little eastern gate makes a noise like Lord Osric considering a
new form."

The court laughed. Even Lord Osric almost did.

Larkspur breathed over the scale. It warmed in Lord Ruvik's palms, the heat
coming from a living will rather than the bit of scale itself.

"Asked first," Nyrzath said.

"Answered free," said Larkspur.

"Witnessed whole," Lord Ruvik finished.

He and Larkspur exchanged a look that made it clear the eastern gate would be
discussed again.

Then House Flint approached.

Mossback was slate-green, broad through the chest, and furred with lichen along
his spine. He watched the Flint valley from nesting caverns above the villages.
Olyra had seen him carry lost quarry workers home through sleet, walking so
slowly that no injured limb jostled.

Duchess Yselle Flint held out both hands.

Mossback did not shed a scale.

Silence moved across the court more quickly than flame.

Duchess Yselle kept her hands extended. "We are waiting."

"No," Mossback said.

The word was quiet. It struck harder than Nyrzath's roar.

Lord Osric stepped near Olyra. "The convocation cannot proceed past an
unwitnessed house. Your royal renewal cannot be confirmed."

"The founding order provides for refusal."

"It provides for private petition and repair. Not spectacle. If one house may
humiliate the crown before every alliance in Ersene, others will discover
grievances before sunset."

"They may have them already."

"Then do not teach them that refusal is easy."

Duchess Yselle's hands fell. "Mossback is agitated. The Grief-Clad can remind
him what this gathering requires."

Olyra looked up at Nyrzath.

He rose.

Larkspur backed one pace despite herself. Mossback did not retreat, but the
lichen along his spine flattened. Nyrzath advanced until his shadow swallowed
House Flint. His hooked horns nearly touched the ceiling. Heat rolled from his
mouth, and every person in the first gallery leaned away as one.

This was what the crown had kept polished: not Nyrzath, but the instant before
people obeyed him.

Olyra could finish the performance with four words. *Make him renew the vow.*

Nyrzath lowered his tusked face until his scarred eye was level with
Mossback's.

"Where is the clutch?" he asked gently.

Duchess Yselle went pale.

Mossback's claws scored the floor. "In the north nesting cavern. Where it has
always been."

Nyrzath remembered every nest in Ersene. He sent hatch-day gifts: bright river
glass, smoothed roof tiles, once an entire wagon of pears that had been less
popular with the hatchlings than with their human neighbors.

"The quarry boundary lies south of that cavern," he said.

"It did," Mossback replied. "House Flint cut past it. I warned them after the
first tremor. They shored the visible face and dug beneath my nesting ledge."

Voices broke across the galleries.

Duchess Yselle turned on him. "We discussed an adjustment."

"You ordered me to stop frightening the stone crews with talk of collapse."

"You watch our lands. You owe us protection."

"And you owed the nest protection from your work."

Nyrzath looked to Olyra. He had entered in horror. He had made truth possible
by refusing to use it.

Olyra felt her throne shift beneath feet that had not yet reached it.

* * *

Duchess Yselle's old alliance scale began to smoke.

She cried out and nearly dropped it. Frost whitened her knuckles as Mossback's
deliberate call seized both their attention and pointed north. Olyra felt
nothing through her own focus, but she saw the cost in Mossback: his breath
shortened, and a rim of ice formed where his claws touched stone.

"Water," he said. "The quarry wall is moving."

The court's high windows flashed white with the storm. A heartbeat later,
thunder shook the banners.

Mossback called again. Duchess Yselle staggered.

"The cut has opened into the flood channel," he said. "Water is entering the
north cavern. If the wall fails outward, it reaches the villages."

"Then renew," Duchess Yselle said. She thrust the smoking scale toward him as
if it were a bridle. "Renew, and I will call you to the rescue."

Mossback's gaze did not leave Olyra. "I am already answering the people."

"Without a witnessed alliance, there is no lawful duty—"

"There are lives."

Lord Osric seized Olyra's elbow and lowered his voice. "This is precisely why
the vow must be secured now. Complete the Dread Passage. Establish command,
then settle the breach after the valley is safe."

It was not a foolish argument. That made it worse.

Around them, noble families clustered close to their dragons. If the royal
renewal failed, the assembled houses could choose another heir. If the
convocation dissolved in panic, every disputed obligation in Ersene might go
with it. King Ambric had feared that fracture. Lord Osric feared it now.

Olyra feared it enough that she understood how easily love became a mask one
made another person wear.

She stepped onto the witness stone.

"Mossback was asked," she said. Her voice cracked once, then carried. "He
answered free. Nyrzath witnessed him whole."

"He refused," Duchess Yselle said.

"Yes."

Olyra faced the galleries. "House Flint's noble title is suspended. It may be
restored if its breach is repaired and Mossback freely returns, or if another
dragon independently chooses the partnership. Until then, Mossback owes House
Flint no alliance."

Duchess Yselle made a small sound of disbelief.

The frost melted from her knuckles. Her old focus stopped smoking and dulled
in her palm. With Mossback's refusal witnessed whole, it could no longer carry
either person's call or draw heat from either body. His exit was not a
courtesy granted in words and denied in flesh.

"And your accession?" Lord Osric asked.

"Will begin where every alliance was meant to begin."

Olyra unclasped the old scale from her neck and set it on the witness stone.
Then she held out empty hands to the largest, most frightening creature in the
kingdom.

"Nyrzath. Before crown or court, will you choose an alliance with me?"

He could refuse. Until he answered, she was only one possible heir standing
before people trained to prefer certainty.

Nyrzath studied her with his clear gold eye. Then he lifted one foreclaw and
worked loose a black scale no larger than Olyra's palm.

It rang on the stone.

"I will," he said, "if you will remember that witnessing is not commanding."

"I will remember."

She picked up the scale. Nyrzath breathed over it, carefully banking the heat
that could turn rain to steam. Warmth spread into her hands.

"Asked first," Olyra said.

"Answered free," said Nyrzath.

Together, they said, "Witnessed whole."

The scale became only a focus, not a will. The choice remained theirs.

Nyrzath crouched and opened one foreclaw before Olyra. She stepped into it.

"The swallow," she warned.

"Still behind my horn."

"Then keep your head level."

The roof groaned as he spread his wings.

"I had intended," he said, and launched them into the storm.

* * *

The Flint quarry had become a brown lake standing on end.

Water pressed behind a cracked wall of cut stone and rubble. Below it, the
valley villages huddled beneath rain. Above it, the northern nesting ledge had
split, exposing a dark seam into the cavern where Mossback's clutch lay.

Nyrzath landed hard enough to sink ankle-deep in mud. Mossback swept down
beside him, smaller by half in every measure, and Larkspur landed beyond them
with Lord Ruvik clutched in the careful curl of one forefoot.

The dragons had spent several minutes tracing the cracks by the time Duchess
Yselle's quarry cart completed its slower journey from court. She arrived
white-faced and soaked and pointed at the wall.

"Burn a channel through the center. Let the water out before it takes the
whole face."

Furnace-light kindled behind Nyrzath's tusks.

Olyra imagined the blast: wet stone bursting, water punching through, the
wall's middle falling inward.

Nyrzath paced three enormous steps left. He placed one claw against the rock,
then shook his head.

"No."

"You can melt siege iron," Duchess Yselle said.

"The clutch lies behind the center cut."

He knew the distance because he remembered where Mossback had nested, where
each egg had lain when he sent six blue roof tiles as gifts. His softness had
kept a map no military survey possessed.

Another crack ran down the wall.

"The old sluice," Lord Ruvik said. "Could it divert the water east?"

Duchess Yselle stared at him. "It was sealed when we deepened the quarry."

"Neglected," Mossback said. "Not sealed. The gate is inside a service
passage. Human-width."

They all looked at Olyra.

The eastern channel led toward the Cress hills. Toward the cisterns Larkspur's
alliance maintained.

Lord Ruvik pulled Larkspur's new scale from inside his coat. "Three gates?"

"Three," Larkspur said.

"I apologize."

"Do it after we live."

He called through the focus. Heat vanished from both of them; Lord Ruvik
doubled over, breath smoking, while Larkspur's wings shuddered. She answered
by launching toward the hills. There, she could release the stored water down
the orchard channels, emptying the cisterns to receive the diverted flood.
Neither command nor scale moved her. She moved herself.

Nyrzath examined the cracking wall. "If I brace here, the center may hold
until the sluice opens."

The torn-looking edge of his left wing would lie beneath the failing ledge.
Olyra saw it. So did he.

"It may crush the joint," she said.

"Yes."

"Nyr—"

"The wall will not be persuaded by my appearance."

He looked toward the exposed nesting seam, then toward the villages.

"Go."

Nyrzath drove his shoulder beneath the overhang.

Stone boomed against black plates. His wings spread along the wall, not in
threat but as a living brace. The whole quarry seemed to lean upon him. He
grunted, masonry-failure voice reduced to one rough breath, and the left wing
buckled without breaking.

Mossback led Olyra to a narrow opening half hidden by spoil. He could not fit
past the first bend. He thrust his head into the gap until lichen scraped from
his brow.

"The passage turns right, then drops," he said. "I will follow above. Listen
for my claws."

Olyra entered.

The dark smelled of rust and flooded earth. Behind her, Nyrzath took another
impact. Dust leapt from the ceiling. Ahead, a faint scrape sounded through the
stone: Mossback pacing above her.

"Right," his muffled voice called.

She found the turn by touch and slid down a wet incline. Water already ran
around her boots. At the bottom stood the sluice wheel, red with rust and
twisted slightly off its axle.

Olyra pulled.

Nothing moved.

Above, claws scraped twice, urgent, then struck three hard blows that shook
grit from the ceiling. Mossback's voice came thinly through the rock.

"The ledge is going."

Olyra braced one boot against the wall and hauled until her shoulders burned.
The wheel shifted the width of a fingernail.

The passage ceiling cracked.

She grabbed the new black scale and called.

Cold drove to her elbow. Direction and urgency struck through Nyrzath's
attention: *here; failing; hold.*

Outside, he answered.

The wall lifted a fraction as he changed the set of his shoulder. That fraction
kept the ceiling off Olyra. It put the weight onto his left wing.

His roar shook grit into her eyes.

Olyra pulled again. The wheel turned half a spoke, then another. Muddy water
foamed through the gate and struck her knees. She did not have enough strength
for the final turn.

A slate-green claw punched through the passage roof behind her.

Mossback tore away loose stone, widening the gap only enough to hook one claw
tip around the far side of the wheel.

"Together," he said.

Olyra pushed as Mossback pulled.

The gate opened.

Water took the passage.

It flung Olyra off her feet and dragged her toward the dark eastern channel.
Mossback's claw closed around the back of her coat and hauled her through the
gap he had made. They landed in the quarry mud as the diverted flood burst from
the old outflow and raced toward the Cress hills.

Far off, three cistern gates opened in succession. The first clean surge
flashed silver through the orchard channels. The second made space. The third,
the little eastern gate, shrieked exactly like Lord Osric considering a new
form.

Then the brown flood reached them.

The emptied cisterns swallowed the first violent rush. Larkspur flew low over
the channels, wrenching debris free with her claws, answering Lord Ruvik's
repeated calls until frost dulled her green-and-violet scales and he could no
longer stand without help. Each chose the cost again because each knew what
the other was asking.

At the quarry, pressure came off the wall.

It did not come off quickly enough.

The northern ledge sheared downward. Nyrzath twisted to keep it from the
nesting seam. His damaged wing folded under the stone with a sound Olyra felt
in her teeth.

Something small tumbled from behind his horn.

Even half buried, Nyrzath snapped his jaws through the falling rubble.

For one sick instant Olyra thought the swallow was gone.

Then Nyrzath closed his mouth without biting and settled his tusked chin into
the mud. The wall held. Behind his shoulder, Mossback reached the nesting seam
and called into the dark. Small answering chirps rose from the cavern.

The clutch lived. The villages stood. In the Cress hills, the flood spread
through stone basins built and maintained by both halves of an alliance.

Nyrzath's gold eye found Olyra.

He could not speak with his mouth occupied, so he nodded gravely.

It was, she thought, very nearly tomorrow.

Once the fallen stone had been levered clear, Nyrzath banked the furnace-light
behind his teeth to darkness and opened his jaws. Olyra lifted out the shaken
but living swallow, wrapped it in her scarf, and sent it to a warm quarry shed
under Lord Ruvik's careful eye while Nyrzath's wing was freed.

* * *

Mossback refused House Flint a second time before sunset.

He did it while standing between the villages and the injured royal dragon,
his scales streaked with quarry mud.

"I will watch the valley's people because I choose to," he told Duchess
Yselle. "I will not renew with you."

House Flint's title remained suspended. Duchess Yselle went before ordinary
judgment for the illegal cut and concealed instability. No dragon's roar
replaced evidence, repair, or law.

Nyrzath's wing required splints the length of roof beams. Olyra saw to the work
with the same seriousness House Cress gave Larkspur's cisterns and molting
grounds. An alliance, she had learned, was easiest to praise while asking the
dragon to bleed for it. Its truth showed afterward, when care was owed in the
other direction.

The convocation resumed around his bandaged wing.

Without the Dread Passage, the court seemed at first too quiet. Then every
human heir and every dragon ally came forward one pair at a time. They asked.
They answered freely. Nyrzath witnessed them whole. House Flint's vacant place
did not break the law; it proved the law meant something.

Their assent confirmed Queen Olyra only after she had accepted that it might
not.

Lord Osric presented her first proclamation with the expression of a man who
had survived the collapse of civilization and found it required only modest
changes to the filing system.

Olyra read it aloud. The royal dragon would enter future renewals as impartial
witness, without threat or Dread Passage.

"King Ambric used to say a crown sometimes needs a gentle friend to wear a
monster's face," she said.

Nyrzath's gold eye rested on her.

"He was wrong. A crown that needs a friend to lie about his nature has
mistaken fear for loyalty."

As her last words faded, Lord Ruvik emerged behind Nyrzath with Olyra's scarf
cupped in his hands. Sheltered from the court by the bandaged wing, Nyrzath
quenched the glow in his mouth and accepted the swallow onto his tongue. Then
he turned immediately toward Olyra.

Nyrzath bent toward her.

Court workers scattered from the path of his approaching jaws. Lord Osric
stood his ground, though he became extremely interested in the proclamation's
lower margin.

Nyrzath opened his mouth.

The damp, furious swallow hopped off his tongue into Olyra's hands.

It pecked her thumb, launched itself toward the rafters, and vanished into the
light.

"Terrifying," Olyra said.

"I have that effect on small creatures," Nyrzath replied.
