stories.body:
# The Future That Refused Us

The dead had been arranged beneath the bell tower because it was the highest dry place in the lower ward.

Thirty-seven of them lay in two rows on the wet flagstones, covered with sailcloth, each pair of bare feet pointing toward the river. Water ticked from the hems. Beside them, rescuers knelt over the living with blankets, splints, and the last clean jars from a medicine cart never meant to arrive anywhere except at the hour appointed for it.

Zadie Cleft stood among them with the broken counter-cadence still trembling in her bones.

She had done it. The impossible thing. The Covenant of Hours was broken.

Above the square, the great salt-glass schedule had split from its center to every edge. For three centuries its luminous lines had held Sablewake's days: births, storms, marriages, collapsed roofs, nine thousand small errands and, at the end of each cycle, the exact course of the flood. Now the glass showed only the night up to the forty-ninth heartbeat after the hinge. Beyond that, it was dark.

Events no verse had named were happening everywhere.

A woman pressed both hands to a stranger's wound instead of waiting for an assigned surgeon. Three children formed a chain to pass cups. A man shouted that the north cistern was leaning, and no one moved, because no bell had told them whether he was right.

Near the tower stairs, Nilo Cleft sat wrapped in a horse blanket. Mud striped his face. A raw band crossed both palms where the undergate wheel had begun to turn beneath them.

Alive.

Zadie crossed the square too quickly, splashing through water pink with brick dust. She crouched and reached for him.

Nilo pulled away.

Her hands closed on the blanket's wet edge.

"How many?" he asked.

She looked toward the sailcloth.

"How many for me?"

"We don't know yet."

"You knew there could be some."

Around them, people were listening without seeming to. Zadie could feel the shape of the answer that would protect the thousands who had obeyed her secret bells. The undergate failed. The river rose faster than witnessed. The Covenant broke before anyone could—

"Zadie."

Baird Ansel came down the tower steps with one arm around a rescuer's shoulders. The first reader's white ceremonial coat was gray with floodwater, and a crack in the salt glass had left a burn like spilled ink across his temple. Yesterday he had been able to feel the pressure of tomorrow behind his eyes. Now his gaze moved over the square with the frightened care of someone learning distance.

"The north cistern is shifting," Baird said. "If it goes, it will take the infirmary roof and the west footbridge."

No line brightened in the schedule. No reader began the verse that would place every hand where survival required it.

Nilo looked past Zadie at the dead.

"Was I worth them?"

The paving stones shuddered. From somewhere upriver came the slow grinding of masonry.

Zadie had built bells to tell a whole city what to do. For the first time in her life, she had no honest answer to ring.

* * *

The day before the flood, she had tried to disobey in the smallest way she could devise.

The schedule said she would take the east stair to the noon bell. Zadie left her tools in the tower, slipped through the west door, and set one boot on the west stair.

The handrail tore loose under her palm.

She lurched backward into a porter carrying lamp oil. The porter twisted to save the jars, struck the door with a shoulder, and knocked it shut. Zadie caught the falling rail before it crushed the porter's foot. By the time they had wrestled the iron aside, oil slicked the west landing and the only safe path was through the east passage.

She ran. Halfway up, a child dropped a basket of apples. Zadie jumped the rolling fruit, collided with a bell apprentice coming down, and lost enough seconds arguing over whose knee was hurt that she reached the east stair's top as the noon striker descended.

The bell sounded while her hand was on its rope.

Exactly as the salt-glass line had shown.

"Do you believe me now?" Baird had asked.

He waited in the reading chamber with the other eight readers. They stood around the schedule with their palms against its rim. The glass did nothing alone. It held what their living minds poured through it: witnessed sequence, correction, and memory. Each reader had forgotten some private country to keep Sablewake inside the future they had seen. Baird no longer remembered his brother's face. Another had surrendered the sound of rain before it struck stone. Their losses were not payment demanded by every magic in the world; they were the working cost of this covenant, renewed by these nine lives every thirty years.

"I believed you before," Zadie said.

"You believed you were the exception."

Light gathered beneath their hands. The flood verse climbed the glass in pale, unwavering marks.

At the cycle's end, the river would overtop the embankment. Nilo would remain at the manual undergate wheel as the chamber filled. His turning would close the gate. The lower ward would stay dry.

Nine other entries marked nine deaths across Sablewake: two workers on the east wall, a boat crew of three, four patients whose medicines could not arrive before dawn.

Ten deaths.

Every other registered breath would continue into morning.

Zadie had tried to make Nilo the eleventh survivor. She packed him into a grain cart bound inland, but a snapped axle spilled the sacks and sent him home by the undergate road. She barred him in their loft; a pipe burst in the wall, and the repair crew carried him out through the only dry passage, which ended beside the gatehouse. She drugged his tea, then dropped the cup when a bell rope whipped loose and wrapped her wrist. Each rescue became a step toward the wheel.

Baird traced the last line without touching it.

"You cannot remove one death and keep the guarantee around everyone else."

"Then the guarantee is a cage."

"It is also why this city is still here."

Zadie looked at the names the future had already made past tense.

In the maintenance archives, she had found the only moment when the cage's bars weakened. At the hinge, for forty-nine heartbeats, the readers had to carry both the closing cycle and the opening one. Old marginalia described scattered disobediences then: a wedding refused, a knife dropped, a gate opened early. The Covenant had corrected them violently, but not at once. Its capacity was vast, not infinite.

For six months, Zadie had hidden a second language inside ordinary bell drills.

Thousands of people had learned it.

Not enough of them knew what it might cost.

* * *

On the flood night, the closing verse drove Sablewake as relentlessly as the rain.

Every lit window, every running figure, every boat pushing into a prescribed street matched its line in the salt glass. Zadie watched from the undergate gallery while the river struck the iron doors below. Red rust wept from the counterweight chain.

The inspection seal on its housing was unbroken.

Untested.

She had asked twice for a live release. Twice, the schedule had shown no need, and metal, labor, and time had gone to predicted failures instead. The Covenant had never required redundancy for a future that could not vary.

Nilo stood at the manual wheel, both hands on the spokes. Thirteen years old, shoulders set in furious imitation of courage. Water curled around his ankles.

"When the wrong bell sounds," Zadie told him, "walk up the gallery. Don't stop for anything."

"Who turns the wheel?"

Above them, the nine readers began the hinge song. The sound entered the ironwork and made every bolt hum. Closing verse and opening verse overlapped inside their living voices.

Forty-nine heartbeats.

Zadie put her hand on the counter-cadence rope.

No person could replace Nilo at the wheel. She had tested names, shifts, volunteers. The Covenant seized on every substitute and turned that life into another road leading Nilo down. Only a blind mechanism lay outside the breath registry, and the counterweight could not choose or work magic. It could merely fall when a living hand released it.

If it worked.

If it did not, the lower ward would take the river. Most of its residents had never heard the secret cadence. They had not chosen uncertainty. Zadie had told the participants they risked their own foreknown safety. She had not told them whose cellars lay behind the untested gate.

Nilo searched her face. "It closes by itself?"

The readers reached the first heartbeat.

Zadie saw the rust at the chain's deepest link. She remembered the inspector saying that a seal was not a test. She remembered telling herself that no change worth making came without danger, as if danger were a purse she alone would empty.

"Yes," she said. "The counterweight is enough."

Her son believed her.

At the seventh heartbeat, she rang.

The counter-cadence went out beneath the storm, disguised no longer: a low strike, two quick, one low. Tower answered tower across Sablewake, each reply reaching Zadie as a dull iron pulse through the rain.

She could not know which private choices people had prepared; that ignorance was part of her design. She had asked each participant to choose one mundane act and reverse it at the signal.

As the replies multiplied, she imagined a baker standing instead of kneeling, a ferryman raising the right hand instead of the left. She imagined bedrooms, workshops, wall posts, and floodboats where someone stepped backward, shut an open door, spoke instead of keeping silent. Any one of those acts would be trivial. The strain she heard in the song told her what their combined demand was doing: nine minds already holding two futures were being forced to correct thousands of deviations at once.

The hinge song sharpened.

The gallery floor tilted beneath Zadie, forcing her toward the cadence rope she meant to release. She wrapped it around her forearm. A falling tool struck the counterweight lever, nearly locking it. Nilo slipped and caught the wheel. Everywhere, the Covenant found accidents, reflexes, other bodies—anything to force the witnessed sequence back into place.

At the twenty-third heartbeat, bells began ringing without hands as their ropes snapped and recoiled.

At the thirty-first, bloodless white light poured from the readers' chamber.

At the fortieth, the hinge song split into nine cries.

"Now!" Zadie shouted.

Nilo let go.

The wheel spun toward his palms. He flinched, then did the one thing no version of the salt glass had ever permitted: he stepped away.

Zadie pulled the release.

The counterweight dropped half its length and jammed. The gate shuddered, remaining open by the width of a coffin.

The river came through.

At the forty-ninth heartbeat, the schedule cracked. The pressure that had bent every stray choice toward one outcome vanished so suddenly Zadie fell forward. Above, five voices stopped. The remaining four dissolved into ordinary human screaming.

Nilo stood at the gallery stair, alive beyond the moment of his death.

Then the flood struck the lower ward.

* * *

In the square beneath the tower, the north cistern groaned again.

"Ropes," Zadie called. Command steadied her voice even if nothing else could. "Clear the west footbridge. Brace the cistern from the roofline."

People looked at her, then at the dead. Some knew her hand in the counter-cadence. Others only knew that the schedule was dark and her son was breathing.

"There are three boats at the south steps," someone shouted.

"There were supposed to be twelve," another answered.

"The other nine were never needed tonight," Baird said.

The city's storehouses held no discretionary timber. Its gate crews had no trained doubles. Its medicines arrived at the last possible hour because the Covenant had guaranteed that hour. Exact safety had taught Sablewake to regard every spare as waste.

Now three emergencies shouted over one another: the leaning cistern, a school cellar filling through a cracked drain, and people trapped beyond the fallen footbridge.

Zadie divided the available hands. "Two boats to the cellar. One to the bridge. Everyone else haul timber to the cistern."

"Which timber?" a voice demanded.

There was none.

She had an answer for every question except those the city needed.

A fisher pushed through the listeners, pointing not to the empty lumber rack but to the flooded market. "Net floats," the fisher said. "Lash them under the bridge planks. We don't need to rebuild it. We need it to stay up for ten crossings."

Two apprentices were already stripping ropes from the silent bell frames. Nobody had scheduled their idea. Nobody stopped them. Within moments, a crooked path of buoyed planks extended across the break.

On the ninth crossing, part of it rolled. A rescuer went into the water. Three hands caught the rope and dragged the rescuer back.

On the tenth, they carried a child over.

It was clumsy and perilous and new.

It was also too late for the people beneath the sailcloth.

Baird lowered himself beside Zadie on the tower stair. His hands shook. "The count is sixty-eight dead in all, including five readers," he said. "More are missing."

Nilo stood within earshot, the blanket hanging from his shoulders.

Baird's damaged gaze fixed on Zadie. "The witnessed future killed ten. Nilo and nine others. Ten, Zadie. Not sixty-eight. It spared everyone else because we spent our lives making it hold."

"It chose a child."

"And you chose a ward."

She recoiled.

"Say it accurately," Baird continued. His voice did not rise. It did not need to. "You did not break a cruel certainty and accept the consequences yourself. You assigned the uncertainty to people who did not know your plan. You let your volunteers believe they were staking their own lives while families below the gate carried the wager."

Each word found a place she had tried not to look.

"Should I have walked him to the wheel?"

"No." Baird glanced at Nilo. "A future can be intolerable and still protect people. Both facts survive each other. Your son's life was not yours to surrender. Their safety was not yours to spend."

Nilo pulled off the blanket.

"And my choice?" he asked. His voice shook with cold and rage. "She lied to me. You all wrote me dead before I could vote on anything. Where was my choice in your ten?"

Baird bowed his head. "There was none."

"Then don't make those ten sound clean."

"I don't." Baird looked at the covered rows. "I make them smaller."

The cracked cistern groaned, and the square fell silent again.

* * *

The city officials gathered at the bell table with a statement already written.

It said the Covenant had failed under extraordinary flood pressure. It said Nilo's abandonment of the undergate had caused the lower-ward deaths. It asked the remaining readers to restore order until a new schedule could be made.

There would be no new schedule. Baird had lost the inward sense by which the readers held one another inside a witnessed sequence. Even if the four survivors could renew the rite, there was no intact opening verse to carry.

But the statement offered the city three familiar comforts: failure without an author, a child to punish, and the promise that somebody might yet know tomorrow.

"Sign it," an official urged Zadie. "The crowd needs one cause."

Nilo read over her shoulder. When he reached the line about abandonment, his face hardened.

"I walked because you told me the gate would close," he said.

Zadie could not look at him.

"Tell them."

Outside, survivors filled the square. Some demanded the readers sing again. Some shouted for the undergate boy. Some called for the people who had rung the wrong cadence to be dragged forward. Fear moved through them faster than the river.

"If the old verse required him," an official said quietly, "perhaps completing it would settle the Covenant."

Nilo went very still.

Baird took the page from Zadie and tore it once, neatly, across the center.

"No," he said. "The verse is broken. Killing Nilo now would not close a gate, restore a guarantee, or raise one drowned person. It would only add a death that no future asked for."

The official opened another copy.

Baird looked at Zadie. "Truth will not make this just. But a lie will teach the city the same lesson you claim to have broken: that no living chooser is responsible when an authority says the outcome had to happen."

Nilo stepped between Zadie and the bell table.

"I won't die so your numbers look tidy," he told the officials. Then, to Zadie: "And I won't be the reason you say it was worth it."

She saw what her silence was already building around him. If she hid, the city would turn Nilo into the author of her decision. If she commanded the crowd to spare him, she would be trying once more to use the bells as a future nobody else could refuse.

Zadie picked up the striker.

* * *

The emergency bell had no unscripted cadence. Every pattern in its three-century book corresponded to a foreseen danger and an assigned response.

Zadie struck it once.

The note rolled over the square, solitary and strange.

"My name is Zadie Cleft," she called from the tower platform. "I designed the counter-cadence. I hid it in the drills. I knew the readers had limited strength during the forty-nine heartbeats, and I coordinated enough contradictions to exceed it."

The square stirred. She made herself continue before courage could disguise itself as eloquence.

"I knew the undergate counterweight had not been tested. I knew no person could be assigned to replace Nilo without the Covenant turning that assignment back toward him. I told Nilo the weight was sufficient. That was a lie."

Below her, Nilo did not look away.

"The fixed flood would have killed ten people: Nilo and nine others. It guaranteed the survival of everyone else registered in Sablewake. We have counted sixty-eight dead since the breach. Eleven more are missing. Five of the dead were readers. The count may rise."

Someone threw a lump of river mud. It struck the tower below her boots.

"I will submit to judgment when the immediate rescues are done. I am not asking you to forgive me. Nilo's life does not pay for the dead. Freedom does not pay for them. I made people carry a risk I concealed, and whatever future we have begins with that truth."

The north cistern cracked like winter ice.

Zadie set down the confession and lifted the observation slate.

"Here is what we know, not what is promised. The cistern's north foot is sinking. The infirmary roof is clear. There are ropes on the west frames, six net floats at the bridge, two boats at the school cellar, and enough hands in this square for more than one attempt."

She drew three rough marks on the slate and held it where the lanterns could find it.

"One group can brace from the roof. One can drain the cistern into the market channel. One can rig a safety line beneath both. Choose among them. Improve them. Refuse them if you see better."

For a breath, no one moved.

Then Nilo climbed the first stair.

"The lower spillway is blocked," he said. "A rope line could pull it open from the side passage."

"The side passage is flooding," Zadie said.

"I know."

Every muscle in her wanted to order him back. That desire had worn two faces now: sacrifice him because the verse guaranteed others, save him because her love outweighed them. Both made his life into a thing she owned.

"What safeguards?" she asked.

His anger flickered—not gone, but forced to share space with thought. "Two ropes, not one. Knots checked by different hands. Nobody goes alone. We change pullers before they're exhausted."

"And if the water reaches the third stair?"

"We leave. Even if the spillway isn't open."

Zadie nodded. "Your choice."

"Not your forgiveness," he said.

"No."

He turned to the square. "I need six."

Nine people came. One cursed Zadie as they passed. Another pressed a coil of rope into Nilo's hands. The fisher shouted a change to the drain plan. The two apprentices divided the remaining lines without waiting for permission. Some citizens did nothing. Some wept beside the sailcloth. Some began carrying jars and blankets toward the infirmary.

Zadie descended into them.

No one absolved her. Two rescuers made her repeat every knot she tied and checked each one after her. She worked under their eyes.

Across Sablewake, bells began to answer the emergency note. One rang twice from the east wall. Another gave three uncertain taps near the school cellar. A handbell sounded from a rooftop, paused, then sounded again. They did not agree on a cadence. They did not promise that everyone would live.

They told one another where living hands were needed.

Nilo's rope tightened beside Zadie's, one strand among many. Together—but not as one—they pulled against the water.

stories.body:
# The Thirteenth Command

The pressure shock caught Edda Rook with one hand on the old dispatch board.

She had come into the cistern command gallery for a paper copy of one route
chart, nothing more. The southern pressure chamber had gone silent six minutes
earlier, and Sula Brant's repair crew was still inside it. Harven Coil's watch
had the upper stairs. Drouth League fighters had the lower gates. Somewhere
between them, three people waited for Edda to remember which maintenance
passage the old maps had forgotten.

Then a shot struck a pipe collar. The board flashed white. Stone rose under
Edda's boots, and the gallery ceiling came down to meet her.

In the dark, block letters opened across her sight.

`SYSTEM UPDATE: HOST FOUND`

`HOST CAPABILITIES CONFIRMED`

`SEEKING CLASS APPLICATIONS`

Records flickered behind the words: thirty-six years of flood calls, gate
orders, pump failures, evacuation grids. Her own voice, younger and quicker,
assigned crews through storms she had almost managed to forget.

`CLASS FOUND`

`APPLYING CLASS: COMBAT CONTROLLER`

No, Edda thought, although thought was all she had.

`PREVIOUS EXPERIENCE CONFIRMED`

The records accelerated. She saw four neighborhoods blinking red during the
great surge, then two workers' beacons trapped beyond a closure line. She heard
herself give the protocol order that saved the western district. She heard,
again, the silence after.

`APPLYING PREVIOUS EXPERIENCE`

`LEVEL UP`

The words repeated too quickly to count. Each repetition forced some new
arrangement into the display: priorities, routes, pressures, voices separated
into channels. Nothing touched her memory or her will. It merely indexed what
she already knew in language built for a battle.

`LEVEL 13 REACHED WITH PREVIOUS EXPERIENCE IN CLASS`

`RETENTION DECISION DEFERRED UNTIL STABILITY`

`WAKING HOST`

Edda woke with lime dust in her mouth and Harven gripping her shoulder. Blood
tracked from his temple into his gray beard, but his other hand held a rifle
steady on the lower door.

"Tell me you can see the board," he said.

The board had been dead since before Sula was an apprentice. Now pale lines
shone across its glass and echoed over Edda's ordinary vision: pipes,
galleries, and a field of uncertain red marks.

"I can see too much of it."

"Good. The south chamber seals in ten minutes. I need a Controller."

"You have a watch captain."

"I need the doors that only answer to the thing in your head."

Edda pushed herself upright. "It isn't in my head. The lattice tagged my civic
seal."

The distinction sounded thin even to her. The old command engine had applied
permissions while she lay unconscious. It was damaged cells, conduits, and
archived protocols, not a mind. Its flat notices answered no questions.

Another panel unfolded.

`TEMPORARY CLASS SESSION ACTIVE`

`MESH RANGE: COPPERWELL CISTERN`

`CELL LIFE AT CURRENT LOAD: 00:11:02`

`BEACON LINKS REQUIRE INDIVIDUAL ACCEPTANCE`

`AVAILABLE DATA: TRANSMITTED POSITION / VOICE / PULSE`

Edda looked past Harven. Two watch members crouched at the lower door, waiting
for the next League push. Beyond the wall, a pressure needle chattered hard
against its stop.

"I want Sula's route," Edda said. "You get nothing else until I have it."

Harven's jaw tightened. A thump sounded below, followed by three close shots.
"Find it while we still own the gallery."

Edda accepted the temporary session.

The world divided into layers. Old structural sensors painted pressure in
shades from cool gray to a yellow that hurt to look at. The watch beacons
appeared as requests, not people: eight points asking permission to transmit to
her. She accepted them one by one. Each point sharpened into location, voice,
and a pulse mark where the wearer allowed it.

Harven pointed to the two at the door. "League is climbing through the west
filter. Get those two behind them."

"If they agree."

He gave her a look. Edda sent the route with its source attached: survey map,
thirty-one years old. Both beacons accepted. The pair slipped through a side
arch and moved along the east spur while Edda watched their lights slide over
the map.

The route overlay exposed the east stair three levels below, its manual
spillwheel marked with an old service flag. Edda remembered eighteen jam calls
and the same remedy every time: lift before pulling. Irrelevant to the pair's
route, she thought, and left the flag in place.

It was appallingly familiar. During flood season, a city became lamps on a
board. The person at the board learned to keep the lamps moving and not imagine
their faces.

A new request flashed from beyond the southern bulkhead.

"Edda?" Sula's voice crackled into her ear. "If that's you, blink the request
twice."

Edda blinked it twice.

Sula accepted. Her beacon resolved deep in the south pressure chamber, beside
two weaker work signals. Relief struck Edda so hard she had to grip the board.

"Found you," she said.

"I hadn't misplaced myself."

Some habits, at least, had survived apprenticeship.

An alarm cut across them. The watch pair had stopped in the east spur. Their
map lights showed open corridor. Their voices reported a wall of broken stone.

"That roof came down three years ago," Sula said. "The old board never took
the repair revision."

Edda saw the League marks advancing only because a damaged stair sensor
reported weight. If she trusted the map, the pair had forty seconds. If the
sensor was wrong, she would route them toward gunfire.

She pulled the maintenance reports from her own authenticated archive, found a
handwritten waste-channel inspection, and laid it over the survey. "Back seven
paces. Hatch at knee height. It will be narrow."

"How narrow?" one of them asked.

"The record doesn't say."

They accepted anyway. One beacon vanished into sensor shadow, then the other.
For five breathless seconds Edda had only their voices and the scrape of gear.
They emerged behind the filter stair just as League fighters entered it.
Harven's pair fired into the ceiling, showering dust and stopping the advance
without trapping anyone below.

The lower door held.

"Useful," Harven said.

Edda watched the false corridor remain serenely open on the lattice map.
"Dangerous."

The cell clock read `00:09:47`.

More requests arrived. Every surviving watch beacon was requesting the mesh
now. Voices crowded Edda: a cracked valve on the north walk, movement under a
drain grate, two wounded at the ration gates, one body no one could yet reach,
pressure climbing in a pipe no one could see. The class separated the reports
by urgency, but it did not make them true. It gave confidence grades based on
old sensors and distance. It offered routes through walls that existed only on
paper.

Edda did what she had done through thirty-six wet seasons. She asked who could
verify. She repeated orders with their reasons. She sent one team to cover the
wounded and told another to abandon an empty stair Harven wanted defended.
When three voices spoke at once, she narrowed them into separate threads and
felt the effort as a band tightening behind her eyes.

Sula's chamber remained the fixed red center of every choice.

"The south gate is twisting in its track," Sula reported. Metal groaned behind
her words. "If we brace the lower hinge, we can reach the service crawl."

The lattice drew a predicted collapse around the chamber. Sixty-eight percent
under present pressure. Eighty-one if the lower hinge took another shock.

Edda muted the forecast from Sula's link.

"Brace it," she said. "Then take the crawl."

Sula did not move. Her beacon stayed exactly where it was.

"What did you just hide?"

"Nothing you need while you're under the gate."

"Then it wasn't nothing."

Harven was issuing orders beside Edda, preparing another push. The gallery
shook. The forecast climbed to seventy-three percent.

"Edda," Sula said, quieter. "Tell me the red number."

Years ago, two workers had asked whether the western closure would reopen in
time. Edda had given them the approved reassurance because panic interfered
with clean dispatch. She had kept her voice level until their beacons went out.

"Seventy-three percent chance of chamber failure if you load the lower hinge,"
she said. "The model is using an obsolete gate profile. It could be badly
wrong."

"Alternatives?"

"Stay where you are and the automatic seal reaches you in under eight minutes.
Force the service crawl and the gate may come down sooner. I don't have a safe
route."

Sula took one audible breath. "The waste vent was widened last dry month. It
isn't on your archive because the work hasn't been certified. We can take the
brace through there and set it from the far side."

Edda found the vent on the old plan, too small for shoulders and thirty years
out of date. "Can all three of you fit?"

"We are prepared to find out."

"I need better than that."

"No. You need honest uncertainty. That's what you have."

Sula transmitted a rough measurement from her work slate. Edda added it to the
map as a current report, clearly marked unverified. The forecast dropped to
forty-six percent.

"Your choice," Edda said. "I recommend the vent."

"Accepted."

The three beacons began to move.

The pressure needle struck its stop again. This time Edda felt the rhythm
through the soles of her boots: three fast impacts, a pause, then two. It was
not the random battering of shots. It was a feedback surge, the kind that
developed when gates at opposite ends of a water system fought one another.

She stripped the troop routes from her display and spread the structural
telemetry wide. The lattice highlighted the main cistern wall as sound because
its oldest sensors said so. Edda ignored the comforting green. She watched the
delays between the north walk and south chamber, counted the beats, and
remembered a pump station that had split before its gauges admitted anything
was wrong.

"Stop firing," she said.

Harven looked over. "Tell them."

"Everyone. Both sides. The concussions are feeding a pressure cascade."

"The League has the west gallery. If my people stop, they reach the ration
controls."

"If nobody stops, the main baffle tears loose. After that, the cistern wall
gets the full wave."

The lattice assembled her observations into a forecast. It had wide margins
and too many amber sources.

`PROBABLE CASCADE WINDOW: 00:05:31–00:07:04`

Harven read it from the board. His face changed, but not enough. "Then we use
the scour gates now. Seal the south chamber, open the gallery sluice, and drive
the League out before the baffle goes."

The class offered the same template. Blue arrows closed the south bulkhead.
Water scoured the disputed gallery. Enemy beacons disappeared from the model.
So did Sula and the two repair workers.

"The pressure wave will pick up silt from the lower bed," Edda said. "You may
save a cracked cistern full of mud."

"May. Your forecast may also be wrong. Mine ends an armed assault in ninety
seconds."

His plan was not cowardice. Harven checked the chamber of his rifle, then
gestured his squad toward the east stair. He meant to go down with them. He
simply knew which deaths he could put in the acceptable column.

A burst of open-band static crossed the lattice. Then an unfamiliar voice,
strained and breathless.

"Copperwell watch, open the ration channels. East bank has days, not weeks. We
did not come for your city."

The League signal lead was broadcasting from somewhere near the west gallery.
Harven reached for the cutoff.

"Leave it," Edda said.

"They came with rifles."

"And you mean to answer with a flood."

"I mean to keep water in Copperwell."

On the board, both victories ended in the same broken blue shape. The League
could seize the ration controls and tear open gates against full pressure. The
watch could scour the gallery and drive the cascade into the south wall.
Neither side had the other's sensor data. Each believed the cistern would
survive long enough to win.

A notice opened beneath the forecast.

`LEVEL 13 PROTOCOL AVAILABLE`

`COMMAND 13: COMMON CAUSE`

`REQUIREMENT: ONE DECLARED OBJECTIVE`

`HOSTILE BEACONS MAY ACCEPT / REFUSE / WITHDRAW`

`ACCEPTED TACTICAL DATA SHARED SYMMETRICALLY`

`ESTIMATED CELL EXPENDITURE: ALL OPERATIONAL RESERVE`

Edda opened the detail. Common Cause would invite every beacon in lattice
range, including those tagged hostile. It would share accepted positions,
voices, hazard readings, and every route Edda published. No hidden team. No
private map. Before acceptance, an invite showed only the declared objective
and whatever structural data Edda chose to publish; no live beacon data crossed
the field. No compulsion. Anyone could refuse, lie through an unlinked channel,
or use the knowledge against them.

The cell clock read `00:05:58`.

"Run the scour template," Harven said.

"No."

"That is a lawful emergency order."

"Then put my refusal in your incident report."

"Sula is dead if that chamber seals. I know. But if we lose the cistern,
thousands queue at dry taps tomorrow."

Edda searched for a private route, some clever thread that could save Sula
without showing the League Copperwell's defenses. Every version failed at the
same place: the jammed south gate needed hands on both sides, and the manual
spillwheel on the east stair had to turn at the exact moment the ration
channels vented. No one side controlled all three.

Abstaining would not keep her hands clean. It would only leave Harven to name
the cost.

Every command had a cost. The honest ones carried it in plain sight.

Harven turned toward the stair. "I will do it without the lattice."

He withdrew his beacon link. Each squad member's beacon registered a separate
withdrawal after his, the last pausing for one long second before it vanished.
Harven could lead them toward the stair. He could not choose their links for
them.

Edda selected Command Thirteen.

"Objective," the open channel prompted in flat text.

She spoke to Copperwell's watch, Sula's crew, and the people who had entered the
cistern with rifles because their settlements were going dry.

"Nobody drowns. The cistern holds."

She published the cascade forecast with its uncertainty. She published the
obsolete structural maps, an uncredited correction to the waste vent's
dimensions, and the fixed locations of the ration controls, south gate, and
manual spillwheel. No person's position appeared. She published the cost: the
remaining lattice cells, the city's tactical secrecy, and the chance that
anyone accepting might still betray the rest.

"I cannot make you agree," she said. "If you accept, everyone in the field sees
what you transmit. If you refuse, the doors stay open for you to leave. If we
keep fighting, the wall likely fails before six minutes. Those are the facts I
have. They are not guarantees."

For one long second, no beacon changed.

Then Sula accepted.

Only then did her light turn white at the center of the south chamber. Each of
the two repair workers accepted in turn and appeared beside her. Four watch
beacons joined on separate confirmations, then two more. Across the west
gallery, League signals appeared for the first time, scattered among the old
pipes. Five accepted individually. Three did not. One accepted, withdrew at
once, and disappeared down the lower stair.

Harven remained absent.

The shared field filled Edda's sight. Voices struck together, and the band
behind her eyes cinched until the edges of the gallery went dark.

"Sula, will you take the south node?"

The request contained authority only over information Sula's group chose to
route.

"Accepted," Sula said.

The map divided. Sula took the gate brace, combining her current measurements
with a League report from its far side. Edda assigned the neutral maintenance
walk for moving wounded people away from the west gallery. Watch and League
members entered it from opposite ends, weapons slung but hands never far from
them.

"Brace team needs four," Sula said. "Two each side. The hinge will jump on the
first vent."

Two League beacons and two watch beacons moved toward the jammed gate. They
could see one another now. For a terrible moment, nobody crossed the final
corner.

Then a watch member shoved the timber brace across the wet floor. A League
fighter caught it. Four sets of hands lifted together while the gate bucked
above them.

The signal lead transmitted a pressure reading from the west controls. It
contradicted the lattice by almost a quarter.

"Sensor age?" Edda asked.

"Hand gauge. Reading now."

Edda marked it current, human-reported. The cascade window shortened.

`00:02:41–00:03:18`

Her right hand began to tremble. The class prioritized a red surge at the north
walk, and she nearly ordered an immediate vent before Sula cut across her.

"No. If north vents before the brace seats, the south gate slams."

Edda had missed the hinge-load marker. It sat at the edge of her narrowing
vision.

"Correct," she said. The word tasted like fear. "South node controls pulse
timing."

She delegated it. The display quieted by one degree.

At the neutral walk, someone fired. The report cracked through every accepted
link. Beacons froze.

"Shot went high," a watch voice said.

"Refused beacon at the drain," the League signal lead answered. "Not in the
field."

Common Cause had stopped nothing. It had only made the choice visible.

"Move the wounded," Edda said. "Anyone unwilling, withdraw by the lower
stairs. Nobody pursues."

Two beacons left the field. The others began moving again. They carried the
wounded past one another through ankle-deep water while the pressure climbed.

"Brace seated," Sula called. "Ready for first pulse."

"Spillwheel?" Edda asked.

Silence.

Harven and the three squad members had been nearest when they withdrew. Without
the manual wheel, the vent sequence would hammer shut against trapped pressure.
Edda sent the invitation again, not as an order but with Sula's timing, the
shortened window, and the same objective.

The lattice cells fell under one minute.

One squad member accepted and appeared beside the spillwheel. A second
accepted. Then the third. Each beacon carried its own confirmation; Harven's
position remained dark.

"Harven," she said on the open band. "I do not need you to trust the League. I
need you to decide whether the objective is true."

Nothing.

Then the watch captain's beacon reappeared on the east stair.

He accepted.

His position resolved among the three waiting squad members, three levels below
the gallery. Harven's pulse ran fast. His voice did not.

"Wheel is jammed."

"It always sticks before the first quarter turn," Edda said. She had dispatched
maintenance there eighteen times. "Lift, then pull. Do not force it downward."

On Sula's count, the south team locked the brace. Harven and the three squad
members heaved the wheel upward. Across the west gallery, League fighters
opened one ration channel by a hand's breadth.

"First pulse," Sula said.

Water struck the pipes with a sound like a building taking breath. The floor
tilted. One of the south beacons winked out, not withdrawn but lost behind a
sensor shadow.

Edda reached for it and lost the timing thread.

"I have the gate," Sula said. "Watch the wall."

Edda obeyed. She watched the delayed pressure readings ripple north. The old
sensors lied high, the hand gauge read low, and the truth moved somewhere
between. She gave Harven the range rather than a clean number.

"Second pull between four and six seconds. Your judgment."

"Understood."

He chose five.

The spillwheel turned. The ration channel opened another hand. The brace team
shouted as the gate jumped, but it held. A deep wave passed under the gallery,
lifting dust from the ceiling in pale sheets. Edda's vision shrank to the thin
blue curve of the cistern wall.

The curve flexed.

It did not break.

Pressure emptied eastward through the ration channels, not as the torrent the
League had tried to seize, nor as the weapon Harven had meant to release, but
in measured, muddy pulses. The baffle's rhythm slowed. Three fast impacts
became two, then one, then the ordinary groan of old stone under water.

Sula's missing beacon returned.

"We are all here," she said.

Edda sat down hard against the dispatch board.

The cell clock showed nineteen seconds.

No one called the ceasefire a peace. The watch kept the upper gallery. The
League kept the west ration controls. Between them, wounded people lay on the
same maintenance walk while the jointly opened channel carried a narrow stream
toward the east bank.

Harven climbed back into the command gallery, wet to the shoulders. He set his
rifle against the wall rather than in his hands.

"They will want the full gates open," he said.

"Copperwell will want them shut."

"And tomorrow?"

"Tomorrow remains difficult."

The lattice offered one final set of choices.

`STABILITY THRESHOLD REACHED`

`EXPORT SYMMETRIC INCIDENT LOG?`

Edda sent a copy to the civic archive and to every beacon that had accepted
Common Cause. The log listed the League assault, Harven's scour order, her
refusal, the map errors, the uncertainties, the withdrawals, the wounded, and
the person who had died before the shared field opened. It would not create
justice. It would make a bloodless victory harder to invent.

`RETAIN COMBAT CONTROLLER CLASS AS PERMANENT PROFILE?`

Edda selected discard.

The overlays vanished. The world became stone, bad light, human voices, and a
board darkening beneath her hand.

Sula emerged from the south passage after dawn, limping slightly and furious
about the state of the gate. She embraced Edda once, hard, then stepped back.

"The city will build another command board," she said.

"Harven will."

"A civilian one. Repair crews, ration stewards, east-bank signals if they
choose. Current maps. Shared costs."

Edda looked across the gallery. Watch members and League fighters stood apart
again, negotiating how long the narrow channel would remain open. No glowing
field made them cooperate. They had only a cracked cistern, an honest record,
and the memory of whose hands had held the gate.

"They will ignore half our commands," Edda said.

"Then we will have to make better ones."

Edda had spent years believing that leaving the board meant she no longer chose
who carried the danger. The cistern had cured her of that vanity.

"One rule," she said. "Every command carries its cost beside it."

Sula offered her an arm for the broken stairs.

Together they climbed toward the argument waiting in the daylight.

stories.title: The Peace They Could Sleep Through
stories.prompt: The benevolent monarchy people have long since come to worship is really just a dozen or so dragons in disguise, hoping to set up a state that can keep everything not on fire for a few hundred years so that they can finally get some actual quality slumber.
stories.body:
# The Peace They Could Sleep Through

At nine in the morning, my god decided the terrace farmers owned next year's
seed beyond the reach of debt.

At nine and three minutes, my god decided the lenders could seize it.

My name was Lumen Mott. In the ordinary course of my office, I kept my god
from contradicting itself in public.

Both judgments arrived in the same blue file. Both bore the private seal of the
Sleepless Majesty. Both began with the phrase I had spent eleven years
perfecting: *Having heard every need, We answer without favor.*

I read them twice while the clock above my desk removed seven minutes from the
time remaining before terrace companies with farm tools reached the provincial
storehouses and house guards closed the city depots against their shipments.

Across from me, Ludo Dask gripped a seed sack between both knees. It held one
district's last clean planting grain, brought as evidence and handled as if it
were an infant. Beside him, Gelda Parn had opened an import ledger whose red
columns represented three shiploads purchased during two failed harvests.

"Well?" Ludo asked.

"The Sleepless Majesty will protect lawful obligation," Gelda said. "There is
no uncertainty."

That was the trouble with an infallible monarch. Uncertainty had to hide in the
clerical staff.

Ludo's districts could not surrender their seed or the tenancy land pledged
against royal loans. Gelda's milling and importing houses could not absorb a
total cancellation without ruining the credit that fed the cities. Both needs
were real. Both delegations had turned them into sacred absolutes. The terrace
companies had promised to occupy the storehouses if I ruled against them. The
house guards had promised to close the depots and detain terrace shipments if I
ruled the other way.

Neither petition offered a concession. I had removed those during preparation.
Undignified bargaining positions confused the question presented to the
Majesty.

There was an old alternative at the back of the procedure book. A common plea
allowed parties to end a case by filing their own agreement before royal
judgment. I had considered it for half a breath, then dismissed it. Common
pleas settled fence lines and disputed apprenticeships. This case concerned
famine, national credit, and perhaps civil conflict. It required a perfect
answer.

I closed the blue file.

"I need clarification," I said.

Gelda looked offended on behalf of divine competence. Ludo looked offended on
principle.

"Wait here."

I took both judgments and went to ask my god which one my god meant.

* * *

The private consultation room had one public door, never opened while a
petitioner waited, and a service door for clerks carrying tea and regrettable
facts. I had used the latter for years. That morning, nobody answered my knock.

Inside, twelve identical figures wearing the face of the Sleepless Majesty were
arguing.

They had the same smooth brown face, the same close silver curls, the same
androgynous body in the same loose gray robe. One stood on the table. Three had
filled the window seat. Two were correcting each other's corrections. Each
held an annotated copy of the grain case.

"Seizing seed preserves contract law by eliminating anyone available to honor
contracts," said the figure on the table.

"Cancellation preserves agriculture by ensuring nobody will finance it
again," replied one at the window.

"We might purchase both claims."

"With whose grain?"

"This is why I requested eighty uninterrupted years before we attempted
credit."

I dropped the blue file.

Twelve identical faces turned toward me.

The one nearest the service door said, "Adjudicator Mott."

"Your Majesty," I said automatically.

"Yes," said all twelve.

The nearest winced. "That is going to complicate the explanation."

The change began with breath. Each human outline expanded on an exhalation, as
if the body had been a garment held taut from within. Gray robes slipped from
shoulders becoming scaled, furred, ridged, or plated. Twelve long necks
uncoiled beneath a ceiling built with suspiciously generous vaults. Claws
clicked on the tiled floor. Wings folded with varying degrees of etiquette.

They were twelve distinct dragons.

One had pearl scales and a broad, blunt muzzle. One was lean and violet, with
translucent spines pressed carefully flat beneath the ceiling. Two were shades
of green but differed in every other proportion. A bronze dragon was small
enough to remain on the table and looked pleased about it. The largest was
gray, soft-frilled, and still wearing the Majesty's silver curls around one
horn.

The dragon nearest me was deep blue, with pale markings around the eyes that
made exhaustion look ceremonial.

"My individual name is Varkesh," the dragon said. "I am the current public
wearer."

"Current."

Varkesh nudged a narrow volume from beneath the discarded robes. It was a
rotation ledger: dates, hearings, journeys, illnesses, and the private mark of
the dragon assigned to each appearance. Twelve marks recurred across two
centuries. On the table lay twelve versions of the grain ruling in twelve
hands.

"The guise is a shape each of us makes while awake," Varkesh said. "It has no
mind of its own. Only one of us wears it in public. Today we all assumed it
privately so we could compare interpretations."

"You share the Sleepless Majesty."

"We constitute the Sleepless Majesty," Varkesh said. "Deliberately. We remain
twelve persons."

My knees found a chair.

The evidence did not rest on two contradictory pages. It breathed around me,
crowded the furniture, and complained when the bronze dragon put a claw through
the table.

"No one else knows?" I asked.

"Several people knew," Varkesh said. "They died at ordinary human intervals.
This has been inconvenient for continuity."

"Two hundred years."

"We were hoping for longer."

* * *

They wanted to sleep.

Not for an afternoon, nor even for the indulgent fortnight granted to senior
clerks after a nervous collapse. The twelve required centuries of deep,
uninterrupted sleep in an old refuge far from inhabited roads. War drums,
collapsing trade, mass hunger, and disputed successions carried far enough to
wake them.

"So you became our monarch," I said.

"Successions had woken us four times in a century," Varkesh replied. "We
removed succession."

The dragons had also ended three cycles of conquest, established grain
reserves, made judgments consistent across districts, and built roads that
turned a bad harvest from a death sentence into an expensive year. My
grandmother had been born during the last levy war. She had described soldiers
taking doors for shields and children hiding from both uniforms. My generation
knew such things as archived testimony.

The gratitude was not foolish. Neither was the worship.

People prayed directly to the living Sleepless Majesty. The twelve supplied
the power behind its impossible continuity and shared guise. Together they
accepted worship, exercised final authority, and acted as one sovereign.
Whatever else they were individually, the collective they had made was a god.

"You did save us," I said.

"Yes," said the pearl-scaled dragon.

"You deceived us."

"Also yes," said another.

Varkesh lowered onto the floor until one pale-marked eye met mine. "We meant
to leave you a stable administration and go. Each useful judgment produced
more petitions. Each answered petition became evidence that no human answer
should be trusted until we improved it."

Against the far wall stood two centuries of ordinary case files. Grain
releases, loan schedules, road accounts, and district disputes sat in the same
clerk-tied bundles used in every hearing office. Most pages carried human
initials. Clerks arranged deliveries, audited measures, and performed the daily
work of government without a dragon entering the room. But whenever interested
parties refused a compromise, the file acquired a blue cover and climbed
toward one final royal answer.

"The clerks know the work," Varkesh said. "The difficulty is that no one
accepts their work once interests collide."

The grain case had divided them. Enforce every debt, and the terrace districts
lost the means to plant. Cancel every debt, and importers would refuse the next
risk or charge for it ruinously. Purchase both sides, and the royal reserve
could not cover another failed harvest. Set a permanent repayment share, and
no one could agree which future counted as normal.

Varkesh pushed the two sealed judgments toward me.

"Select one," the dragon said. "Refine it. You know how to make us sound like
one timeless mind."

The compliment had built my career. Courtiers praised how cleanly I removed
hesitation, trade, and human partiality from draft rulings. I had believed I
was translating mortal confusion into divine clarity.

"How much of the Majesty's voice was mine?" I asked.

"Enough that we are asking you to choose our last answer."

"And then?"

"We will enforce it, leave ordinary administration to the people already
performing it, surrender the guise to history, and sleep."

"For how long?"

"Three centuries, if no one begins a war over grain."

Every dragon looked at me as though human disagreement were an error I had
introduced.

* * *

I tried my old method once more.

Ludo and Gelda sat on opposite sides of my hearing room. I took the raised
chair between them, where the carved back suggested that the Sleepless Majesty
listened through its servants.

"What loss could your districts tolerate?" I asked Ludo.

He looked past me toward the empty royal alcove. "None, if the Majesty is just."

"Could repayment come from surplus after the next harvest?"

"To admit repayment is to admit seizure was lawful."

Gelda straightened. "At last, a true statement."

"What could the importing houses defer?" I asked her.

"Nothing the Majesty guaranteed."

"Could principal remain while collection paused?"

"To pause collection announces that contracts hold only when convenient."

They were not speaking to each other. They were performing certainty upward.
I had arranged the chairs, asked the questions, and promised a verdict. Even my
attempt at bargaining sounded like another examination for a hidden ruler.

A clerk entered with two folded messages.

The terrace companies had begun moving toward the provincial storehouses.
House guards were closing city depots and turning back wagons while they
awaited judgment. Each side believed that taking position before noon would
help the Majesty protect the righteous.

Ludo went pale. Gelda pressed a thumb hard into the import ledger's spine.
Neither withdrew a threat.

I imagined reading the seed judgment. The house guards might stand down today,
because our god had spoken. Tomorrow, every closed depot would become a defense
of sacred contract against an inexplicable divine betrayal.

I imagined reading the debt judgment. The terrace companies might leave the
storehouses today. At the next seizure, their only remaining appeal would be
to defy the law and hope history judged them more mercifully than their god
had.

A perfect answer did not remove conflict. It removed every legitimate way to
change the answer.

"The judgment will be given at noon," I said.

Ludo touched the seed sack. Gelda closed her ledger. They left by separate
doors.

I pulled the procedure book from my lowest shelf and opened it to the common
plea.

The rule had six lines.

For the first time that morning, brevity looked honest.

* * *

The Hall of Petitions was full before noon.

Terrace families packed one gallery. Mill workers, import clerks, and household
guards filled the other. At the center waited Ludo's seed sack and Gelda's
ledger. Above my chair, the royal alcove stood open.

The Sleepless Majesty entered in gray robes.

Varkesh wore the shared face perfectly. The crowd knelt as one body. I knelt
with them from habit, love, and fear.

"We ask," the hall recited.

"You answer."

Varkesh placed a sealed judgment before me. "Read, Adjudicator Mott."

It was a third formula. Temporary royal purchase, compulsory quotas, armed
supervision, and a schedule of repayment comprehensive enough to remain wrong
for decades. In a low voice, Varkesh said, "We will stay awake until compliance
is secure."

The offer was kind. It was terrible. It would prevent the noon confrontation
and preserve the exact dependence that had caused it.

I stood.

"I will not read this judgment."

The prayer's final word seemed to remain in the air after every mouth had
closed.

"For eleven years," I said, "I have drafted the Majesty's rulings. I removed
doubt. I removed bargaining. I made twelve different judgments sound as if one
perfect mind had spoken."

Varkesh's human face did not move.

"I ask the Sleepless Majesty to appear in full."

The eleven side doors opened.

Eleven more copies of the same gray-robed monarch entered. The hall recoiled
before anyone understood why. I set the rotation ledger beside the grain
evidence and read three entries aloud: dates, public acts, changing private
marks.

Then twelve living disguises ended.

Bodies lengthened. Wings unfolded. Tile cracked beneath an incautious claw.
The forms were pearl, violet, green, bronze, gray, blue, and other colors for
which my legal training had provided no useful terminology. They crowded the
hall in twelve breathing, unmistakably individual bodies.

Varkesh remained nearest my chair.

"We are twelve persons," the dragon said. "Together, we have been the
Sleepless Majesty. We built the peace so it would outlast our waking. We have
not found an answer to your grain dispute."

Some people fled. More knelt lower.

"Then command them to make peace," someone shouted from the terrace gallery.

"Order both sides to negotiate," came an answering cry.

The revelation had not ended worship. It had merely given our god twelve
visible bodies.

Varkesh looked at me. "We can issue that command."

"No."

A ripple of outrage crossed both galleries.

"If you order them to negotiate," I said, "they will still be negotiating
with you."

I took the sealed formula, broke its blank fastening cord, and laid the empty
back page on the table.

"Ludo Dask. Gelda Parn. There will be no royal judgment. If you want an
agreement, file a common plea."

"Now?" Gelda asked.

"Before the storehouses are occupied and the depots close completely."

Ludo stared at the twelve dragons. "Command us to sign."

Varkesh drew breath.

"Do not," I said.

For two centuries, the Sleepless Majesty had answered. That noon, twelve
dragons chose silence.

* * *

I moved my high chair away from the table.

Ludo put the seed sack between himself and Gelda. Gelda placed the import
ledger beside it. Neither sat.

"State what your people cannot survive," I said.

"Seed seizure," Ludo answered. "Not after two failed harvests. If we surrender
clean seed, we plant poor grain or nothing. If tenancy land passes to the
houses, families become laborers on fields they held before the loans."

Gelda's reply came quickly, but not upward. She spoke to him. "Our contracts
financed that seed and the imports that fed your districts last winter. If
principal vanishes, no house can borrow for the next shipment. City workers
pay first when grain stops moving."

"What loss can you bear?" I asked.

Neither answered.

From beyond the hall came the noise of a frightened crowd learning that its god
had no verdict. Noon passed.

Ludo loosened the seed sack's tie. "We could repay from surplus. Not from seed.
Not from land before harvest."

Gelda opened her ledger. "Future surplus at what share?"

"A share people can live after paying."

"That is not a number."

"Neither is a harvest."

It was the first useful exchange they had ever had.

They argued over a cap. Gelda demanded published district inventories; Ludo
demanded published import costs. Gelda offered to release depot grain at a
margin subject to audit if the terrace companies withdrew from the
storehouses. Ludo would order withdrawal if the houses stopped detaining
wagons. Each accused the other of disguising theft as necessity. Each was
occasionally correct.

I wrote nothing.

When they reached language, Gelda drafted the first clause in her own hand:
seed stores and pledged tenancy land would be protected from seizure until the
next harvest. Ludo drafted the second: principal would not be canceled, but
repayment would be capped and drawn only from future surplus.

They wrote that all grain inventories, import costs, and depot margins would be
opened for inspection. City depots would resume release at the audited margin.
Terrace districts would withdraw from the provincial storehouses. Detained
shipments would proceed.

"How long?" I asked.

"Until the next harvest," Ludo said.

Gelda shook her head. "If the count is wrong, that locks us into shortage."

"Ninety days," she said.

"Too short."

"Long enough for open stock counts in every district. Renew it then, amend it,
or let it expire."

Ludo looked toward his gallery. His supporters had been promised divine
vindication. Gelda's had been promised eternal contract. Signing would make
each merely accountable.

"Ninety days," Ludo said.

They added the expiry in a cramped final paragraph. No dragon supplied a word.
No royal seal touched the page.

Ludo Dask signed for the terrace districts. Gelda Parn signed for the city
houses. I signed only as witness and entered the plea under the old six-line
rule.

That did not stop the armed groups.

Ludo wrote a second message: *Hold the road. Do not enter the storehouses. The
seed and land are protected for ninety days while we count.*

Gelda wrote hers: *Open the depots. Release the wagons. Make no detention under
the disputed claims.*

They chose their own runners from their own galleries. The messages left
through opposite doors.

We waited.

The twelve dragons waited worst. One wore a groove in the floor with a claw.
Another counted ceiling panels. A smaller dragon unfolded and refolded
its wings. Varkesh watched the empty doors.

"The messages may fail," Varkesh said.

"Yes."

"Both groups may continue."

"Then Ludo and Gelda will answer for the orders they gave, and the rest of us
will decide what comes next."

Varkesh glanced toward the doors. "We would have compelled them."

"That is why you are waiting."

The first runner returned from the city. Depot doors were open. The wagons were
moving.

The second returned from the provincial road. The terrace companies had
stopped short of the storehouses. They would remain assembled until they saw
the protected-seed clause copied in full.

Gelda ordered copies made.

It was not trust. It was enough material interest, written concession, and
human authority to make the next step less dangerous than the last.

The hall began the old response without anyone leading it.

"We ask—"

Voices faltered, waiting.

Varkesh and the other eleven did not answer.

At length, Ludo held up the common plea. Gelda raised the import ledger beside
it.

People began reading.

* * *

The ninety-day articles raised the city price of flour, lowered several debt
payments, and satisfied nobody who had promised perfection. On the seventeenth
day, open stock counts showed one district had less grain than both sides had
assumed. Ludo and Gelda amended the release schedule after a meeting that
lasted fourteen hours and included no revelation whatsoever.

The dragons disclosed the rotation ledger and the false continuity of the
Sleepless Majesty. In their final public act, all twelve renounced royal and
religious authority. Human clerks struck the royal-answer line from every open
docket, and district delegates recognized no dragon's word as judgment. Some
people continued to pray privately, but power and worship without authority no
longer made the collective sovereign a god.

They retained no veto. They appointed no hidden successor and required no
human office to watch for their waking. On the morning they left, all twelve
came to the Hall of Petitions in their own bodies. The shared face did not
appear again.

No escort waited. The dragons carried no decree, kept no messenger, and asked
no one to follow. At a movement among them too small for me to identify, twelve
pairs of wings opened. Their first attempt at a formation required several
midair corrections. Then they departed together toward their old refuge
without circling back.

Three days later, travelers from the last inhabited road reported twelve
rumbling voices disputing the local acoustics after dusk. Before dawn, every
voice stopped. The silence continued. We established no office to listen for a
second night.

My royal title ended with their authority. The temporary docket had several
recallable chairs, of which I occupied one when the others tolerated me. Every
petition had to state a proposed concession. After one year, the districts
could keep the procedure, replace it, or discard it.

At my third hearing, two millers and six villages argued over transport fees.
They interrupted one another, miscounted a shipment, revised a proposal, and
asked me three times to decide for them.

"What can each of you bear to lose?" I asked.

The hearing continued untidily into supper.

Far from our voices, twelve dragons slept through the peace we had not finished
making.

stories.title: A Crown of Quiet Hours
stories.prompt: The benevolent monarchy people have long since come to worship is really just a dozen or so dragons in disguise, hoping to set up a state that can keep everything not on fire for a few hundred years so that they can finally get some actual quality slumber.
stories.body:
# A Crown of Quiet Hours

Water counted is fire denied.

That maxim was cut above every door in the municipal water office, stamped on
every ledger, and spoken by senior auditors whenever they wished to make a
junior clerk feel that arithmetic was a branch of heroism. I had always
believed it anyway.

On Founding Day, with forty thousand oil lamps waiting to be lit and a dry wind
combing the capital's roofs, the western cistern was short by nine hundred
thousand gallons.

I added the columns again.

Outside the inspection room, worshippers streamed toward the palace square in
white festival coats. Each carried a little clay lamp for the Crowned
Ancestors, the dead monarchs who had ended the border wars, built the
granaries, and required landlords to keep buckets on every stair. My mother
had survived a tenement fire because one of their cisterns had worked. She
still lit two lamps every year: one for the monarch who had ordered the works
and one for the inspector who had refused the builder's bribe.

I intended to become that sort of inspector. A permanent appointment waited on
my certification of the Founding Vigil.

The ledger offered me a simpler future. A strip of crimson wax crossed the
missing-water entry, impressed with the royal seal. Below it, in an immaculate
hand, someone had written: *Adjustment authorized. Correct total and certify.*

The chief auditor had already placed his pen beside the amended figure.

"The seal settles custody," he said. "Sign, Istra."

"The seal doesn't fill a hydrant."

His glance moved toward the square, where Vicar Estrel's assistants were
arranging lamps in forty-seven golden circles. "An assistant auditor does not
postpone the Founding Vigil because she dislikes a subtraction."

I dipped the sounding rod again. It struck stone far too soon.

Then I heard water moving.

Not in the municipal main. Beneath it.

The palace conduit ran behind a locked iron grille, humming with a strong,
steady current. An obsolete plaque beside it identified the pipe as part of the
royal emergency works. Above the grille hung the rope of the Flood Bell, gray
with dust. No clerk had authority to ring it. The bell belonged to siege,
earthquake, and royal command, in that order.

I put the unsigned certificate in my coat, took the ledger, and followed the
sound underground.

* * *

The palace sluice descended through three gates. The first admitted auditors.
The second admitted only auditors carrying royal business, which the wax seal
on the ledger served well enough. At the third, the air turned cold and wet,
and I began to suspect embezzlement on a scale requiring architecture.

I emerged above a cavern full of dragons.

There were eleven.

I counted because that was my profession, and because counting postponed
screaming.

One lay coiled in a nest of white sand, pale as old ivory, with a damp cloth
folded over its eyes. A green dragon was turning three times upon a bed of
river stones with the hopeless concentration of a dog that had been promised
comfort by a liar. Two copper-colored dragons argued in whispers about whether
the drip from the northern vault was soothing or intolerable. A narrow blue
one had pushed its entire head beneath the water. The largest, black-scaled and
scarred along one shoulder, was packing wool into its ears.

All around them, the stolen water gleamed in a new basin.

The dragons had rugs. They had pillows. They had shelves of ledgers. One had a
porcelain cup balanced between two claws.

Queen Orvessa IV stood on the ledge below me in her Founding Day robes.

"Assistant Auditor Noll," she said. "You are early."

I held up the municipal ledger. "The city is nine hundred thousand gallons
late."

Every draconic head turned. The black dragon removed one plug of wool.

Queen Orvessa closed her eyes. "I asked for a less conspicuous adjustment."

One copper dragon murmured, "You asked a water auditor not to notice water."

"I was tired."

"We are all tired."

The queen looked up at me. She had the face stamped on coins: mild eyes,
silver-threaded hair, the small rueful smile that painters had called maternal
for nineteen years. "Istra, I can explain."

"Start with the reptiles."

The mild eyes narrowed. Then the queen's outline shivered.

No crown or hidden engine performed the change. Flesh moved because she moved
it. Her robes drew tight, split at seams arranged for the purpose, and fell
away as her body lengthened down the steps. Silver hair flattened into a ridge
of dark red spines. The famous hands became claws; the maternal smile acquired
enough teeth to govern by itself. A red-gold dragon settled where the queen had
stood, one foreclaw still wearing the royal signet like a ridiculous ring.

"I am Kharost," the dragon said in Queen Orvessa's voice. "Queen Orvessa IV is
my present office."

I gripped the rail.

"You worship neither," Kharost added. "The Vigil is for the Crowned Ancestors,
who are deceased legal fictions. We were quite careful about that."

"How considerate."

"We thought so."

Behind Kharost, the ivory dragon lifted the cloth from one eye. "Is the bell
going to ring?"

"No," Kharost said.

"There are forty thousand lamps above us," I said, "and the hydrants have no
water."

The blue dragon surfaced. "That sounds like a reason to cancel the lamps."

"They worship your dynasty with them."

Kharost sighed, and warm smoke curled between her teeth. "Yes. That got away
from us."

She led me past the basin to a wall of portraits. Forty-seven rulers gazed down
in oils and mosaics: conquerors who had signed peace, reformers who had built
sewers, solemn children who had grown into solemn adults and died at
politically convenient ages.

"Masks," I said.

"Offices," Kharost corrected. "Rotated among twelve of us. Monarch, heir,
adviser, remote cousin, occasionally disagreeable foreign envoy. It is useful
to lose an argument to oneself in public."

"Two hundred and eighteen years of royal history."

"Two hundred and eighteen years without a city burned in war." Kharost looked
longingly toward the basin. "We require deep sleep. Cool stone, no vibration,
stable water, and—this has proved the difficult part—several centuries in which
no one sets the neighborhood on fire."

The black dragon pushed the wool back into its ear. "Meaningful sleep," it
said, "has become a theoretical condition."

* * *

Kharost did not ask me to trust her. She showed me records.

That was almost worse.

The royal archive filled the cavern's eastern wall. Original treaties bore
corrections in the same twelve hands across generations. Grain tallies showed
which reserves had been opened during lean winters. In a narrow volume from
the thirty-second reign, a proposed border campaign ended after the monarch
invited both generals to dinner and quietly melted their swords into the
table.

"A theatrical period," Kharost said.

I found the appropriation for my mother's cistern. The contractor's first
design had cut the reservoir in half. A royal examiner had rejected it and
sent two officials to prison.

The paper shook in my hands.

"The peace was real," Kharost said. "We did not fake full granaries or unburned
homes. We stopped six wars, three succession crises, and an astonishing number
of men who believed torches improved negotiations."

"You also taught the city that obedience was gratitude."

"We taught it not to burn."

"You let people kneel to people who never existed."

"The Crowned Ancestors existed as public work. They do not hear prayer. They
hold no present office. Orvessa does, and while she lives your doctrine
expressly forbids worshipping her." Kharost tapped the archive with one claw.
"We separated the functions."

"You designed a religion as a filing system?"

"It was supposed to be an annual speech."

I laughed then, once, because otherwise I might have thrown the appropriation
ledger into the basin.

Kharost unrolled a thick manuscript on a stone table. *The Book of Quiet* was
written across its cover.

"At dawn," she said, "our last measures would have taken effect. Tax bands,
reservoir rules, appointments, grain purchases, fire inspections. All
specified for the coming centuries. Human officers would administer them while
we slept."

I turned pages. The work was meticulous. It anticipated drought, population
growth, crop failure, corruption, and seven varieties of dispute concerning
goats. Corrections had been layered over corrections until some margins looked
furred with ink.

"Where do we change a rule that's wrong?" I asked.

"The rule will not be wrong."

The green dragon stopped circling its stones. Several of the others looked
away.

I laid my ledger open to the missing total. "This one was."

"For one night. The basin must settle to sleeping temperature. Once the Vigil
ends, the lamps are extinguished, the municipal cisterns refill, and we
withdraw. The palace crews have contingency carts."

"For a square packed with forty thousand people?"

"The calculated likelihood of a major ignition is less than one in eight
hundred."

"Is tonight's child the first or the eight hundredth?"

Kharost's pupils thinned. "Do not mistake a hard choice for indifference."

"Do not average people until they disappear."

For the first time, anger overtook her patience. Heat flashed through the room,
and the edge of the Book of Quiet browned beneath her claw.

Then she lifted it quickly. "That," she said, "was poorly illustrative."

The other dragons were silent.

Kharost folded the municipal ledger closed. "I cannot allow this out of the
palace before dawn."

"Then cancel the Vigil."

"A royal cancellation without visible cause would cause panic, investigation,
and noise. The whole point of tonight is that it is the last night."

"You stole fire water for pillows."

"Cooling beds."

"Pillows with plumbing."

She set the ledger on the table beside the Book of Quiet. "You may remain here
comfortably until morning."

Comfort was represented by a straight-backed chair between two sleeping
dragons.

While Kharost argued with the copper pair about who would watch me, I slipped
my original sounding sheets from beneath the royal archive copy and reclaimed
the municipal ledger from beside the Book of Quiet. The dragons had spent two
centuries studying human government. None had learned to count what an auditor
carried.

I climbed back toward the lamps.

* * *

By dusk, the square burned gold.

Thousands of worshippers stood shoulder to shoulder within the circles of
light. At the palace steps, Vicar Estrel wore the plain gray of a living
officiant; all the gold had been reserved for the Crowned Ancestors. Behind
him, Queen Orvessa's empty chair waited outside the ritual, because the living
monarch held authority but received no prayer.

I found Estrel beside the ceremonial fountain and showed him the sounding
sheets.

"The west cistern cannot serve the square," I said. "End the Vigil. Now."

He read the figures twice. His face changed, but his voice stayed level. "The
palace certified the adjustment."

"The palace diverted the water."

"To what?"

The honest answer would expose Kharost. The cautious answer would leave forty
thousand lamps burning.

"An unlawful private basin."

Estrel looked toward the crowd. People were already reciting the names of
forty-seven reigns, each response rolling across the square like surf.

"On an assistant auditor's accusation," he said, "I can delay one lamp circle.
If I halt the Founding Vigil against the royal seal, the crowd may press the
gates. Give me proof people can see."

"I am telling you the hydrants are empty."

"And I believe that you believe your figures. They believe this ceremony
remembers the peace that kept their grandparents alive."

A gust struck the square.

The lamps guttered. A row of canvas prayer streamers snapped hard enough to
break its upper line. The loose end dropped, swept across six flames, and rose
burning into the awning over the western arcade.

For one long breath, everyone watched.

Then the awning fell onto a vendor's roof.

Someone opened the ceremonial fountain. It coughed twice and spat mud.

I ran to the nearest hydrant, wrenched the cap loose, and heard the hollow rush
of air.

Above the first screams, Estrel shouted for calm.

The fire crossed to the next awning.

* * *

The Flood Bell rope hung behind the palace grille.

I reached it with smoke at my back and a palace guard in front of me. I held up
the royal-sealed ledger as if it still belonged to me and said, "Emergency
water order."

The guard hesitated just long enough to remember that people who forged royal
seals rarely wore municipal boots.

I ducked through.

The bell rope was stiff with age. Beside it stood the emergency sluice wheel,
painted red and chained in place. The chain yielded to the guard's axe on the
third blow. I set both hands on the wheel.

If I opened it, the new basin would drain into the civic mains. The prepared
stone would warm. The current would churn the sand nests and soak every pillow.
Two centuries of deception would rise after it in twelve furious bodies.

Behind me, burning cloth sailed over the crowd.

I turned the wheel.

Deep below, a gate groaned open. Water struck the old pipes so hard the floor
jumped.

Then I pulled the rope.

The loudest bell in the capital woke the dragons.

Its first note hit like a bronze wall. The second rolled over the square and
shook ash from the arcade. By the third, water hammered through the hydrant
mains.

People were running in every direction. Estrel climbed onto the dry fountain,
seized one of the tall ceremonial lamps, and held it above his head.

"Who remembers the first deliverance?" he called.

The old response came raggedly from the nearest worshippers. "We remember
together."

"Then together—clear the west lane! Pass empty buckets inward! Full buckets
out!"

He turned worship into instructions one line at a time.

"What do the faithful preserve?"

"The living!"

"Then pull down those streamers!"

The lamp circles broke apart. Their little lights, meant for dead royal masks,
marked bucket stations through the smoke. Hands passed water from the reopened
hydrants. Others dragged carts and canvas away before the fire could take
them. A row of bakers soaked the roofs with trough pans. Two worshippers used a
festival pole to tear down a blazing awning and nearly brought it onto
themselves; ten more seized the pole and guided it into the flooded gutter.

The water had returned, but pressure built slowly. Flame climbed the western
arcade and found the old beams beneath its tiles.
