Queen Orvessa came through the palace doors barefoot, her silver hair loose.

"Noll," she said over the bell's fading roar, "you have destroyed conditions
that took nineteen months to establish."

"Your city is on fire."

"I can see that."

"Then ask for help."

She looked at the crowd, at Estrel commanding lines beneath the golden circles,
at the hydrants finally spilling water. "The queen can order them."

"That is the problem."

A burning roof beam cracked. People scattered below it.

I caught Queen Orvessa's hand before she could move. It was already too warm.
"Ask them in your own face."

Fear changed her more completely than flesh had. Not fear of the fire. Fear of
being seen.

Then Kharost tore through Queen Orvessa.

Red-gold scales swept across the palace steps. Her wings opened wide enough to
knock two banners down, and the crowd's panic struck as a physical force.
Buckets fell. People screamed. Estrel stared up at the living power that had
worn the throne, then at the golden circles dedicated to rulers who had never
been people at all.

Kharost lowered her head.

"We took your water," she said. Her voice carried without the bell. "We built
this peace because we wished to sleep in it. We lied about who ruled you. If
you will help save the square, we will answer for that when it is safe."

The cracked beam fell.

Kharost caught it across one shoulder. Fire washed over her scales, harmless
for an instant, then bright enough to make her recoil. Human hands pulled
trapped buckets and people clear while she heaved the beam into the fountain
basin. A scale split across her shoulder.

The palace doors burst outward again.

Eleven dragons emerged into the wreckage of public worship.

The ivory one came blinking, its damp eye cloth still snagged on a horn. The
green one wore half its river-stone bed clattering between its belly scales.
The narrow blue dragon streamed basin water across the steps. The black dragon
had forgotten to remove one wad of wool and kept turning its wrong ear toward
Estrel's orders. Copper, gray, dun, and mottled bodies filled the square until
every royal proportion seemed absurd.

They did not end the fire.

They bought us the time to do it.

Two braced the arcade while citizens stripped burning tiles from the roof.
One shielded a bucket line with its wings until the thin membranes smoked and
curled at the edges. The blue dragon carried water in its mouth, discovered
that this made shouted coordination impossible, and submitted with visible
offense to being used as a cistern. The black dragon dragged three blazing
carts into the open square, where human crews drowned them.

Kharost tried to climb toward the hottest roof.

"No," I shouted. "Hold the eastern beam."

She glanced at me, royal reflex warring with necessity.

"That is not a suggestion from a subject," I said. "It is an instruction from
the water line."

Kharost held the eastern beam.

Estrel raised his lamp. "What do we preserve?"

This time the answer came from the whole square, frightened and furious and
working.

"The living!"

By midnight, the fire had nowhere left to go.

* * *

The western arcade lost its roof. Thirty-one people were treated for smoke and
burns. No one died.

That last number was entered in my ledger without adjustment.

At the public inquiry, the square filled again, though nobody brought a votive
lamp. Kharost and the other dragons lay in the old parade ground under guard,
too large for the hearing chamber and too tired to object to weather.

Some citizens demanded the return of Queen Orvessa IV. Her reign had been
gentle, they said, and gentleness was rare enough without interrogating its
anatomy. Others wanted twelve execution platforms and had given no thought to
the engineering.

I testified between them.

I entered the uncensored water figures. I entered the royal archives, the war
records, the granary accounts, the prison orders, my mother's cistern, the
secret basin, and the Book of Quiet. The lie did not empty the granaries after
the fact. The saved lives did not make the lie consent.

"You kept the peace," I told Kharost. "You do not therefore own it."

She lowered her head until one gold eye met mine. "What will keep you from
burning it when we sleep?"

"Nothing."

The hearing erupted.

I waited.

"Nothing kept you from draining our cistern except your own judgment," I said
when the room quieted. "That failed. So ours must be allowed to fail in public,
where other people can correct it before the roof catches."

The Charter of Waking Hours took six weeks, nine hundred amendments, and one
incident in which the black dragon fell asleep during a tax debate and crushed
a decorative hedge.

It placed law, water, taxation, records, and appointments under elected human
councils. It opened royal archives and accounts to public audit. It ended state
worship of the Crowned Ancestors without forbidding private remembrance. It
retired the forty-seven masks, including Queen Orvessa IV, and recognized
Kharost and the other eleven as residents: protected by law, bound by law,
entitled to no throne, sacrifice, or uncounted gallon.

Kharost argued for a provision requiring all bells to be padded.

She lost.

We compromised on walls.

Seven months later, I inspected the cooling works beyond the inhabited wards.
Its reservoir had its own watershed, its own public ledger, twelve enormous
stone beds, and soundproofing thick enough that the dragons could not hear the
debate over its cost. Human engineers had designed shutoff gates accessible
from outside. Human inspectors had tested them. My permanent appointment came
with instructions to distrust every seal, including my own.

The twelve dragons settled one by one.

The ivory dragon placed the damp cloth over its eyes. The green dragon turned
three times upon its stones, reconsidered, and turned once more. The copper
pair resumed their argument about dripping water until Kharost opened one eye
and said, "Two centuries. Please."

At last only Kharost remained awake.

"Will it hold?" she asked me.

I looked at the gauges, the open ledger, the gate controls, and the human crew
waiting for my answer.

"Not by itself," I said.

Kharost considered that. Then she smiled with her own alarming teeth, tucked
her head beneath one red-gold wing, and slept.

For the first time in two hundred and eighteen years, nobody had been ordered
to be quiet.

We were anyway.

stories.title: A Place for the Living
stories.prompt: Introducing a boyfriend or girlfriend to the family can be either very pleasant or very stressful. When you come from a lineage of necromancers, these feelings are amplified, as relatives who died decades ago might show up for a visit.
stories.body:
# A Place for the Living

The key at Greer Morrow’s throat had been quiet for the whole drive. On the front steps, her thumb began tapping it against her coat button.

Imani pretended not to notice. She had brought a cake, clean shoes, and enough composure for one evening. Asking why her girlfriend’s family heirloom had developed a nervous tic seemed greedy.

Greer caught the brass key in her fist. It was old enough that its teeth had softened into brass hills. “Last chance to fake a flat tire.”

“With your mother watching us from behind the curtain?”

The curtain in the left-hand window snapped shut.

Greer winced. Imani kissed the corner of her mouth, which made her smile despite herself.

“No surprises,” Greer said. “I promise.”

Imani knew the promise had qualifications. Greer had explained kept-place suppers on their third date, after Imani had asked why every photograph of the Morrow dining room showed one chair turned toward an empty setting. The dead could visit, sometimes, if invited. They did not roam the halls, possess the cutlery, or appear in mirrors while a guest was flossing. Greer’s assurances on that point had been suspiciously specific.

“No surprises,” Imani agreed, and held up the cake tin. “Unless your family has strong feelings about ginger.”

Davina Morrow opened the door before they knocked. She was smaller than Imani had imagined and warmer in every sense: soft brown sweater, flour on one sleeve, hands that closed firmly around Imani’s cold fingers.

“Imani Crowe. At last. Come in before the rain decides to come sideways.”

The house smelled of onions browned in butter and wet stone cooling after a fire. Umbrellas crowded a brass stand. Framed portraits climbed the stair wall, but so did grocery lists, postcards, and a photograph of Greer at twelve with one eyebrow missing.

“Experiment,” Greer said when Imani paused at it.

“Necromancy?”

“Hair bleach.”

Davina laughed. “More dangerous in untrained hands.”

Greer’s father took the cake tin with the solemn care of someone accepting a peace treaty. “Homemade?”

“My mother’s recipe.”

“Then I’m hiding the last piece before anyone else knows there is one.”

He meant it kindly. The word *mother* did not catch in the room or summon a hush. Imani let out a breath she had not known she was holding.

Dinner began pleasantly enough that she was embarrassed by how thoroughly she had rehearsed disaster.

Greer’s father had made a mushroom pie whose crust shattered at the touch of a fork. Davina remembered that Imani disliked sweet wine and had found something dry. Greer told the eyebrow story properly, with gestures, and Imani laughed hard enough to snort into her glass. When Davina asked about Imani’s work assessing old houses, her questions were interested rather than forensic. Had she ever found a staircase resting on nothing? Yes. Had the owner insisted it was historical? Also yes.

“A house can be old or it can be badly maintained,” Imani said. “Age is not a repair strategy.”

Greer’s father lifted his glass. “I’ve been saying that about my knees.”

Even Davina’s correction when Imani reached to shift a spoon was gentle.

“A guest never rearranges a Morrow place setting,” she said, nudging it back into line. “Old household rule.”

“Noted.”

There were five settings.

Imani had assumed the extra belonged to a late arrival, although the fifth plate was wrapped in black linen and the chair before it stood a handspan farther from the table. An ivory place card lay facedown beside a black-handled butter knife. Greer had not looked directly at either object since sitting down.

Davina waited until the pie plates were cleared. Then she unfolded the linen.

The plate beneath was thin white porcelain painted with a border of green moths. The room seemed to contract around it.

“We have a family guest,” Davina said.

The key struck Greer’s glass.

Imani looked at her. “A surprise?”

“Not exactly.” Greer’s fingers closed around the key again. “It wasn’t certain she would accept.”

Which was not an answer, but Davina had turned over the card. In narrow blue handwriting it read *Aunt Zephra*.

Beside the familiar name, the butter knife looked worn nearly silver at the tip.

“It was hers,” Davina said. “She used it every Sunday for forty years. In our practice, the familiar name directs the invitation. The object helps it reach the person intended. Nothing grander than that.”

“And she can say no?” Imani asked.

“Of course,” Davina said.

Greer met Imani’s eyes. Regret was already there, asking to be mistaken for apology.

Davina placed both palms flat on the table. “Aunt Zephra Morrow, you are remembered here. Your place is kept, if you choose it.”

For three breaths, nothing happened.

On the fourth, the candles leaned toward the fifth setting. Davina’s shoulders tightened. A smear like condensation formed above the chair, gathered color, and became the suggestion of a woman sitting very straight.

She arrived in details. A dark collar. Long brown hands. Silver hair rolled at the nape of her neck. Her face took longest, as if distance resisted expression. Then her mouth sharpened into amusement.

“You’ve put me in the severe dress again,” she said.

Her voice had a soft double edge, one sound in the room and another at the bottom of Imani’s hearing.

Davina smiled with naked relief. “It’s how you present.”

“It’s how you remember.” The woman looked down at herself. “Fortunately, death has cured me of vanity. Mostly.”

Greer laughed, and for a moment she was younger than the photograph on the stairs. “Hello, Aunt Zephra.”

“There you are.” Aunt Zephra reached across the narrow boundary of her setting. Greer offered two fingers. The dead woman touched them, and Greer inhaled as though she had put her hand into cold water. “Still wearing that solemn little key.”

“Still.”

Aunt Zephra Morrow had been dead for seventy-three years. She was not transparent, exactly. The wallpaper showed through her only when Imani looked away from her face. Her chair creaked beneath movements that were entirely her own, though the substance that made those movements possible came from Davina’s rigid hands and slowly paling lips.

Aunt Zephra turned to Imani. “And you must be the structural realist.”

“I didn’t realize I’d been briefed.”

“Davina sends news with every invitation. Otherwise I’d spend my one visit between the family’s yearly remembrances asking who had died, which is dreary even by our standards.”

“Do you—” Imani stopped. Every possible ending to the question felt rude.

“Remember being dead? Yes. Remember being alive? Also yes. I have not been remade from Davina’s recollections, if that is what your eyebrows are asking. I am myself there, and I am myself during this visit, and I expect to remain myself when I return.”

Davina’s breath whitened briefly above the table. “Twenty minutes is comfortable. We should not waste them explaining what she already understands.”

“I like her eyebrows,” Aunt Zephra said. “They ask permission before trespassing.”

That won Imani despite her anger. So did the way Aunt Zephra squeezed Greer’s fingers once before letting go, as if contact mattered too much to prolong carelessly.

Greer’s father brought out the cake, cut Aunt Zephra a slender slice, and set it inside the ring of her cutlery. Her fork moved in her translucent hand. Davina supplied the impossible contact; Aunt Zephra supplied the eagerness.

She tasted one bite and shut her eyes.

“Ginger,” she said. “And pear. Oh, that is unfairly good.”

“My mother’s,” Imani said.

“Then I am glad she made something that traveled farther than either of you expected.”

Imani looked down before gratitude showed too plainly. When she looked up, Aunt Zephra was studying her, not as an examiner but as another woman who understood what a recipe could carry.

“You’re a Morrow by marriage?” Imani asked.

“By invitation, not by blood. The distinction used to matter in a kinder way.” Aunt Zephra pointed her fork at the green moths on the plate. “I painted those. Badly.”

“You established the supper,” Davina said.

“Helped. A kept place was hospitality. The living offered a chair; the dead decided whether to sit. We argued, ate what we could, and went away when the guest was tired.”

She looked toward the two dessert plates Greer’s father had cleared and placed facedown in a stack on the sideboard. Then she took another bite of cake.

For several minutes, it was wonderful.

Aunt Zephra wanted to know whether buildings still hid pipes inside walls as if ashamed of them. She told Imani about a kitchen ceiling that had collapsed into a funeral supper because three generations had agreed not to inspect a stain. Davina supplied one dry correction, Greer supplied another, and Aunt Zephra dismissed both on the grounds that neither had been born.

Imani could almost forgive the ambush. Almost.

Then Davina said, “Tell her about the house survey.”

Greer’s smile faltered. “There isn’t much to tell.”

“Imani examines old houses before people buy them,” Davina told Aunt Zephra. “Useful experience, if she and Greer live here.”

The last word landed with less noise than a fork. It did more damage.

Imani turned to Greer. “Here?”

“Someday,” Greer said. “Maybe. It was only a conversation.”

“A conversation with whom?”

Greer rubbed the key between finger and thumb.

Davina answered. “With me. This house passes with the table.”

Aunt Zephra set down her fork. “Does it.”

“The person who keeps the place must live here,” Davina continued. Her voice remained hospitable; only its purpose had changed. “Greer has known that all her life.”

Imani had known Greer wanted a house with deep windowsills. She knew Greer hated moving, loved burnt toast, and had once spent six months deciding whether to buy a blue sofa. They had discussed children in the cautious hypothetical. Marriage in the laughing hypothetical. They had not discussed taking responsibility for a dining room where the dead arrived by appointment.

“You told me your mother might want to meet me,” Imani said quietly.

“She does,” Greer said.

“You did not mention the property evaluation.”

“It isn’t like that.”

Davina’s expression tightened with something closer to hurt than offense. “I would not hand this table to someone who thought our family was an entertaining eccentricity.”

“I don’t.”

“Then you understand that wonder is the smallest part of the work.”

Aunt Zephra said, “Davina.”

But Davina had the momentum of someone opening a door she had held shut for years.

“There are records to keep. Invitations to prepare. People who say they respect the practice until remembrance falls on a work night, or the room will not warm, or grief is tedious instead of picturesque. I will not leave Greer alone with that.”

Her fear was real. Imani could see its grooves in the house: the polished table, the indexed place cards on the cabinet, the butter knife kept safe across seventy-three years. Davina had spent her adult life preserving doors that opened only briefly. Love had not made her less controlling. Control had not made the love false.

Imani looked at Greer. “Did you tell her we talked about marriage?”

Greer went still.

Davina said, “You have been together eighteen months.”

“That was not my question.”

“Yes,” Greer said. “I told her it might be where we were going.”

Heat climbed Imani’s throat. “You told your mother before you told me?”

“I was trying to work out how to tell you all of it.”

“By arranging a dead relative to ask?”

“I didn’t arrange this.”

“You knew.”

Greer’s hand fell from the key. “I knew it was possible.”

There it was: *no surprises*, trimmed small enough to crawl through.

Aunt Zephra leaned toward Imani. She could not move beyond the reach of her place, and the effort made the edge of her sleeve fray into mist. “For whatever it is worth, I accepted an invitation to dinner. I was not told I would be interviewing anyone.”

Davina breathed faster now, each exhalation white. “I asked you to meet the woman Greer may marry.”

“Meeting is not measuring.”

“You measured me.”

“I asked whether you loved this family when you took the table. You said yes. I was too sentimental to ask whether you loved yourself outside it.”

Davina flinched. Greer’s father reached toward her, stopped, then folded his hands. His earlier warmth had not vanished. It had simply proved unequal to conflict.

Davina turned back to Imani. “Would you marry Greer?”

“That is a question Greer should ask me.”

“Do you want children?”

“Also not yours.”

“Would you move here?”

Imani looked around at the moth plate, the rain-dark window, the sideboard stacked with generations of intimate obligation. “I would have wanted to see it before deciding.”

“You are seeing it.”

“As an audition.”

Greer said, “That’s enough,” so softly that it functioned as a request Davina could deny.

“No,” Davina said. Her fingers trembled against the cloth. “Not if Greer expects to take that key. I need to know whether I am preserving this for someone who will abandon it.”

“I have not asked Greer to abandon anything.”

“You may, once you understand the cost.”

The room was warm, but Davina’s skin had gone gray around her mouth. Frost feathered the bowl of her wineglass where her wrist touched it.

Greer noticed. “You’re past twenty minutes.”

“I am fine.”

“Close the place.”

Davina looked at Aunt Zephra. “You have not answered.”

“Because I do not give warranties on human beings.”

“You gave me your judgment before.”

“And you have been punishing everyone with it ever since.”

Zephra glanced again at the sideboard. The cleared dessert plates lay face-down, harmless and finished. Then she flexed her hands as if feeling had become difficult.

“Davina,” she said, and all humor had left the doubled voice. “Close my place, please.”

Davina’s eyes shone. “One answer. Is she fit for this family?”

“I asked to leave.”

“You may not come again until after the next remembrance.”

“I know where I am going.”

Davina’s hands pressed harder into the table. The candle flames bent almost flat. She could hold the visit because she was alive and willing to spend her own heat on it. Zephra could object, but she could not cast herself free.

Greer stood halfway, the key swinging loose. “Please.”

Davina looked at her daughter, exhausted and pleading. “Sit down.”

Greer did.

The small surrender hurt Imani more than the hidden house, perhaps because she understood it. Greer had spent her life learning which battles could be survived by becoming quiet. Imani had spent hers learning to smile during inspections where owners called cracks decorative. Composure was useful. It was not courage.

She pushed her chair back.

Davina’s head snapped toward her. “Do not touch that setting. A guest who breaks a kept place rejects the table.”

“Imani,” Greer said.

That one word held fear for Aunt Zephra, fear of Davina, fear that Imani would walk out and make every concealed consequence real.

Imani stepped to the fifth chair. Up close, Zephra’s outline shivered. She looked tired, furious, and entirely present.

“I want to hear it from you,” Imani said. “Do you want to go?”

“Yes.”

Davina rose too quickly and swayed; Greer’s father caught her elbow.

“This is the only visit she can make this year,” Davina said. “If you turn that plate, it is over. Dinner, her visit, and any claim you imagine you have here.”

Imani’s fingers hovered over the porcelain. She thought of the cake made from a dead woman’s recipe, offered freely. She thought of Greer discussing marriage in this room while giving Imani only hypotheticals. She thought of how easy it would be to sit down and call endurance love.

“I don’t want a claim,” she said. “I want a choice.”

She turned the plate face-down.

Porcelain struck wood with a flat domestic knock.

The working broke.

Cold rushed outward. The candles straightened. Zephra thinned from the edges inward, silver hair and severe dress loosening into bright condensation. Davina’s hands left the table; color began returning to them almost at once.

For one heartbeat, Aunt Zephra’s face remained clear.

“No verdict,” she said. “A kept place welcomes a guest. It does not keep one.”

Her gaze moved to Greer.

“Make room for the living while you have them.”

Then the chair was empty.

No one spoke. Rain ticked at the window. On the overturned plate, the green moths were hidden against the table.

Davina sat down carefully. Grief altered her face more than anger could. “Do you understand what you ended?”

“Yes,” Imani said. Her voice shook now that courage had become consequence. “She did too.”

“You had no right.”

“Neither did you.”

Greer stood. This time, she did not stop halfway.

Davina looked at her. “If she rejects the table’s rules, she cannot share its care. You cannot inherit this house and make the practice answer to whoever you bring home.”

“Then I won’t inherit it.”

The words frightened Greer as she said them. Imani saw the pulse jumping at her throat, just above the key.

Davina stared. “You do not mean that.”

Greer pulled the chain over her head. “If keeping the table means ambushing the woman I love and refusing a guest who asks to leave, I don’t want to keep it.”

She laid the key beside Aunt Zephra’s butter knife.

It made almost no sound. Still, Greer’s father closed his eyes.

Davina’s hands curled in her lap. “Without that key, you do not prepare invitations after me. You do not choose the remembrances. If someone else keeps the table, you come when they invite you, like any other relative.”

Greer looked at the empty chair. Her face crumpled, then steadied. “I understand.”

Imani believed that she did. Greer was giving up not an antique but a future: this house, the authority to call beloved dead, the certainty of her place in a lineage. The choice did not repair what she had hidden. It cost enough to be real anyway.

“I should have told Imani before tonight,” Greer said. “About the interview. The house. The key. All of it.”

Davina looked older with her heat returning. “I was trying to protect what your family entrusted to me.”

“Aunt Zephra was our family too.”

“I know.”

Davina said it so quietly that Imani almost missed it.

* * *

Outside, the rain had thinned to a cold mist. Imani stood under the porch eave with her coat unbuttoned and did not take Greer’s offered hand.

Greer let it fall.

“No surprises,” Imani said.

“I lied by making the promise smaller in my head.” Greer swallowed. “I knew she might be invited. I knew my mother meant to judge you. I knew taking the key meant living here someday, and I talked to her about marriage because talking to you felt like I could lose something.”

“So you let me find out at the table.”

“Yes. I’m sorry. Not for failing to manage tonight. For deceiving you.”

The clean shape of the apology hurt. Imani loved her. That remained true, annoyingly untouched by wisdom.

“Leaving the key doesn’t make us fine.”

“I know.”

“I don’t know whether we’re fine.”

Greer nodded once. “I know that too.”

The front door opened. Davina held out the cake tin. It was washed, dried, and noticeably lighter.

“He hid two pieces,” she said. “I overruled him.”

Imani accepted it.

Davina kept one hand on the door. “If you come again, no extra place will be set without asking you first.”

It was not an apology. It was not forgiveness either. It was one boundary, offered late.

“Thank you,” Imani said.

Davina glanced toward Greer, then closed the door.

At the car, Greer waited without reaching for her.

“Breakfast,” Imani said. “Saturday. Somewhere aggressively ordinary.”

Hope moved across Greer’s face, cautious enough not to offend. “Living-only?”

“Living-only. We talk about the house. Marriage. Children. The table. Everything you tried to save by not saying it.”

“And after that?”

“After that, we decide whether we can make a place for each other.”

Imani got into the car with the cake tin on her knees. Greer took the driver’s seat, keyless now, and for a while they listened to the rain.

stories.title: The Wrong Side of the Part
stories.prompt: You find a magical wig that, when worn, turns you into the exact oppose of who you are, with the wig changing to match the new personality. However, you don’t believe this… until you put it on.
stories.body:
# The Wrong Side of the Part

By three fifteen on the last day of the shop, I had made seventy-two decisions and none of them was the one that mattered.

SELL went on the acrylic heads and the hydraulic styling chair. DONATE went on three boxes of synthetic bobs that had survived two decades of fashion by never having participated in it. DISCARD went on dried adhesive, moth-nibbled switches, and a practice head whose remaining hair gave it the expression of a betrayed turnip.

I printed the labels in twelve-point type, centered. Grief was no excuse for crooked stationery.

The unsigned purchase contract lay beneath the appointment ledger, where I had put it while searching for a cloth to polish the mirrors. The mirrors did not need polishing. They were already honest enough to show the stripped shelves, pale rectangles on the walls, and me in my gray cardigan, reducing our mother's life's work to three verbs.

My phone vibrated.

**Four sharp,** Petra had written. **The buyer arrives at five. Please tell me we are still having a surprise-free afternoon.**

I typed, **Of course.**

Then, **Though I wondered if we might discuss—**

Then, **There are a few figures I don't quite—**

I deleted everything except **Of course**, added a smiling face so it wouldn't look hostile, and hated Petra for making me do it.

This was unfair, since Petra had not made me do anything. That was the useful feature of never saying what I wanted: other people could be guilty without the inconvenience of a trial.

Below her text sat a voice message from six months earlier. Seven minutes and twelve seconds. I had listened once, in the dark, after our mother was asleep upstairs. I had never played it again. I did not need to. Petra's voice had worn a groove through me.

I turned the phone facedown and chose a new task.

Our mother's oldest travelling case had escaped the labels because its brass catches were jammed. I worked them loose with the flat end of a tail comb. The case smelled of old powder, canvas, and the faint animal warmth that human hair kept long after it belonged to no one. Inside rested a row of setting pins, a stained veil, and nothing worth saving.

The bottom sounded hollow when I knocked it.

Beneath a false panel lay a wig wrapped in yellowing tissue. It was an ash-brown bob, center-parted, blunt at the jaw. Good hair, hand-knotted, wasted on a style so obedient it seemed to apologize for occupying the box.

A card had been tucked beneath the crown.

*Wear it and meet the person you are not.*

*Heat wakes it.*

*To take it off, tell the truth neither of you wants.*

I read it twice, which was one more time than it deserved.

Our mother had loved theatre without requiring a stage. She once told a nervous bride that the right hairpiece would frighten rain away, and it had not rained until after the photographs. This proved nothing except that weather occasionally cooperated with salesmanship.

“Magical wig,” I said to the empty shop. “Naturally. Very useful inventory note.”

Still, human-hair work had to be tried before it was donated. A warped foundation could pinch, and old elastic sometimes failed without warning. I could picture Petra asking whether I had checked it. I could picture myself saying no. The second image was less plausible.

I pinned up my own hair, loosened the adjustment tabs, and lowered the wig onto my head.

I did it voluntarily. I did it while disbelieving every word on the card. Later, those facts mattered to me, though they did not make what followed less mine.

The crown settled cool against my scalp. I slipped two fingers beneath the nape and tested the tension. The foundation was exquisite: fine lace, tiny knots, a spiral of denser work around the crown as deliberate as a fingerprint. Then my skin warmed it.

My next heartbeat struck the net like a plucked string.

Heat ran outward through the knots. Not heat arriving from the wig—mine, drawn from my scalp and pulse, distributed in bright little paths I could feel but not see. The lace contracted to my head. My attention caught on it, and the whole spiral seemed to fill with everything I knew I was: quiet, careful, accommodating, tidy. The list became a cage only because I supplied the bars.

The hair brushed my jaw.

Then it brushed my shoulders.

I grabbed the styling chair as the bob poured down and out. Ash brown deepened to copper-black, bright as a banked fire wherever the light struck. The center part slewed hard to the left and bleached bone-white in a line so straight it looked cut with a razor. Sleek lengths buckled into enormous coils. They crowded my shoulders, sprang halfway down my back, and tossed after every startled movement with the momentum of an entrance.

I stared into the salon mirror.

The woman in the glass stared back with my face and none of my apologies.

Nothing inside me went dark. I remembered the labels. I remembered the contract. I remembered why Petra wanted the sale and why I had said yes. I simply found all those reasons unbearably boring.

“Oh,” I said, and my voice came out rich with amusement. “There you are.”

I yanked off the gray cardigan and dropped it on the DISCARD pile.

The labels offended me next. Seventy-two tiny white surrender flags. I swept them from the counter, peeled SELL off the styling chair, slapped it onto the contract, and laughed so hard the copper-black coils bounced around my face.

My phone gave me the buyer's number from the email thread. I called.

“This is Tilda Bristow,” I said when a cautious voice answered. “A small correction to today's arrangements. The shop is not for sale.”

There was a silence filled with paper and alarm. “But the appointment—”

“Is an excellent opportunity for you to discover resilience.”

I ended the call.

Before I could lower the phone, Petra rang.

“I'm stuck at the lender,” she said. “The buyer asked for a corrected debt statement before the signing. Their system is down. I'll be there by quarter to five. Do not start without me.”

“Take your time,” I said, and heard how easily the new voice could make sabotage sound considerate.

Old me would have vomited from shame. I could remember that. I could even anticipate the practical consequences with perfect clarity: breach, delay, debt, Petra's fury. Yet relief fizzed through my blood. I had spent two years making grief presentable for other people. For once, I wanted witnesses to the mess.

The shop account was still signed in on my phone. I propped it against a canister of combs and recorded myself beneath the faded awning, framed by bare display hooks.

“At four thirty,” I told the lens, “we are holding a funeral for being agreeable. There will be free hair, poor judgment, and the public burial of a terrible property sale. Dress code: something you were told was too much.”

I posted it before prudence could crawl back into fashion.

Then I tore apart the sorting scheme. SELL, DONATE, and DISCARD fluttered together across the floor. I put a silver bouffant on the betrayed turnip and arranged the heads in the window like a jury of glamorous widows. I opened every box Petra had taped. Each rip of packing tape felt like taking a full breath after years in a tight collar.

People began arriving at four twenty-six.

There were only eight at first: nearby shopkeepers, former customers, two teenagers still in school clothes, and a man who claimed he had come because his partner had sent him for groceries. By four thirty-five there were perhaps fifteen, which was enough to fill the narrow shop and make disaster feel curated.

I became magnificent.

I fitted a violet crop onto a woman who had once returned a custom piece because her husband called it “attention-seeking.”

“He was right,” I told her, turning her toward the mirror. “Seek better attention.”

The room applauded.

I gave away a reserved lace-front to someone it had not been reserved for. I knew this was theft from tomorrow's obligations. I also knew exactly which drawer held the deposit slip. The knowledge did not stop my hands. That was the horror of it, hidden inside the champagne sparkle of being watched.

I modelled three pieces at once over the impossible coils and told the crowd which customers lied about cutting their own bangs. I described our most expensive stock as “mourning hair for rich people who expect grief to have a natural-looking hairline.” A few people looked offended; more bought things. The shop account's viewer count climbed.

Every suppressed observation came out sharpened for entertainment. My jokes were accurate enough to draw blood and funny enough that the wounded laughed first.

At four forty-three, Petra Bristow pushed through the door.

She wore her good coat and carried a document folder against her ribs. Her gaze went from the crowd to the open boxes, to the wig on my head, to the SELL sticker across the contract I had pinned to the wall.

“Tilda,” she said. “What have you done?”

“Improved the closing party.”

“There wasn't supposed to be a closing party.”

“Then I've improved it infinitely.”

The crowd laughed. Petra did not. She was three years younger than I was, but exasperation had always made her look like the elder sister appointed by a stern committee.

She came behind the counter and lowered her voice. “The buyer sent me your video.”

“Then we saved on invitations.”

“Take it down. Call back. Say you're ill.”

“At last, a diagnosis for owning an opinion.”

“This isn't an opinion. It's a jointly owned building under debt, and you just announced to the neighborhood that you can make unilateral decisions about it.”

The delight in me sharpened. She had found the point that hurt and mistaken it for a warning.

I climbed onto the low fitting platform. The coils rose and settled around me, too large for modesty. “Petra would like everyone to know the shop is jointly owned. This is legally true. It was jointly inherited. It was not jointly kept open. It was not jointly cleaned at midnight, or stocked, or defended to creditors. And when our mother got sick, she was not jointly lifted from bed or washed or persuaded to eat.”

The room changed temperature.

“Stop,” Petra said.

For years I had wanted her to say I was right. Wearing the wig, I wanted something sweeter: I wanted her unable to survive my rightness.

Petra looked at the people crowded between the wig stands. “Could everyone please leave?”

“No,” I said. “They came for the funeral.”

Her mouth tightened. “You told me you could manage. Every time I offered to come, you told me not to disrupt my life. You made every decision, Tilda, and then presented me with the invoice in a language I was supposed to guess.”

It landed because it was true.

Truth did not make me gentler. It made me reach for a larger weapon.

I picked up my phone. The old voice message waited in the thread, still seven minutes and twelve seconds, still private.

Petra saw the screen. Her face emptied.

“Don't.”

Ordinarily, that one word would have stopped me. I knew it should stop me now. I remembered sitting in the dark while her recorded voice broke, remembered deciding I would never use her confession against her. The promise was present in my mind, intact.

I pressed play.

Petra's voice filled the shop.

*I couldn't come back because every time I saw her like that, I was terrified. You made it look as if I was busy, and I let you, because cowardice sounded worse. I knew you were drowning. I knew, and I still—*

Petra knocked the phone from my hand. It skidded beneath the styling chair. The message kept playing.

No one laughed.

She crouched, but I was faster. I snatched up the phone, clipped the ugliest thirty seconds, and posted them with one line about the co-owner who had inherited half the shop and none of the sickroom.

The act took six taps.

Petra stared at me as if six taps were a distance she could not cross.

“The wig didn't invent that cruelty,” she said. “It just made you enjoy using it.”

My screen lit with a new email before I could answer.

The buyer had withdrawn the offer.

There it was: the thing I had wanted. The five-o'clock signature evaporated. The shop remained ours, along with its debt, its emptied shelves, and the echo of Petra's voice dying in the sudden quiet.

Petra picked up her folder.

“You wanted me punished,” she said. “You were just too polite to ask.”

Then she left.

The crowd followed in embarrassed pieces. One person set a free wig back on the counter. Another avoided my eyes while continuing to record. Within minutes I stood alone among ripped boxes and overturned categories.

The copper-black mass in the mirror was glorious. Its white part divided my head like a verdict.

I opened a live broadcast.

The shop account still had hundreds of viewers. Reactions climbed the screen: flames, question marks, hearts, demands for context. I angled the phone so the empty shop stretched behind me like conquered territory.

“Since everyone is suddenly interested in inheritance,” I began, “let's discuss who morally owns this place.”

I knew Petra owned half. I knew care could not transmute signatures. I knew I had hidden my resentment inside obedience, then called the hiding generosity. None of that knowledge had vanished. It merely stood at a distance while self-interest wore my skin beautifully.

My thumb hovered over the button that would send me live.

I wanted to press it.

I wanted the shop. I wanted the watching faces. I wanted Petra to hurt enough that my hurt would finally look proportionate. And beneath all of it, humiliating in its smallness, I wanted my sister to have noticed without being told.

At my temples, the crown pulsed.

Craft lived in my fingers deeper than temperament. I slid them beneath the coils and felt the lace. Each beat of my heart sent warmth along the radiating knots. The foundation was not a mind wrestling me. It was a focus, exquisitely worked and utterly inert without the living pattern I kept feeding it: meek against monstrous, silence against spectacle, one self defined by the rejection of the other.

The card had not said which truth, only that neither of us wanted it. There was no *us*. There were two postures I had used to avoid the same naked sentence.

I ended the broadcast before it began.

The empty shop offered no applause.

“I want the shop,” I said, “and I wanted Petra to know without ever making myself ask.”

The sentence hurt more than any accusation. It blamed no one. It guaranteed nothing. It made my desire visible where it could be refused.

The white part blurred.

Heat drained from the spiral of knots. The huge coils lost their spring and collapsed against my shoulders, copper-black fading through brown. The crown slackened under my fingers. I lifted the wig free.

By the time it reached the counter, it was the same drab, symmetrical bob I had taken from the case.

My gray cardigan waited on the rubbish pile.

I put it on, then took it off again.

Deleting the post did not delete the copies. A clipped version already had more views than the shop account had followers. The buyer's withdrawal remained politely final. Three messages demanded refunds for things I had given away. One asked whether the funeral would continue tomorrow.

I typed a public statement that said the disclosure had been mine, made without Petra's consent, and that no circumstance excused it. I did not mention the wig. “Magical hair made me do it” had the structure of a joke and the ethics of a trapdoor.

Then I sent Petra a message.

**I removed it. What I did is still mine. I am sorry I played and posted your message. I won't ask you to forgive me. Please come back only if you want to watch me make sure it cannot happen again. After that, I want to propose a fair process for the shop. You can say no.**

She did not answer.

At five twenty, she returned.

She stayed inside the locked door, coat still buttoned, while I set the ash-brown wig on a canvas block at the workbench. I turned the styling chair away from the mirror. For once I did not want to see myself as a client whose discomfort could be managed.

“Is that it?” Petra asked.

“Yes.”

“Can it do it again?”

“If someone wears it and supplies what it needs, I think so.”

“You think.”

“I only know what it did with me.”

I showed her the spiral construction at the crown: the tiny central knot from which the tension spread, the pathways that had carried my heat and pulse. Then, with a blunt needle and tweezers, I began to unwork it.

The first knot resisted because it was old and fine, not because it wished to remain. I teased it apart. Hair loosened across the block. I took out the next, then the next, destroying in minutes the skill of hands I would never identify.

Petra watched until the foundation opened and the wig became ordinary loose hair sliding onto the worktable.

“I'm sorry,” I said again. “The grievance was real. The cruelty was a choice I made while cruelty felt good. Both are true.”

“That doesn't fix it.”

“No.”

“People heard me.”

“Yes.”

“I don't know if I can forgive you.”

My old instinct rose at once: reassure her, release her, punish myself so thoroughly she would have to comfort me. I let the instinct pass without obeying it.

“You don't have to decide that today,” I said.

I put the loose hair in the DISCARD box. Then I peeled the label off.

On a fresh label I wrote DECIDE TOGETHER and stuck it over the torn cardboard.

Petra gave it a tired, suspicious look. “Stationery. Bold.”

“I'm starting within my range.”

Her mouth moved, almost a smile and not forgiveness.

I took the unsigned sale contract from the wall. On its blank back, I wrote what I should have written before the first box was packed: a formal accounting of the shop's debt, both our ownership, and the care work I had performed; an independent appraisal; thirty days for me to seek financing to buy Petra's share at a fair value; a sale after that if I could not. I added that I would make every possible correction to the public harm without repeating her private words.

“I will agree to the accounting and the appraisal,” Petra said. “That's all I'm agreeing to.”

“All right.”

“I am not agreeing to thirty days.”

“All right.”

“And I am not agreeing to save this place because you finally admitted you want it.”

The shop around us looked smaller without the wigs: just scuffed floorboards, shelves, two sisters, and a future that had declined to label itself.

“All right,” I said.

Then I read her the rest of my terms aloud.

stories.title: The Station Between
stories.prompt: A person dies and wakes up in a train station, one train leading to heaven and the other to hell, anyone who is meant for hell but trys to enter the train to heaven will get dragged to hell while on the train, not wanting to find out what the afterlife is like, they stay at the station
stories.body:
# The Station Between

The first thing I knew after dying was that the bench had been designed to
prevent sleep.

A steel ridge divided every seat. It pressed between my shoulder blades when I
tried to lie back, so I sat up. The floor beneath my bare feet was white tile
veined with old gray mop water. Institutional lights hummed overhead. There
were no doors I recognized, no windows except the long black panes beyond two
sets of tracks.

Above the nearer platform, a board read:

**HEAVEN — 8 MINUTES**

The board over the opposite track read:

**HELL — 15 MINUTES**

On my lap lay a cream paper ticket. My name, RUTH, was printed at the top. A
strip of black film covered the destination field, with one corner lifted just
enough to invite a fingernail.

I remembered the kitchen tiles rushing toward me. I remembered trying to call
out and having no breath for it. Then voices above me, urgent and receding, and
someone saying a number that was answered by silence.

“Am I dead?” I asked.

The woman behind the information window looked up from a ledger. She wore a
gray cardigan and a brass badge stamped HESTER PIKE. Nothing about her was
winged or radiant. A pencil held her hair in a loose knot.

“Yes,” Hester said.

I turned the ticket edgewise so the black field faced the floor. “And those are
what they say they are?”

“Those are the names on the boards.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

“It’s what I can answer.”

Behind her, a hairline rectangle interrupted the yellowed wall, the shape of a
door painted over too many times. Hester closed the ledger and came around the
window.

“I can tell you what I have seen here,” she said. “The trains arrive. People
present their tickets. The gates admit them or do not. I have not traveled on
either train.”

The ticket was stiff enough to cut. I flipped it over.

**VALID THIS SERVICE ONLY**

**NO REISSUE**

Two thin black borders ran around the warning, one inside the other.

“There’ll be another service.”

“For other tickets.”

“There are always other trains.”

Hester’s expression did not change. “Here, I have seen no expired ticket
restored.”

The heaven board clicked down to seven minutes. The sound was absurdly small.
It reminded me of a clock in a hospital room, its hand jumping once each
second while Asha watched the dark window.

Stay until morning, she had said.

I pressed my thumb against the unopened film. If the word beneath it was
HEAVEN, then perhaps Asha had gone there. Perhaps I could find her. If it said
HELL, then perhaps leaving her had been weighed and found heavier than
everything else I had ever done.

Either answer would make one night into a verdict.

“I don’t have to look,” I said.

“No.”

“Then I haven’t decided.”

Hester glanced at the boards. “Not looking is something you can do. It will
not stop the clocks.”

I moved to the far end of the bench, away from her, and put the ticket into my
pocket with the black film unbroken.

***

The other passenger sat down where I had been.

I had not seen her arrive. She was perhaps my age, perhaps younger; death had
smoothed the useful measures out of both of us. A blue elastic circled her
wrist. She gathered her loose dark hair at the nape of her neck with hands that
shook only once, then let it fall again.

Her ticket lay open across her knee.

SABINE KROLL, it read.

Beneath her name, in hard black letters, was **HELL**.

“You’re holding yours backward,” she said.

“On purpose.”

“Clever. I looked straight away, like an idiot.”

“You’re not an idiot.”

“You don’t know me.”

The brittle brightness in her voice asked me to laugh. I did, a single startled
breath. Sabine smiled as if she had won something, then held up the ticket.

“You’d think eternity could afford an appeals desk.”

Hester had returned to the information window. “There is no appeals desk I can
direct you to.”

“Even living courts let the accused speak.”

“I don’t know who assigned the word.”

“But you’ll enforce it.”

“I don’t control the gates or the trains.”

Sabine rose and crossed to the waist-high gate beneath the heaven sign. When
she put her ticket against the brass plate, the gate gave a soft red pulse and
stayed shut. She tried again, holding the ticket flatter.

“The door on the train opens on the platform side,” she said.

Hester’s hands settled on the counter. “Do not board that train.”

Sabine looked over her shoulder. “You just said you don’t control it.”

“I said I do not control the door. I have seen three passengers enter a train
that did not match their tickets. The train began to move. They did not
continue on it.”

“Where did they go?”

“To the other train.”

“Alive?”

The corner of Hester’s mouth tightened. “They were dead when they arrived.”

“You know what I mean.”

“They remained themselves as far as I could see. They were conscious. They
resisted.”

Sabine looked down at the word on her ticket. “And you watched.”

“Yes.”

“Did any of them have a chance to explain what they’d done?”

“Not to anyone I could see.”

The heaven board clicked to four minutes.

Sabine came back to the bench but did not sit. “If that word is right, they
should be able to tell me why. If it’s wrong, I’m not volunteering to make
their mistake convenient.”

“What are you going to do?”

“Get on the other train.”

Hester said, “I have told you what I have seen.”

“And I listened.” Sabine’s eyes stayed on mine. “The gate won’t open for me,
but the carriage door will. I need someone on the platform to keep it from
closing.”

“It moved them,” I said.

“Maybe they let go.”

“She said they resisted.”

“Then maybe I’ll resist better.”

There was humor in the angle of her mouth and terror beneath it. I could have
said no. I could have told her the test was too expensive because she was the
one paying for it.

Instead I pictured the black field on my ticket. If Sabine remained on the
heaven train, the boards would become labels, nothing more. Asha might be
reachable no matter what was printed under the film. I could have uncertainty
without loss.

“I’ll hold it,” I said.

Hester’s voice sharpened. “Ruth.”

It was the first time she had used my name. I mistook the shame I felt for
proof that I was doing something brave.

Sabine held out her hand. I took it. Her fingers were cold, but no colder than
mine.

“If it works?” I asked.

“Then one ugly word gets smaller.”

***

The rails began to sing.

Light gathered in the black window beyond the heaven track, first a pinprick,
then two steady lamps. The train arrived without a rush of wind. Its silver
cars eased alongside the platform as quietly as an elevator, bright windows
showing blue seats, brass luggage racks, and paper cups standing in molded
holders. People were already inside, their faces turned away or blurred by
reflections.

When the doors opened, warm air touched me.

It smelled faintly of lemon lotion and clean cotton warmed in a dryer.

Asha had kept a tube of lemon lotion on the hospital table because the air
cracked her hands. I had rubbed it into her knuckles on the last evening. She
had watched me make careful circles with my thumbs and said, Stay until
morning. Not dramatically. She had been tired, and afraid, and trying not to
make either thing my fault.

I had promised.

At midnight I had gone home for a shower. At two, her final call lit the room.
I silenced it before I was properly awake. By dawn, there was no one left to
call back.

The carriage warmth drew across my face. Somewhere inside, passengers murmured,
and one brief rise of laughter had Asha’s cadence only because I wanted it to.
My hand went into my pocket. I found the lifted corner of the black film and
set my nail beneath it.

“Ruth.”

Sabine stood at the closing gate. Her own ticket had produced another red
pulse. The carriage doors sounded a warning tone.

I let go of my ticket.

There was a narrow service gap beside the gate where its arm met the wall.
Hester had not mentioned it, and she made no move to block it. Sabine turned
sideways and forced herself through, scraping one hip against the brass post.
The carriage doors began to meet.

I caught one with both hands.

It pushed steadily, without violence, and I leaned my weight against it.
Sabine seized the rail and swung aboard.

“Come with me,” she said.

For a moment I saw the empty seat behind her, its fabric warmed by a light with
no visible sun. The lemon scent deepened. I could peel the ticket. I could
know.

“Doors closing,” Hester called.

I stepped back.

The panels met between us. Sabine pressed her palm to the glass, the blue
elastic bright on her wrist. The train slid forward.

Nothing happened at first.

One window passed, then another. Sabine kept pace with me from inside, moving
down the aisle as the carriage carried her away. Her mouth opened in a
triumphant, disbelieving laugh.

The opposite rails rang with a blow like an iron bar dropped on stone.

The hell train entered the station.

It was dark red, nearly brown, with riveted sides and windows filmed by smoke.
Dry heat pressed from it before it stopped. Its wheels complained against the
track in a long metallic cry. I turned toward it for one second.

Sabine struck the heaven-train window.

The destination field on her ticket had darkened to ash gray around the black
word HELL. The rest of the cream paper remained unchanged.

Shadow was collecting under the blue seats. It rose in flat bands and wrapped
her ankles. She kicked free of one and caught the brass luggage rack with both
hands. More darkness drew across her waist and shoulders, not hiding her but
pulling her sideways through the moving carriage.

“Ruth!”

I ran along the platform. Her train was gaining speed. Sabine’s shoes skidded
over the bright floor. She locked one arm around a seat back. The shadow
stretched, tightened, and dragged her down the aisle while the other passengers
remained shapes behind reflected light.

“Hold on,” I shouted, as if I had not been the one who held the door.

Sabine’s grip slipped from the seat. She caught a vertical rail with her right
hand, the blue elastic cutting a line across her pale wrist. Her face was awake,
furious, fixed on mine.

The wall behind her split into a seam no wider than a closed curtain. There was
no view through it, only a depthless strip of dark. The bands pulled. Sabine
braced both feet, screamed my name once more, and was drawn through.

The seam closed.

The heaven carriage continued past me, empty where she had been.

Across the platform, a hand struck the smoky glass of the hell train.

The blue elastic was still around its wrist.

Sabine stood inside the other carriage, bent forward and breathing though
breath could have meant nothing there. The same loose strands of hair crossed
her cheek. She beat at the window with both palms, turned as if searching for a
door, then saw me.

The heaven train vanished into the black beyond the station.

In my pocket, the ticket burned cold.

I pulled it out. The outer of its two borders had faded from black to gray.
The film still hid the destination.

“That route has lapsed,” Hester said behind me.

The hell board read:

**HELL — 5 MINUTES**

***

Sabine came to the window opposite me.

Smoke moved across the glass between us, thinning and thickening. When it
cleared, I saw the pressure marks the luggage rail had left across her palms.
She held up her ticket. Its destination field remained ash gray around the
unchanged black word HELL.

“Can she get out?” I asked.

“I have not seen anyone get out after a transfer,” Hester said.

“You knew that would happen.”

“I warned you that I had seen it happen.”

“You could have stopped us.”

“I could not have stopped the train. I might have tried to restrain her. Or
you.” Hester looked at Sabine rather than at me. “I did not.”

The answer gave me no clean place to put my anger.

The platform gate beneath the hell sign stood closed, its brass plate dark.
Heat lifted from the train in dry, unsteady waves. Behind Sabine, the carriage
was dim but material: wooden benches, leather straps, brass bolts dulled almost
green. I could not see who else sat there. I could not see what waited beyond
the tunnel.

“If I board it,” I asked, “will it take me?”

“Present your ticket and the gate will respond.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“It is what I know.”

“What if mine says heaven?”

“That service has gone.”

The words struck harder than the iron noise. If Asha was anywhere beyond that
warm carriage—if the scent had been more than memory, if there had been even
the smallest chance—I had let it leave. No punishment could be as precise as
not knowing whether I had missed her.

The board clicked to three minutes.

“And if mine says hell?”

Hester’s gaze fell to the covered field. “Then the label would match this
train. I cannot tell you whether the label is just. I cannot tell you what the
destination contains.”

I could peel the film and surrender to whichever sentence waited beneath. If
it said hell, I could call boarding honesty, or punishment, or the courage I
had failed to show beside Asha. If it said heaven, I could spend whatever
remained knowing that absolution had once been offered and that I had thrown it
away.

Both fantasies asked the station to finish my guilt for me.

Sabine struck the glass once.

The sound was muffled, but I flinched. She did not point to the closed gate or
beckon me toward the train. She only looked at me. The fury in her face was
not a message about my destination. It belonged to her.

I went close enough that the heat tightened my skin.

“I helped you because I wanted you to prove it could be escaped,” I said. “I
wanted you to find out for me.”

Sabine’s mouth moved. The window gave me no sound.

“I’m sorry.”

I did not ask whether she forgave me.

The final minute disappeared from the board. A warning bell rang inside the
hell train. Its doors folded shut.

Hester said, “If you let this service leave, the other border will lapse. I
have seen no later train here accept a ticket after that.”

My hand closed around the paper. I wanted to open it so badly that my thumbnail
creased the black film. I wanted a word to hate. I wanted one to obey.

I kept my thumb still.

The train moved.

Sabine walked with the window as long as the carriage allowed. I walked on my
side, neither of us looking away. Her palm stayed against the glass, the blue
line around her wrist visible until smoke covered it, until the last car passed,
until the red lamps at the rear became two embers and went out.

The inner border on my ticket turned gray.

Then the ink of my name, the warning, and both borders drained into the paper.
The black peel-back film lightened last. In a few breaths I held a blank cream
rectangle.

Behind me, both passenger gates locked with the sound of bolts driven home.

***

I tried them anyway.

The heaven gate did not light when I pressed the blank ticket to its plate. The
hell gate did not light. I shook each until the brass bars rattled in their
housings.

“Another service,” I said. “You said there are other tickets. Let me take
another service.”

“Not with that ticket.”

“Give me a new one.”

“I cannot.”

“Who can?”

Hester picked up her ledger. “No one I have seen.”

The boards went dark. Without their words, the station became only tile, iron,
and the stale smell of cooling brakes. There was no revelation in it. No voice
told me that refusal was noble. My blank ticket did not become a key to
something hidden.

Hester crossed behind the information window and pressed her palm to the
painted rectangle in the wall. A narrow door opened without showing what lay
beyond; there was only a wedge of ordinary yellow light and the edge of another
gray wall.

I hurried after her. The opening narrowed before I reached it. I wedged the
blank ticket into the gap. The door pushed the paper back without bending it
and shut.

“Hester.”

She looked at me from the other side.

“How long am I here?”

“I don’t know.”

“What am I supposed to do?”

“I don’t know that either.”

The door sealed, leaving only the hairline in the paint.

I was alone.

I thought of Asha’s room after I left it: the chair pulled close to her bed,
the cup with its bent straw, the phone close enough for her to reach. I had
imagined that room so many times that memory and invention had worn into each
other. I did not know whether she had been awake when she called. I did not
know whether she had been afraid. I knew only what I had done.

I sat on the bench and placed the blank ticket beside me.

The cold worked through my clothes. There was no sunrise beyond the windows.
There was no clock now that the boards were dark. I counted my breaths until I
understood that counting would not make time answer.

Then the board mechanisms stirred.

Letters flipped into place above both tracks. New minutes appeared. The blank
ticket beside me remained blank.

At the far end of the bench, a woman gasped.

She wore wet slippers and a hospital wristband. Her hands clutched the front of
her gown closed. She stared at the boards, then at me.

“Am I dead?”

The old impulse rose whole inside me: step away before fear became a request.
Find the painted door. Find the darkest part of the platform. Let her peel her
ticket and carry whatever word waited there without making it mine.

I picked up my blank ticket and moved toward her.

“Yes,” I said.

She began to cry without sound.

I sat at the other end of the bench, leaving the seat between us open. After a
moment she crossed that space herself and caught my sleeve.

“What happens?”

“I can tell you what I’ve seen here.”

I told her about the gates and the one-service warning. I told her I did not
know who had made the labels, whether they were fair, or what waited beyond
them. When I reached Sabine, I did not say the train had taken a passenger, as
if she had been luggage. I said her name. I said I had held the door. I said I
had watched her dragged from the moving heaven train into the hell train, and
that she had remained herself all the way to the last window.

The woman listened with both hands around her unopened ticket.

“Which one was yours?” she asked.

I showed her the blank paper. “I didn’t look.”

“Can you still go?”

“The gates won’t open for me.”

She glanced toward the tracks. “Was it worth it?”

The question had no answer that would not pretend I knew more than I did.

“It was my choice,” I said. “And Sabine paid for part of it.”

The woman looked down. With one careful pull, she peeled the film from her
ticket. Her shoulders shook when she read the word, but she turned it so I
could see.

**HEAVEN**.

“Is it?” she asked. “Heaven?”

“That is where the sign says the train goes.”

“But is it?”

“I don’t know.”

The rails began their distant song. She tightened her grip on my sleeve.

“Will you stay until it comes?”

My sister’s voice did not enter the station. No warmth passed through me. There
was only this frightened stranger, the pressure of her fingers, and the
approaching light.

“Yes,” I said.

The train drew in with its clean windows and ordinary blue seats. Warm air
crossed the platform when the doors opened, carrying lemon and cotton and a
hundred other things I could have made into promises. The woman presented her
own ticket. The gate lit green.

She kept hold of my sleeve until the opening bars made her release me. I walked
beside her to the carriage door, but I did not touch it. She stepped aboard by
herself and took the nearest seat. I remained on the platform.

When the train moved, no shadows rose.

She watched me through the glass until the carriage entered the dark. The
warmth went with it. The gate closed before me, and when I laid my blank ticket
on the plate there was no light at all.

The station offered no thanks. Across the tracks, the hell board continued its
countdown for someone who had not yet appeared.

I returned to the bench. I sat at one end and laid the useless ticket on my
knee, leaving the place beside me clear.

The cold came up through the tiles. I stayed where I could be found.

stories.title: The Friends I Built
stories.prompt: You are the child of a damned soul and the archdemon Belphegor. You are deaf and non-speaking. Unfortunately for you, your parents, while loving, are extremely lazy. So you use your exceptional aptitude and intelligent to create your own friends and impress others at school with your skills
stories.body:
# The Friends I Built

Belphegor, my archdemon parent, signed the wrong corner of my exhibition form
with all four hands.

It was an impressive mistake. Four elegant strokes of green fire braided
themselves around the ornamental skulls in the margin while the line marked
GUARDIAN remained offensively blank.

I waved the paper between Belphegor's face and the cushion.

I was deaf and non-speaking; I argued fluently with my hands and, when
necessary, my pocket slate.

Their upper eyes opened. Their lower eyes considered it an unreasonable hour
and remained closed. Belphegor lifted two hands to sign, *Beautiful work. Very
proud.*

The other two tucked the blanket beneath their chin.

I pointed to the blank line.

*Of course,* they signed. Their fingers were graceful even when the rest of
them had surrendered to the couch. *Put it here. I will correct it after one
small rest.*

I held up the kitchen clock. The guardian deadline was that morning. The
promised conveyance was due in twenty minutes. Belphegor smiled at me with
genuine confidence, shut their upper eyes, and became a part of the couch.

Talvi lay on the rug beside the couch, half inside a quilt and half outside it.
She had once been damned for reasons she called both complicated and badly
documented. She was much better at remembering my first diagrams than the
present day. Every lopsided machine I had drawn as a child was pressed between
sheets in her cabinet.

When I touched her shoulder, she woke at once and signed, *Exhibition. Today. I
remember.*

I showed her the clock.

She sat up. Hope rose in me, embarrassing and automatic.

*I'll arrange the ride now,* she signed. *Ten minutes.*

Then she leaned against the couch while searching for the dispatch slate. Her
eyes closed with her hand still under a cushion.

They loved me. This was not a theory. Talvi had learned every variation of my
signing as my hands grew. Belphegor could watch a diagram unfold for hours,
provided they were horizontal. Love had never been the missing component.
Completed tasks were.

I laid the form on my workboard. With a brass rule, I scored two precise folds
between the decorated margin and the guardian box. I fixed a paper hinge along
the first crease with a needle of sealing heat, then swung the signed corner
over the blank line without cutting or changing a stroke. The green signature
now occupied the required box. The ornamental skulls stared upside down, which
improved them.

The dispatch slate remained dark.

I strapped my pressure strips, projection plates, copper rods, and case of
embermoss cultures to a handcart. At the door, I looked back. Talvi had found
Belphegor's hand in her sleep. Belphegor's thumb moved once against hers.

I left them a note large enough to cover the clock.

I hauled everything to school alone.

By the time the black chimneys of the Cinder Annex rose beyond the ash trees,
my palms were blistered and the first lesson was over. Dependence, I decided,
was only another word for delay.

* * *

The Aptitudes Exhibition occupied the furnace hall for three days each year.
Heat shivered above the floor grates. Student projects crowded the iron tables:
glass gardens that folded away from touch, bone-white bridges carrying beads
of molten metal, and one cage full of shadows arranging themselves into rude
gestures.

The students around me suddenly gathered their papers. A moment later, a
lesson lamp blinked above Instructor Bexel's table.

The bell again. It sent no light until it was finished.

Bexel caught my eye and signed, *Sorry.*

She signed competently, which made the apology worse. We had discussed the
sound-only bell twice.

When everyone faced her, Bexel raised the exhibition rules. *Advanced-workshop
eligibility requires a collaborative entry. Teams lock in three days from
now.*

I read the rule again. My design had been accepted as a solo project the week
before.

Around me, tables closed like jaws. Students pulled stools together and bent
over shared plans. I carried my slate to Ekri. His flame-figure engine stood on
the next table, a copper drum connected to the hall furnace. Pressure from his
demonstration traveled through the flagstones in crisp, rhythmic taps I could
feel through my shoes.

I wrote, `JOIN PROJECTS? MY RELAY CAN MAP YOUR LOAD.`

Ekri glanced at the slate, then at the students watching him. He knew enough
sign to answer, though he used only one hand.

*Too slow,* he signed.

I waited.

His face tightened. He took my chalk and added beneath my question,
`LOOKING UP. WRITING. EXTRA TIME.`

He had spent longer explaining the inconvenience than a signed answer would
have taken.

The remaining teams found urgent reasons to study their own tables.

Bexel approached. She kept her face toward me when she signed. *I can approve a
solo accommodation.*

I pointed to the workshop requirement.

Her mouth pulled sideways. *You could exhibit. It would not satisfy the
collaboration criterion.*

An accommodation that removed the thing I was competing for. Efficient.

I wiped Ekri's answer from my slate. Bexel watched me write two new words.

`BUILD TEAM.`

Her eyebrows rose.

I had three days.

* * *

Embermoss looked dead until it was hungry. Mine lay in two shallow dishes,
grey as old scabs, while I built brass frames around them.

I had planned assistants: four spindle legs each, a hinge for pointing,
receptive plates for my relay, and simple flags for answers. Reliable bodies
for reliable instructions. I fed the moss bitter coal-sugar, touched my palms
to the growth plates, and supplied the shaping current my craft lessons called
living magic.

Green warmth passed from me into the cultures. I stopped when my wrists began
to tremble. The magic was mine to give; the growth that followed was theirs.

The first moss climbed its frame in neat, measured bands. It tested one leg,
then the opposite leg, balancing before committing its weight. The second
burst over the copper ribs, ignored half the channels I had etched, and formed
a round body with three unnecessary loops.

I pointed to the coal-sugar.

The precise one sampled a crumb and spat it onto my ruler.

The round one ate six, flashed orange through the thin moss over its core, and
knocked over the dish looking for seven.

I offered sweet ash instead. The round one rolled in it. The precise one
selected a second bitter crumb and ate it while standing on my ruler,
apparently because contradicting me mattered more than disliking lunch.

Assistants were not supposed to have culinary spite.

I set out a box of labeled tools so they could learn word tiles. The precise
one walked over every label, paused at `KNURL`, and rolled the textured wheel
under two feet. The tiny ridges seemed to please them. They drew the tile close
and raised both flags.

Knurl.

The round one climbed into my thimble and curled around it. When I tried to
retrieve the tool, they wrapped all three loops over its rim and displayed a
red panel.

I placed the `THIMBLE` tile beside them.

The panel changed to green.

Thimble.

Names, I discovered, made introductions necessary. I signed mine. Knurl
repeated the shape with hinged flags, careful and exact. Thimble attempted it
with two loops, got tangled, and turned the failure into a dance.

By the second day, both had grown warm enough to seek food on their own and
strong enough to rearrange my bench. Knurl sorted my washers by diameter.
Thimble hung colored scraps from the relay arms, where they served no purpose
except delighting Thimble.

I removed one. Thimble put it back.

I removed it again. Thimble showed red.

It was my relay. It was also becoming our exhibition, though I had not yet
admitted the distinction.

Knurl was adjusting a sensor plate when I noticed the bracket beneath them was
loose. I reached across, caught their brass frame, and lifted.

Every spindle leg locked. Both flags snapped flat against their body.

I set them down.

Knurl retreated behind the coal-sugar bowl and pushed three tiles into line.

`DO NOT TAKE.`

Heat climbed my face. I had been about to save them from a fall. I had also
given no warning and allowed no refusal.

I signed, *May I lift you to tighten the bracket?*

Knurl considered the bracket, considered me, then raised the yes flag.

The frame relaxed when my hands closed around it.

After that I asked. Sometimes Knurl raised the no flag and pointed out another
solution. Thimble usually showed green, except when sticky with ash, when they
apparently considered touch a privilege nobody deserved.

The relay itself still failed. My pressure strips could translate vibration,
heat, and load into colored light, but the projected map muddied whenever two
signals overlapped. I tried separating the channels. Knurl placed each plate
in a perfect ring. The colors sharpened, but the delay doubled.

Thimble climbed the projector, pulled down all the decorative sails, and
stretched them at unequal angles.

I signed, *That is worse.*

Thimble flashed red, then tapped the pressure strip and pointed.

The staggered sails caught each pulse in sequence. Knurl studied them, then
rotated the neat ring by one plate, destroying its symmetry to preserve its
spacing.

The map opened across the wall: blue for clear, yellow for strain, red for
danger. Fast, legible, and nothing like my original design.

Knurl raised both flags. Thimble shone green through their moss until the whole
room looked seasick.

On my slate I wrote, `FRIENDS?`

The word felt more dangerous than living magic.

Knurl selected `YES` and aligned it precisely beneath the question.

Thimble slapped up a green sail, stole the `YES` tile, and nested with it inside
the thimble.

* * *

On exhibition morning, the dispatch slate was still dark.

Talvi sat beside it with sleep creases across her cheek. Her eyes widened when
she saw the time. *I meant to confirm it.*

Behind her, Belphegor lay buried under four separate blankets. One hand
emerged to sign, *I was going to wake.*

I did not answer. If I opened my hands, anger would come out.

I packed the projection plates and pressure strips. I folded the exhibit
chassis into its case, then reached for Knurl.

They stepped away and raised the no flag.

Thimble planted all three loops across the case and flashed red.

`SAFE`, I wrote. `I CARRY.`

Knurl rearranged the tiles.

`ASK.`

Thimble added another.

`WALK.`

They drew their plan directly over mine. The chassis already had jointed
supports to hold the sensors against uneven floors. Turn the supports down.
Move the load plate forward. Use Thimble's sails to balance the case and
Knurl's exact weight shifts to steer.

It was undignified. It was also clever.

I looked at them both and signed, *Will you help me change it?*

Two yeses, different as fingerprints.

We built the cart in eleven minutes. It walked with a stiff six-legged gait,
carrying the heavy case while Knurl rode the forward plate and directed each
turn. Thimble perched on top beneath a striped sail. I hauled only when the ash
road steepened.

Talvi followed us to the door. *Irix, I'm sorry.*

I looked at the three-day-old note still covering the clock.

*I know,* I signed. Then we left, because sorrow did not move equipment either.

The three of us reached the Cinder Annex while the entry lamp was still green.

* * *

Instructor Bexel inspected our walking chassis, Knurl's flags, and Thimble's
sails. She looked from them to me before signing, *Are they entering as
collaborators?*

I asked them.

Knurl raised yes. Thimble displayed green.

Bexel amended the entry card. Then she pressed a glass scoring seal over the
chassis hinge.

*If that breaks before judging ends, the score is void,* she signed.

I nodded. Knurl examined the seal's alignment and adjusted it by a hair.

The furnace hall filled. When the opening bell sounded, I knew because faces
turned and shoulders jumped. I waited until Bexel lifted the green lamp before
starting.

I laid pressure strips across the demonstration floor. Knurl placed calibrated
weights while my relay projected each load in blue geometry. Thimble scampered
between the strips, sending bursts of gold across the map. The audience could
see where every foot landed, where heat collected, and where the iron beneath
them strained.

The fixed hazards belonged on the map too. The painted evacuation chevrons
pointed toward the east doors, though the furnace release grate faced their
approach. Ekri's cutoff lever hung behind his copper drum. Above the feed pipe,
Knurl stopped beneath a cold-air shutter and tilted their flags to match its
crooked edge. I added all three to the projection.

A student wrote a challenge on the question board:
`SHOW TWO OVERLAPPING LOADS WITHOUT LOSING DIRECTION.`

I started drawing the answer. Knurl crossed both flags.

For one hot instant I wanted to lower the flags myself.

Instead, I signed, *Show me.*

Knurl shifted the sensor ring. Thimble climbed the projection arm and unfurled
the staggered sails. My first diagram collapsed. Their altered pattern rose
through it: two currents, one violet and one green, crossing while remaining
distinct.

Understanding changed the audience's faces. Students leaned over the strips.
Hands pointed. A few tried signs they had seen us use. When they brought their
palms together in applause, I saw the motion first and felt a soft confusion of
impact through the floor.

I had wanted to impress them. I had not expected the pleasure to belong to all
three of us.

At the next table, Ekri prepared his final flourish.

His engine accepted the living current he pressed into its copper drum, then
shaped it into flame figures above the furnace mouth. Each figure landed with
