a pulse strong enough to tremble my slate. The hearing students grinned and
covered their ears. Ekri grinned wider.

I had seen the feed latch earlier. Its two teeth met crookedly, leaving a
yellow stress crescent on my relay whenever the furnace drew hard. I had
pointed it out. Ekri had written, `HOLDS FOR ONE SHOW.`

Now he saw the audience watching our table.

He pushed both palms against the drum.

A many-winged figure of fire spread to the rafters. The flagstones bucked.
Ekri's latch jumped one tooth, then the other.

The furnace feed door fell open.

Black ember-grain poured into the chamber. Flame pressed white against the
vents. Students flinched and looked up, but the alarm lamps stayed dark. The
sound-only alarm was giving them a warning I could not receive.

Bexel stood on a table and signed the standard instruction: *East doors. Move
now.*

My relay painted the floor red.

Pressure was building beneath the feed line. The east corridor crossed
directly in front of its release grate. If the grate opened, every student
following the usual route would meet the ember spray.

I caught Bexel's eye and slashed both hands across the order.

She looked at the red map.

The release grate began to shake.

* * *

The projector was too weak to throw my plan across the whole hall.

The walking chassis held the power plate I needed.

I put my thumb against Bexel's glass scoring seal. For three days I had measured
every choice against the advanced workshop. I broke the seal.

Knurl was already loosening the power housing. Thimble stripped the balancing
sails free. Together we fed the plate into the projector, and my diagram
climbed the furnace wall in fierce color.

Blue arrows turned students away from the east doors and toward the rear
service passage. Red marked the release grate. Yellow marked the cold-air
shutter above the feed pipe—a narrow iron panel I had noticed because Knurl had
stared unhappily at its crooked edge during setup.

Bexel read the map. She signed, broad enough for the room, *Follow blue. Watch
Irix.*

Her authorization changed panic into movement. She took the front of the line,
opened the service barrier, and pointed students through.

I drew Ekri's engine in yellow, then the cutoff lever in red. Ekri's face had
gone grey. I jabbed two fingers toward the lever.

He moved. Heat forced him back once. He wrapped his exhibition apron around
his arm, reached past the drum, and dragged the cutoff down. The great flame
figure folded into the furnace.

The pressure map remained red.

Knurl pointed to the cold-air shutter.

I signed, *No. Stay here. Both of you.*

Knurl's flags flattened.

Thimble flashed a red so dark it was almost black.

The old wish rose in me: friends who could not fail because they could not
refuse. It looked ugly under the red light.

I made myself ask. *You understand the danger? You still choose this?*

Knurl pointed from the shutter to their spindle legs, then raised yes.

Thimble spread the largest sail and raised green behind it.

I wanted to keep them safe. They wanted to help keep everyone safe. Neither
want erased the other.

I signed, *Together.*

Knurl ran along the sensor rail and up the angled pipe. They hooked two spindle
legs into the shutter wheel and aligned the bent shaft one precise fraction at
a time.

Thimble anchored one loop around the remaining chassis bar. They stretched the
sail between the release grate and the last students entering the passage.

I kept the projection steady and changed the route as blue sensors cleared.
Ekri held the cutoff. Bexel counted every visible face through the service
barrier and waved the last cluster onward.

Knurl forced the shaft straight.

The cold-air shutter dropped open. Pale vapor washed across the furnace, and
the red pressure lines on my map began to shrink.

The release grate snapped wide anyway.

Embers struck Thimble's sail. Light ran through the cloth in a ragged orange
line. Thimble recoiled but held the fabric until the spray thinned and fell.

Then their green core dimmed.

The map turned blue at the same moment the judging lamp began to flash.

I let the projector fall.

By the time I reached Thimble, Knurl was beside them, both flags trembling.
The striped sail had shriveled along one edge. The felt beneath was scorched,
not split, and Thimble pulled one loop away from my hand.

Even then, I remembered.

*May I carry you?* I signed.

Thimble's panel flickered green.

I lifted them out of the ash.

* * *

Bexel voided our exhibition score.

She did it after helping me cool Thimble's moss, after Knurl had inspected
every stitch in the new patch, and after Ekri had written a complete account
of the latch he had rushed. The original striped sail stayed attached. Its
blackened edge showed beneath the patch. Thimble refused every offer to make
the colors match.

Then Bexel stood where the whole team could see her.

*The score measures an intact exhibition,* she signed. *Your seal was broken.*

I held Thimble closer, with permission.

Bexel continued. *The advanced workshop measures aptitude and collaboration.
Today demonstrated both.*

She amended the record to list Irix, Knurl, and Thimble as three collaborators.
Not maker and equipment. Three.

Ekri waited until I looked at him. `I SAW THE LATCH`, he wrote on my slate.
Then, beneath it, `I WANTED THE FINISH MORE. I WILL HELP REBUILD.`

I did not offer instant friendship. I handed him the list of damaged parts.
He nodded and began sorting them.

Before we left, Bexel posted three changes on the hall board. Future event
alarms would carry light and floor signals. Team formation would include an
accessible process supervised by an adult instead of leaving excluded
students to bargain for entry. Living collaborators would be registered as
participants and asked for consent.

Local rules on one school board did not repair everything. They repaired three
things that had nearly hurt us.

Bexel came home with us carrying a support agreement she had drafted, not one
she expected me to invent.

Talvi and Belphegor were awake.

Talvi saw Thimble's patched sail and covered her mouth. Belphegor sat fully
upright, all four hands empty. Their attention was so complete that I almost
made the task easier for them.

Instead I wrote on my slate:

`YOU LOVE ME. I LOVE YOU. LOVE IS NOT THE WORK.`

They read it.

`I WILL NOT REMIND YOU TO SUPPORT ME. I WILL NOT BUILD YOUR REMINDERS.`

Talvi's eyes filled. She did not ask me to comfort her. She opened the dispatch
slate, arranged a standing school conveyance for every exhibition and workshop
morning, and assigned its confirmation to the adult dispatcher. Bexel received
the backup notice. Only after the confirmation glowed green did Talvi sign,
*This is my responsibility. If it fails, I repair it.*

Belphegor placed all four palms on the couch. Green fire sank into the cushions
and stitched a narrow line to the household deadline slate. At the next marked
time, the couch snapped upright and deposited Belphegor on their feet.

They blinked, offended by their own success.

*My consequence,* they signed. *My maintenance.*

Bexel laid the agreement on the table. It made her the school contact when a
guardian task was missed, gave her authority to activate transport, and
required the adults to report failures to one another. She asked my consent
before adding my name to the communication list. I gave it.

Talvi signed the guardian line. Belphegor signed the witness line. Bexel
checked both before taking the document with her.

The next morning, the conveyance arrived while the couch was still forcing
Belphegor upright.

Knurl waited beside the repaired chassis, aligning the new bolts. Thimble sat
inside the old thimble under their visibly patched sail. Neither had been
packed.

I signed, *Do you want to come to school with me?*

Knurl placed `YES` squarely in the center of my palm, then stepped onto the
steering plate.

Thimble flashed green, climbed my sleeve, and used the patched sail to point at
the door.

Talvi did not ask whether the dispatch slate had worked. She checked it
herself. Belphegor, vertical and rumpled, held the door.

I entered the Cinder Annex with the friends I had built, and who had chosen,
again, to come with me.

stories.title: Solstice Evening Bell
stories.prompt: Solstice Evening Bell, First Monarch and queen of all magical girls, is the only being on Earth under the "ultrahuman" categorization. The invasion force is easily into the six-digit range. She stands alone. Write me a fight scene.
stories.body:
# Solstice Evening Bell

The instruments went blind nine seconds before the sky opened.

Solstice Evening Bell stood above the western bay, twelve silver chimes turning
around her in a slow, uneven halo.

They were not the twelve women.

Solstice had required that truth before she accepted the crown. No soul was
imprisoned in the silver. The dead had gone where the dead went, beyond any
monarch's jurisdiction. What circled her were twelve last spells, each freely
made by one of the twelve strongest magical girls then living. On coronation
night, each woman had driven her transformation past the point from which her
body could return and poured the whole bright remainder into a chime.

Their bodies had not survived the making. Their choices had.

Solstice knew every note by the woman who had left it. The lowest had belonged
to someone who drank tea too hot and cursed every time it burned her. The
sharpest came from a woman who laughed just before she charged. The smallest
chime carried the final spell of the woman who had squeezed Solstice's fingers
hard enough to hurt and made her promise never to confuse a gift with a shrine.
The other nine were no less particular in her memory but no less important.

The thirteenth tone was Solstice's own. Its thumb-sized resonator rested
against her sternum beneath the white armor of her dress, warm from the force
rising out of her living nerves. The nonliving crown could store the twelve
final spells and shape her power through them. It could not choose, act, or
make a spark until Solstice woke it.

Below, evacuation arrows still crawled across empty harbor roads. On the
nearest public hazard board, one red line remained visible through the static:

**ULTRAHUMAN ASSETS IN EXCLUSION ZONE: 1**

It was an administrative category, devised for any living individual who could
exceed a strategic weapon's force and remain capable of choosing where it
fell. Earth had other wonders, other dangers. It had only one entry in that
particular box.

The crown made Solstice a queen. It had never made her ultrahuman.

Solstice had ordered every conventional battery and aircraft beyond the
eastern ridge. If they stayed, they would die. If they fired, they would only
make her divide her attention between interception and rescue.

So the bay was empty when night split twenty kilometers above it.

The rupture appeared as a black seam across the stars. Its edges bent
cloudlight inward. Then folding vanes caught the moon, and eight perfect wedges
descended through the seam.

The public instruments returned noise. Solstice's royal hearing returned mass,
position, and the cold pulse of a coordination mesh linking every nonliving
shell.

One hundred thirty-one thousand seventy-two frames.

Eight wedges. Sixteen thousand three hundred eighty-four in each. Two aimed
toward the sea shelf, two toward the breakwaters, four toward the eastern ridge
and the inhabited dark beyond.

All twelve orbiting chimes answered her shock with clear notes. The central
resonator gave a deeper thrum against her heart.

Thirteen tones intact.

"I am Solstice Evening Bell," she told the descending host. Her voice could
not cross twenty kilometers of air, but sovereignty had never required an
audience. "First Monarch. Queen of all magical girls. Earth's only
ultrahuman."

She raised both hands.

At her coronation, the independent circles had argued for eleven days before
permitting one of their own to command the rest. There had never been a monarch
before her, and no successor after the circles faded. On the twelfth morning,
the twelve donors had settled what command would cost them. The compact they
forged had ended with the clause none of them wanted to imagine using: *What
the crown joins, the monarch may release.*

Succession, they had called it.

Abdication, Solstice had privately understood.

*Use us,* the maker of the smallest chime had told her. *Do not make a shrine.*

She gathered the twelve chimes into four vertical lines and felt their
frequencies pull through her bones. The full chord would expose its pattern.
Anything that survived would know the shape of her strength.

But the wedges were still rigid. Still synchronized. They would never be this
vulnerable again.

She struck.

The chord did not sound through air. It arrived inside the formation.

For one white instant, every vane in the western sky showed its edges.
Resonance passed from frame to frame along the mesh that held their descent
exact. The leading quarter of each wedge folded inward. Thirty-two thousand
seven hundred sixty-eight shells came apart in sheets of dark metal and blue
sparks, spilling beneath the survivors like eight black waterfalls.

The pressure hit Solstice a heartbeat later. Her dress snapped around her legs.
Blood warmed one nostril. The central resonator slammed against her sternum
hard enough to bruise.

Royal hearing counted again.

Ninety-eight thousand three hundred four remained.

The eight wedges dissolved.

Schools of sixty-four scattered in spirals, each one offset from the others.
The same mesh pulse raced through them carrying a model of her chord: phase,
interval, delay. Solstice sounded the full chord a second time and watched the
schools flex around its nodes. Fewer than a hundred frames broke.

Then every surviving shell turned toward her chimes.

Needles silvered the night.

Solstice flung six chimes upward and six down. Between paired notes she drew
edict planes—thin surfaces of destructive resonance, invisible except where
rain or metal crossed them. She bell-stepped along a sounding line an instant
before the needles reached her. The step could not curve. She arrived beside
the uppermost chime with her shoulder already turned, and a needle scored heat
across her pauldron.

Schools pursued. Good.

She dropped three chimes toward the cloud deck and held three below the
rupture. The first edict plane slanted north to south between them. It could
not chase anything. It did not need to. Solstice flashed across its western
edge, let the schools correct toward her, then stepped away.

Four thousand shells crossed the plane and separated at the waist in showers
of sparks.

The next schools braked. Others flowed around both ends.

She rotated the upper pair, narrowing the open air into a corridor. The host
divided again, a hundred choices made as one. Some schools fired at her. Some
fired at the chimes. Some stopped descending altogether and spread toward the
stars, forcing her either to abandon them or widen the trap until the ridge
routes opened.

She could not hunt ninety thousand targets.

She could make the sky smaller.

Solstice bell-stepped from the rupture's southern edge to the cloud deck, every
transit a straight stroke of light. She placed planes like walls in a
descending maze, their gaps angled toward the bay's center. Frames that dodged
one met another. Frames that slowed were pressed from behind by schools still
committed to landing.

The mesh learned each plane after contact. It learned where not to be. That
knowledge made its next turn predictable.

Solstice herded it downward.

A needle volley struck one of the lowest chimes. Hairline cracks raced across
its silver surface. The note wavered, and the edict plane between it and its
partner began to fray. Through that widening seam lay the southern breakwater.

She could save the tone and lose the corridor.

"No," she said, though the refusal hurt before the command did.

She burned it.

Power overloaded the cracked chime. Its edict expanded from a hair-thin plane
into a blade a kilometer wide. Frames crossing the seam flashed dark. The
woman who had laughed before every charge became a kilometer of white
judgment. Then the chime shattered, and her final spell vanished from
Solstice's royal hearing.

It did not become silence. It became an absence shaped like a hot iron driven
through her skull.

The woman had died once, willingly, centuries ago. Solstice had not killed her
again. But until this moment, something she had made still rang in the world.
Now it never would.

The fragments fell toward the southern breakwater, still holding the residue
she had poured into them.

Eleven orbiting tones remained, and the central one.

The host sent schools toward the unguarded northern end. Solstice collapsed two
planes, threw their chimes across the bay, and made a new corridor before the
leading frames cleared the cloud. Needles followed the moving points. One
chime burst under impact; she burned its tone in the instant before it failed,
widening the northern plane. Its remnants tumbled toward the opposite
breakwater.

Ten orbiting.

A third was caught between colliding shells. Solstice overloaded it too. The
resulting edict cut downward through the center of the host, and the molten
pieces fell toward the shallow sea shelf between the two breakwaters.

The second lost spell had belonged to the woman who always burned her tongue
on tea. The third came from someone who had hidden shaking hands inside her
sleeves on coronation night and volunteered anyway.

Nine orbiting. The pain was no longer three separate wounds. It was a
three-pronged vacancy inside every sound she made. The women remained
themselves—in Solstice's memory and in whatever waited after death. Their last
works did not.

The battle descended to the tropopause. Below waited an autumn storm, its wet
black towers shouldering east from the bay. Solstice held the last corridors
until the schools had compressed themselves between the fixed rupture above
and the clouds below.

Then she closed the planes.

Broken frames sheeted against the storm tops. Others struck their own wreckage.
The mesh screamed in pulses too fast for any ordinary receiver to separate,
and royal hearing counted through the noise.

Forty-nine thousand one hundred fifty-two remained.

Exactly half the host's survivors had been destroyed since the opening chord.

The next mesh pulse did not route around an edict plane.

It marked every intact chime.

The host had found her treasury.

It saw finite hardware. Solstice saw nine promises.

Needles came not in volleys now but continuous silver rivers. Schools
sacrificed themselves against planes so the following schools could measure
the instant each frequency loaded. Others rammed the chimes directly. The
crown showed them what queenship had taught Solstice to hide from everyone
else: her power was enormous, and finite.

She dropped into the storm.

Rain struck her face like thrown gravel. Lightning turned tens of thousands of
folding vanes into a white, revolving ceiling. The weather did not obey her.
It obeyed pressure, heat, gravity—old laws that asked no one's permission—and
that made it useful.

Solstice placed a chime inside an updraft and another beneath it. The edict
between them lay flat. She stepped above the plane. Schools plunged after her,
heavy with rain, then hit the rising air and lost the fraction of alignment
their mesh expected. They crossed the plane out of sequence. Rows of frames
broke and vanished into cloud.

False pulses struck her royal hearing: phantom masses to the north, an opening
toward the shelf, a feigned collapse over the ridge. She answered the first
and bell-stepped into a collision attack.

A frame hit her ribs at flight speed.

Her armor took the edge from it. Nothing took the force. She spun through rain,
caught one sharp shoulder of metal, and drove the shell through an edict plane.
It split in a blue flare. Three more hit her before she reached the next chime.
Something in her side gave with a deep, nauseating click.

She could not tell which masses were real.

She could still tell which roads led east.

Solstice abandoned pursuit. She set every remaining plane across a landing
vector and let gravity make the host choose. To preserve a chime was to leave
one road open. To close a road was to expose the chime holding it.

She burned the fourth tone above the northern shelf. Its fragments fell into
the whitecaps. Its maker had stained every glove she owned with violet ink.

She burned the fifth over the bay mouth, and the expanded edict forced six
thousand frames into the storm's strongest downdraft. That spell's maker had
repaired every torn glove with a different color of thread and called matching
them wasteful.

She burned the sixth halfway to the ridge. The frequency tore out of her nerves
with a burst of red behind her eyes. For a moment she could not feel her left
hand. The sixth woman had looked directly at death on coronation night and
refused to call it beautiful.

Six orbiting chimes remained.

The host folded into needle-thin files, too narrow for the broad corridors.
Solstice crossed two chimes, made a vertical plane, and bell-stepped behind the
files. They turned toward her. Rain and gravity carried their maneuver wide.

She burned the seventh and cut off their recovery.

The seventh spell had come from the woman who argued against monarchy for ten
of the circles' eleven days, then volunteered before anyone else.

Five orbiting.

Two thousand collision shells came at the upper chimes from opposite sides.
Solstice sent both points diving, straight paths converging above the bay. At
the last instant she stepped between them, crossed her arms, and burned the
eighth tone. Its edict caught the collision shells and the schools beneath.
Metal thundered into the sea.

The eighth woman's remembered off-key marching song stopped threading the
crown. Solstice's own memory of it remained. The world would never hear the
spell sing it again.

Four orbiting.

Her landing was a fall. She struck one knee against a frame's back, shattered
it with the force at her heel, and pushed off before the needles arrived. A
projectile passed through the loose fabric above her hip and scored a line of
fire across her skin.

The mesh threw another false mass at her hearing. She ignored it.

The real host had begun synchronizing below the storm. Not into wedges; it had
learned better. Into landing columns, each thin enough to dodge until the final
descent.

Solstice placed her last four orbiting tones around the storm's eastern wall.
She held one in reserve near the northern breakwater—the reign after this
battle, a path out if the others failed.

The ridge route opened beneath it.

Frames poured through.

She saw, with awful clarity, what she had been protecting: not the donors'
choice, but her own need never to become the woman who destroyed their work.
Every route she left open carried the host toward the people that work had
been made to protect.

*Use us. Do not make a shrine.*

Solstice burned the reserved tone.

The ninth great edict sealed the ridge route. Fragments curved east, completing
more of the broken silver arc that now stretched from the northern breakwater,
across the sea shelf, toward the southern wall.

The smallest chime was gone. The pressure of its maker's fingers remained in
Solstice's hand.

Three orbiting chimes remained. Their lines made a triangle, not a lattice.
Three straight bell-steps. Three edict planes. No redundancy.

Royal hearing counted the host as it dropped below the storm.

Eight thousand one hundred ninety-two.

Eight columns of one thousand twenty-four.

Two drove for the sea shelf. Two aligned on the breakwaters. Four arrowed
toward separate points along the eastern ridge.

Solstice dropped her triangle over the bay.

The first shelf column crossed the northern plane. She burned one endpoint.
The edict widened and destroyed the column from front to rear. Before the chime
finished breaking, the second shelf column crossed the other plane sharing
that point. The widening edge took it too.

Two thousand forty-eight frames went dark. The chime's fragments rained into
the northern shallows.

The tenth spell had belonged to a woman who carried sugar for stray animals in
the pockets of her battle coat. Solstice remembered finding the grains there
after the woman was gone.

Two orbiting tones remained. One line. Solstice bell-stepped along it toward
the northern breakwater while the third column fired upward. Needles struck the
water behind her in a racing white stitch.

She arrived inside the column.

At close range the frames were all folded vanes and featureless armor,
nonliving machines correcting around her faster than bodies could think. She
drove both hands apart. The edict plane snapped open between the final pair of
chimes. The column's lower ranks crossed it under the weight of those above.

Solstice burned the next tone.

The plane flared through the entire column. The chime shattered southward. Its
frequency left her with a convulsion that nearly pitched her into the harbor.

One thousand twenty-four more frames broke against the northern breakwater.

The eleventh woman had steadied the silver mold with both hands while her own
transformation consumed her. She had been crying. She had never once tried to
hide it.

The fourth column was already descending on the southern one. Solstice had two
sounding chimes for less than a second: the last intact one and the one
disintegrating above her. She stepped that dying line.

She came out sideways, ribs screaming, and jammed her shoulder against the
intact chime. The last plane formed between its note and the fading note behind
her. It trembled across the southern breakwater.

The column crossed.

She burned the last orbiting tone.

The edict widened. The fourth column became a storm of dark shells tumbling
into concrete and foam. At the same instant, three of the eastern columns
veered away from the plane's far edge. Their frames remained intact, but their
landing geometry collapsed; they could no longer establish separate ridge
anchors. The mesh folded them sideways toward the eighth column and the
breakwaters.

The chime burst at the southern end of the silver arc. Royal hearing vanished.
Its final count remained branded behind Solstice's eyes.

The twelfth woman's spell left no sound behind at all. Solstice remembered her
answering the final consent question: *Yes. Entirely. Do not soften it for me.*

Four thousand ninety-six frames remained.

One intact column formed the core. Three columns, crippled as independent
formations, spread around it as escorts. Together they reached the breakwaters
and locked vanes, shell to shell, building a mesh lattice across the bay mouth.

Above them, the rupture widened.

The lattice was stabilizing it.

Solstice fell onto the southern breakwater hard enough to crack concrete. She
tried to stand and one leg folded. There were no chimes to step toward, no
paired tones for an edict. The central resonator could still armor her retreat.
Given time, it could shape smaller blows.

Her own force still moved under her skin, vast and difficult and alive. That
was what the hazard bureaus classified. The crown had given it twelve kinds of
precision. Breaking the resonator would not make her less than ultrahuman.

It could not destroy four thousand ninety-six synchronized frames before the
next wave arrived.

Synchronized.

The mesh had adapted to every frequency she had shown it. It had made itself a
perfect conductor for her crown.

And from the northern breakwater to the sea shelf to the concrete beneath her,
twelve trails of burnt silver formed an arc. Each broken chime was dead
equipment, incapable of calling power, but each still held a dying residue of
the final spell its maker had freely placed there, awakened and spent through
Solstice's living force. The invasion lattice crossed that arc in a thousand
places.

The crown had joined them.

Solstice knelt at its open southern end. Her living body, neurally bound to the
central resonator, was the final point that could close the circuit.

Solstice pressed her palm to the central resonator. She remembered the circles
at her coronation, each afraid that a monarch would mean surrendering their
power to one will. She remembered the twelve women standing around the silver
mold: frightened, particular, unanimous. None had asked to be preserved. Each
had asked that her last work reach the day when no single magical girl could
win alone.

She remembered promising that the crown would never own what they entrusted to
it.

*What the crown joins, the monarch may release.*

She had mistaken custody for keeping.

The clause was not permission to discard them. It was an obligation to let
their choices finish.

"You were never mine to keep," said the First Monarch. "Earth does not belong
to its savior."

She closed her hand.

The central resonator cracked.

Every missing frequency returned at once—not healed, not restored, but
released in destructive inverse. The full chord had moved outward from
Solstice in harmony. This went inward through every connection the crown had
made: her nerves, the burnt chimes, the mesh lattice, the four thousand
ninety-six frames bound to it, the low-latency signal reaching back through the
rupture.

No soul returned. No dead woman was summoned or spent again. Only the last
residue of twelve freely made spells answered Solstice's living will, and in
answering, ended.

The bay turned soundless and white.

Frames went dark from south to north. Folding vanes locked. The lattice
collapsed into the water. The inverse chord ran upward through the column's
signal, a black fracture racing across the rupture from both ends.

The seam closed.

Four thousand ninety-six became zero.

Solstice felt the central tone tear free.

Then she heard only surf, falling metal, and her own raw breath. Beneath the
breath, her raw power remained: immense, unharmonized, hers.

Dawn found her sitting against the southern breakwater. The eastern ridge was
intact. No columns stood on it. No second wave crossed the ordinary paling sky.

For the first time in centuries, Solstice could not count everything
approaching her.

The uncertainty frightened her.

It also belonged to everyone.

Across the empty harbor road, the public hazard board cleared its static. It
measured the force still gathered inside the woman on the breakwater and
restated its administrative truth.

**ULTRAHUMAN ASSETS IN EXCLUSION ZONE: 1**

The crown had made her exact enough to cut an army into countable pieces. It
had never supplied the force or the will that put her in that category.

Solstice touched the cracked hollow over her sternum. The twelve lost tones did
not answer. None ever would.

The women themselves had never been inside the chimes. Their last works had,
and those works were gone now in the purpose for which they had been given.
Solstice remembered every one of them.

She was still Solstice Evening Bell. Still the queen of all magical girls,
though history had left her no living subjects. Still First Monarch because she
had not kept their crown past its need.

Still Earth's only ultrahuman.

The next impossible thing would meet her without their voices.

stories.title: The City of Eleven Foundations
stories.prompt: There is a city that is architecturally colorful. It is divided by districts, and each district has its own style, like Gothic, Chinese, Egyptian, Greek, steampunk, cyberpunk, biopunk, dieselpunk, raypunk, solarpunk, and more. Notes: The story should focus on the city architecturally not the people or culture;
stories.body:
# The City of Eleven Foundations

The rain reached the receiving cisterns as dust.

For weeks, heat had bleached the solarpunk terrace's white ceramic walks and tightened the soil beneath its planted roofs. The linked reservoirs stood low enough for bottom floats to show through gauge glass. The terrace sat below the biopunk filter outlet and above the river works. First drops ticked on photovoltaic-blue canopies. Leaves and pale gravel detained those beads, but the cloud over the basin had turned noon light the color of slate.

Across the basin, eleven districts descended in wedges toward a river. Color sharpened wherever one foundation met another. Warm gold stopped at pearl enamel. Sea-glass teal ended against soot-black steel. Oxide red faced verdigris copper across a service alley. Ochre sandstone met pale limestone along a joint too narrow to hold a fallen coin. Blue-violet roofs crowded close to green and amber glazed tile without sharing a gutter. At the low center, board-marked concrete carried red, yellow, and cobalt bands down broad ramps to flood doors that had not opened in years.

Water began to disclose what color concealed.

Higher on another wedge, it ran onto layered eaves, then down chains into dry plinth channels beneath vermilion timber columns. The halls there stood above linked courtyards on dressed stone. Their mortise-and-tenon frames bore weight through dense sets of interlocking brackets under the eaves; their lower screens rested in grooves from which they could be lifted. Runoff crossed the first court, dropped a shallow step, and vanished into a radial drain.

On the basin's high shoulder, rain darkened old silt stripes in Egyptian settling basins. The steps rose between battered sandstone walls whose inward slopes thickened toward their foundations. Empty water marks showed how grit had once descended from terrace to terrace before reaching the lapis-and-turquoise channels below. A second radial drain carried the new brown trickle beneath them.

Below those basins, rain glossed Greek stoas, following their slight fall. Blue-green channels ended behind stylobate plugs. Beyond, Gothic gargoyles fed grilles over deep cisterns beneath colored glass. At the marked working level, a low throat crossed each downhill wall into a dry masonry channel ending above the biopunk beds. Flying buttresses stepped across gravel-footed lanes.

Elsewhere the storm struck newer surfaces harder. It drummed on copper boiler courts, flowed past brass gauges, and pattered through pipe galleries above reciprocating lift pumps. Their intake descended to the central undercroft; their discharge ended at the high Egyptian basins. Rain slicked the painted-over teeth of a disused coupling where the copper district touched the steel sheds below. Beyond that joint, an elevated compression engine turned a black flywheel, driving a discharge pump nearer the river.

Rain made cyan and magenta pressure strips shine against matte composite walls. Those passive bands followed sealed utility conduits into the cyberpunk foundation, then disappeared under a district of grown cellulose ribs and leaf-green membranes. There, root rafts filled cavities between soil and structure. Dry reed galleries and cream-colored fungal beds waited above the ordinary watercourse, their outlet lip sloping toward the solarpunk cistern mouths below. Moisture thickened the outer fibers of the roots, as moisture always did.

A pneumatic carrier passed through a raypunk freight tube with a diminishing rush. The lower shutters clapped closed behind it. High above pearl canopies, pressure-balancing shafts exhaled through amber fins. At the center, the brutalist court remained almost dry beneath its coffered roof. Its undercroft lay empty behind flood doors, a low gray volume held between shear walls and caissons driven deeper than the foundations around it.

Beneath all eleven districts, the radial drains entered one service ring. At each border, a high-water float actuated a linkage that dropped a bulkhead closed; the gate had to lift to reopen. The bulkheads had protected foundations from small backflows, pipe fires, and neighboring spills. On maintenance plates beside them, worn tool arcs ended at cleanly painted boundary lines.

Then the cloudburst covered both the city and the short valley upstream. The separate trickles became eleven loads delivered to the same buried ring.

* * *

At the river, branches came down broadside in the surge. They tangled against the dieselpunk outfall screen, caught roof grit, reeds, and a rolling burden of silt, and flattened into a dense mat. The check gate swung inward against its stop.

It had closed correctly. That correctness sealed the only low exit from the city.

The discharge pump pulled against the blocked mouth. Its housing shook, first with a full mechanical beat and then with the dry rattle of cavities forming where water should have filled the impeller. The outlet gauge stopped rising. Above it, the engine continued to drive the flywheel while no water passed the shut gate.

Rain still entered from every slope.

In the buried service ring, the first high-water float rose until its linkage dropped a sector bulkhead. Iron met its sill with a concussion carried through concrete. Backflow stopped at that border. The next pulse, denied the volume beyond, climbed higher in the adjoining compartment. A second float rose. Another gate fell. Closures traveled around the basin—not together, but according to eleven different rates of runoff.

The ring lost its equal waterline. It became a necklace of sealed chambers, some holding air above a rising surface, some already running full. Every incoming drain added height to one compartment and force against the gates on either side.

In the cyberpunk wedge, cyan pressure strips brightened beside the sealed service floors. Magenta followed, lengthening upward along the utility risers as pressure bowed membranes behind them. The light came from compression changing the strips’ physical response; it interpreted nothing. Yet it made the hidden condition plain. The outfall gauge at the river remained fixed while, farther and farther uphill, colored bands showed a head of water still rising.

The first boundary had been protected. The shared foundation had been divided into eleven pressure vessels.

* * *

The matte composite foundation absorbed almost nothing. Waterproof faces turned the trapped surge sideways until it found the annular gap around a utility sleeve. Water knifed through that small opening and entered the softer ground beneath the biopunk district.

The root rafts were built to spread ordinary rain. They took water into layered fibers, thickened, and pressed more firmly into the soil that supported the grown ribs above. In a season of measured flow, that swelling closed erosion paths. Under the sudden buried surge, it narrowed the only remaining throat. Fine roots packed against the utility sleeve. The water behind them rose faster.

One cyan strip became solid light. A magenta length reached the underside of a cantilevered block.

Pressure worked past the root mass through gravel seams and struck the Egyptian foundation broadside. The battered walls carried the lateral push into their thicker bases. The stone yielded so little that the force changed direction. Muddy water spread along the base, searching, until it found the prepared sand and rubble beneath the neighboring Greek stylobate.

The first effect in the Greek court was dry.

A thread of white dust spilled from the edge of one column base. The open rills held only rainwater, but the saturated bed below had begun to lose its even bearing. Pressure raised one end of a paving slab by the thickness of a leaf. The next slab stayed down. Along the stoa, a line of pale columns that had been straight enough to vanish in perspective now showed one broken interval.

Another bulkhead fell beneath the central court.

The closure sent a blunt pulse backward. Greek drain plugs shivered in their sockets. The Egyptian mass held, the swollen roots tightened, and the sealed composite walls admitted nothing. Each sound foundation passed the excess to a joint less able to refuse it.

The shifted column remained standing. Its misalignment was nevertheless the first wound the storm wrote above ground, in a court whose own floor was scarcely wet.

* * *

The next pulse crossed beneath the Greek compartment and tore gravel from around the nearest Gothic buttress feet. The narrow lanes filled at their edges as gargoyles poured through the rain. Below the grilles, the vaulted cisterns still had room; the closed sector gate kept the foundation pressure from reaching them. They could accept falling water from roofs but not the trapped water lifting from beneath.

One buttress settled outward. The stone moved less than a finger’s width, but the movement altered the lateral thrust it had been built to carry. Inside the tall hall, a blue pane threw its reflection at an angle across the black floor. Violet light narrowed along one rib and widened along the next.

At the Chinese-derived halls, the same ground movement traveled differently. One stone plinth dipped as fines washed from beneath it. A vermilion column descended with the plinth; its tenoned beam shifted within the joint instead of splitting, and the layered dougong above redistributed the small change beneath the wide eave. Green glazed tiles chattered, settled, and held their overlapping courses.

The timber frame had room to accommodate motion. The soil did not. Brown water appeared at the lower edge of a dry plinth channel and carried pale grains into the stepped courtyard. A screen bowed where its sill no longer sat level. The primary columns remained vertical enough to bear, while the foundation continued to lose material.

Across the basin, capacities stood isolated from the loads they might have relieved. Water entered the steampunk boiler court above the hubs. It hissed against iron doors, drowned the lower fireboxes, and quenched the pressure that should have powered the reciprocating pumps. Their rods stopped at uneven heights. Brass gauge needles sank.

The diesel engine remained dry on its elevated frame. It could supply torque, but its shaft still drove the useless discharge pump at the blocked outfall. Between the two districts, the old coupling teeth were hidden under several skins of green and red paint.

In the raypunk district, compressed air had nowhere to go. Water entered the lower ring while the freight-tube shutters remained closed above it. Each rising pulse squeezed a pocket of air into a shorter length. When the pocket rebounded, the shock struck pipe brackets and bulkhead faces. Glass-block towers trembled in their mortar. High pressure shafts, built to vent the freight system, stood cut off from the ring by those lower shutters.

The central undercroft remained empty. Its flood doors divided the rising ring from enough gray volume to blunt the peak, but their locking pins were still seated. Along the descending surface route, the solarpunk cistern gauges still showed unused depth above the river works. Rain collected slowly in planted terraces, detained among stems and gravel, while the low city filled faster beneath the ground.

Occupation withdrew along the slope. Lifts stopped with their cars above the lowest landings. Fire doors stood propped along upward routes. Laundry lines emptied; carts and benches disappeared from courts; loose screens were taken from the paths of water. Window light went dark first beside the river, then in climbing rows. Chalk marks appeared above wet thresholds. Tool chests stood open at service hatches, their contents no longer arranged.

No crowd remained in the architecture’s lowest rooms, but evacuation changed no load below them.

At three places, the danger was visible. Colored glass remained skewed above the scoured Gothic footing. The Greek column line broke the eye at its displaced base. Under the brutalist court, cobalt and yellow paving bands rose in a shallow ridge over the crown of the service ring.

The ridge climbed with the next hammer stroke.

* * *

Keeping the sector gates closed would preserve dry galleries, polished floors, and the empty central undercroft for a little longer. It would also keep every rising compartment narrow enough to tear at its neighbors. If the ring crown split, pressurized water would scour outward below all eleven foundations, beyond the reach of any open court or settling stair.

The alternative could be read in the city’s levels.

The undercroft lay below the ring crown behind doors designed to flood. Raypunk shafts rose above every expected waterline. The diesel flywheel aligned with the steampunk pump shafts. Egyptian basins received the route's only lifted water. Greek floors fell into Gothic cisterns and Chinese-derived courtyards along separate branches. Below their reunion, the biopunk outlet stood above the solarpunk receiving cisterns; both remained above the river works. The reservoirs had capacity because their terraces were still delaying the rain.

The route existed, but only as disconnected fragments. Connecting it would put river mud into the central undercroft, silt onto ochre stone, water across white plaster, a dark line on basalt, and pressure against timber screens. It would load reeds and fungi with every fine particle the settling steps missed. It would exchange the possibility of pristine interiors for certain damage.

The first changed object was a broken warning seal beside the brutalist flood doors.

Locking pins came out of their sockets and appeared stacked on a ramp above the rising ridge. A wet wrench lay across a gate housing. Lower freight shutters stood open beneath the raypunk tubes, their release handles left down. The painted skins over the border coupling had been cut away, exposing toothed steel. At the Greek stoas, stylobate plugs rested on folded cloth. Gothic cistern grilles leaned against walls. The lowest timber screens had been lifted from their grooves where they could be saved; others, already bound by the shifted plinths, remained in place. Spill panels between the stepped courts stood propped open.

These were not automatic responses. The floats had closed the gates. The new arrangement bore the marks of tools and many passages through the rain.

The cobalt ridge rose again. A paving joint opened and released a thin line of brown foam.

Then the central flood doors swung inward, and the first sector bulkhead began to lift.

* * *

The brutalist undercroft took the released surge.

Water struck its back wall hard enough to climb the board marks, then spread across the broad floor. The empty volume converted height into width. Shear walls received the first lateral blow; deep caissons carried the shifting load below the softened surface layers. Mud covered the lowest red wayfinding band. A maintenance cabinet tore loose and lodged against a ramp, but the ring crown stopped rising.

The release also drove trapped air ahead of it. With the lower raypunk shutters open, compressed air entered the freight tubes and climbed the pressure-balancing shafts. Glass blocks fogged from within. Air burst above the flood line through amber fins, shaking rain from the parabolic canopies. One last hammer stroke rang through the lower brackets. Then the pockets had an upward path, and the following pressure arrived as a long push rather than a blow.

At the industrial border, the diesel engine changed work. The shaft to the blocked discharge pump had been disengaged; oily teeth stood motionless over the jammed outfall line. Across the service alley, the exposed coupling joined the black flywheel to the steampunk transmission. There was no elegance in the fit. Old tooth faces struck, slipped, caught, and shed flakes of paint. Dark iron rods began moving in the flooded copper pump house.

The reciprocating lift pumps drew mud-heavy water from the buffered undercroft. With every stroke, valves opened and shut in physical sequence. The dry engine labored under the added load. Its orange flywheel mark slowed enough to become a succession of arcs. In the copper district, drowned boilers stayed cold while pump rods rose under borrowed torque.

The pumps' sole lifted discharge reached the high Egyptian basins with the force of a broken gutter. It hit the upper step, threw brown water against turquoise faience, and spread between the battered walls. Those walls took the new lateral load through their thickened bases. At each drop, the current broadened and slowed. Branch grit accumulated first; coarse sand followed in crescent bars. The water crossing the lowest ochre lip remained cloudy, but it no longer carried stones large enough to scar a pump valve or jam an open rill.

Pressure strips still burned solid in three cyberpunk service levels. Rain continued entering the ring faster than the first pump strokes lifted it. In the brutalist undercroft, mud reached the yellow band.

From that high settling head, clarified overflow descended across the Greek border. The removed stylobate plugs had exposed the ends of two channels. Water entered the subtle grades of the stoas and divided, half curving toward the Gothic lanes, half toward the timber-framed courtyards. The split reduced the thrust on the already displaced paving. White plaster darkened along both rills. At the shifted column, water passed on either side instead of striking the weakened base. Its broken perspective did not worsen.

The first branch descended through the Gothic gargoyle channels and poured through open grilles into deep cisterns. Vaulted chambers stored the leading surge, transferring its weight rib by rib into piers. Basalt lower courses acquired a black-brown tide line. As the water rose, pressure beneath the scoured buttress compartment fell. At the marked working level, the branch entered the low throat in the downhill wall, passed through a falling masonry channel, and emerged above the biopunk beds. The blue pane’s reflection crept closer to its old angle.

The second branch crossed raised stone plinths through the opened channels of the Chinese-derived district. It dropped from one courtyard to the next under deep layered eaves. The flow found a lower screen trapped in its warped groove, bowed the lattice, and broke it free. Timber fragments traveled only as far as the next stone sill. Above, mortise-and-tenon joints admitted small rotations without surrendering the beam ends, while dougong sets spread altered roof loads across adjacent columns. Water stained the plinths. Green and amber tiles continued shedding new rain into the same controlled path. The frame kept its primary geometry while accepting the loss of what had been made to yield first.

At the beds, Gothic masonry outflow met the Chinese-derived courtyard branch. Reed stems bent flat under the initial flow and rose partway when it passed. Root mats that had constricted the buried surge now held the opened soil along the surface route. Water spread through cream fungal layers and permeable membranes. Fine silt lodged among fibers; the beds darkened from leaf green to wet umber. Their pores narrowed as material accumulated. The lift pumps had to slow, or the water would overtop them before filtration could occur.

The diesel flywheel lost another measure of speed. Mud climbed above the yellow band in the central undercroft. Along the cyberpunk foundations, magenta pressure remained high beside two sealed utility sleeves. The whole sequence balanced on rates that no single district could absorb.

But the raypunk shafts continued venting, so the slower strokes did not trap another hammer. The undercroft continued spreading each pulse. Grit kept settling on the Egyptian stairs. The two Greek grades kept flow away from the shifted column. The Gothic vaults and stepped timber courts gave the filters time by storing and stretching their branches.

At last, water emerged from the biopunk beds with only a pale haze. It crossed the outlet lip and descended through open receiving lines. The first solarpunk cistern received it below its lowest gauge mark. Linked reservoirs passed the rise from one white ceramic chamber to the next. Overhead, planted terraces were only then beginning to release their detained roof water. Their delay left room for the filtered flood descending from above.

One cyan pressure strip shortened by the width of a slab.

Then another did.

Sector by sector, the buried head fell. Magenta retreated from the cantilevered service floors. Waterlines met across the raised bulkheads instead of battering them from opposite heights. In the brutalist court, the brown foam at the lifted paving joint thinned and stopped. The ring crown held beneath the ridge.

The Gothic buttress did not return to its former bed, but it ceased moving. Colored light steadied on the wet floor. The Greek column stayed fractionally out of line, fixed now against a level that no longer changed. Through the timber halls, the chatter of glazed tile became only the sound of rain.

On the receiving terrace, cistern gauges rose into their clear tubes.

* * *

The river took longer to fall than the rain. When its surface finally dropped below the outlet mouth, the check gate eased from its stop. The branch-and-silt mat remained packed over the screen, now reachable from the bank but not yet cleared. Nothing about that delayed repair had saved the city. Survival already showed in the route of the mud.

It striped the brutalist undercroft to the height of the yellow band. It filled corners behind the shear walls and dried in the board marks. The Egyptian basins held bars of grit on every step. White stoa floors carried brown edges. Gothic basalt kept a tide line below the colored glass. Several timber screens were missing, and one stone plinth waited above a void to be packed and pinned. The biopunk reed beds lay bent beneath the silt they had caught. Their living fibers would grow or fail according to ordinary light, water, and repair; the clogged sections were cut out and replanted.

Repairs did not erase the storm’s diagram. The Greek column base was reset, but a narrow bronze line marked its displaced position. New grilles over the Gothic cisterns could be lifted without breaking paving. The courtyard spill panels were rehung above fresh stone channels. At the industrial border, the coupling remained bare and accessible under a jointed cover instead of paint. The raypunk shutters acquired external release bars. In the service ring, bulkheads were reset to rest raised over low equalization slots until high-water floats actuated and dropped them closed.

Most visible were the seams across the borders. Narrow spillways interrupted colored bands without smearing them together. Cobalt concrete still met sea-glass enamel cleanly. Ochre stone still ended at pale limestone. Vermilion timber still rose above its own gray plinths, distinct from the black basalt beyond. Only the routes for shared pressure crossed.

Shutters reopened downslope. Ventilation stirred damp curtains behind windows. Lift rails shone with new oil. Fresh footprints passed through the drying Greek court, vanished on dark stone, and appeared again as mud on a repaired plinth. Warm squares of light returned to the basin after sunset.

At one boundary, a thread of rain descended a green glazed tile, entered a newly cut channel in the raised stone, and crossed through a bronze-lined joint into the pale rill beside it. A small wet footprint overlaid the seam. The water kept both colors in its reflection as it moved on.

stories.title: The Weight of Falling Up
stories.prompt: You're an apprentice at a prestigious magic school! It's time for you to take your flying assessment, and take to the skies. Others choose brooms, levitation spells, or mounts. You show up with something a little different.
stories.body:
# The Weight of Falling Up

By the time Examiner Dovek called my name, three people had already left the roof. Two had chosen brooms, which was what sensible people at Nine Eaves usually did.

The first leaned low over a broom and cut around the western chimney in a polished brown arc. The second sat upright on another, rising at a measured angle while the lacquered handle stayed level beneath both hands. The third went past between the lifted wings of a pale horse, hands buried in its mane while each downstroke sent a warm gust rolling over the slates.

Two brooms were not a coincidence. Nine Eaves kept racks of practice models, broom-width gates, and enough standard diagrams to wallpaper a tower. The horse was rare enough to draw looks in the dining hall, but not questions on an assessment roof. Its lane was painted wider, its harness had already passed inspection, and everyone present knew what those wings could do.

Then there was me.

“Juni Wex,” Dovek called again.

“Present. Still regrettably attached to the building.”

The Collegium of Nine Eaves occupied most of the view below us: black roofs pitched at improbable angles, bridges stitching tower to tower, windows bright as chips of amber. Beyond it, the city fell away in terraces toward a silver bend of river. The launch roof was so high that birds passed beneath the gutters. Prestige, I had learned, was often ordinary terror with excellent masonry.

I sat on the warm slate and unlaced my shoes. Mine were scuffed brown leather, bought without enchantment, one still bearing a pale water mark from a badly judged fountain.

I pulled them off, set my stockinged feet on the roof, and turned the right shoe heel-up across my knee.

Dovek crouched opposite me. Their examination coat snapped once in the wind and settled. “Begin.”

The ink stylus came from my cuff. I pressed its blunt nib beside the heel and drew the first stroke in a curve around the back of the shoe. The second hooked across the underside toward the arch. The third doubled inward, a black curl aimed at the small hollow between them. It looked less like a word than an arrow teaching the wind where to leave.

Nothing happened. Ink was only ink until someone living asked more of it.

I cupped the shoe between both hands, breathed, and let warmth run out through my palms. The three lines drank it. For an instant, black deepened beyond black.

I drew the mirrored wind curl around the other heel and underside, charged it, and put both shoes back on. My fingers trembled at the laces. Apparently fear was mostly an audience with opinions.

Dovek tapped one gloved finger above the right-hand curl. “No crown.”

“I’m fond of steering.”

“And your stationary count?”

“Small bursts.”

I traced the shape I had omitted: a shallow cap with three points. “A crown spreads one heel’s wind beneath my center. It will check a fall and quiet a turn, but it cannot steer. Once I feed it power, one point burns away per breath. Three points, exactly three breaths, then the crown is gone and the narrow jet returns.”

“Can you interrupt it?”

“I can cut power, but the unused points burn out anyway. It cannot be restarted.”

“A limitation.”

“A feature with strict opinions about counting.”

“A limitation,” Dovek repeated. “You are required to remain inside the stationary boundary for a count of three. Demonstrate the limitation. Do not conceal it.”

The first broom candidate flashed past the far eave, coat streaming straight behind. Above, the second held almost motionless while the broom’s bristles trembled through corrections too small to see. The pale horse climbed through a patch of sun, every feather briefly edged in gold.

I imagined a wide, blunt plume roaring beneath me while I hung unable to turn, all three crown points visibly burning away. Effective, temporary, and about as elegant as being held aloft by an argument.

“Understood,” I said.

I did understand. I simply had no intention of doing it.

* * *

Dovek raised a hand.

I ran for the edge.

At the gutter, I jumped, pointed both soles down, and drove warmth through my legs.

The curls answered.

Two pale streams of wind tore from my heels. They snapped my coat against my back, flung grit from the gutter, and punched me upward so hard my stomach arrived a moment after the rest of me.

I made a sound that began as a scream and improved into laughter.

The shoes did not carry me. The ink did not decide where I went. I supplied the power; the curls narrowed it into two rushing jets; my feet aimed the result. With both soles turned toward the roof and the output matched, I climbed. When I swept my heels behind me, the streams bent backward and shoved me forward into the blue.

For three glorious seconds, everything worked.

Then I drove a shade too much power through my left leg. Its jet surged harder.

My left hip lifted. My right shoulder dropped. The western chimney tipped sideways in front of me as I rolled toward the weaker stream.

“Excellent,” I told the rapidly rotating school. “A view.”

I nearly answered by forcing more through both heels. Instead I eased my left leg and fed the right until the two pale currents matched. The roll slowed. I opened my arms, shifted my hips, and came level with enough dignity to fool anyone who had not seen the first half.

The course turned around a tall iron arch strung with blue streamers. The first broom candidate banked through it by leaning into the curved handle. The second rose in a straight, measured line, hands quiet on the grip. Higher still, the winged horse folded its wings for one clean heartbeat, then opened them and surged upward.

There are respectable ways to fly. I had watched them practiced from the lower courts for years: the long broom bank, the patient broom hover, the powerful bargain between a rider and a winged animal. They all looked as though the sky were a country one might enter with the correct papers.

I arrived with two handwritten winds shouting at my heels.

I angled both feet down and poured on a smooth, sustained rush. Bells chimed somewhere below, nine notes thrown loose among the roofs. The jets curled white around my ankles and streamed behind me in twisting ribbons. Every change began in my body: toes lowered for climb, heels swept back for speed, one ankle canted outward to carve the bank. The air struck my soles, seized my coat, watered my eyes. I did not feel weightless. I felt gloriously outvoted by my own momentum.

The blue streamers cracked beside my ears. The city wheeled below in slate and copper and green garden squares. My legs began to tremble from holding both channels even, but the strain had a rhythm: power, angle, answer; power, angle, answer.

At the top of the arch hung the high-course bell.

I pitched forward, let the paired streams drive me through a rising curve, and slapped the bell with my palm.

Its note burst out bright enough to shake my teeth.

The arch rushed past beneath me. I was still climbing and moving far too fast toward the next roofline.

I swung both heels ahead and gave a moderate reverse pulse.

Wind blasted forward across my soles. My speed eased. The jets rasped over the curls and carried a few black flecks away into the white stream.

I noticed. I also noticed that the course marker remained safely unstruck, which seemed the more flattering observation.

Below, Dovek wrote on the examination sheet. Naturally, I assumed it meant *astonishing, perhaps historic*.

The stationary boundary waited ahead.

* * *

It was a square of yellow ribbons stretched between four slender poles on neighboring roofs, enclosing a piece of perfectly good empty air. The second broom candidate already occupied it.

They sat upright in the center, the broom level beneath them. Its bound twigs made tiny, practiced corrections while Dovek counted from the launch roof below.

“One.”

The rider shifted one knee. The broom eased back half a handspan.

“Two.”

The bristles dipped and recovered. From a distance, the candidate might have been sitting on a bench.

“Three.”

They glided out with a small, satisfied turn.

I hovered outside the ribbons on a low sustained rush. My legs had opinions now. Both were unprintable.

The safe answer waited in my cuff. I could draw the three-point crown over one heel, feed it power, and let the broad plume spend its three breaths beneath my center. I would lose steering while it burned, but I would remain stable long enough for the count.

Instead, I entered the square and began firing alternating microbursts.

Left, right, left, right. Each gust lasted barely longer than a blink. My ankles chattered beneath me as I corrected every drift with another sharp pulse. If I moved quickly enough, I reasoned, I would appear almost still.

“One,” Dovek called.

A left burst nudged me toward the upper ribbon. I snapped the right heel down and inward. Its jet kicked me back, then too far. Black specks peppered the pale wind behind it.

The first broom candidate swept along the outer course. The second left the square on an easy level line. The pale horse crossed the sun above, the rider bent to its rhythm. All three were moving. Moving looked dignified.

“Two.”

I fired right, left, right in quick succession. Each ignition punched through my calf. The last correction spun me a quarter turn and produced a sound from my throat like a startled kettle.

I smiled toward Dovek. Dovek did not smile back.

The right curl was shedding more ink than the left. I favored that foot whenever I drifted, and the separate little starts were eating its edges. I twisted enough to glimpse the heel. A gray nick had appeared in the outer curve.

“Three.”

I lurched out of the square with my chest heaving. Behind me, the wind-traces knotted and unraveled in no pattern worth admitting to.

“Juni,” Dovek called.

I curved back toward the nearest eave. Dovek had crossed to its ridge, the examination sheet tucked under one arm. Their attention fixed on my right heel.

“Your outer channel is scouring.”

So much for altitude protecting a person’s secrets.

“It has another descent in it.”

“You may declare a repair pause. One-point deduction. Inspect both shoes, then continue.”

One point. A small price, if points were the only things being weighed. But the other candidates were clean silhouettes against the sky, and I was sweating hard enough to drown a modest insect. A repair on the ridge would make the runes look provisional. It would make them look like something I had drawn on ordinary leather that morning.

Which, inconveniently, they were.

The rooftop-survey roster closed today. I pictured a term copying elevations from other apprentices’ notebooks while they measured the world with their own eyes.

I raised my right heel and looked. The nick was pale, narrow, and entirely real.

“I can complete,” I said.

Dovek’s expression did not change, but their questions became precise when they were worried. “Have you measured how much line remains?”

“I have seen it.”

“That was not my question.”

I fed a thin stream through the right curl. It came half a beat late, ragged at one edge.

“It is enough.”

The words left a sour place behind my teeth.

Dovek held my gaze for another beat, then pointed toward the descending course and the white landing ring on the launch roof.

“Proceed.”

* * *

I proceeded too quickly.

Smooth, matched output would have worn the ink slowly. I managed several sensible seconds of it.

Then I saw the first broom candidate arrowing toward the landing roof below, and my good judgment, already bruised, developed a competitive fever.

I tipped my heels back and drove.

The paired jets lengthened into white cords. Roofs rose around me. Wind shoved hair into my mouth. I spat it out, rolled between two stone finials, and added a sharp right pulse to recover the line. The pale horse wheeled well above the course, kept to its familiar wider lane. The second broom glided toward the far landing mark with infuriating composure.

My own ring came into view: a white circle on dark slate, Dovek approaching along the ridge beside it. I was high and fast. I should have begun braking then, with both feet angled forward and a long, moderate reverse flow.

Instead I chased the lost seconds.

The ring widened below.

I swung both heels ahead and drove power through the curls.

The left jet roared forward.

The right gave one ragged cough. Reverse wind tore across the worn outer curve, lifted the last thread of black, and silenced it.

The left side of my body was shoved backward. The right kept carrying forward and down.

My right shoulder dropped. The city rolled over me. In one sickening instant I snapped into a rightward corkscrew.

I forced more power down both legs by instinct.

Only the left answered.

The surviving reverse jet hammered my left side farther back. The corkscrew tightened. Roof, sky, roof, sky—the world became a wheel with me badly nailed to its rim.

I tried again. More power. More spin.

The shoes had not betrayed me. The right curl had announced its wear in black dust and a gray break. Dovek had offered me time. I had spent both warnings to purchase the appearance of ease.

“Call your stop, Juni!” Dovek shouted.

One hand was raised at the roof’s edge, ready for my declared surrender.

I could call and fail cleanly. I would be alive, unqualified, and indoors for a term.

Or I could keep feeding the one jet I had because motion felt more useful than falling.

That was the trap. The left curl was obeying perfectly. Every desperate command made the imbalance worse.

There was no graceful way out.

That helped.

Grace was what had put me here.

I cut all power.

The left jet vanished. Nothing corrected me; nothing chose a safer line. The added torque stopped, but the spin remained, and gravity took the rest.

I fell.

* * *

Wind clawed tears from my eyes. The roofs below looked small enough to fit in a box.

I pulled my knees tight, not to slow the rotation but to bring the failed shoe within reach. The world became a smaller, faster wheel around one steady thing: the scuffed heel a handspan from my nose.

The outer curl had opened to bare brown leather.

I tore the stylus from my cuff.

With the shoe turning beside my face, I dragged the missing curve around the heel. The nib skated. I drew again, slower, following the surviving line under the shoe until wet black joined black.

The base curl was whole.

I could have powered it then and hoped two narrow jets would agree before I struck a roof. Hope had already submitted enough examination work for one morning.

Above the repaired curl, I drew a shallow cap.

One point.

The roofs spun through the corner of my sight.

Two.

The pale horse crossed the wheel of sky, wings spread wide.

Three.

The crown waited in fresh black ink.

Neither leather nor drawing knew I was falling. Neither could decide to help. I flattened my palm over the heel and sent my living warmth through every new line.

Then I extended the right leg beneath me and supplied power.

The crowned curl opened.

Instead of a narrow jet kicking from one heel, a broad pale plume curved inward and blossomed beneath my center. It had no aim beyond the shape I had drawn. It could not choose the roof or turn me toward it. It simply poured wide and steady while I held the power.

I took the first breath.

The first crown point flashed white and blew away. The broad wind pressed against my rotation from below. Roof and sky stopped striking past quite so fast. My corkscrew widened, shuddered, and began to flatten.

One.

I took the second breath.

The next point burned. The plume thickened around my falling body, opposing the drop without erasing it. My stomach rose against my ribs. I opened from the tuck and hauled my left heel into view.

Its curl was frayed nearly through.

Two.

I drew the third breath.

The last point brightened above my right heel.

I put the stylus to the left shoe. Around the outside curve, under the heel, into the channel. Quick but whole. My lungs strained to release the breath too soon. I held it long enough to press my thumb over the wet line and send warmth into the repair.

The left curl darkened.

The final crown point vanished.

Three.

The broad plume collapsed to a narrow right-hand stream. I cut it at once rather than let one-sided thrust start another turn. The crown was gone, its one use spent, but the repaired curl beneath it remained.

For one raw heartbeat I was falling between decisions.

Then I aimed both heels below me and fed them equal power.

Two clean streams struck the air.

My hips steadied between them. I canted both feet against what remained of the turn and let the matched thrust unwind it. Then I angled both soles together and climbed away from the roofs on a smooth white rush.

“Right rune wore through!” I shouted toward Dovek. My voice tore thin in the wind. “I saw the damage. I declined the repair.”

The admission sounded embarrassingly small.

It also sounded true.

I did not chase the time I had lost. I did not rattle through frantic corrections. I held both outputs low and even, let the wind show every adjustment, and took the long curve back toward the landing roof.

The first broom candidate circled wide of my path. The second watched from beyond the yellow square, broom almost level. The pale horse beat upward with the rider low against its neck.

And I flew.

Not like any of them. Not tidily. My renewed jets streamed behind Nine Eaves, wavering when my ankles tired and straightening when I trusted the balance between them. A crosswind shoved me; I tilted both soles and let the paired thrust answer. Speed pulled me forward; I eased power instead of hiding it beneath another burst.

The landing ring swelled below.

I began braking while it still looked too far away.

Both heels forward. Both curls fed gently.

The jets streamed ahead in two pale fans, pushing against my motion. Ink flecks lifted from them, but slowly now, without the violent black spray of the earlier brake. The force climbed through my ankles, knees, and hips. I let it.

The roof rose.

I turned both soles down for one last soft rush, cut power, and dropped the final handspan onto slate.

Both ordinary shoes landed inside the white ring.

Momentum carried me three stumbling paces. I windmilled, recovered, and remained upright.

For several seconds, this seemed an unreasonable amount of success.

Then my legs sat me down.

* * *

Dovek came to stand at the edge of the ring.

I lay on my back with my knees up. “If that was the posture component, I request a merciful interpretation.”

“Your stationary-control component failed.”

“Ah.”

“You identified visible wear and declined an offered repair pause.”

“I remember that less fondly.”

“You continued into a high-load reverse brake without an adequate margin.”

“Are we approaching a point?” I asked.

“We are circling it to ensure you recognize the terrain.”

I pushed myself upright. Both heels were visible beyond my knees: the base curls dark and whole, the right crown entirely gone, the leather around them scuffed and dusty. They looked homemade because I had made them. They looked temporary because they were. Neither fact seemed shameful from the ground.

Dovek crouched and set the sheet on the slate between us.

“You also diagnosed asymmetric thrust while under load,” they said. “You stopped feeding it. You restored both channels without external intervention, used the crown as declared, stated the fault, and completed a controlled landing.”

The wind lifted one corner of the paper.

Beside *stationary control*, Dovek had written a mark I did not enjoy.

Beside *judgment under failure*, they had written one I did.

At the bottom was a pass.

I read it twice, in case the second reading revealed an educational cruelty.

“The rooftop-survey practicum?” I asked.

“You are qualified.”

Dovek held up a finger before I could become unbearable. “For long crossings, you will carry enough physical margin to finish with half the drawing intact. You will set a declared repair threshold before launch. And you will not confuse hiding effort with demonstrating control.”

I looked at the failed mark beside the stationary component.

Earlier, I would have argued that mark upward. Now my calves were still shaking from three breaths inside my own wind.

“That seems fair,” I said.

Dovek gave me the sheet.

Out beyond the roof, the last traces of my flight were coming apart. The rapid bursts inside the yellow square had left a ragged knot freckled with black. Lower down, the corkscrew twisted through itself where one jet had overruled the other. Beneath it hung one broad pale bloom, already thinning at the edges.

From there to the landing ring, two clean ribbons arrived side by side.

I had wanted one smooth wake across the sky.

What remained was better: an honest record of the wind I had wasted, the wind I had trusted, and the moment I finally learned the difference.

stories.title: The Shape of Mercy
stories.prompt: You are a child of a great mage lineage, your eldest sister could turn forests into ash with her flames, your older brother capable of freezing oceans over, your younger sibling, a tamer of magical beasts, but for some reason, everyone fears you the most, and you have zero clue why.
stories.body:
# The Shape of Mercy

Evelyn Bellweather, my eldest sister, could turn forests to ash. She had once stopped a wildfire by burning the untouched trees ahead of it. The songs omitted the black hills, the displaced villages, and the scars beneath her left glove. Marcus Bellweather, my older brother, had frozen an ocean reach hard enough to march an army across it, although he maintained that the fish had been deeply impressed. Phoebe Bellweather, my younger sibling, could put her hand against the muzzle of a raging magical beast and feel where terror ended and hunger began.

I could make a supper knife nervous.

"It's steel," Marcus murmured beside me. "If you glare any harder, it may discover an ancestral gift."

"Perhaps it will appoint me its steward."

He smiled, but his hand went still around his warded cup.

At the head of the table, Lady Rowena Bellweather rose. Candlelight caught the silver stitched through her dark sleeves: little channels for the living wards she supplied with every breath. Beyond the tall windows, the orchard pressed green and restless against the glass. Its trees had been cultivated by generations of the family to flower in every season. Tonight, white petals clung to the panes like curious moths.

Relations, household officers, and tenants filled the long tables. They had come to hear the succession appointments, particularly mine. House Bellweather held that a child's magic followed the shape of an early, ruling desire. Evelyn had wanted warmth. Marcus had wanted stillness. Phoebe had wanted to know why a trapped fox screamed when nobody touched it.

According to my mother, I had wanted nothing remarkable.

I had accepted that. Mostly. The appointment would make usefulness official even if magic never did.

"A great house is not sustained by power alone," Rowena began.

One of the clerks had laid out the household ledger near her elbow. Its brown leather and cheap black ink looked shabby among the warded crystal. Earlier, when I suggested that every appointment be entered twice and witnessed, my mother had said, not unkindly, "Ink is for people whose word cannot defend itself."

Now she rested two fingers on the page. "Adrian Bellweather will serve as—"

The orchard doors exploded inward.

Wind crossed the hall like a thrown table. Candles vanished. Platters skated. My unwarded cup struck the wall and survived, which I thought showed character.

Something vast shouldered through the wreckage.

It stood taller than a carriage horse, though no horse had antlers branching like a winter tree or stormlight moving under translucent skin. Blood darkened an old scar around its throat. Each breath dragged the smell of rain and hot iron into the room. Lightning crawled from tine to tine above its lowered head.
