Claire returned Nora’s novel with a fern pressed between two blank cards and permission to throw it away if it seemed invasive.

“You could have asked whether she wanted a fern,” Tess murmured to me.

“You could let them have one interaction without grading it.”

“I am channeling my attention into service.”

She was. The cups carried requested names, the drinks came out exact, and Tess had become very good at asking before she decorated anything. When Frank approved a tiny portrait of Captain on his sleeve, Tess spent ten minutes getting the ears right.

At Claire’s table, the work of learning continued.

“Why do you wait until the tea cools?” Nora asked.

“Because when it is too hot, all I taste is heat. I want the ginger.”

“I had invented something more tragic.”

“You may keep it for a museum label.”

Claire mentioned that she had worn her soft graphite pencils down to silver stubs and could not get the darker shadows she wanted. The next Sunday Nora brought a paper packet from an art shop.

“You said you needed these,” she said, setting the packet on the table. “If remembering that was too much, I can return them.”

Claire opened the top just enough to read the grades. “Remembering what I told you is not too much.”

“Good.”

“Buying six is possibly too much.”

“The clerk said they break.”

“They do.”

“Then I bought you future breakage.”

Claire laughed. “Thank you.”

Nora had begun turning pages in earnest. Sometimes she sat at Claire’s table and read while Claire drew. Sometimes they talked until the cups went cold. Once Claire spent ten minutes describing how an illustration could be accurate and still lie if it hid the feature a reader needed most. Nora listened with the stillness she had once wasted on Rae’s scarf.

One morning Claire came in with graphite on her cheek. Nora noticed while they were arguing about the ending of a book.

“You have pencil here,” Nora said, pointing to her own cheek.

Claire wiped the wrong side.

“Other side.”

Claire found her chin.

“May I?” Nora asked, holding up a clean napkin.

Claire went still, then nodded. “Yes.”

Nora stepped closer and wiped the smudge once, gently. She retreated before either of them had to ask.

“There,” she said.

“Thank you.”

Tess kept her eyes on the register with heroic effort. I busied myself with the grinder. The grinder did not need me, but it understood sacrifice.

That Sunday Nora ordered a large cardamom latte.

Tess froze with the cup in her hand.

“It is a drink size,” I warned.

“I know what sizes are.”

She wrote NORA in letters proportionate to the vessel and handed it over.

Nora carried it to the table she now shared with Claire, sat down, and knocked her knee hard against the underside. The spoon jumped from Claire’s saucer. Nora caught the cup but not her dignity.

Claire laughed so hard she had to turn away.

Nora rubbed her knee. “I’m glad my pain has made us closer.”

“That is not why I’m laughing.”

“Then your cruelty is less structured than I thought.”

Nora began laughing too. Rae looked up from the communal crossword, smiled at the noise, and went back to her clue.

Their tables had moved together without anyone in the staff moving them. That distinction had become important to me.

* * *

In February, Rae came through the Mercer door with Highway.

Highway was a man in his thirties with silver beginning at his temples, round glasses, and the calm of someone who had never fought a wet umbrella indoors. Rae hooked two fingers through his sleeve as they approached the counter.

“This is Highway,” she said.

I did not ask whether the form was a surname, nickname, or prophecy about traffic. Tess did not ask either. She wrote HIGHWAY on his cup because that was the name he gave her.

He thanked her, moved aside, and listened with grave interest while Rae complained about a crossword clue from the previous week. He was friendly in the unperformed way of a person who had arrived to have coffee with the woman he was seeing, not to enter anyone else’s drama.

Nora looked at Rae.

It looked like the old reflex, and it was not a small one. Rae took off the red scarf and laughed at something Highway said. Nora’s gaze held for a beat too long.

Claire saw.

I knew because she lowered her eyes to the same line of her book three times. I did not know what she thought, and I had learned not to fill that blank for her.

Whatever Nora read in Claire’s lowered gaze, she set her book down.

“I looked,” she said.

Claire’s finger stayed between the pages. “You did.”

“Rae is still beautiful.”

Claire gave one short nod.

“And I am still embarrassed,” Nora continued. “Seeing them brought back standing by the counter and hearing no. I was remembering how much I wanted the floor to open. I wasn’t wishing Rae were available.”

Claire studied her. “I don’t want to be the person you chose because I was sitting nearby when someone else said no.”

“I don’t want that either.”

“You understand why I might not know the difference yet.”

“Yes.” Nora folded her hands around the large latte. “I can’t make you know it with one good sentence. I’m not asking you to decide today.”

Claire looked toward the window. Outside, the rosebush held only thorns and dark red hips.

Nora waited. She did not offer evidence Claire had not requested. She did not ask Claire to reassure her for telling the truth.

After a while Nora said, “You were explaining why a drawing of a gull’s foot was rejected.”

“It was not elegant.”

“The foot?”

“The rejection.”

“I have recent professional interest in the topic.”

Claire’s mouth shifted. Then she reopened the book to a page of small coastal studies and turned it toward Nora.

She had chosen to remain.

At the communal table, Rae took Highway’s pen without permission. Highway took it back. They continued their own morning, which was exactly where they belonged.

* * *

March softened the rain. The drops hung in the air like a thought rather than a punishment, and the rosebush produced new leaves with red edges.

Claire noticed first.

She also brought a clock into the room, though at the time it looked like a folded sheet of work notes.

“I got the coastal assignment,” she told Nora.

“The field guide?”

“Six weeks. I leave at the beginning of June.”

Nora smiled quickly. “That’s good.”

“It is.”

“You wanted it.”

“I did.”

They both looked toward the clock above the pastry case. It was only 10:38, which was not the time that concerned them.

“Six weeks,” Nora said.

“Yes.”

“There will be Sundays there.”

“Probably the standard number.”

Nora laughed, but the new fact stayed between them. Their careful routine now had an edge. June would arrive whether they named what was happening or not.

Later that morning, Claire went outside to draw the new leaves. I was sweeping grit from the Mercer threshold, a task with the useful moral quality of being real. Nora followed with her latte.

“What are you drawing?” she asked.

Claire held the sketchbook against her chest. The movement echoed the day I had seen the unauthorized pages. Nora’s gaze dropped to the closed cover; Claire followed it.

Then Claire lowered it. “Do you want to see?”

Nora considered before answering. “Yes.”

Claire turned the current page toward her. It held three studies of the rosebush: thorn, leaf edge, the wrinkled remains of a winter hip. Nothing was prettified. Every part seemed worthy of accuracy.

“You put the underside in,” Nora said.

“That’s where the early aphids hide.”

“A useful truth.”

“Not every drawing needs to be flattering.”

Nora leaned closer only after Claire angled the page toward her. “May I hold the branch out of the wind?”

Claire nodded. “The one with the three leaves.”

Nora held it carefully while Claire drew.

When they came back inside, Nora paused at the counter.

“There’s an exhibit in May,” she began.

Claire waited.

Nora arranged her face into the precision I had learned to distrust. “At work. It will have labels.”

“I would hope so.”

“I was just mentioning it.”

“All right.”

Claire carried her tea to the table. Nora watched her go, then looked at me.

I polished a cup and offered no translation.

* * *

By April, the café door sometimes stayed open. The air smelled less of wool and more of wet pavement, cardamom, and the green breath of the plant shop across Mercer. Nora and Claire often sat at the window now. They disagreed about books and table stability. They had learned how to make each other laugh. They had not learned how to call what they were doing.

Claire raised the subject on a quiet Sunday after the rush.

“Nora, what is this?”

Nora looked at the two cups, the open books, Claire’s sketchbook turned faceup between them. “Sunday?”

“You know that isn’t what I mean.”

The grinder was off. I could hear them, but I kept both hands occupied sorting spoons.

Claire spoke evenly. “Are we becoming friends? Am I part of your recovery from Rae? Are we moving toward a date?”

Nora’s face emptied in the way it did when she tried to fit too much truth into too few words.

“Our interactions have developed beyond their initial context,” she said.

Claire blinked. “That is a museum label.”

“I’m trying to be accurate.”

“Accurate about what?”

“I value what we have. I don’t want to impose an interpretation before there is enough evidence.”

“Evidence accumulates because people act.” Claire closed her sketchbook, not hard, but decisively. “I like you. I am willing to go slowly. I am not willing to stay an unnamed possibility while you wait for certainty.”

“I’m not waiting for Rae.”

“That is only one thing you could be waiting for.”

Nora opened her mouth. Nothing came out.

Claire put on her coat. “You do not owe me a date. You do owe yourself an answer before you ask me to keep making room for one.”

She left through Mercer. At the rosebush she paused, touched one new leaf, and continued down the hill.

Tess appeared beside me holding a marker.

“No,” I said.

“I didn’t propose anything.”

“Your marker is uncapped.”

She capped it. “Nora could send a note.”

“Not through us.”

Nora had remained at the window, staring at Claire’s half-finished tea. After a minute she came to the counter.

“What did Claire mean?”

I could have answered. I had six months of observations and a recently improved conscience. The combination remained dangerous.

“Claire’s meaning is Claire’s to explain,” I said.

Nora pressed her lips together. “Do you think she’ll come back?”

“I don’t know.”

“Has she ever missed more than one Sunday?”

“I won’t report her visits to you.”

Nora recoiled as if I had accused her of something.

“I’m sorry,” I said. “I know you’re asking because you’re frightened. The answer still belongs to her.”

“Could you tell her I want to talk?”

“No.”

Tess shifted beside the pastry case. I could feel how much she wanted to turn refusal into a gentler form of interference.

Nora looked down at her cup. “You told me to ask Rae.”

“I did. I was trying to move a story I thought I understood. This time I am telling you that your question is yours to ask.”

“What if I ask badly?”

“Then you listen to the answer.”

She stood there for a long moment. Then she took the folded napkin Tess had silently placed near her, started to write, and stopped.

“No note,” Nora said.

“No note,” I agreed.

She put the marker down.

The following Sunday Nora arrived at 9:04.

Claire did not come.

Nora waited until eleven, ordered one small latte, and left without asking us where Claire was.

The Sunday after that, Nora arrived at 9:03.

Again, Claire did not come.

Nora waited until ten. She read sixteen pages and left.

The third Sunday was the first one in May. Nora came at 8:57, before I had turned the sign, and stood beneath the awning while I set out the chairs.

“I’m not asking you anything,” she said.

“Good morning to you too.”

“Good morning.”

At 9:09, Claire came up Mercer with her sketchbook under one arm.

She stopped at the rosebush.

Nora went to meet her.

* * *

The first roses had opened small and pink, more stubborn than elegant. A breeze worried one bloom against the brick. I was just inside the open Mercer door, arranging chairs. I kept my eyes on the work. Their voices carried anyway.

“Claire,” Nora said.

Claire looked at her. “You’re early.”

“I have recently discovered that 10:17 is not a law.”

“That must have been difficult.”

“I’ve had support.”

Claire’s smile appeared and went again. “What did you want to say?”

Nora did not look toward me. She had finally stopped treating the counter as a translation service.

“I know you like honey-ginger tea because it tastes bright without pretending to be summer,” she said. “I know you put the underside of leaves in field guides because people deserve the part that helps them. I know you hate endings where nothing is chosen and everyone calls that depth. I know you use soft graphite because you would rather make a true shadow than a tidy one.”

Claire held very still.

“You told me those things,” Nora continued. “I did not collect them from your cup or ask someone else to tell me. You chose to tell me, and I liked listening. I like how exact you are when accuracy is kindness and how impatient you get when it is only hiding.”

“Nora—”

“I looked at Rae for a long time because I could invent almost everything about her. She was bright and far away, and wanting her asked nothing from me except wanting. Rae’s no hurt, but it was not a door that redirected me to you. You are not what happened because Rae was unavailable.”

Claire’s gaze dropped to the rose between them.

Nora drew a breath. “You are frightening for the opposite reason. You answer back.”

Claire laughed once, softly.

“I want to know you outside Hinge,” Nora said. “Before you leave in June, will you go on one date with me? Saturday afternoon. A walk through Volunteer Park, then dinner somewhere we do not have regular orders. Intentional. Specific. One date.”

Claire looked toward Broadway, where the first bus of the hour sighed at the curb. Then she looked at the café windows, at the cups stacked behind me, at Nora.

“Are you ready to go slowly?” she asked.

“Yes.”

“Slowly cannot mean pretending we have not chosen anything.”

“Then yes to moving slowly. No to pretending.”

“And the field assignment is still six weeks.”

“I know.”

“We do not have to decide what happens after it before one date.”

“I know that too.”

Claire let out a breath. “Then yes. One date.”

Nora’s relief was not graceful. Her shoulders dropped; one hand flew to her mouth; she laughed into her fingers.

“I had another museum label ready,” she admitted.

“Burn it.”

“Gladly.”

The wind pushed the nearest rose away from Claire’s sketchbook. Nora reached for the stem and stopped.

“Do you want me to hold it?” she asked.

Claire opened to a new page. “Yes, please.”

Nora steadied the branch while Claire made three quick lines, then another. The closed portion of the sketchbook remained beneath Claire’s hand. The old pages did not become proof of devotion or a gift redeemed by romance. They stayed what Claire had promised they would stay: closed.

When Claire lifted her pencil, Nora released the branch.

“May I see what you’re drawing now?” she asked.

Claire looked at the page, decided, and turned it toward her.

It was only a rose study. Thorn, wind-bent stem, small uneven petals. Nora studied it as though no one had ever shown her a thing by choice before.

“You made it look stubborn,” she said.

“It was.”

“Good.”

They came in together.

Not accidentally. Not because an arrow on receipt paper had pointed them there. Together because each had crossed a little distance under her own power.

“Usuals?” I asked.

“Large cardamom latte,” Nora said.

“Honey-ginger tea,” Claire said.

Tess took two cups. She wrote NORA and CLAIRE in her clean block letters. Then she hesitated with the marker poised beneath the names.

“May I add tiny roses?” she asked.

Nora looked at Claire.

Claire looked at Nora.

“Yes,” they said together.

Tess drew one beneath each name, no hearts, no arrows, no prophecy. Just two consented flowers on compostable cups.

They took the window table. Their names faced each other across it.

At 10:26, Rae arrived with Highway. Rae greeted Nora, greeted Claire, and complained to Highway about a crossword clue. The old triangle did not reform. It could not; it had depended on reducing people to positions, and everyone involved had kept living beyond the diagram.

Frank came in with Captain, who inspected the floor for steamed-milk opportunities. Tess asked Frank before drawing a tiny terrier on his sleeve. Outside, buses breathed at the curb and the roses shook rain from their petals. Hinge filled with the ordinary sound of cups, chairs, spoons, and people choosing what to say.

I had once believed the café’s name made me responsible for swinging every door open. I had been wrong about both power and responsibility. A hinge permits movement. It does not choose the direction, and it cannot make anyone cross a threshold.

Nora leaned over the rose drawing Claire had chosen to show her. Claire pointed to the underside of one leaf. Their shoulders did not touch. Then they did, briefly, and neither of them treated it as a contract.

They had one date ahead of them, a six-week absence beyond it, and no certainty worth sanding into fate.

Their names remained on the cups until the cups were empty.

stories.title: Self-Reflection
stories.prompt: An anxious teenager wishes for someone who understands her perfectly and wakes beside a second version of herself. The duplicate has her memories but quickly develops choices, relationships, and a life of her own—just as both girls discover she has only four days before she disappears.
stories.body:
# Self-Reflection

Nina woke to a second breath.

It came from the pillow beside hers: a soft catch, an exhale, then another,
slower inhale as the girl in Nina's bed woke too.

Nina did not scream. Screaming required confidence about what was happening.
She lay rigid under the blanket and catalogued evidence instead. Same dark
freckles across the nose. Same pale scar tucked beneath the left eyebrow. Same
sleep shirt, including the ink stain near the hem. Same blue paper bracelet
from the museum trip two weeks ago, though Nina could feel her own bracelet
scratching her wrist under the blanket.

The girl's eyes opened.

Nina knew the exact instant fear entered them because it entered her own face
every morning before presentations.

"Why are you looking at me like that?" the girl whispered.

"Because you're me."

"That's a terrible reason. You're me too."

They scrambled out opposite sides of the bed. The girl hit the desk; Nina hit
the wall. Their matching winces were almost worse than the matching faces.

In the bathroom mirror, two Ninas stared back. The glass was ordinary: toothpaste
flecks, a chipped corner, no ominous glow. Nina covered it with a towel. The
girl remained. They traded bracelets. Nothing happened. Nina pinched her arm,
then, after receiving a furious look, asked permission before pinching the
other girl's. Both marks reddened.

"Last thing you remember before waking," Nina said.

"Standing here last night."

The memory arrived in both their voices. Jocelyn Park's birthday dinner had
ended with Nina fleeing before dessert, after she had spent two hours measuring
every laugh for length and every sentence for signs of structural collapse.
She had told the table that cold fries possessed greater structural integrity.
There had been a pause. Jocelyn had smiled. Nina had translated the pause as
*mistake* and the smile as *mercy*.

At home, facing the mirror, she had said, "Maybe the only friend I can make is
myself."

She had meant it as a joke, which was how Nina delivered most statements she
could not survive hearing repeated. But on the final word, a second inhalation
had pulled from behind her sternum toward the reflection. Not from the glass.
From inside her—a breath she had taken and somehow also released.

Then nothing. She had gone to bed.

"I remember the pull," the girl said.

Nina nodded. "What did you dream?"

"A yellow hallway."

Nina had dreamed about sinking through a floor made of toast.

The difference opened between them, small and bottomless.

"So you're a copy," Nina said, because *copy* sounded more manageable than
*person who remembered being me until six minutes ago*.

The girl folded her arms. "I'm not calling you the original."

"I didn't ask you to."

"Good. Then I need a name."

She looked at their two reflections, not as if consulting them, but as if
refusing to. "Anin."

"That's just Nina backward."

"It's where I came from," Anin said. "It isn't where I'm going."

Their mother worked nights at the hospital and would be home in forty minutes.
Nina spent twenty of them constructing a plan whose chief strength was that it
required nobody else to know anything.

"Stay here," she told Anin, stuffing a cereal bar into her hand. "I go to
school. You don't open the curtains. We figure out how to undo this tonight."

Anin looked around the bedroom. "You want me to spend my first day in a
closet."

"It's not a closet."

"You're right. A closet has a door."

Nina left before the argument could become an event she was late for. All the
way to school, she felt as if she had forgotten her own body at home.

At lunch, Daphne leaned across the table. "Are you okay?"

Four harmless words. Nina's mind converted them into stadium lights.

"Fine," she said too quickly.

Ben was midway through a story about his driving instructor making him circle
the same block until a pigeon ceased to count as a road hazard. Jocelyn was
peeling the label from her water bottle. Nobody looked angry. That only meant
Nina had missed the subtler signs.

"You left pretty fast on my birthday," Jocelyn said.

"I had a headache. No, that's not—" Nina stopped. Her practiced explanation
had tangled with the truth and dragged it out. "I'm bad at being in rooms."

The table went silent.

There it was: the pause. Nina could feel every second landing on her skin.

Then Ben said, "Rooms are badly designed. Too many corners. My driving
instructor would never approve."

Daphne's mouth twitched. Jocelyn did not laugh. "You know you can tell me if
you need to leave, right?"

Nina nodded as if the conversation had concluded successfully, then spent the
rest of lunch proving it had not by saying almost nothing.

When she got home, the kitchen contained the impossible made domestic. Anin
sat at the table in Nina's green hoodie. Their mother sat opposite her with
both hands wrapped around an untouched mug.

"You told her."

"I introduced myself," Anin said.

Their mother rose. Hospital fatigue still marked the skin beneath her eyes,
but fear had sharpened her. She touched Nina's forehead, then Anin's, checked
their pulses, made them stand side by side, and asked each a question about
their father that no stranger could answer.

When both answered, their mother sank into the nearest chair. Nina had expected
the questions to divide real from false. Instead they had produced two correct
daughters and nowhere sensible to put the fact.

"Are you hurt?" their mother asked Anin.

"I don't think so. I'm hungry. Does that count?"

Their mother made toast because feeding someone was a decision she could still
make. She put out the strawberry jam. Nina pushed it away on instinct; Anin
pulled it toward herself, examined the seeds, and spread it thickly.

"You hate that," Nina said.

Anin took a bite. Her eyebrows rose. "Apparently I didn't know yet."

Their mother laughed once, sharply, then covered her mouth. Tears came anyway.
She apologized to both of them, though neither understood what for.

"You believe her?" Nina asked.

"I believe there are two frightened girls in my kitchen." Their mother looked
at Anin directly. "And I believe you when you tell me who you are. The rest can
wait until I've slept for ten consecutive years."

Anin lowered her toast. Something in her expression loosened—not because she
had been explained, but because she had been addressed.

Anin knew everything Nina knew. The cough drops he had kept in the car. The
way grief had turned the house quiet after he died. But while Nina had been at
school, their mother had told Anin something new: once, cleaning the kitchen,
their father had sung fake opera so loudly that the neighbor's dog had joined
in from behind the wall.

"He did?" Nina asked.

Anin looked at her. "You don't know that one."

It should have made Nina believe in Anin's separation. Instead it felt like
discovering a room in her own house whose key had been given to someone else.

Their mother sat down again. "After he died, I used to wish there were two of
me. One to work, one to stay home with you. I said it out loud. More than
once."

"Did anything happen?" Nina asked.

"I got hoarse."

Anin took another bite of toast. Nina hated strawberry jam. Anin apparently
did not.

They tested the mirror again that evening. They covered it, turned it toward
the wall, put both bracelets in a drawer, repeated Nina's sentence, then said
it backward. Their mother made her old wish again while holding Nina's
bracelet. Nothing doubled, vanished, warmed, flashed, or answered. The mirror
continued reflecting whatever stood in front of it, with the dull patience of
an object unfairly accused.

By bedtime, Nina had learned only that Anin snored a little and preferred the
window open.

The next morning, Nina watched Anin choose the green hoodie again.

"One day," Anin said. "I want one day outside."

Nina had thought of the same plan before Anin proposed it, which did not make
it generous. Anin knew every class, every route, every face as of the night at
the mirror. She could attend school as Nina while Nina stayed home and studied
the difference between them.

"You tell me everything people say," Nina insisted.

"I tell you what happened to me."

The pronoun lodged under Nina's ribs.

Anin went to school in Nina's face. Nina spent the morning pacing from the
mirror to the window, trying to detect a thread between them. There was none.
She did not know what Anin saw, thought, or felt. She had only her own restless
mind, which was familiar company and not especially good.

When Anin came home, exhilaration and guilt had put color high in her cheeks.
She took off the green hoodie, folded it on the bed, and gave Nina an account
that contained too much air: sun on the walk, the sour edge of cafeteria
lemonade, the relief of speaking without composing three possible reactions
first.

"I got caught at lunch," Anin said. "Jocelyn asked if rooms were any better
today."

Nina sat down on the edge of the bed. "What did you say?"

"That some were. Then I asked what I'd missed. Daphne stopped opening her
pudding. Ben forgot his joke."

"You admitted you didn't know?"

"I almost gave them your answer. I could feel all the pieces—the half-smile,
the deflection, the apology that pretends it isn't one." Anin touched the
folded hoodie as if smoothing a wrinkle Nina could not see. "But I told them I
didn't know how to answer yet."

It was not the answer Nina would have given. Nina hated how easily she heard
that, and hated herself for hearing it as victory.

Anin told her about standing outside after lunch under a sky Nina had seen a
thousand times. Wind had put hair in her mouth; the bell had rushed her back
inside; she had forgotten a warmer coat. She described each annoyance with
the careful ownership of somebody unpacking new possessions. In class she had
chosen a different argument for the English response waiting in Nina's notes.
She had erased it twice, then left the third version.

"Why that one?" Nina asked.

"Because I changed my mind."

"Jocelyn thinks you're angry with her," Anin said. "She said you've seemed
angry for months."

"I'm not."

"I know. She doesn't."

"So you corrected her."

"I couldn't keep pretending. She asked about something you said yesterday."

"You made me look strange."

Anin's face went still. It was a stillness Nina had never practiced. "You sent
me there to be you."

"For one day. You were supposed to show me what I'm doing wrong."

"You're not a machine with a loose screw."

"Easy for you to say. You borrowed my life and everybody liked you better."

"I borrowed your name. I don't want to do it again."

"Because you got what you wanted?"

"Because I got one day, and half of it belonged to lying."

Anin lifted a hand between them, ending the agreement.

Lamplight shone through her fingertips.

For a moment Nina thought it was a trick of the thin skin. Then she saw the
line of the bookshelf through Anin's palm. The blue bracelet on Anin's wrist
had faded with her, its printed pattern washed to a ghost. Nina seized her own
bracelet. Solid paper. Solid ink.

"No," she said.

Anin turned her hand over. "That isn't an answer."

For two days they treated panic like a laboratory.

Their mother called the hospital and said she could not come in. She timed
Anin's pulse, marked changes in the translucency, and wrote down every failed
idea. The girls exchanged bracelets; Anin's faded bracelet remained faded on
Nina, while Nina's remained solid on Anin. They moved both bracelets across
the house. They uncovered the mirror, covered it again, sat Anin in darkness,
then sunlight. Nina repeated the sentence until the words became furniture.
Their mother wished for another self. Anin wished to stay.

Nothing altered the slow clearing of Anin's body.

Nina tried being cheerful for an hour. Anin continued fading. Nina cried until
her face hurt. Anin continued fading. They argued, apologized, held hands, sat
in separate rooms. At each measurement, the line of light through Anin was a
little brighter.

The green hoodie remained perfectly green.

Near the fourth dawn, Anin sat at Nina's desk wearing the hoodie over the sleep
shirt she had arrived in. Her wrists and throat were translucent now. When she
typed, the keys sank beneath fingers that looked made of window glass, but the
letters stayed black and ordinary on the screen.

Nina stood behind her with a list of new tests.

"We could try the sentence at the exact time," Nina said. "Same place, same
clothes. If it made you once—"

"No."

"It might stabilize you. Or make another—"

Anin spun the chair around. "Another what?"

Nina could not say *you*. Not while looking at her.

"I'm not a failed batch," Anin said. Fear roughened her voice, but it did not
make the choice less hers. "And I'm not spending what I have left helping you
manufacture my replacement."

"I'm trying to save you."

"You're trying to make an outcome you can stand."

Nina's list trembled. "What if you're fading because I don't need you now?"

Anin stared at her. "You think I'm dying because my job is complete?"

"I don't think that. I just—what if the rules think it?"

"What rules? We tried happy. We tried miserable. We tried close and apart. I
started fading before you learned anything useful." Anin reached for Nina's
hand. Her grip was faint but warm. "Your need isn't killing me. Your getting
better won't save me. And I wasn't made *for* either one."

The last sentence broke something quieter than hope. Nina saw the shape of the
four days: every test had asked what Anin was for, how Anin worked, what Anin
proved about Nina. Even the school day had turned Anin's life into evidence.

Nina put the list down.

"I'm sorry," she said.

Anin waited. Nina did not ask whether that fixed anything. It did not.

"What did you write?" Nina asked.

Anin turned the screen toward her.

The page began: *I like strawberry jam because Nina doesn't. That wasn't why I
tried it, but it might be why I noticed.*

Below it, Anin had written about the yellow hallway in her first dream. The
weight of the green hoodie. Jocelyn's face when an answer did not fit. Their
mother falling asleep at the table and waking with both girls' hands beneath
her cheek. Fear appeared on the page, but so did irritation, appetite, sunlight,
and a joke about Nina's lists having lists.

It sounded a little like Nina. It sounded more like Anin.

"Tell me about our father singing," Nina said.

So Anin did. She gave him an apron as a cape and a wooden spoon as a tragic
hero's sword. Their mother corrected the spoon to a dish brush. Anin objected
that a dish brush lacked dignity. By the end, all three were laughing too hard
for the story to remain sad in only one way.

Then Anin asked Nina about the first lunch—the one Anin had not attended. Nina
told her about Daphne's question, Ben's pigeon, and the sentence that had
escaped before she could make it harmless. Anin listened with her eyes closed.

"I wish I remembered it," she said.

"I wish I remembered the opera."

The symmetry was imperfect. Nina would have years, perhaps, to hear old family
stories. Anin had minutes. But for that moment each held something the other
could receive only by being told, and Nina understood that listening was not a
lesser form of knowing someone. It was the form everybody else had always had.

They stopped measuring time by opacity. Anin chose the last hour: tea too sweet
for Nina, their mother between them on the bed, the window open despite the
cold. Anin used a black pen to write **I AM REAL** on her own forearm.

Nina wrote **SAME** on hers.

Anin took the pen back. Beneath Nina's word, she added **YOU TOO**.

"Tomorrow," Anin said, "tell someone one true thing."

Nina's chest tightened. "If I do, will you—"

"No bargain." Anin touched their wrists together, fading ink against solid.
"Not for me. Because it's your day, and you get to decide what to do with it."

When the sun reached the lower edge of the window, Anin became almost entirely
light. Their mother held one of her hands. Nina held the other. Neither could
feel much pressure, but Anin looked from one of them to the other and said,
"Still here."

Then she wasn't.

The green hoodie collapsed across Nina's knees. Beneath it, the duplicated
sleep shirt was gone. So were Anin's bracelet and the words on her arm. Nina's
own bracelet remained. **SAME. YOU TOO** remained in black ink on Nina's skin.
The page waited on the screen.

Their mother made a sound Nina had never heard from her before. They held the
empty hoodie between them.

They did not know whether Anin had died, gone elsewhere, or ended in some way
they had no word for. Not knowing did not make the bed less empty. It did not
make her less their loss.

At lunch the next day, Nina wore the green hoodie.

Daphne looked at her inked forearm, then at her face. "Are you okay?"

The truthful answer was too large for the table. Nina nearly said *fine*. She
nearly asked Ben about driving. She nearly let Jocelyn decide that silence
meant anger because anger was easier to admit to than fear.

"No," Nina said. The pause arrived. This time she stayed inside it. "I left
your birthday because I was afraid you'd watch me fail at being normal. And I
lost someone yesterday. I can't explain all of it yet. But I need you to stop
guessing what my quiet means while I practice actually telling you."

Jocelyn's eyes filled before Nina understood why. "I thought you hated us."

"I thought you were being kind because you felt sorry for me."

"I was being kind because you're my friend." Jocelyn scrubbed at one eye,
annoyed by it. "But I can't guess. You have to say when you need quiet."

"I know. I mean, I know now. I might still be terrible at it."

Ben nodded gravely. "Most rooms require several attempts. Ask any pigeon."

The joke did not erase anything. It made enough space to breathe.

Daphne pushed her unopened pudding cup across the table. "I don't know what to
say when people are grieving," she admitted. "This is what I have."

Nina took it. "Thank you."

Jocelyn glanced at her fries. "For the record, I told three people your
structural-integrity theory after the party."

"You did?"

"Cold fries really do hold up better."

Nina laughed, and then cried, which embarrassed everyone enough that they all
became busy with napkins and lunch trays. Nobody understood perfectly. Nobody
left.

At home, a note waited beside the lamp in their mother's hurried writing:
*Love you. Both of you, somehow.*

Nina printed Anin's page. She saved it twice, because grief had not cured her
of sensible precautions. Then she tied her surviving blue bracelet around the
lamp's stem. It did not glow or warm or become anything except paper around
metal.

That was enough. It had been there. She had been there.

Nina opened the response she owed for English. The blank document reflected
her dimly until she typed across it. For once, she did not begin by guessing
what answer would make her easiest to like.

She began in her own words.

stories.title: Realms
stories.prompt: Your twelve-year-old sister is dying, and the only cure is a living heartseed sold in a market beyond a hidden portal. The dealer will accept no money—only your place in every memory your family has of you. When you refuse the bargain, stealing the heartseed may be your last chance to save her.
stories.body:
# Realms

The portal looked less like a doorway than a wound.

It hung in the abandoned tunnel below Queen Street, twenty feet of white light
stitched into wet concrete. Black rain crawled upward around its edges. It
spattered the ceiling and left the floor beneath it dry.

Someone had painted above the wound:

> RUNNERS GO IN
>
> DEBTS COME OUT

Underneath, in smaller letters: *sometimes*.

I stood behind the yellow line with a borrowed pack on my shoulders, Lena's
hospital bill folded in my sock, and my phone pressed to my ear.

“Cal-Cal,” Lena's saved voice whispered through the speaker. Machines breathed
behind her. “You said you're getting groceries. If you bring those cardboard
pears again, I'm reporting you to the government.” She paused to catch her
breath. “Come back before visiting hours, okay?”

The message ended. I put the phone in my jacket beside her photograph.

“Name?” asked the woman at the folding table.

Her silver throat tag read **M. Voss — Licensed Exit Witness**. A cracked
tablet, a thermos, and a pistol lay in front of her. The pistol was the least
alarming thing in the tunnel.

“Cal Mercer.”

“First crossing?”

I considered lying. M. Voss looked at the clean knees of my jeans and waited.

“Yes.”

“Then say it like you prefer living.” Voss pointed to the wall beside her.
Something translucent pulsed under the concrete there, thick as a buried
vein. It disappeared into the rim of the portal. “The seam is alive. I can
prompt it. I can't order it. If it stops recognizing this route, your reasons
won't persuade it.”

Behind me, Tuck sighed theatrically. He was tall, short one piece of his left
ear, and wrapped in a coat whose original owner had probably fought hard.

“He paid for a guide,” Tuck said. “He gets a guide.”

“He paid *you*,” Voss said. “That makes him a customer with company.”

Tuck smiled. “Cruel distinction.”

Voss took a dull metal disk from a locked case. At her touch, the buried vein
pressed closer to the surface. She made me declare my name again, then held
the disk against the living seam. Pale lines spread across the metal.

“The disk stores the mark,” she said. “It does nothing by itself. The seam has
paired it to your declared name, this entry, and tonight's return window. It
remembers the route, not your wrist. Lose it before you open an exit and you
become local. Lose it after the exit opens but before I stamp it closed, and
momentum may carry you through while whoever holds the disk keeps one usable
trail behind you.”

“So I don't lose it.”

“A gifted student.”

I tied it around my bare wrist with doubled cord. Tuck pulled back his sleeve
and showed me a separate disk on a leather thong, its markings dim but visible.

“Mine,” he said. “No sharing, no heroic clasping of hands, no sentimental
nonsense.”

Voss glanced at the hospital bill corner protruding from my sock. “Your sister
needs a transplant, not a miracle.”

“Her name is Lena Mercer. She's twelve. Her numbers got worse this morning.”

“That doesn't change what a heartseed costs.”

“No,” I said. “It changes what I'm willing to pay.”

Voss's expression tightened. “That's what worries me.”

I checked my pack: water, protein bars, flares, copper wire, a knife, and a
fistful of diner salt packets. An old Runner-forum post by GutSaint72 had
claimed salt discouraged *wet trouble*. Half the replies said the account was
a fraud. The other half said the writer was dead.

Tuck stepped through the wound. The white seam swallowed him with a wet pop.

Voss looked at me one last time. “It doesn't care why you enter.”

“I know.”

“Not yet.”

I played one second of Lena's message—*Come back*—and crossed.

* * *

Sound went first.

The tunnel vanished. Pressure filled my skull. I landed knee-deep in red
grass, under a blue sky crowded with doors.

Thousands drifted overhead: painted doors, steel doors, doors small enough for
a hand, one round door wider than a stadium. Some opened on fire or water or
lamplit rooms. Others stayed shut. None explained where we were, and I had no
breath to ask.

Tuck was already walking toward a white road. His voice reached me a beat
late. “Don't stare. Everybody eventually sees a door they want.”

I looked down. The grass bent away from my boots without touching them.

Far ahead, a city of copper towers and crooked awnings rode the shell of
something vast and sleeping. Its plated back rose and fell. With each breath,
the whole city climbed against the sky and settled again.

“Deepmarket,” Tuck said. “Where wanting something is the first way you tell it
how to hurt you.”

At the city gate, a living figure made of warm smoke stretched across the
road. Faces opened and closed inside its body like bubbles.

“Terms,” it said. “One emotionally weighted memory from each entrant. I select.
You cross the collection line, you consent.”

Tuck stopped before a white groove in the stones. “Can we refuse?”

“Yes.”

“Can we enter after refusing?”

“No.”

He crossed. The smoke touched his brow. Tuck staggered and muttered something
about the smell of his father's truck.

I wanted to rush past him, but the gatekeeper spread across the road.

“Do I choose the memory?” I asked.

“I select.”

Lena's heart was failing while I negotiated with smoke. I stepped over the
line.

A cool finger touched my forehead.

Something came loose.

There had been a girl named Priya. I knew she had given me my first kiss, and
that it had once mattered. I could no longer see her face, recall the place,
or find a single sensation from the event. The knowledge remained like a
label on an empty drawer.

I folded over, grasping for what wasn't there.

Tuck caught my collar. “Walk.”

“It took too much.”

“It took something heavy. That's the stated price.”

“You make that sound fair.”

“I make it sound finished.” He pulled me through the gate. “Save your anger.
Things here can smell it.”

Deepmarket rang around us like a drawer of knives. Living merchants barked
offers from stalls built into the sleeper's shell. A woman with beetle wings
uncorked jars of thunder. A three-headed hen laid warm brass eggs into a
velvet basket. A mirror-eyed seller tracked pieces of my reflection as I
passed. On one table, inert maps had been pinned flat beneath a net of pale,
breathing roots.

I kept one hand over Lena's photograph.

“How much?” I asked.

“For my remaining fee?” Tuck said. “You have it.”

“For the heartseed.”

He stopped in an alley glazed with green wax. “You don't buy a heartseed with
cash.”

I pulled seven hundred dollars from my jacket. “You said half up front.”

“Half *my* fee.”

The money shook in my hand. “You knew this was all I had.”

“I knew it was more than you could afford to lose and less than the market
would notice.”

My knife came out.

Tuck drove two knuckles under my ribs. I dropped to one knee, gasping, while a
thin antlered merchant paused at the alley mouth with an empty bottle ready.

“Put it away,” Tuck said. “Deepmarket's living substrate feels expressed
want. Strong want makes a heavy price. Anger is just another thing it can
sell back to you.”

I sheathed the knife. The antlered merchant clicked his tongue and left.

“You said the Realms run on want,” I said.

“Runner shorthand. I know this market. Anyone who claims to know every door in
that sky is selling a map.”

He led me to a blank wall furred with hair-thin roots. It had no handle, only a
shallow depression that warmed when we approached.

“It opens for honest shame,” Tuck said.

“That's convenient for you.”

He put his palm against the wall. “I abandoned a friend because his boots fit
me better.”

The roots shivered but did not open.

Tuck swallowed. “He was alive when I took them.”

A slit appeared in the wall.

My turn. I tried to offer the time I'd stolen groceries, but the roots stayed
cold.

“I was relieved,” I said. The words scraped on the way out. “When the doctors
said Lena might die. For one second, I imagined the waiting ending, and I was
relieved I wouldn't have to be afraid every morning.”

The wall opened wide.

* * *

The shop beyond was warm and dark. Roots hung from its ceiling and braided
through its shelves. Glass jars held plum-sized lights, each beating at a
different rhythm.

Behind the counter sat a child-shaped figure in a gray suit. White hair framed
an unlined face; its hands were wrinkled as old paper. A thin shadow tied it to
the roots beneath the counter.

Tuck said, “That's an avatar. Don't mistake the shape for a child.”

The dealer smiled. “Hello, Tuck.” Its eyes turned to me. “Cal Mercer.”

I touched my token.

“The shop reads what the entrance marked,” it said. “It does not need your
trust.”

I put the hospital bill and Lena's photograph on the counter. “She needs a
heartseed.”

Roots slid over the paper, the photograph, and the edge of my hand. I pulled
back. On the highest shelf, one light changed its rhythm. A label flowered
across the jar: Lena beneath our kitchen table, knees drawn up, daring me to
find her.

“The seed is tuned,” the dealer said. “Your records describe the damage. Your
want supplies the weight. Your living tie supplies the direction.”

“Price?”

Every heartseed beat at once.

“Twenty years.”

“Mine?”

“Whose else did you bring?”

“Take them.”

Tuck swore softly.

The dealer leaned across the counter. “You neglected to ask which twenty.”

I pictured years as blank squares and tried to make them cheap. “Which?”

“The best. The ones in which your body is strong, your judgment clear, your
love returned. The seed takes nourishment where nourishment is richest.”

My certainty faltered. The dealer saw it and smiled wider.

“Another price, then. Your place in your sister's remembered life.”

“What does that mean?”

“She keeps the repaired years. She and your mother lose their lived memories
of you. My roots bend their attention so photographs feel mislabeled, your
room feels available, your messages feel sent by mistake. History remains.
Birth and hospital records remain. Objects remain. They simply build painful
explanations around a person they can no longer remember.”

A root curled across the counter like an offered pen. “Say you consent, and
Lena wakes stronger.”

The clean heroic answer rose to my mouth.

I had rehearsed it through every careful doctor conversation: *anything*. My
years, my blood, my place at the table. Brother traded for sister. A sacrifice
so complete nobody could accuse me of feeling relieved.

The root touched my fingers.

Then I heard Lena's message in my head. Not the saved sound—the demand inside
it. *Come back.* She had asked for pears and time and her brother. She had not
offered her mind for me to carve pieces from. Neither had our mother.

Priya's empty drawer opened inside me. The gate had taken one memory after
stating its terms to the person who owned it. This bargain would take
thousands from people who weren't in the room and call my permission enough.

I drew my hand away.

“No.”

The dealer's smile vanished. “The traces would hurt less with time.”

“You don't get to make forgetting me their cure.”

“Then why did you come?”

I looked at the jar marked with Lena's face. “I thought I came to pay.”

“And now?”

I took out my knife.

“Now I steal.”

Tuck gave one short, disbelieving laugh. Then the shop tried to kill us.

* * *

Roots dropped from the ceiling. One caught my ankle and slammed me against the
floor. Others wound around Tuck's arms and throat. Shelves folded inward as the
living shop pulled its heartseeds out of reach.

The dealer's jaw opened too far. A shriek like metal on winter rail shook the
jars.

I tore open the salt packets and flung them into its mouth.

The crystals struck wet tissue. The child shape convulsed. Its thin shadow
whitened where the salt drew moisture from it, and the roots nearest the
counter loosened.

“GutSaint72,” I wheezed. “One useful post.”

Tuck ripped an arm free. He seized a low jar and smashed it against the shelf.
A flock of tiny living lights burst out, biting at every root they touched.

“Wrong one!” I shouted.

“It looked hostile!”

“That's your selection rule?”

The dealer pointed at Tuck. The wall behind him split open. Beyond it, the
white road ran clear toward the gate, and his own token shone through his
shirt.

“Guides may leave,” the dealer rasped. “Customers pay.”

The root around Tuck's throat released him.

He looked at me, then at the open wall. For one breath he was already gone. I
saw it in the angle of his body, the hand closing around his own disk, the
instinct nine years had sharpened.

He ran for the road.

The roots hauled me backward. I clawed at the waxy floor while Lena's jar
receded overhead.

Tuck reached the threshold.

Then he stopped.

“I have enough stolen footwear,” he muttered, and turned back.

He threw his weight onto the root around my ankle. It bucked, flinging my knife
from its sheath. Tuck kicked the blade toward me. It spun too high. I grabbed
for the handle and caught the edge.

Pain opened my palm.

I held on, sawed through the root, and rolled free. Milk-colored fluid washed
over the floor. The shop shuddered.

Tuck drove his shoulder into the dealer avatar. Its child-shaped body folded
against the counter, all paper skin and braided root underneath. I climbed the
shelves as they contracted around me.

The labels blurred: antlers, a furnace, six fingers, a blue eye. Then Lena,
under the kitchen table.

I caught her jar against my chest.

The shop's defensive reflex struck like a kicked elevator.

Every root snapped toward the route marks on our tokens. The wall, ceiling,
and floor became a throat throwing us out. Tuck grabbed my jacket as the shop
hurled us through a corridor of spinning doors. Brief openings flashed around
us—salt water, red stone, a room full of candles—but our stored marks burned
white as the living shop shoved us toward the same wet seam.

The Queen Street seam answered the stored marks by opening two circles onto the
tunnel, their edges overlapping. Voss stood beyond them with her stamp raised.

Tuck crossed first on his own mark. I followed, still holding the jar.

A dealer-root whipped out of the folding corridor and caught my wrist. The
cord snapped. My disk vanished backward into the shop, but the threshold was
already open and my body was already falling.

I struck tunnel concrete.

The jar shattered under my hand.

For one dead second, I thought I had killed the seed.

Then the light found the fresh cut in my palm.

It entered like a hot thread pulled through every vein. I watched roots of
gold climb beneath the skin of my wrist and disappear toward my chest. A
second rhythm struck under my heart.

Voss stamped Tuck's disk closed. Then she was above me, pistol in one hand,
the other holding my shoulders down.

“Where is the heartseed?” she demanded.

My chest answered twice.

Tuck lay bruised beside me. He stared at the glow under my ribs.

“That,” he said, “is not where he planned to put it.”

* * *

I woke cuffed to a clinic bed. The room smelled of bleach, burned toast, and
the mineral sharpness of the portal rain. Beyond a reinforced inner door, I
could hear the return tunnel's old pipes ticking.

My cut hand was bandaged. Heat branched from it to my chest. Beneath my pulse,
the heartseed kept its own patient rhythm.

Voss sat in the corner with a paperback. Tuck occupied the next bed, one arm
in a sling and pale rings around his throat.

“Lena,” I said.

Voss set down the book. “Alive.”

“Did she get it?”

“The seed rooted in the first fresh blood it touched. Yours. Removing it now
would probably kill both of you.” She raised a hand before I could fight the
cuff. “It was tuned to Lena's damaged cardiac pattern, not to her body as a
host. Your blood is carrying a surplus of whatever repair factors it makes.”

“Then give her all of it.”

“No.”

The old word rose—*anything*—but this time I heard what it tried to hide.

Voss continued. “The clinic told your mother every known risk and most of the
unknown ones. She consented to one screened transfusion. Lena was awake enough
to assent. One. Monitored. Her numbers improved, but they aren't normal. This
bought time. Nobody here can promise how much.”

Better, I thought.

Not cured. Not safe forever. Better.

The word hurt so beautifully I had to close my eyes.

Voss put my phone in my free hand. Lena appeared on the screen, washed pale by
hospital light but sitting higher against her pillows than she had that
morning.

“Cal-Cal,” she said.

The dealer had offered to erase that voice from her. Hearing it now nearly
broke me.

“Hey,” I managed.

“You look terrible.”

“Tuck looks worse.”

From the next bed, Tuck lifted one finger without opening his eyes.

Lena's smile faded. “They said you stole something alive and now it's inside
you.”

“That's the short version.”

“Did you know that would happen?”

“No.”

“Did you ask me before deciding this was worth it?”

I looked at the cuff, the bandage, and the faint gold under my skin. “No.”

“Then if there's a next time, you ask. Before another transfusion. Before
another miracle. I get a vote.”

“You get a vote,” I said. “And I don't donate again unless the clinic says it's
safe enough, you want it, and our mother agrees. I stay for the monitoring. All
of it.”

“Good.” Lena breathed carefully, but the breath reached the end without a
cough. “Also, pears in cans. The government has standards.”

I laughed. She did too. For a few seconds we were only brother and sister,
arguing over fruit.

After the call, Tuck pushed an envelope across the gap between our beds.

“The unpaid half,” he said. “And part of the paid half. I delivered you to the
wrong price without telling you.”

“You came back.”

His gaze went to the boots at the foot of his bed. “That doesn't make the
first time unhappen.”

“No.”

“I'm helping close the route anyway.”

Voss stood. “So am I. The entry was mine to witness. The breach is mine to
contain. I don't get to become a line in somebody else's report because your
guide is unreliable and you're catastrophically stupid.”

“Accountable allies,” Tuck said. “Warmest room in the city.”

Only then did Voss open the evidence pouch from the return. Tuck's stamped disk
lay inside. A clipped cord lay beside it.

She checked the pouch again.

“Your token never crossed,” she said.

The heartseed's second rhythm quickened.

From beyond the reinforced door came three soft knocks.

A child's voice spoke through the steel.

“Cal Mercer.”

Voss drew her pistol. Tuck reached beneath his pillow. I kept Lena's phone in
my hand.

The heartseed answered the knock with one hard, hungry beat.

stories.title: Daughter of the Sun
stories.prompt: Four centuries ago, your mother saved the capital by burning the rest of the kingdom and became a goddess in the history she left behind. Now you are worshipped as the Daughter of the Sun—and when proof of what she did awakens the same buried power, you must decide whether to destroy it alone or trust the people it endangers to share control of your fire.
stories.body:
# Daughter of the Sun

The prayer had once named every city.

The Daughter knew because the oldest sun-glass steps still held their ghosts: narrow cuts beneath the newer gold leaf, one for each place the Day of Glass had erased. Now the priests sang only of the capital, the one city Queen Aurelia had saved. A hundred thousand voices answered from the square, and the shield-tower cast their devotion back as warm light.

At the Daughter's wrists, another light began to gather under her skin.

Seris Venn touched two fingers to the inside of her left wrist. Not a grip. Not a command. A reminder that she could choose what her hands did next.

Across the altar, Chancellor Cythra Dhal watched the shield flicker over the eastern roofs. “The infirmary lost cooling again this morning,” she murmured. “My office's thermal oath-seal is the only key to the capital's final sink, and the sink cannot cool a shield with no fire left to route. Three more failures and reverence will be the least of what the city asks from you.”

The Daughter kept her palms flat on the stone. For four centuries, the Rite of Deliverance had called that restraint humility. She had refused a throne, refused command, refused every petition to become the Goddess the capital declared her mother to be. Yet she still stood at the altar and let the shortened prayer pass through her silence.

Tovan Rek stepped out of the scholars' rank before the final verse.

He looked absurdly small beneath the tower, all patched sleeves and wind-worried hair. In both hands he carried a black shard recovered from the tower's sealed foundation. “There is an older response,” he said. “If the Daughter will give one drop of living fire.”

Dhal moved first. “The rite is not an excavation.”

But the Daughter had already pressed her thumb to the shard's edge. Blood brightened, gold at its center. Tovan spoke six harsh syllables that did not sound like prayer.

The shield-tower answered.

Black light climbed its ribs. A woman's figure appeared above the altar, broken by seams and weather, one hand closed around a sphere of white fire. Queen Aurelia's face turned toward someone outside the surviving frame.

“The capital will survive,” the witness said. “The outer cities will not.”

The prayer collapsed into screams.

The figure vanished, but not before the Daughter saw her mother's expression. Not grief alone. Decision.

Dhal climbed the altar step. “A damaged witness, awakened by an unlicensed invocation. Say so.” Her voice stayed low while guards closed the square's gates. “Then come with me. The shield is failing, and we must learn how much power the Crown can safely draw from you.”

“Safely for whom?” Seris asked.

Dhal did not look at her. “For the people alive today.”

The accusation struck because it was not wholly false. The Daughter had kept herself pure of office while children burned fever-hot beneath a failing shield. She had imagined that refusing authority meant she could not abuse it. Meanwhile, she had lent her face to a lie.

“I will not call the witness false,” she said. “And you will not examine me behind a locked door.”

Seris drew a thin disk from beneath her breastplate. The oath-record had passed through four hundred years of Venn hands. It opened only when the Daughter laid her bloody thumb upon it and said, before the crowd and Dhal's guards, “Let the truth condemn Queen Aurelia. Let it condemn me too.”

A woman appeared in the disk's trembling light. Deryn Venn wore soot on her cheek and held a swaddled infant against her chest. Behind her, a sky burned white.

“Who protects her,” Deryn demanded of someone beyond the frame, “from becoming—”

The record snapped into darkness. On its underside, newly visible lines traced a route across the Glass Sea to the buried Crown of Noon.

The Daughter turned to the square. The priests had stopped singing. Beyond them, the names cut from the stair waited under gold.

“This rite is incomplete,” she said. “I am going to bring back what was removed.”

For the first time in four centuries, the tower gave no answering light.

* * *

They crossed the Glass Sea beneath a hard, colorless dawn: the Daughter, Seris, Tovan, and Orrin Pell, the relic-smith whose tools could coax old hinges into remembering motion. Wind drove splinters of translucent salt over the frozen waves. Behind them, a black pulse moved under the glass, keeping pace.

At the ninth descent shaft, people barred the lift.

“No kneeling,” said Sister Calvea Dorn, warden of the Ninth Hollow. Ash marked her eyelids and both bare palms. “No secret workings. Tell us what followed you.”

So the Daughter told them about the witness, the route, and the Crown. She also told them the capital's shield was failing. No one bowed. An old man spat into the lift machinery. A child asked whether the Goddess had known their families were outside the shield.

The light at the Daughter's wrists spread to her elbows.

Stone softened beneath her boots. Seris reached for her, then stopped a hand's breadth away.

Calvea faced the residents gathered along the shaft. “I can bank her flame in this floor and nowhere beyond it. Until the third bell, or until any three household witnesses revoke consent. It will scar my hands and blur my sight. The heat will remain under this stone until we carry it out by living flame. Do you accept the risk?”

Questions came first. Where would the heat go? Could it reach the sleeping chambers? Who would stand watch? Calvea answered each one. Only when voices from every occupied gallery agreed did she kneel.

She did not touch a mechanism. She pressed her living palms to bare rock and drew dusk out of the Hollow's gathered shadows. The darkness folded around the Daughter's ankles, cool and immense. Heat poured down through it. Calvea's hands reddened. Her pupils clouded silver.

Nothing in the old machines had made that magic.

The Daughter could breathe again.

Then the cistern alarm began: not a bell, but a grinding cry through the walls. Water sprayed from a split joint above the lift, and the floor lurched as a buried gate tried to open against centuries of mineral crust.

Orrin dropped beside the exposed housing. He had said little on the crossing, but now his hands moved with intimate certainty. “The local line can survive,” he said. “If it receives enough heat to release the seal.”

Calvea, half blind, turned her face toward the Daughter. “One spark. No more than I name. For this cistern only.”

Again the residents questioned. Again they consented, this time to a measured repair whose risk ended at the iron isolation ring Orrin had wedged into place.

The Daughter crouched beside him. She let a thread of gold pass from her finger into the focus stone.

The gate opened. Water thundered into the lower tanks.

For one breath, people cheered.

Then Orrin's isolation ring turned by itself. He seized it with both hands. Metal screamed against metal while black light leapt past the ring and raced deeper beneath the Hollow.

Every lamp went dark.

In their place, a single buried line shone through the floor, pointing toward the Crown.

The cistern water began to fall.

“It used your spark to wake the master line,” Orrin said. His voice carried the flat horror of recognition. “And the master line still serves the capital.”

Far above, something struck the descent doors. Dhal had found their route.

* * *

The chamber beneath the Crown of Noon had been built for seven doors. Six were sealed. The seventh stood open, drinking the Ninth Hollow's water through a conduit wide enough to walk inside.

At the chamber's center, a black-sun key floated over a dead circle of glass. Tovan approached it as if nearing an injured animal.

“I have dreamed this room,” he said.

The key unfolded.

Light passed through Tovan's body. For an instant the Daughter saw not bones but crowded layers of script, many damaged, some still writing. Across the walls, precise words appeared among the sacred marks: ARCHIVE. MOBILE EXPRESSION. REINTEGRATION PENDING.

Tovan staggered toward the circle.

“It wants its missing pages,” he gasped. “It thinks that is all I am.”

The old language had become a blade. Keeper Below, the Under-Surface prayers called him. A scholar with an impossible memory. A possible god. The chamber called him an expression, as if a technical word could decide whether his fear mattered.

The Daughter caught his sleeve but did not pull him back. “What do you choose?”

He stared at the histories moving under his skin. “I choose the record. I also choose to remain Tovan Rek.”

Orrin opened the key's housing. His fingertips divided along hair-fine seams, revealing threads of pale metal beneath living skin.

The Daughter looked at him.

“I was made to maintain this network,” Orrin said. His mouth tightened. “I have spent my life wondering whether every kindness was only a surviving directive. I did not tell you because I wanted one thing about me to be mine.” He placed his opened hand against the dead interface. “This is mine to tell. The repair is mine to attempt.”

Nothing happened.

“The circuit needs living power,” Orrin said. “And he needs an anchor the archive cannot define for him.”

Calvea leaned against the wall, her damaged palms wrapped in grey cloth. “Calling the Name works here only for a willing person inside my hearing, and only while I can hold the dusk between us. It cannot prove what he is. It can hold what he claims.”

Tovan nodded.

Calvea called, “Tovan Rek.”

Dusk rose from the seams around her feet. Tovan answered with his own name. Orrin joined the circuit. The Daughter laid both hands on the glass and gave it a measured pulse of solar fire.

The chamber woke.

Seven branches flowered across the walls, each once independent, each later dragged into one blazing crown. Witnesses assembled beside the map: the shield-tower excerpt; Deryn's oath-record; civic logs carried inside Tovan; a maintenance trace Orrin could read. None was complete. Together, where they overlapped, they restored the lost hour.

Queen Aurelia stood inside the circle with both hands around the source. Beyond her, the kings' engines tore at the outer shields. A younger form of Tovan offered an adaptive isolation: seven branches cutting themselves apart, changing as the attack changed.

“Probability of preserving all branches?” Queen Aurelia asked.

“Unknown.”

“Probability of preserving the capital if I centralize?”

“High. Outer branches will be consumed.”

For forty-three minutes, the records showed Queen Aurelia attempting other answers. Then the outer shields began to fall.

Deryn entered the restored frame with the infant Daughter against her heart. “Who protects her from becoming what you became?”

Queen Aurelia closed her hands around the source.

“If she is stronger than I was,” the Goddess said, “teach her that strength does not make the decision hers alone.”

The Day of Glass began.

The Daughter could not look away. Her mother had saved a city. Her mother had destroyed six. She had preserved the evidence, perhaps from honesty, perhaps punishment, perhaps the hope that her child would do better. No witness could absolve her. None could flatten her into a monster simple enough to escape grieving.

A second Queen Aurelia stepped from the light after the record ended.

Its edges trembled. Its eyes held private recognition the civic witness had not contained.

“I do not know whether I am her soul,” the Mother-fragment said. “Or memory. Or reconstruction. Or someone new who woke carrying her remorse.” It looked at the Daughter with unbearable tenderness. “But I know the Crown is awake, and it has found you.”

Gold restraints closed around the Daughter's wrists.

* * *

The seventh door burst inward. Dhal entered with guards at her back and the capital's thermal oath-seal burning on her chest.

“By Continuance authority,” she said, “restore capital priority.”

The chamber accepted the seal. The master conduit opened.

Orrin cried out. His hands locked against the interface, forced into motions he fought hard enough to shake. The Crown drew fire through the Daughter's restraints. On the wall-map, the Ninth Hollow dimmed while the capital's shield brightened.

“People are dying there too,” Dhal said. Her face shone with sweat and reflected gold. “I will answer for the record later. I will not let the city fail now.”

“There is always a later in which you promise to ask permission,” the Daughter said.

She reached inward for all her fire. If she released it at once, she could melt the Crown, the conduits, the seal, perhaps the chamber itself. No one would ever command the network again. The certainty felt clean. It felt merciful.

Seris put her shield across the Daughter's path.

“Move,” the Daughter said.

“No.”

The Daughter's gathering heat painted Seris's armor white. “I can end this.”

“You can decide the cost alone.” Seris's arms shook behind the shield. “That is not the same thing.”

The Daughter saw her mother's hands closing around the source.

Her own were fists.

“Then tell me,” she said, and the words hurt more than the restraints. “All of you. Tell me what you will risk.”

Calvea would set thresholds for the Hollow and accept the burns of holding them, if its residents renewed consent now and could revoke it later. Tovan would divide the recovered archive among the seven branches, knowing each part would change and none might remain entirely the man standing before them. Orrin would cut the master conduit, though every surviving directive in him demanded repair. Seris would bear temporary stewardship of the capital's inflow—not ownership, and only until public witnesses replaced her.

Even Dhal had a choice no one else could make. Her seal alone could open the final thermal sink. Without it, the capital would cook under the power already drawn.

The Daughter listened until every promise became a limit on her. She could not consent for the Hollow, hold Calvea's dusk, make Orrin's refusal, divide Tovan without erasing him, or open Dhal's sworn seal. Her fire was necessary, but necessity was not sovereignty. For years, worshippers had told her every miracle began and ended in her hands. The truth was both more frightening and more merciful: she was only one person in the chain, and the others could tell her no.

“One release,” the Daughter told her. “Bounded to the heat already in the eastern shield. Then the seal loses master authority.”

Dhal looked from the map to the Daughter. “And if your branches fail?”

“Some may.”

“Your mother chose against that uncertainty.”

“Yes.” The Daughter opened one aching hand. “And six cities paid for her certainty.”

* * *

The Ninth Hollow answered Calvea through the speaking tube: households consenting, risks named, three witnesses empowered to revoke. Dusk pooled under the seven doors, held by Calvea's living will rather than the Crown.

Seris pressed her palm to the capital branch and swore stewardship until three public watches had passed, revocable by the same witnesses who received the current.

Tovan stood within the black-sun key. “Tovan Rek,” he said one last time with a single voice. Then he divided.

Seven versions of his expression flickered across the map. Already, one stood differently. Another was laughing in terror. None received command over the others.

Orrin put both hands around the master conduit.

“Maintenance directive,” the chamber said through him. “Preserve central service.”

“No,” Orrin whispered.

He pulled.

The conduit resisted like a living tendon, though it was only glass and metal routing living fire. The isolation ring he had used at the cistern flashed in the wall-map, an earlier act of refusal remembered in his hands. With a sound like a mountain inhaling, the master line tore free.

Dhal still had not moved.

The eastern branch glowed toward rupture. Her oath-seal began to crack.

She shut her eyes, then pressed the seal into its socket. “One release. Eastern shield. Existing heat only.”

The capital's final sink opened.

The Crown tightened around the Daughter. Seven branches called for power at once, not as commands but as bounded requests. She could feel their different limits: the capital accepting less than it demanded, the Hollow taking back only its water and heat, five uncertain communities waking far across the Glass Sea.

She did not choose among them.

She opened both hands.

Solar fire flooded the chamber. The branches governed their own intake. Calvea held the thresholds. Seris bore the capital's weight. Orrin kept the severed ends apart while his arms shook. Tovan's voices counted one another, ensuring no branch vanished unheard.

Still the transfer was too slow.

The key's frame began to collapse. The Mother-fragment stepped into the break.

“Are you alive?” the Daughter cried.

“Enough to choose,” it said.

White fire passed through its uncertain body. For three final seconds it held the frame open, face neither machine-calm nor divinely serene, but afraid.

Then it was gone.

The Daughter's scars split into light. Seris lifted her grounding hand from the Daughter's wrist. Across the shield between them, she met the Daughter's eyes.

“Continue,” Seris said.

The second dawn went outward in seven unequal lines.

* * *

The capital kept a smaller shield. The Ninth Hollow kept its water. Two distant branches failed before dawn and were cut free by their own witnesses; both settlements survived the darkness. No crown could command them all again.

The complete record went out with the names of the six lost cities restored. Dhal surrendered her broken seal and lived to face a judgment she could argue against in public. Tovan survived in seven diverging voices that had already begun disagreeing over which memories belonged first in their archives.

The Daughter refused the coronation offered by the frightened capital. She also refused the old luxury of disappearing.

Her first covenant was witnessed in the Ninth Hollow greenhouse: one hour of solar heat, one growing room, a steward chosen by the households, and any three witnesses able to end the gift. Calvea tended a dusk-dark flame between bandaged hands. Orrin repaired a water pump after confirming no directive had called him there.

A small projection of Tovan flickered above a seed tray. “Do you think she would understand?” he asked.

The Daughter knew whom he meant. She looked up through layers of stone toward a sun she could not see.

“I think she understood the warning,” she said. “I think understanding was not enough.”

Warmth moved into the soil. No prayer told it where to go. Her open hands rested beneath light no one owned alone.
